COMMENTARIA IN CANTICUM CANTICORUM

PL 195, coll. 1001–1278  ·  Latin from the Migne printing  ·  First English translation  ·  column numbers follow the original plates, not the Garnier reprint

Wolbero of St Pantaleon

Wolbero S. Pantaleonis

fl. 1167

Benedictine abbot of St Pantaleon in Cologne, whom Migne places under the year 1167. His one surviving work is a long commentary on the Song of Songs, written for a community of nuns on an island in the Rhine and sent to a neighbouring abbot for his judgement before it circulated. It lay unprinted in his abbey's library until Henricus Gravius, a monk of the same house, published it at Cologne in 1630, and Migne reprints that edition.

Commentaria in Canticum canticorum

qui operantur in me non peccabunt, et qui elucidant me vitam aeternam habebunt (Eccli. XXIV).

Commentaries on the Canticle of Canticles

who work in me shall not sin, and who make me plain shall have life everlasting (Eccli. XXIV).

EPISTOLA NUNCUPATORIA

1001Reverendissimo in Christo Patri Domino venerabili Henrico Spichernagell, D. Pantaleonis abbati et 1002S. Unionis Barsfeldinae praesidenti principali meritissimo, nec non reverendis admodum et amplissimis 1003ADD. Henrico Liblero, Joanni Munch, Paulo Vrechen, Henrico Goermanno et Gabelo Scaffenio, monasteriorum ordinis Sancti Benedicti observantiae ejusdem in Sancto Martino, Brawiler, Tuitio, Gladbach et Graffscafft abbatibus dignissimis, dominis et praelatis suis observandis.

Mirabuntur non abs re, R. admodum et amplissimae DD. vestrae cur commentator hic super Cantica canticorum Salomonis tandiu sub modio latuerit, ac nunc primum lucem aspiciat: ad quod verisimiliter ego cum Judaeo illo Mardochaeo dilectam suam compellente Esther, et quis novit utrum idcirco ad regnum veneritis, ut Wolbero iste tali in tempore pararetur? Quare nec pro anima sola sufficere arbitratus fui, si auctor talis in domo D. Pantaleonis 1003Bscriptus tantum delitesceret, nisi plurimorum utilitati et spirituali gustui profuturus, sub incudem datus, nova quadam occasione opportunus prodiret in lucem.

Et quaenam, dicetis, occasio isthaec est? Annus jam tertius est quo tempore annalis capituli in monasterio Sancti Pantaleonis celebrati Kalendas Septembris B. Aegidio abbati sacris, vestri quoque sacrati vertices, pontificali infula noviter decorati fuerint. Nullis profecto verbis aut scriptis comprehendere valeo, quantum hinc gaudiorum accreverit charissimis vestris confratribus, quanta etiam laetitia tam meo quam publico pariter nomine ex hoc perfusus sim, vobisque ex animo gratulari desideraverim, posteaquam intellexeram a sanctissimo domino nostro 1003CUrbano VIII, auctoritatem hanc episcopalem RR. admodum Dominationibus vestris super additam, et a R. domino episcopo Cyrenensi solemni ordine pontificales mitras, capitibus vestris impositas fuisse. Eccur enim tam sanctam, tamque honorificam et novam Dominationibus vestris non gratularer gloriam? gloriam, inquam, qua, praeter omnem quod mihi persuasum ambitionem, solo clarissimarum virtutum merito (utpote qui inter sacrae unionis nostrae Bursfeldensis columnas praecipuas annumeramini, eamque indeclinabiliter suffulciendo constabilitis), donati et affecti estis?

Quid agerem? Honorem hunc novum R. domino praelato meo ut descenderem acclamaturus filialis 1003Dpostulabat amor; cidares RR. Dominationum vestrarum veneraturus pariter ut occurrerem gratitudo exigebat, aliorum exempla provocabant. Sed nolui in summorum conspectu sacerdotum apparere vacuus, nec etiam munus quod offerrem prae manibus erat. Cum subito, Deo ita inspirante, memor fui commentatoris hujus Wolberonis coabbatis vestri, et delectatus sum, et quia religiosorum plurimi lectione suavissimarum interpretationum illius antebac illecti, summopere mecum dolebant inter caeteram bibliothecae nostrae supellectilem tam pia et profunda latere commentaria, neque thesaurum talem pluribus communicari ad testandam mei 1004Aerga RR. admodum DD. vestras promptitudinem beneque merendi studium, quod dudum in votis habueram, fiducialiter aggressus fui, et Commentaria Wolberonis nostri non modo revidi, verum etiam revisa meliorem in ordinem disposui, atque ita disposita et renovata eadem nominibus RR. admodum DD. vestrarum inscribenda, typo ut subjicerentur, omnem coepi movere lapidem. Caeterum cum Salomone ipso attestante, plures faciendi libros nullus sit finis, adeoque saeculi hujus ingeniis nova magis arridere soleant quam vetera, erat fortasse quod verebar, ne vel commentatoris hujus antiquitas, vel verius personae meae exiguitas, a qua renovatus nonnihil liber non exiret, obstaculo forent, quo minus feliciter in manus multorum transiret. 1004BPorro RR. admodum Dominationum vestrarum animatus auctoritate, a metu simili, imo Zoilorum omnium, qui bonis conatibus deesse non solent, obtrectatu, facile liberandum me duxi, cum quod in apothecam et horreum Dominicum non semper centesimus aut sexagesimus, quin saepius tricesimus fructus inferatur: tum quod per cornua vestra Aaronica protegendus, eodem anni decurso tempore a praelato redeat, quo in pontificales mitras abbatialia vestra mutata fuerunt almucia.

Quamobrem, reverendissime domine praeses, praelate mi observandissime, suscipe minimi clientis tui hanc qualemcunque curis meis pastoralibus superadditam et huc usque variis militum incursionibus obstantibus protacta operam; et quia juxta elogium 1004CSapientis: Vir qui diligit sapientiam laetificat patrem suum (Prov. XXIX): laetifica per conatum hunc meum in sapientia et cantico spirituali libri hujus spiritum tuum, et refocilla infirmos et seniles artus tuos, multis pro monasterio et unione nostra Bursfeldica exantlatis laboribus debilitatos, sed nondum fractos. Suscipite et vos, antistites venerabiles, observantiae meae erga vos tesseram exiguam Wolberonem coabbatem vestrum, RR. admodum Dominationibus vestris humiliter a me nuncupatum; sitque novi honoris vestri particeps, qui religionis avitae aeque monasticae relator exstitit egregius. Quae eadem praesulibus vobis ut, in incepto spiritualis disciplinae incremento succrescat et propagetur, 1004DDeum optimum, maximum sanctissimumque legislatorem nostrum Benedictum ejusdemque patrones ordinis jugiter exorabo. Qui etiam patientissima sua benignitate RR. admodum et amplissimas Dominationes vestras cum omnibus sibi commissis per quam diutissime felicissimeque superstites atque incolumes servare dignetur. Ita fovet et apprecatur ex pastoratu Laugelensi ipso B. Aegidii abbatis anno 1629.

RR. ad. et amplissimarum Dominationum vestrarum, humilis servus et frater Henricus ERSMERS Graviensis Pantaleonita, ordinis S. Benedicti.

NUNCUPATORY EPISTLE

1001To the most reverend Father in Christ, the venerable Lord Henry Spichernagell, abbot of St Pantaleon and 1002most deserving principal president of the holy Union of Barsfeld, and also to the very reverend and most ample 1003ALords Henry Libler, John Munch, Paul Vrechen, Henry Goermann and Gabel Scaffenius, most worthy abbots of the monasteries of the order of Saint Benedict of the same observance at Saint Martin, Brawiler, Tuitium, Gladbach and Graffscafft, his lords and prelates to be revered.

Your very reverend and most ample Lordships will wonder, and not without cause, why this commentator on the Canticles of Canticles of Solomon has lain so long under a bushel, and only now for the first time looks upon the light: to which, in all likelihood, I [answer] with that Jew Mordecai pressing his beloved Esther, and who knows whether you have come to the kingdom for this, that this Wolbero might be made ready at such a time? Wherefore I did not judge it enough for one soul alone, if such an author, 1003Bwritten, should only lie hidden in the house of St Pantaleon, unless, given over to the anvil, he should come forth into the light, opportune upon some new occasion, to profit the use and the spiritual taste of very many.

And what, you will say, is this occasion? It is now the third year since, at the time of the annual chapter celebrated in the monastery of Saint Pantaleon on the Kalends of September, sacred to blessed Aegidius the abbot, your consecrated heads too were newly adorned with the pontifical infula. By no words or writings am I able to comprehend how much joy grew from this for your dearest confreres, and with how great gladness I too was filled by it, in my own name as much as in the public one, and how heartily I desired to congratulate you, after I had understood that from our most holy lord 1003CUrban VIII this episcopal authority had been superadded to your very reverend Lordships, and that pontifical mitres had been placed upon your heads in solemn order by the reverend lord bishop of Cyrene. For why should I not congratulate your Lordships on a glory so holy, so honourable and so new? a glory, I say, with which, beyond all ambition, as I am persuaded, you have been gifted and endowed by the sole merit of your most illustrious virtues (inasmuch as you are numbered among the chief pillars of our sacred Union of Bursfeld, and establish it by unswervingly supporting it)?

What was I to do? Filial love 1003Ddemanded that I go down to acclaim this new honour of the reverend lord my prelate; gratitude required that I go likewise to meet [you], to venerate the tiaras of your very reverend Lordships; the examples of others provoked [me]. But I did not wish to appear empty in the sight of the highest priests, nor was there even a gift at hand that I might offer. When suddenly, God so inspiring, I remembered this commentator Wolbero, your co-abbot, and was delighted; and because very many of the religious, enticed heretofore antebac by the reading of his most sweet interpretations, grieved exceedingly with me that commentaries so pious and profound lay hidden among the other furniture of our library, and that such a treasure was not communicated to more, I set about it with confidence, to testify my 1004Areadiness toward your very reverend Lordships and my zeal to deserve well, which I had long had among my wishes; and I not only reviewed the Commentaries of our Wolbero, but also, reviewed, arranged them into a better order, and I began to move every stone that, so arranged and renewed, and to be inscribed with the names of your very reverend Lordships, they might be put under the type. For the rest, since, as Solomon himself attests, of making many books there is no end, and so new things are wont to smile upon the wits of this age more than old ones, there was perhaps something I feared: lest either the antiquity of this commentator, or, more truly, the smallness of my own person, from which the book, not a little renewed, might not go forth, should be an obstacle, whereby it should pass less happily into the hands of many. 1004BBut, animated by the authority of your very reverend Lordships, I thought that I should easily be freed from a like fear, nay, from the detraction of all the Zoiluses, who are not wont to be wanting to good endeavours: both because into the Lord's storehouse and barn not always the hundredfold or sixtyfold, but more often the thirtyfold fruit is brought in; and because, to be protected by your Aaronic horns, it returns from its prelate at the same time, the course of the year having run, as that in which your abbatial almuces were changed into pontifical mitres.

Wherefore, most reverend lord president, my most revered prelate, receive thou this work, such as it is, of thy least client, superadded to my pastoral cares and hitherto drawn out protacta by the various incursions of soldiers standing in the way; and because, according to the saying 1004Cof the Wise Man: A man who loveth wisdom maketh his father glad (Prov. XXIX): gladden thy spirit, through this endeavour of mine, in the wisdom and spiritual canticle of this book, and refresh thy infirm and aged limbs, weakened by many labours endured for the monastery and our Union of Bursfeld, but not yet broken. Receive you also, venerable prelates, this small token of my regard toward you, Wolbero your co-abbot, humbly dedicated by me to your very reverend Lordships; and let him be a sharer in your new honour, who stood forth as the eminent narrator of the ancestral, and equally monastic, religion. That the same, under you as prelates, may grow and be propagated in the begun increase of spiritual discipline, 1004DI will unceasingly entreat God, best, greatest, and our most holy lawgiver Benedict, and the patrons of the same order. May he also deign, by his most patient kindness, to keep your very reverend and most ample Lordships, with all committed to them, surviving and unharmed for as very long and as very happily as may be. So he cherishes and prays, from the pastorate of Laugel, on the very [day] of blessed Aegidius the abbot, in the year 1629.

Of your very reverend and most ample Lordships the humble servant and brother, Henry ERSMERS of Grave, a Pantaleonite, of the order of St Benedict.

EPIGRAMMA AD AUCTOREM ET LECTOREM COMMENTARIORUM HORUM.

1005AUt superes Pylei doctissime tempora scriptor, Et tua sit cunctis cognita fama locis, Hoc opus eximium praelo mandare, decorum Pluribus est visum non sine laude tua. Ergo securus prodi, Wolbero; latere Non decet ingenii tam pia scripta tui Quem modo dulcis amor pangendi cantica tangit, 1006AEn Wolberonem, quo duce pangat, habet. Talia non lusit Dircaeus cantica vates, Ad tactum citharae quando salivit aper. Wolbero meres, vitam canit ille pudicam, Sponsi cum sponsa mystica verba refert. I nunc quisquis amas animae et connubia Christi Quem tibi concilies, en paranymphus adest.

EPIGRAM TO THE AUTHOR AND THE READER OF THESE COMMENTARIES.

1005AThat thou mayest outlast the times of the Pylian, most learned writer, And that thy fame may be known in every place, To commit this excellent work to the press has seemed Fitting to many, and not without praise of thee. Go forth then secure, Wolbero; it befits not That the so pious writings of thy genius lie hid. Whom the sweet love of composing canticles now touches, 1006ALo, he has Wolbero, under whose leading he may compose. Not such canticles did the Dircaean bard play, When at the touch of the lyre the boar leapt up. Wolbero, thou deservest; he sings a chaste life, He tells the mystic words of the Bridegroom with the bride. Go now, whoever thou art that lovest the nuptials of the soul and of Christ: Whom thou mayest win to thyself, lo, the paranymph is here.

FRATER HENRICUS GRAVIUS LECTORI BENEVOLO.

Commentaria venerabilis domini abbatis Wolberonis, licet devotis ac Deo consecratis virginibus quondam ita postulantibus, ab auctore ipso conscripta et inscripta fuerint, volueritque cum sanctimonialibus solis illa delitescere, neque communem in lucem prodire nisi, ab aliquo correcta in opus elaboratum ac masculinum evaserint: nolim tibi persuasum habeas, lector benevole, quasi opera mea hoc ipsum assecutus fueris. Haec namque vere de se humiliter sentientium virtus est magna et praeclara agere aut scribere et nihilominus parve et mediocriter de se, suisque sentire. Emicat in hac virtutis specie non vulgariter abbas noster Wolbero. in cujus commentariis licet antiquissimis, sed assiduo annorum novem studio congestis tantum abest ut informe aliquid, vel muliebre aut lima emendatiori indigens offenderim (licet in dedicatione religiosis sororibus suis nuncupata, aliisque operis, hujus praefationibus hoc ipsum innuere videatur) ut divino magis quam humano spiritu conceptum et calamo exaratum opusculum hoc videri merito debeat. Quapropter latere te nolim quicunque operis hujus lector futurus es parum me Commentariis hisce de proprio aut addidisse aut miscuisse, nisi ubi sensus ambiguitas, periodorum dissolutio versuumque disjunctio simile quid desiderare visum fuerat. Haec fortassis erant, quae lectorem delicatum in Wolberone antiquo offendere potuissent. Quibus cum labore et conatu meo sat subventum, nescio qua typographi vel correctoris incuria aut festinatione errata nonnulla hinc inde irrepserint, quae sub finem libri hujus emendata, videre liceat, operam hanc meam qualemcunque aequi bonique consulito, et dum ea frueris in tui emolumentum suscipe, et suscipe benigne perpetuum auctoris hujus monumentum. Vale Haec nova editio multis erroribus typographiae et correctionis purgata cum securitate fructuque consuli potest. EDIT..

BROTHER HENRY GRAVIUS TO THE KIND READER.

The Commentaries of the venerable lord abbot Wolbero, although they were composed and inscribed by the author himself for devout virgins consecrated to God, who once so requested, and he wished them to lie hidden with the nuns alone, and not to come forth into the common light unless, corrected by someone, they had turned out a finished and masculine work: I would not have thee persuaded, kind reader, that thou hast obtained this very thing by my labour. For this is the virtue of those who truly think humbly of themselves: to do or to write things great and splendid, and nonetheless to think meanly and moderately of themselves and of what is theirs. In this kind of virtue our abbot Wolbero shines forth in no common way. in whose commentaries, most ancient indeed, but gathered by the assiduous study of nine years, I am so far from having met with anything shapeless, or womanish, or wanting a more correcting file (although in the dedication addressed to his religious sisters, and in other prefaces of this work, he seems to hint at this very thing), that this little work ought deservedly to seem conceived by a divine rather than a human spirit, and traced by the pen. Wherefore I would not have it hidden from thee, whoever thou art that shalt be the reader of this work, that I have added or mixed little of my own into these Commentaries, save where ambiguity of sense, looseness of periods and disjunction of verses had seemed to want some such thing. These perhaps were the things that might have offended a delicate reader in the ancient Wolbero. Since these have been sufficiently relieved by my labour and effort, [and] through I know not what carelessness or haste of printer or corrector some errors have crept in here and there, which it is permitted to see corrected at the end of this book, take this labour of mine, such as it is, in good part; and while thou enjoyest it, receive it to thy profit, and receive kindly this perpetual monument of this author. Farewell.

EPISTOLA DEDICATORIA WOLBERONIS ABBATIS.

1005BDilectissimis sororibus in Insula Rheni Deo et beatae Mariae militantibus, WOLBERO peccator.

Dum mecum saepius tractarem et ancipiti animo frequenter revolverem quidnam dulce, quid jucundum, quid utile interioribus sanctae charitatis vestrae auribus, o sanctissimae sorores, decantarem, cujus dulcedine et incitamento ad majorem coelestis vitae amorem vester erigetur animus, occurrit repente animo meo illud cantabile sponsi et sponsae epithalamium, quod pro sui excellentia dicitur Canticum canticorum. Hoc nempe genus cantionis valde competit dignitati vestrae professionis, quia haec omnium praecellit ordinem professionum sicut illud omne genus canticorum.

1006BTria quippe sunt genera professionum, unum conjugatorum, alterum viduarum, tertium virginum. Legimus autem quia est Canticum laudis, canticum laetitiae, canticum novum. Ponamus ergo quasi quibusdam gradibus canticum laudis conjugatis, canticum laetitiae viduis, canticum novum virginibus, quod nemo potest dicere, nisi qui sequuntur Agnum quocunque ierit (Apoc. XIV). Canticum quippe laudis cantant conjugati, qui initium aliquod religionis et bonae conversationis acceperunt, sed nondum tribulationem carnis evaserunt; canticum vero laetitiae cantant viduae, quae aliquid altius sunt assecutae, majori praestantes religione et experta jam tribulatione carnis absolutae ac propterea possunt 1007Aet laudem et laetitiam canere. Porro virgines cantant canticum novum, quae summum retinent gradum nunquam praedictam carnis tribulationem expertae, atque ideo potentes canere et laudem, et laetitiam, et novitatem singularem ac caeteris inedicibilem.

Sed valde attendendum his quae virgines dicuntur, cujus partis sint; in duas quippe partes hanc professionem Dominus divisit, hoc est in virgines prudentes et stultas (Matth. XXV); quia hoc novum canticum non possunt dicere, nisi quae sunt ex parte prudentium: prudentes autem sunt quae et corpore et mente virgines sunt; stultae vero quae, quamvis virgines sunt corpore, corrupta tamen vivunt mente. Tales nimirum non possunt cantare 1007Bcanticum novum, sed neque ultimae professionis canticum; quae nec ad ipsius pertingunt meritum, quia non habent in vase oleum, quin imo pro hac negligentia sui non intrant thalamum sponsi.

Quocirca valde attendere et sollicita esse debet charitas vestra, quae estis virgines corpore ut etiam sitis mente; quia nihil vobis confert virginitas carnis, si jam mente, nupsistis. Si ergo rectam virginalis professionis normam tenetis, singulare canticum, et ut ita dicam, non simpliciter canticum, sicut conjugatae et viduae, sed Canticum canticorum cantatis, quod solum possibile est illis cantare, qui sunt ante thronum Dei sine macula, quia non inquinaverunt vestimenta (Apoc. XIV), id est corpora 1007Csua.

Auctoritates sane harum trium professionum in sacra reperiuntur Scriptura, quia castitas conjugalis praedicatur in Elisabeth, sanctimonia vidualis in Anna, perfectio virginalis in beata Dei genitrice Maria. Singularum autem meritum ipse Dominus in Evangelio demonstrat, ubi dicitur semen cecidisse in terram bonam et fructum fecisse, aliud tricesimum, aliud sexagesimum, et aliud centesimum (Luc. VIII).

Tricesimus namque fructus conjugatorum est caste viventium, quas hoc numero ostendit computus digitorum, indice pollici superposito, pondus tribulationis et depressionis ipsarum indicat viduarum sustentatione et consolatione virili destitutum. 1007DPorro numerus centenarius, qui pro perfectione ponitur, perfectionem sanctarum demonstrat virginum, qui de sinistra ad dexteram translatus, juncta summitate indicis ad summitatem pollicis, coronam exprimit virginitatis.

Pensate ergo professionis hujus excellentiam cujus est praemium fructus centuplicatus, cujus est meritum dicere canticum novum, cujus dignitati maxime congruunt, pro speciali divina gratiae conjunctione, ista quae vobis pro modulo nostro canere intendimus Cantica canticorum. Nequidem vobiscum, quaecunque vere virgines estis, haec cantica non dico canere, sed nec susurrare possum, qui longe 1008Aa vestra sanctitate differo; sed sicut aliquis qui scientiam alicujus artis verbo tantum insinuare potest, actu vero exprimere non potest, ita et ego quamvis haec vobiscum cantare, culpa obstante, non possim, tentabo tamen cum Dei adjutorio aliquid dicere, unde possitis horum excellentiam et singularem dignitatem Canticorum aliquatenus cognoscere. Ergo ut dicit gentilis poeta: Fungar vice cotis, acutum Reddere quae novit ferrum, exsors ipsa secandi: (HORAT., Ars poet., 304.) et quia non licet cantare, liceat saltem cantandi consilium dare. Nam et sanctus Moyses cum quo Deus facie ad faciem loquebatur, Jethro cognati sui viri gentilis consilium audivit et fecit, cum ipse plenus 1008Besset sapientia et sanctitate, iste vero longe valde ab eo distaret gentilitate et vitae qualitate. Sed hoc quia Deus dedit velle, det etiam posse. Scio equidem multis indignum fore, qui veterum tantum scripta suscipiunt, Miraturque nihil, nisi quod Libitina sacravit. (HOR., Ep. II, I, 49.) Quod post dicta majorum quae firmavit charitas, meas quoque ineptias impudenter detexerim, sed vestra me apud eos excusabit dilectio quorum solummodo proposui satisfacere desiderio. Quod si nimis simplicem pro causae majestate reprehendunt orationem, meminerint quia in constructione tabernaculi, non tantum aurum et argentum, byssus 1008Cet purpura, sed etiam pili caprarum sunt oblati, (Exod. XXV), et magis a Domino laudata sunt duo parva viduae minuta quam immensa divitum donaria (Luc. XXI). Et si compositionem verborum calumniantur, causam tamen materiae venerentur, et tenuitatem orationis sive compositionis excusent, et materiae dignitas et devotae supplicationis obediens charitas. Nam et plurimos metrica arte compositos libros in Ecclesia habemus de Evangeliis et sanctorum gestis, humili stylo et simplici oratione, qui tamen propter materiae dignitatem, obtinuerunt jam auctoritatem. Unde Arator Actus apostolicos scripturus, dicit: Jejuno sermone quidem, sed pinguia gesta Scripsimus, ac pelagi pondere gutta fluit Arator, Epist. ad Flor. v. 7. Patrol. t. LXVIII, p. 64.. 1008DNemo ergo simplicitatem nostram contemnat, quia cum simplicibus sermocinatio nostra (Prov. III), quin potius eo magis nobis peccantibus indulgeat, quod plus libuit aliquid, quamvis simpliciter scribere, qui inani otio, torpore, cum etiam hoc opus nusquam prodire velimus, sed cum solis tantum quibus missum est sanctis delitescere sororibus; nisi forte alicui benignitatis intuitu placuerit hoc ad corrigendum suscipere, et de informi et molli compositione aliquod pulchrum et masculum opus elaborare.

Suscipite itaque hanc meae parvitatis operam, in qua non piguit me laborare gratia dilectionis 1009Avestrae, in vestri quidem emolumentum, in mei vero perenne monumentum; quatenus cum haec aspicitis 1010Aet legitis, memores mei sitis et pro me sive vivo sive mortuo communem Deum exoretis.

DEDICATORY EPISTLE OF ABBOT WOLBERO.

1005BTo his most beloved sisters on the Island of the Rhine, serving as soldiers to God and to blessed Mary, WOLBERO, a sinner.

While I was often treating with myself, and frequently turning over with a doubtful mind, what sweet thing, what pleasant, what useful thing I might sing to the inward ears of your holy charity, O most holy sisters, by whose sweetness and incitement your mind would be raised to a greater love of the heavenly life, there suddenly occurred to my mind that singable epithalamium of the bridegroom and the bride, which for its excellence is called the Canticle of Canticles. This kind of song, indeed, greatly befits the dignity of your profession, because this surpasses the order of all professions, as that surpasses every kind of canticles.

1006BFor there are three kinds of professions: one of the married, another of widows, the third of virgins. Now we read that there is a canticle of praise, a canticle of gladness, a new canticle. Let us assign therefore, as by certain steps, the canticle of praise to the married, the canticle of gladness to widows, the new canticle to virgins, which no man can say, save they who follow the Lamb whithersoever he shall go (Apoc. XIV) [Vulg. Apoc. 14:3 nemo poterat dicere canticum, nisi illa centum quadraginta quatuor millia, "no man could say the canticle but those hundred forty-four thousand"; Hi sequuntur Agnum is 14:4]. For the canticle of praise the married sing, who have received some beginning of religion and of good conversation, but have not yet escaped the tribulation of the flesh; while the canticle of gladness widows sing, who have attained something higher, excelling in greater religion, and, having now experienced the tribulation of the flesh, are set free from it, and therefore can 1007Asing both praise and gladness. But virgins sing the new canticle, who hold the highest step, never having experienced the aforesaid tribulation of the flesh, and therefore able to sing both praise, and gladness, and a newness singular and unutterable to the rest.

But great heed must be taken, in those who are called virgins, of which part they are; for the Lord divided this profession into two parts, that is, into wise and foolish virgins (Matth. XXV); because this new canticle they cannot say, save those who are of the part of the wise: and the wise are those who are virgins both in body and in mind; but the foolish, those who, although they are virgins in body, yet live corrupted in mind. Such, assuredly, cannot sing 1007Bthe new canticle, nor even the canticle of the last profession; who do not even attain to its merit, because they have no oil in the vessel; nay rather, for this negligence of theirs, they do not enter the bridegroom's chamber.

Wherefore your charity, you who are virgins in body, ought greatly to take heed and be solicitous that you be so in mind also; because virginity of the flesh confers nothing on you, if you have already married in mind. If, then, you hold the right rule of the virginal profession, you sing a singular canticle, and, so to speak, not simply a canticle, as married women and widows do, but the Canticle of Canticles, which it is possible to sing only for those who are before the throne of God without spot, because they have not defiled their garments (Apoc. XIV) [Vulg. Apoc. 14:5 sine macula enim sunt ante thronum Dei; the clause qui non inquinaverunt vestimenta sua is Apoc. 3:4], that is, their 1007Cbodies.

Authorities for these three professions are indeed found in Holy Scripture, because conjugal chastity is proclaimed in Elizabeth, widowly holiness in Anna, virginal perfection in the blessed Mother of God, Mary. And the merit of each the Lord himself shows in the Gospel, where the seed is said to have fallen into good ground and to have made fruit, some thirtyfold, some sixtyfold, and some a hundredfold (Luc. VIII) [Vulg. Luc. 8:8 fecit fructum centuplum, "made fruit a hundredfold", with no thirty or sixty; these stand in Matt. 13:8 and Mark 4:20].

For the thirtyfold fruit is that of the married living chastely, whom the reckoning of the fingers shows by this number, the forefinger being laid over the thumb; it indicates the weight of the tribulation and depression of the widows themselves, destitute of the support and consolation of a man. 1007DBut the hundredfold number, which is put for perfection, shows the perfection of holy virgins; which, carried over from the left hand to the right, the tip of the forefinger being joined to the tip of the thumb, expresses the crown of virginity.

Weigh therefore the excellence of this profession, whose reward is the hundredfold fruit, whose merit is to say the new canticle, to whose dignity, by reason of the special divine conjunction of grace, these Canticles of Canticles which we intend to sing to you according to our small measure are most fitting. Not even with you, whichever of you are truly virgins, can I, I say not sing these canticles, but not even whisper them, I who differ far 1008Afrom your holiness; but as someone who can convey the knowledge of some art by word only, but cannot express it in act, so I too, although I cannot sing these things with you, my fault standing in the way, will nevertheless try with God's help to say something from which you may in some measure know the excellence and singular dignity of these Canticles. Therefore, as the gentile poet says: I will serve as a whetstone, which knows how to render iron sharp, itself without share in cutting: (HORAT., Ars poet., 304.) and since it is not permitted to sing, let it at least be permitted to give counsel for singing. For holy Moses also, with whom God spoke face to face, heard and did the counsel of Jethro his kinsman, a gentile man, although he himself was full 1008Bof wisdom and holiness, while the other stood very far distant from him in gentilehood and in the quality of his life. But since God has given to will this, may he give also to be able. I know indeed that it will be unworthy in the eyes of many, who receive only the writings of the ancients, And admire nothing save what Libitina has hallowed. (HOR., Ep. II, I, 49.) that after the sayings of the elders, which charity has confirmed, I have shamelessly laid bare my own follies as well; but your love will excuse me before them, whose desire alone I have set myself to satisfy. And if they reproach the speech as too simple for the majesty of the cause, let them remember that in the construction of the tabernacle not only gold and silver, byssus 1008Cand purple, but also goats' hair were offered, (Exod. XXV), and the two small mites of the widow were more praised by the Lord than the immense gifts of the rich (Luc. XXI). And if they cavil at the arrangement of the words, let them nevertheless venerate the cause of the matter, and let both the dignity of the matter and the obedient charity of devout supplication excuse the thinness of the speech or composition. For we have in the Church very many books composed by metrical art, on the Gospels and the deeds of the saints, in a humble style and simple speech, which nevertheless, on account of the dignity of their matter, have already obtained authority. Whence Arator, when about to write the Acts of the Apostles, says: In fasting speech indeed, but deeds that are rich Have we written, and a drop flows with the weight of the sea. 1008DLet no one therefore despise our simplicity, because discourse with the simple is ours (Prov. III); nay rather, let him indulge us sinners the more, in that it pleased [us] more to write something, however simply, who in empty leisure, torpor, since we even wish this work to go forth nowhere, but to lie hidden only with the holy sisters alone to whom it has been sent; unless perhaps it shall please someone, out of a regard of kindness, to take this up for correcting, and out of a shapeless and soft composition to work out some beautiful and masculine work.

Receive therefore this work of my littleness, in which it has not irked me to labour for the sake of your 1009Alove, for your profit indeed, but for my own perpetual monument; so that when you look upon these things 1010Aand read them, you may be mindful of me, and, whether I am living or dead, entreat our common God for me.

CENSURA ABBATIS GERODHENSIS Super Commentaria Wolberonis abbatis in Canticum canticorum.

  • 1009

1009ADomino venerabili et intime amabili WOLBERONI Sancti Pantaleonis abbati frater GERODHENSIS coenobii dictus abbas non modo cellarium, sed et cubiculum sponsi introductum inebriari consummata charitate ab ubertate domus Dei et torrente voluptatis ipsius potari in aeternum (Psal. XXXV).

Scribitis enim et familiari omnibus et sapientia spiritus utentibus humilitate, rogando monetis et 1009Bmonendo rogatis, ut opus vestrum super Cantica canticorum, remota penitus omni captatione benevolentiae vestrae, diligentius consideratum, quidquam tamen mihi videatur, videlicet sive in lucem proferendum sentiam, vel abscondendum et deponendum intelligam, vos scripto certificem; quia nulli me melius credatis quod et consanguinitas stringat ad benevolentiam et sapientia correctionis non deneget sententiam. Et quidem sicut nonnisi his duobus prudentia et benevolentia, omnis intelligens recognoscit cuncta contineri judicia, ita cum benevolentiam certo adesse, prudentiam abesse non sine dolore recogito, illum secutus qui orabat, dicens: Ut sciam quid mihi desit (Psal. XXXVIII), non 1009Csufficiens ferre onus quod imponitis, non immerito subterfugio.

Verum cum haec omnium etiam otio torpentium sit excusatio et mihi credens et a me id fieri posse sperans, vestra charitas facere moneat, non ut judex, sed ut voto amicus sponsi, dum audio vocem 1010Aipsius, suam cordi vestro in libertate spiritus doctrinam subministranti, ad vocem sponsi vos utentis pro organo, in charitate veritati congaudenti congaudeo, et opus istud non abolendum, imo ad gloriam Dei, gloria enim revelare sermonem (Tob. XII), et ad utilitatem Ecclesiae Dei illarumque institutionem quibus scribitur, manifestandum omnimodis censeo. Revera et fide catholicum, et moribus 1010Binstruendis, omnis Christianus bene in domo Dei vivere disponens, judicabit aptissimum.

Moleste aliquantum vos accepisse comperi, quod codicem subito perfectum non remisi, sed impedimento fuerunt aliqua, tum quia nulla res festinata simul et examinata esse potest, quod et a vobis didici, cum in novum pene presseritis annum; quare cum diligentia scriptum, cum negligentia non judicari legendum. Ad hoc accessit quod fratres nostri contra voluntatem quidem vestram, sed me volente et super hoc gaudente certatim hunc rapuerunt et sedulo et diligenter legerunt, et studio lectionis commendabilem reddiderunt, sed ita tamen ipsius lectionem mihi etiam et nolenti aliquam 1010Csubduxerunt. Nunc vero et non sine diligentia perlectum, vobis omnibus in Christo legere communicandum remitto; superest, ut cui laborem judicastis participandum, non negetis fructus participium. Vale.

CENSURE OF THE ABBOT OF GERODHEN On the Commentaries of Abbot Wolbero on the Canticle of Canticles.

  • 1009

1009ATo the venerable and inwardly lovable lord WOLBERO, abbot of Saint Pantaleon, brother, called abbot of the monastery of GERODHEN: [may you,] led not only into the cellar but also into the chamber of the bridegroom, be inebriated with consummate charity from the plenty of the house of God, and with the torrent of the pleasure of him be given to drink for ever (Psal. XXXV).

For you write, and with a humility familiar to all and to those who use the wisdom of the spirit, you admonish by asking and 1009Bask by admonishing, that I should certify you in writing concerning your work on the Canticles of Canticles, considered with more diligence, every courting of your good will being wholly put away, what nevertheless it may seem to me, namely whether I think it should be brought forth into the light, or understand that it should be hidden and laid aside; because you would trust no one better than me, in that both kinship binds [me] to good will and the wisdom of correction would not deny a verdict. And indeed, as every man of understanding recognizes that all judgments are contained in nothing but these two, prudence and good will, so, since I reflect not without grief that good will is surely present and prudence absent, following him who prayed, saying: That I may know what is wanting to me (Psal. XXXVIII), not 1009Cbeing sufficient to bear the burden that you lay on me, I not undeservedly shrink from it.

But since this is the excuse even of all who are torpid in leisure, and your charity, trusting me and hoping that this can be done by me, admonishes me to do it, not as a judge, but as a friend of the bridegroom by desire: while I hear the voice 1010Aof him ministering his doctrine to your heart in the liberty of the spirit, at the voice of the bridegroom using you as an organ I rejoice together in charity rejoicing with the truth, and I judge that this work is not to be abolished, nay, to the glory of God, for it is glory to reveal the word (Tob. XII), and for the profit of the Church of God and the instruction of those for whom it is written, it is by all means to be made manifest. Truly both catholic in faith, and, for morals 1010Bto be instructed, most apt, every Christian disposing himself to live well in the house of God will judge it.

I have learned that you took it somewhat ill that I did not at once send back the codex, finished; but some things were an impediment: first, because no thing can be at once hurried and examined, which I learned from you also, since you pressed on almost into the new year; wherefore what was written with diligence [should], as it is read, not be judged with negligence. To this was added that our brothers, against your will indeed, but with me willing and rejoicing over it, eagerly snatched it and read it sedulously and diligently, and by the study of reading made it commendable; yet so that they withdrew from me, even unwilling, some of the reading of 1010Cit. But now, read through, and not without diligence, I send it back, to be communicated to all of you in Christ for reading; it remains that you not deny a share in the fruit to him whom you judged fit to share the labour. Farewell.

PRAEFATIO GENERALIS WOLBERONIS IN CANTICUM CANTICORUM SALOMONIS.

  • 1009

1009DIn sancta Scriptura multa dicuntur cantica quae diverso causarum genere differentia, nunc generaliter, nunc specialiter pro loco et tempore sunt decantata; loco, quia vel in patria vel in aliena terra; tempore, quia vel in pace vel in captivitate. Dicitur enim Canticum Moysi, Canticum Annae, Canticum Habacuc prophetae, vel alia hujusmodi; sed haec omnia simpliciter cantica. Hic autem dicuntur Cantica canticorum, eo quod omnia canticorum genera mystici intellectus majestate praecellant.

Et alia quidem cantica habent causam quare fuerint 1010Ddecantata, sicut Moyses decantavit canticum laudis pro victoria celebrata, quando submersus est Pharao cum curribus et equitibus suis in mari Rubro. Anna quoque canticum Domino cecinit, pro collata fecunditate sublato sterilitatis opprobrio. Ezechias quoque canticum cantavit pro reddita sibi sanitate. Ergo cantica singula cuique fuerunt gratiarum actio pro beneficio sibi a Deo collato. Istud vero canticum summae illius perfectaeque charitatis repraesentat harmoniam, qua sopitis omnibus rerum mundanarum curi, anima quaeque fidelis 1011ACreatori suo veluti sponsa sponso ineffabili amoris dulcedine conjungitur, in cujus complexibus tanta pacis et quietis suavitate commoratur, ut nihil sit quod praeter eum cupiat, nihil quod tam magnificae gratiae praeponat, quia nihil certe est quod spiritui resistat, qui calcato carnis bello cum subjugata sibi carne, eadem felici concordia in Christo sabbatizet. Magna quippe pars et optabile Sabbatum, id est requies est, quando caro non concupiscit adversus spiritum, sed sedato vitiorum tumultu, tanta internae tranquillitatis dulcedine mens perfruitur, ut nihil aliud quam Dominum desiderans, velit et possit Canticum canticorum dicere, hoc est veram et perfectam charitatem habere. Omnibus enim virtutibus supereminet charitas, sicut Canticum canticorum 1011Bomnia supergreditur cantica. Ascensiones autem in corde sunt disponendae, ut quasi quibusdam gradibus perveniatur ad cantanda Cantica canticorum; ut sicut qui ingreditur sancta adhuc multa habet necessaria ut possit ingredi Sancta sanctorum; et qui celebrat Sabbata longe altioribus indiget, ut pervenire possit ad Sabbata sabbatorum: sic qui canit cantica, ad majora semper debet proficere, ut possit cantare Cantica canticorum.

Septem quippe cantica in divina reperiuntur pagina, quorum decantatorum causae, mystice nobis quasi per quosdam gradus indicant animae profectus, qui reguntur per gratiam septiformis Spiritus. 1011CExeundum namque est de Aegypto hujus mundi et transeundum mare Rubrum per baptismum, vel per lacrymas poenitentiae, ut submerso vitiorum satellite primum decantemus canticum cum Moyse: Cantemus Domino, gloriose enim honorificatus est, equum et ascensorem projecit in mare (Exod. XV). Deinde relicto saecularium negotiorum tumultu perambulanda est spiritualis solitudo donec inveniamus puteum quem foderunt patres, quorum doctrinis et exemplis informati, ad recte vivendi modum secundum concinamus canticum quod cecinerunt filii Israel pro invento puteo. Ascendat, concinebant, puteus quem foderunt principes et praeparaverunt duces multitudinis in datore legis et baculis suis (Num. XXI). Cumque ad viciniam terrae promissionis 1011Dvenerimus, ad possidendam ipsam beatam terram nos praeparantes, et nobiscum spirituales et carnales invitantes, tertium cum Moyse decantemus canticum: Attende, coelum, et loquar; et audiat terra verba ex ore meo (Deut. XXXII). Sed ut hanc terram spiritualiter inhabitare possimus, depugnandi sunt hostes animae, contra quos tota intentione militandum nobis est, ut his effugatis, quartum cum Debbora concinamus canticum: Salvatae sunt reliquiae populi, Dominus in fortibus dimicavit (Jud. V). Superatis tunc hostibus, quintum cum David canticum pro evasione et liberatione nostra Domino decantemus, quod videlicet canticum David cecinit, quando liberatus est de manu omnium inimicorum suorum et de manu Saul et dixit: Dominus, petra 1012Amea et robur meum et salvator meus (II Reg. XXII), et reliqua. Postquam videlicet repressis spiritualium adversitatum motibus omnibusque saecularium rerum postpositis curis, optata tandem mentis quiete positi fuerimus, surgendum et properandum est profectibus animae ad promerendos illius coelestis Sponsi amplexus, cujus intentionis canticum sexto loco cum Isaia cantabimus: Cantabo dilecto canticum patruelis mei vineae suae (Isai. V). Processu videlicet hujus angelicae conversationis cum in tantam celsitudinem pennis sanctae contemplationis evolaverimus, ut jam in ipsius Sponsi amplexibus commorantes cum Apostolo dicere possimus: Nostra autem conversatio in coelis est (Philip. III). Tunc demum septimum decantabimus canticum, 1012Bquod non tantum canticum sed Canticum canticorum dicitur, quando ab omni opere saeculari feriantes, cum ipso sponso jugi quiete sabbatizare coeperimus.

Tria autem sunt consideranda in hoc libro: materia, intentio, finalis causa. Materia est sponsalia Christi et Ecclesiae, sive cujusque fidelis animae, quae constant vera et perfecta ejus dilectione, quae videlicet dilectio demonstratur mortificatione vitiorum et delectatione virtutum atque observatione ipsius mandatorum. Intentio est legentes et audientes hortari ut ita studeant Christo per charitatem adunari, ut digni sint sponsae vocabulo nuncupari. Finalis causa est summum inde consequi bonum quod Deus est, de quo bono scribitur: Quod nec 1012Coculus vidit, nec auris audivit, nec in cor hominis ascenderunt ea quae praeparavit Deus diligentibus se (I Cor. II).

Attendendum videlicet in hoc libro nihil secundum litteram carnaliter intelligendum, sed totum ad spiritualem sensum referendum, quia littera occidit, spiritus autem vivificat (I Cor. III). Nam quia Deus per se humano cordi loquens, capi non poterat, per aenigmata misericorditer movet et revocat, et per res cognitas latenter ei amorem rerum incognitarum insinuat, ut dum allegorice alloquendum esset per exteriora quae cognosceret intelligeret interiora, quae amare et servare debet. Nam hic quasi amoris corporei verba ponuntur ubi oscula, ubera, genae, femora nominantur; ut a torpore suo 1012Danima per sermones consuetos discussa recalescat et per verba amoris qui infra est excitetur ad amorem qui supra est. In quo non irritanda neque contemnenda est descriptio sacra, sed misericordia Dei consideranda, in hoc et amplior, quia ut nos ad amoris sacri amplexus accendat, usque ad infirmitatis nostrae verba se inclinat. Sed unde se locutione humiliat inde nos intellectu exaltat, quia ex sermone hujus amoris discimus, qualiter in Divinitatis amore serviamus. Valde aut solerter intuendum est, ne cum exteriora audimus, ad ipsa exteriora sentiendo remaneamus et machina quae ponitur ut levet, ipsa magis opprimat et gravet. Debemus ergo in verbis exterioribus quidquid est intus quaerere et loquentes de corpore extra corpus fieri, 1013Adebemus ad nuptias sponsi et sponsae cum intellectu charitatis (cum veste nuptiali venire, ne si ista careamus, in tenebras exteriores (Matth. XXII) ) in caecitatem ignorantiae repellamur.

Sciendum praeterea quod Salomon tres edidit libros, primum Proverbiorum, secundum Ecclesiasten, tertium Cantica canticorum, qui singuli singulis tribus philosophiae supponuntur partibus, videlicet Physicae, Ethicae, Logicae, hoc est naturali, morali, rationali scientiae. In Ecclesiasten nempe de naturali rerum statu disputat; in Proverbiis de morum honestate perorat; in Canticis canticorum de rationabili divinorumque mysteriorum dispositione decantat. His enim tribus modis quasi quibusdam gradibus mentis profectus ducitur, hoc est naturalitate, 1013Bmoralitate, rationalitate. Naturalitas est rerum ordinabiliter conditarum spectabilis variatio; moralitas honestae vitae informatio; rationalitas spiritualis divinaeque scientiae optabilis assecutio.

Sane ex naturalitatis consideratione, dum attenditur quantae pulchritudinis, quantae utilitatis, quam decenter, quam rationabiliter, et quam ordinabiliter creata sint disposita, quam immutabiliter, loco et tempore jussas servet vices, satis perpendi potest, qualis et quantus, quam speciosior, quam sublimior, quam potentior; ac ideo quam juste colendus, quam digne adorandus sit ipsius creaturae conditor Deus. Unde Apostolus: Invisibilia, inquit, ejus a creatura mundi per ea quae facta sunt, intellecta conspiciuntur, sempiterna quoque ejus virtus et divinitas, 1013Cita ut sint inexcusabiles (Rom. I). Non ergo excusari poterit homo, quia hujusmodi consideratione deducitur ad cognitionem Creatoris et fidem quae credit vera esse quae promittit Deus justis comminatur injustis, atque ex hoc prius timore compungitur post amore.

Primo namque timore surgit ad moralitatis honestatem, donec processu conversationis ipsa moralitas assumitur per charitatem, quae foras mittit timorem (I Joan. IV). Cum enim homo omni terrena creatura excellentior sit; ipsa autem creatura tantae, ut diximus, pulchritudinis sit, nimirum perpendere poterit, quam longe pulchrior futurus sit, si per mortalitatis decorem Creatori suo adhaeserit. Ad imaginem quippe 1013Det similitudinem Dei factus est homo (Gen. II) qui ex duabus substantiis, hoc est anima et corpore concretus: similitudinem habet Dei ex eo quod vivit et inter reliquas creaturas valde bonus dicitur, ipsa corporis habitudine ad coelestia suscipienda et terrena calcanda, originaliter evectus. Sed quia sicut ipse Deus nec crescentibus creaturis crescit, nec decrescit, cum tamen in omnibus sit; sic nec anima minutis membris minuitur, nec adauctis augetur et tamen est in omnibus.

Porro imaginem Dei habet ex meliori portione, scilicet anima, quae viget ingenio, ratione, intellectu, in quibus profecto Dei ostenditur imago, qua ei conformatur per moralitatis honestatem ut, sicut portavit imaginem terreni terrena diligendo, portet 1014Aet imaginem coelestis (I Cor. XV), coelestia ardenter exquirendo et exercendo. Non enim pueriliter cogitandum quod Deus qui incorporalis et incomprehensibilis est, aliquibus corporalibus lineamentis comprehendi possit, ut habeat imaginem ad quam factus sit homo, sed imago ejus est ratio humanae menti insita, qua differt ipse homo ab irrationabilibus, quaque discernit justum ab injusto, honestum ab inhonesto, utile ab inutili, qua denique reprimit bestiales animi motus, ne corrumpant mentis integritatem; quod si fragilitate aliqua impellente corruperint, denuo duce eadem ratione per sanctae moralitatis studium reformare possit.

Quo studio moraliter homine instituto rationalitatis illum gratia dignanter provehit, qua sui ipsius 1014Bet Dei cognitionem accipiat: sui quidem qua perpendet quid sit, et unde donum quod accipiat, quod non suo merito sed Dei gratia salvatur, in libertate gloriae filiorum Dei (Rom. VIII) assumptus sit: porro Dei, qua intelligat nihil melius, nihil potentius, nihil sublimius Deo, quem solum scire, timere, venerari, diligere et colere tota animi virtute debeat. Et haec est sapientia quae non introibit in malevolam animam, nec habitabit in corpore subdito peccatis, quia Spiritus sanctus disciplinae effugiet fictum, et auferet se a cogitationibus quae sunt sine intellectu, et corripietur a superveniente iniquitate (Sap. I).

Virtus ergo moralitatis assumit gratiam rationalitatis, quia mens quae Deo per disciplinae honestatem appropiat, magis scientiae ipsius subtilitatem 1014Cconsiderat, juxta Jacobi vocem qui suos auditores hortatur, dicens: Appropinquate Deo et appropinquabit vobis (Jacob. IV).

Hunc triplicem animae profectum Psalmista precatur, dicens: Bonitatem et disciplinam et scientiam doce me (Psal. CXVIII): primo namque bonitatem deinde disciplinam, tertio loco ponit scientiam. Deus enim naturaliter bonus existens hominem naturaliter bonum condidit, quoniam ad imaginem et similitudinem suam fecit, data ei ratione qua posset discernere bonum et malum, sed ipse horum alterum bonum non a se, sed a Deo posse intelligens, bonitatem se doceri postulat ut per naturalitatis bonitatem affectu sanctae moralitatis disciplinam, 1014Dper quam proficere possit ad illam incomprehensibilem et divinam rationalitatis scientiam, hujusque profectus ordinem toto mentis desiderio semper flagitans proclamat, bonitatem, inquiens, et disciplinam et scientiam doce me. Ac si aliis verbis dicat: Quia me, Domine Deus, naturaliter bonum condidisti; qualiter ipsum bonum naturae non meo vitio corrumpatur, sed tua gratia propagetur, doce, quatenus hoc modo velim et possim tuo adjutorio recte vivere et recte vivens tuorum mysteriorum arcana mentis arce penetrare.

Huic igitur tertiae parti quam rationalitatem diximus iste liber subscribitur propter excellentiam sacramentorum quae in Christo et Ecclesia, sive in qualicunque, Deo dilecta animi inibi decantantur qui 1015Aet merito inscribitur hoc nomine quod est Cantica canticorum, quia omnibus canticis perfectius et sublimius quasi quodam privilegio spiritualis harmoniae insignitus mystica intonat. Nam si subtilius consideres omnia fere Christi et Ecclesiae sacramenta in eo decantari intelliges. Namque ut verbi gratia dicam, in ipso cantici principio dum dicitur ex persona Ecclesiae: Osculetur me osculo oris sui, adventus Christi per carnem optatur, quasi aliis verbis Ecclesia dicat: Qui mihi quondam per ora prophetarum tuorum caeterorumque Patrum locutus es, jam nunc te ipsum praesentialiter secundum carnem natus offer, et proprio ore mandatorum tuorum decreta mihi porrige. Passionem quoque Christi et resurrectionem eo loco denotat; ubi dilecta 1015Bloquitur fasciculus myrrhae, dilectus meus mihi, inter ubera mea commorabitur, ac subinde, botrus cypri, dilectus meus mihi (Cant. I), ubi per myrrham amaritudo passionis; per botrum dulcedo resurrectionis exprimitur. Et alibi: Fuge, inquit, dilecte mi, et assimilare capreae aut hinnulo cervorum super montes aromatum (Cant. VIII); per capream hinnulumque ascendentis in coelum Domini potentiam insinuans. In grege detonsarum ascendente de lavacro (Cant. IV, VI), populus baptizatorum onera peccatorum deponentium accipitur, in gemellis fetibus gemina charitatis, in oculis vero, dentibus, genis, capillis, caeterisque quae ibi nominantur membrorum compositionibus, spiritualis ornatus et compositio sanctae Ecclesiae, sive cujuslibet sanctae animae describitur. Haereticorum ibi 1015Cpravitas, doctorum suavitas denotatur, et ut totum comprehendamus, quidquid in sancta Ecclesia generaliter vel specialiter agitur vel actum celebratur pulcherrimis allusionibus decantatur, ut merito tali nomine, quod est Cantica canticorum iste liber pro sui excellentia appelletur.

Igitur nostrum in hoc opere propositum est ipsorum sacramentorum rationalitatem ut possumus investigare; maxime vero ad aedificationem vestram, sanctae sorores, moralitatem inspicere et vestrum in amore sponsi vestri Domini Jesu Christi animum excitare.

Totum vero librum in quatuor divisimus tomos, propter quatuor periocharum recapitulationum subdistinctiones 1015Dquae signantur capitulo hoc tertio repetito: Adjuro vos, o filiae Jerusalem, per capreas cervosque caprarum, ne suscitetis neque evigilare faciatis dilectam quoadusque ipsa velit.

Harum ergo periocharum prima est ab eo quod ait: Osculetur me osculo oris sui, usque: Adjuro vos, filiae Jerusalem, secunda ab eo quod dicit: Vox dilecti mei; ecce iste venit, saliens in montibus, transiliens colles, usque itidem: Adjuro vos, filiae Jerusalem. Tertia prolixior quae sic incipit: Quae est ista quae ascendit per desertum, usque ad tertiam adjurationem: Adjuro vos, filiae Jerusalem. Quarta. Quae est ista quae ascendit de deserto deliciis affluens, usque ad finem.

Harum sane quatuor partium decantationes in quatuor 1016Adistinximus libellos: vel propter quadrigam Aminadab evangelicam, sive moralem quae constat quatuor virtutibus cardinalibus, quam sponsa turbata expavit, vel ut moneatur animus moralitati, studens quadratus esse debere virtutibus, ut sicut quadratu quocunque utitur stat; sic ille nec elevetur prosperis, nec dejiciatur adversis, sed veluti lapis quadratus in aedificio Domini positus, mortificatione vitae carnalis Christi passioni conformetur, crucis suae bajulus, ut possit comprehendere cum omnibus sanctis, quae sit longitudo, latitudo, sublimitas et profundum (Ephes. III). Cujus comprehensionis virtus sola perfectorum est, qui in charitate radicati et fundati (ibid.) ita Creatori suo inhaerent ut Canticum canticorum amplitudine charitatis jugiter decantent in quibus 1016Bhaec quadratura charitatis consistit. Longa enim in sanctis est charitas, quia non horaria sed perseverans et continua; lata, quia etiam usque ad inimicos extenditur; alta, quia propter spem et remunerationem vitae aeternae habetur; profunda, quia etiam Dei secreta penetrat; nemo autem cognovit quae sunt Dei, nisi Spiritus Dei (I Cor. II), per quem ipsa charitas in sanctorum cordibus diffunditur (Rom. V).

In ipso quoque capite vero exemplari nostro Domino, id est Christo, hujus quadraturae pulchritudo delectabiliter refulget, figurata in passionis suae genere, crucis videlicet specie. A summitate quippe crucis usque deorsum longitudo charitatis ejus exprimitur, de quo Joannes dicit, quod cum dilexisset 1016Csuos qui erant in mundo, in finem dilexit eos (Joan. XIII): latitudo vero a dextera in sinistram porrecta ad dilectionem inimicorum protenditur, pro quibus supplicans: Pater, inquit, ignosce illis, quia nesciunt quid faciunt (Luc. XXIII); sublimitas in tituli inscriptione attenditur: vix enim considerare potest altitudo benignitatis ejus, qua nos regit, fovet et custodit; profundum per partem terrae infixam, quae caetera sustinet, abyssum judiciorum Dei occultat, quia cum tanta Deus egerit et passus sit pro salute hominum, cur hunc assumat, illum repellat, inscrutabile et investigabile est.

Vos igitur, o dilectae sorores, cum Domino crucifixae mundo, discite comprehendere cum omnibus 1016Dsanctis, longitudinem, latitudinem, sublimitatem et profundum charitatis, quatenus in thalamum Domini nostri sponsi vestri cum accensis lampadibus, hoc est bonis operibus introductae, canticum illud novum solis virginibus cantandum, vere Canticum canticorum valeatis jugiter ante thronum Dei decantare.

Sed jam nunc ad ipsius seriem libri veniamus, hoc praemonentis, ut si quem movet quod ultra mensuram sermo porrigatur, et explanationis modum supereffluat oratio, noverit nos non tantum explanandae gratia id opus assumpsisse; sed hac potius intentione, ut inde nobis materiam superemus, unde sanctarum sororum religioso desiderio, quibus non potuimus verbis, saltem satisfaceremus scriptis.

GENERAL PREFACE OF WOLBERO ON THE CANTICLE OF CANTICLES OF SOLOMON.

  • 1009

1009DIn Holy Scripture many canticles are spoken of, which, differing by a diverse kind of causes, have been sung now generally, now specially, according to place and time; place, because either in the fatherland or in a foreign land; time, because either in peace or in captivity. For there is spoken of the Canticle of Moses, the Canticle of Anna, the Canticle of Habacuc the prophet, or others of this kind; but all these are simply canticles. Here, however, they are called Canticles of Canticles, because they surpass all kinds of canticles by the majesty of mystical understanding.

And the other canticles, indeed, have a cause why they were 1010Dsung, as Moses sang the canticle of praise for the victory celebrated, when Pharaoh was drowned with his chariots and horsemen in the Red Sea. Anna too sang a canticle to the Lord for fruitfulness bestowed, the reproach of barrenness being taken away. Ezechias too sang a canticle for health restored to him. Therefore the several canticles were, for each one, a thanksgiving for a benefit conferred on him by God. But this canticle represents the harmony of that highest and perfect charity, by which, all the cares curi of worldly things being lulled to sleep, every faithful soul 1011Ais joined to her Creator as a bride to the bridegroom with the ineffable sweetness of love; in whose embraces she dwells with such sweetness of peace and quiet that there is nothing she desires besides him, nothing she would set before so magnificent a grace; because certainly there is nothing that resists the spirit which, the war of the flesh trodden down, with the flesh subjugated to it, keeps sabbath in Christ in the same happy concord. For a great part, and a Sabbath to be desired, that is, rest, is when the flesh does not lust against the spirit, but, the tumult of the vices being stilled, the mind enjoys such sweetness of inward tranquillity that, desiring nothing else than the Lord, it wills and is able to say the Canticle of Canticles, that is, to have true and perfect charity. For charity towers above all the virtues, as the Canticle of Canticles 1011Bgoes beyond all canticles. But ascents are to be disposed in the heart, so that, as by certain steps, one may arrive at singing the Canticles of Canticles; that just as he who enters the holy place still has need of many things to be able to enter the Holy of holies; and he who celebrates Sabbaths needs far higher things to be able to arrive at the Sabbaths of sabbaths: so he who sings canticles ought ever to advance to greater things, to be able to sing the Canticles of Canticles.

For seven canticles are found in the divine page, the causes of whose singing mystically indicate to us, as by certain steps, the progresses of the soul, which are ruled through the grace of the sevenfold Spirit. 1011CFor we must go out of the Egypt of this world and cross the Red Sea through baptism, or through the tears of penitence, that, the attendant of the vices being drowned, we may first sing the canticle with Moses: Let us sing to the Lord, for he is gloriously honoured; the horse and the rider he hath thrown forth into the sea (Exod. XV) [Vulg. magnificatus est … dejecit, "is magnified … hath cast down"]. Then, the tumult of worldly business being left behind, the spiritual solitude is to be walked through until we find the well which the fathers dug, by whose doctrines and examples being informed in the manner of living rightly, we may sing together the second canticle, which the children of Israel sang for the well they had found. Let it ascend, they sang together, the well which the princes dug, and the leaders of the multitude prepared, in the giver of the law and with their staves (Num. XXI). And when we have come to the neighbourhood of the land of promise, 1011Dpreparing ourselves to possess that blessed land, and inviting with us the spiritual and the carnal, let us sing with Moses the third canticle: Attend, O heaven, and I will speak; and let the earth hear the words from my mouth (Deut. XXXII) [Vulg. Audite, caeli, quae loquor: audiat terra verba oris mei, "Hear, O heavens, the things I speak: let the earth hear the words of my mouth"]. But that we may inhabit this land spiritually, the enemies of the soul must be fought down, against whom we must war with our whole intention, that, these being put to flight, we may sing together the fourth canticle with Debbora: The remnants of the people are saved, the Lord hath fought among the mighty (Jud. V). The enemies then being overcome, let us sing to the Lord the fifth canticle with David, for our escape and deliverance, that canticle namely which David sang when he was delivered from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul, and said: The Lord is my rock 1012Aand my strength and my saviour (II Reg. XXII), and the rest. After, namely, the motions of spiritual adversities having been repressed and all the cares of worldly things set aside, we shall at last have been placed in the longed-for quiet of mind, we must rise and hasten with the progresses of the soul to merit the embraces of that heavenly Bridegroom; the canticle of which intention we shall sing in the sixth place with Isaias: I will sing to the beloved the canticle of my cousin, of his vineyard (Isai. V). When, namely, by the progress of this angelic conversation, we shall have flown up to such a height on the wings of holy contemplation that, dwelling now in the embraces of the Bridegroom himself, we can say with the Apostle: But our conversation is in heaven (Philip. III). Then at last we shall sing the seventh canticle, 1012Bwhich is called not only a canticle but the Canticle of Canticles, when, resting from every worldly work, we shall have begun to keep sabbath with the bridegroom himself in continual quiet.

Now three things are to be considered in this book: the matter, the intention, the final cause. The matter is the espousals of Christ and the Church, or of each faithful soul, which consist in true and perfect love of him; which love, namely, is shown by the mortification of the vices and the delight of the virtues and the observance of his commandments. The intention is to exhort those who read and hear so to study to be united to Christ through charity that they may be worthy to be called by the name of bride. The final cause is thence to attain the highest good, which is God, of which good it is written: That which neither 1012Ceye hath seen, nor ear heard, nor into the heart of man have those things ascended which God hath prepared for them that love him (I Cor. II).

It is to be heeded, namely, that in this book nothing is to be understood carnally according to the letter, but the whole is to be referred to the spiritual sense, because the letter killeth, but the spirit quickeneth (I Cor. III). For because God, speaking by himself to the human heart, could not be grasped, he mercifully moves and recalls it through enigmas, and through known things secretly insinuates to it the love of unknown things, so that, since it had to be addressed allegorically, through the exterior things which it knew it might understand the interior things, which it ought to love and keep. For here words as it were of bodily love are set down, where kisses, breasts, cheeks, thighs are named; that the soul, shaken out of its torpor 1012Dby accustomed speech, may grow warm again, and through the words of the love which is below may be stirred to the love which is above. In which the sacred description is not to be made void nor despised, but the mercy of God is to be considered, and in this the ampler, because, to kindle us to the embraces of sacred love, he inclines himself even to the words of our infirmity. But whence he humbles himself in speech, thence he exalts us in understanding, because from the speech of this love we learn how we should serve in the love of the Godhead. Greatly, or skilfully, must we look to it, lest, when we hear exterior things, we remain in those exterior things by our perceiving, and the machine which is set to lift should itself rather press down and weigh down. We ought therefore in the exterior words to seek whatever is within, and, speaking of the body, to become outside the body; 1013Awe ought to the nuptials of the bridegroom and bride with the understanding of charity (to come with the wedding garment, lest, if we lack it, into the outer darkness (Matth. XXII) ) we be driven back into the blindness of ignorance.

It is to be known besides that Solomon put forth three books, the first of Proverbs, the second Ecclesiastes, the third the Canticles of Canticles, which are placed, each under each, beneath the three parts of philosophy, namely Physics, Ethics, Logic, that is, natural, moral, rational science. For in Ecclesiastes he disputes of the natural state of things; in Proverbs he discourses of the honesty of morals; in the Canticles of Canticles he sings of the rational disposition of divine mysteries. For by these three modes, as by certain steps, the progress of the mind is led, that is, by naturality, 1013Bmorality, rationality. Naturality is the visible variation of things created in order; morality, the informing of an honest life; rationality, the desirable attainment of spiritual and divine knowledge.

Indeed, from the consideration of naturality, while it is heeded of how great beauty, of how great utility, how becomingly, how rationally, and how orderly the created things have been disposed, how unchangeably it keeps its appointed turns in place and time, it can be sufficiently weighed of what kind and how great, how much more beautiful, how much more sublime, how much more powerful, and therefore how justly to be worshipped, how worthily to be adored, is God, the founder of this creature. Whence the Apostle: The invisible things, he says, of him from the creation of the world through the things which are made, being understood, are clearly seen, his eternal power also and divinity, 1013Cso that they are inexcusable (Rom. I). Therefore man will not be able to be excused, because by consideration of this kind he is led to the knowledge of the Creator, and to the faith which believes to be true the things which God promises to the just, threatens to the unjust; and from this he is pricked, first by fear, afterwards by love.

For first by fear he rises to the honesty of morality, until, by the progress of conversation, morality itself is taken up through charity, which casteth out fear (I Joan. IV). For since man is more excellent than every earthly creature, and the creature itself is, as we have said, of such great beauty, surely he will be able to weigh how much more beautiful he will be, if through the comeliness of mortality he cleaves to his Creator. For to the image 1013Dand likeness of God man was made (Gen. II), who is compounded of two substances, that is, of soul and body: he has the likeness of God in this, that he lives and among the other creatures is called very good, raised up originally by the very bearing of his body for receiving heavenly things and trampling earthly ones. But because, just as God himself neither grows with growing creatures nor decreases, although he yet is in all; so neither is the soul diminished when the members are diminished, nor increased when they are increased, and yet it is in all.

But he has the image of God from the better portion, namely the soul, which thrives in wit, reason, understanding, in which the image of God is indeed shown, by which he is conformed to him through the honesty of morality, so that, as he bore the image of the earthly by loving earthly things, he may bear 1014Aalso the image of the heavenly (I Cor. XV), by ardently seeking out and exercising heavenly things. For it is not to be thought childishly that God, who is incorporeal and incomprehensible, can be comprehended by any bodily lineaments, so that he should have an image to which man was made; but his image is the reason implanted in the human mind, by which man himself differs from irrational things, and by which he discerns the just from the unjust, the honest from the dishonest, the useful from the useless, by which finally he represses the bestial motions of the mind, lest they corrupt the integrity of the mind; and if, some frailty impelling, they have corrupted it, he may reform it anew, the same reason leading, through the study of holy morality.

By which study, man being morally instructed, the grace of rationality worthily advances him, by which he may receive knowledge of himself 1014Band of God: of himself indeed, by which he will weigh what he is, and whence the gift which he receives, that he is saved not by his own merit but by the grace of God, [and] has been taken up in the liberty of the glory of the sons of God (Rom. VIII): but of God, by which he may understand that nothing is better, nothing more powerful, nothing more sublime than God, whom alone he ought to know, fear, venerate, love and worship with all the virtue of his mind. And this is the wisdom which will not enter into a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins, because the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee the deceitful, and will withdraw himself from thoughts that are without understanding, and will be rebuked by iniquity coming upon it (Sap. I).

Therefore the virtue of morality takes up the grace of rationality, because the mind which draws near to God through the honesty of discipline considers the more the subtlety of his knowledge 1014C, according to the voice of James, who exhorts his hearers, saying: Draw nigh to God and he will draw nigh to you (Jacob. IV).

This threefold progress of the soul the Psalmist prays for, saying: Goodness and discipline and knowledge teach me (Psal. CXVIII): for first he puts goodness, then discipline, in the third place knowledge. For God, being naturally good, created man naturally good, since he made him to his own image and likeness, reason being given to him by which he could discern good and evil; but he himself, understanding that he can [do] the one of these, the good, not from himself but from God, asks to be taught goodness, that through the goodness of naturality, by the affection of holy morality, discipline, 1014Dthrough which he may be able to advance to that incomprehensible and divine knowledge of rationality; and, ever demanding the order of this progress with the whole desire of his mind, he cries out: goodness, he says, and discipline and knowledge teach me. As if he said in other words: Since thou, O Lord God, hast created me naturally good; how that very good of nature may not be corrupted by my fault, but propagated by thy grace, teach [me], so that in this way I may will and be able by thy help to live rightly, and, living rightly, to penetrate the secrets of thy mysteries with the citadel of the mind.

To this third part, then, which we have called rationality, this book is subscribed, on account of the excellence of the sacraments which are sung therein in Christ and the Church, or in any whatever, beloved of God, of the mind; which 1015Ais also deservedly inscribed with this name which is the Canticles of Canticles, because, marked as by a certain privilege of spiritual harmony, more perfectly and more sublimely than all canticles, it intones mystical things. For if you consider more subtly, you will understand that almost all the sacraments of Christ and the Church are sung in it. For, to speak by way of example, in the very beginning of the canticle, when it is said in the person of the Church: Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth, the coming of Christ through the flesh is longed for, as if the Church said in other words: Thou who once spokest to me through the mouths of thy prophets and of the other Fathers, now at length, born according to the flesh, offer thyself in presence, and with thine own mouth hold out to me the decrees of thy commandments. The passion also of Christ and the resurrection it denotes in that place where the beloved 1015Bspeaks: A bundle of myrrh is my beloved to me, he shall abide between my breasts, and presently after, a cluster of Cyprus is my beloved to me (Cant. I), where by the myrrh the bitterness of the passion, by the cluster the sweetness of the resurrection is expressed. And elsewhere: Flee, she says, my beloved, and be like to a roe or to a young hart upon the mountains of spices (Cant. VIII) [Vulg. capreae, hinnuloque cervorum, "to a roe and to a young hart"]; by the roe and the young hart suggesting the power of the Lord ascending into heaven. In the flock of shorn ones coming up from the washing (Cant. IV, VI), the people of the baptized laying down the burdens of sins is understood; in the twin offspring, the twin things of charity; and in the eyes, the teeth, the cheeks, the hair, and the other arrangements of members which are named there, the spiritual adornment and arrangement of holy Church, or of any holy soul, is described. There the depravity of heretics, 1015Cthe sweetness of doctors is denoted; and, to comprehend the whole, whatever in holy Church is done, generally or specially, or is celebrated as done, is sung with most beautiful allusions, so that deservedly this book is called by such a name, which is the Canticles of Canticles, for its excellence.

Our purpose, therefore, in this work is to investigate, as we are able, the rationality of these sacraments; but chiefly, for your edification, holy sisters, to look into morality and to stir up your mind in the love of your bridegroom, the Lord Jesus Christ.

We have divided the whole book into four tomes, on account of the four subdistinctions of the recapitulations of the periochae, 1015Dwhich are marked by this chapter thrice repeated: I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes and the harts of the goats, that you stir not up nor make the beloved to awake, till she herself will. [Vulg. Cant. 2:7 filiae Jerusalem, per capreas cervosque camporum, "daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes and the harts of the fields"]

Of these periochae, then, the first is from where it says: Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth, up to: I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, the second from where it says: The voice of my beloved; behold he cometh, leaping upon the mountains, skipping over the hills, up to, likewise: I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem. The third, longer, which begins thus: Who is she that goeth up by the desert, up to the third adjuration: I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem. The fourth. Who is she that goeth up from the desert, flowing with delights, up to the end.

The singings of these four parts we have distinguished into four 1016Alittle books: either on account of the evangelical chariot of Aminadab, or the moral one, which consists of the four cardinal virtues, which the bride, troubled, dreaded; or that the mind studious of morality may be admonished that it ought to be squared by the virtues, so that, as by squareness it stands on whatever [face] it uses, so he is neither lifted up by prosperity nor cast down by adversity, but, like a squared stone placed in the building of the Lord, is conformed to the passion of Christ by the mortification of the carnal life, the bearer of his cross, that he may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the length, breadth, sublimity and depth (Ephes. III) [Vulg. latitudo, et longitudo, "breadth, and length", the reverse of the order the exposition follows]. The virtue of which comprehension belongs to the perfect alone, who, rooted and founded in charity (ibid.), so cleave to their Creator that by the amplitude of charity they continually sing the Canticle of Canticles; in whom 1016Bthis squareness of charity consists. For charity in the saints is long, because it is not for an hour, but persevering and continual; broad, because it extends even to enemies; high, because it is had for the sake of the hope and reward of eternal life; deep, because it penetrates even the secrets of God; no man, however, hath known the things which are of God, save the Spirit of God (I Cor. II), through whom charity itself is poured forth in the hearts of the saints (Rom. V).

In the head himself also, our true exemplar, the Lord, that is, Christ, the beauty of this squareness shines forth delightfully, figured in the manner of his passion, namely in the form of the cross. For from the top of the cross down to the bottom, the length of his charity is expressed, of whom John says that having loved 1016Chis own who were in the world, he loved them unto the end (Joan. XIII): and the breadth, stretched from the right to the left, is extended to the love of enemies, for whom, supplicating, Father, he says, pardon them, because they know not what they do (Luc. XXIII); the sublimity is regarded in the inscription of the title: for scarcely can the height of his kindness, by which he rules, cherishes and guards us, consider; the depth, through the part fixed in the earth, which sustains the rest, hides the abyss of the judgments of God, because, though God has done and suffered so much for the salvation of men, why he takes up this one, repels that one, is inscrutable and unsearchable.
