Pulchritudo quippe appellationis est, dicere: Amicam, columbam, formosam; pulchritudo adhortationis, surge, propera, veni; pulchritudo causae, hiemem et imbrem recessisse, flores apparere, tempus putationis adesse, vocem turturis auditam esse, ficus protulisse grossos suos, vineas florentes odorem dedisse.

1111B104 Ordo vero non sine consideratione disponitur in hac appellatione, adhortatione et causa. In appellatione quidem, dum primo dicit amicam, deinde columbam, postremo formosam; in adhortatione vero primo surge, dein propera, postremo veni. Porro in causa primo loco hiems transiit, secundo imber recessit, tertio flores apparuerunt, quarto tempus putationis advenit, quinto vox turturis audita est in terra nostra, sexto ficus protulit grossos suos, septimo vineae florentes odorem dederunt. Causa adhortationis hujus qua monetur dilecta surgere, properare, venire, sunt hiemis et imbris recessus, florum apparitio, et tempus putationis; vox turturis et ficus proferentes grossos suos, vineaeque florentes.

1111CSed videndum unde locutio ista procedat: supra dixerat, vox dilecti mei, quam vocem Scripturam sanctam diximus, tota enim divina pagina vox Dei est, per quam legendo dilecta saltus induti pariete mortalitatis nostrae, et loquentis ad se per fenestras et cancellos miraculorum et doctrinarum, nam quoties Scripturas sanctas videmus vel legimus, Deus ad nos vel nobiscum loquitur. Hoc ergo modo loquentem ad se dilectum, dilecta, id est Ecclesia sive quaevis fidelis anima advertit, quando divinae dispensationis ordinem, sacramentorum religionem, praeceptorum divinorum utilitatem audit, legit, intelligit.

Verum ipse dilectus veluti e salute dilectae sollicitus 1111Din hujus modi locutione assumunt sibi officium boni oratoris, ut audientem tribus attrahat modis hoc est ut faciat attentam, docilem, benevolam: nam dum non semel, sed ter inclamitat, dicens, surge, propera, veni, ac si dicat non segniter sed celeriter et studiose te offer, veluti aliquid ratum et insolitum auditura attentam facit; cum vero vocabulo dilectionis et gratiae frequenter appellat dicens: Amica mea, columba mea, formosa mea, benevolam reddit ut majorem pariat voluntatem praeparandi et audiendi.

Porro causam hujus advocationis eum docet distincte per numerum dicendo: Jam enim hiems transiit, imber abiit et recessit, flores apparuerunt, tempus putationis advenit, vox turturis audita est, 1112Avineae florentes odorem dederunt, docilem facit ut agnoscat tempus magnae salutis et gratiae quod debeat cum magna veneratione et gaudio suscipere.

Et hoc est magnae pietatis indicium, qua ad nos frequenter intendit dilectus iste per fenestras et cancellos, infinitae clementiae suae stans post parietem malorum nostrorum quasi nubem ne transeat oratio oppositam (Thren. III), loquens quotidie et admonens quatenus istum parietem vel hanc nubem ariete virtutum et afflatu sancti Spiritus dissipemus.

Quid ergo loquitur dilectus dilectae? Surge, inquit, propera, amica mea 105 columba mea, formosa mea, et veni: surge per fidem, propera per spem, 1112Bveni per charitatem: sive, surge per intentionem, propera per operationem, veni per contemplationem: haec est enim totius tui cultus et religionis perfectio, credere, sperare, diligere: nam reliqua tria, videlicet intentio, operatio, contemplatio ex his constituuntur. Si enim recte credis, recte quoque ad bona agenda intendis; operaris vero propter spem praemii consequendi, subtilius autem contemplaris, quo magis ad Deum per charitatem sublevaris.

Et hoc facere poteris, si amica fueris, hoc est si abjecto errore infidelitatis mihi per fidem reconciliari; si columba fueris, hoc est si simpliciter vixeris, neminem laeseris et tuis tantum contenta fueris, spe futurae remunerationis, vel si fragilitate aliqua 1112Ccompellente de arca, hoc est de Ecclesia male agendo exieris, non in saeculo remaneas, sed citius revertas ferens ramum olivae in ore, hoc est spem habens misericordiae per confessionem et modum poenitentiae.

Si formosa fueris, hoc est dilectione Dei sola servans omnes mundi curas, vel si qua pulchritudinem mentis tuae inficere possunt, postposueris, ut non lippientes Liae oculos, sed formosam et pulchram Rachelis faciem habens in illam supernae beatitudinis majestatem, quae Deus est, purgato mentis oculo intendere possis.

VERS. 11, 12.-- Jam enim hiems transiit, imber abiit et recessit.

1112DFlores apparuerunt in terra nostra, tempus putationis advenit: vox turturis audita est in terra nostra.

Cur autem ad haec tantopere se invito? Quia frigus infidelitatis et tempestas caecitatis et ignorantiae, quae totam mundi obduxerat faciem, recesserunt; et flores apparuerunt, id est initia bonorum operum jam pullulare coeperunt, et tempus putationis advenit, hoc est consilium et regula, vitia et peccata amputandi tempore gratiae jam habentur. Vox quoque turturis audita est, id est sonus praedicationis, ex qua resonant consilia, praecepta et exempla castitatis, solitariae conversationis, supernae speculationis et poenitentiae quae omnia exprimit turtur castus et gemebundus, amator solitudinis et 1113Anidificans in excelsis. In ipso namque principio evangelicae vocis clamat turtur verbis et moribus, sive ipse Dominus Jesus Christus virginitatis filius, sive ipsa ejus genitrix beata virgo Maria, sive praecursor ipsius beatus Joannes Baptista. Denique ipse Dominus de Virgine natus castitatis est praenuntius, solitudinem consecrat in desertum ductus, contemplationi monet studendum in monte orans, ad poenitentiam hortatur quasi gemebunda voce proclamans: 106 Poenitentiam agite, appropinquavit enim regnum coelorum (Matth. X). Beata quoque Dei genitrix singulare est speculum castitatis, quae solidaria et in divina contemplatione posita ab angelo salutatur, et Christi mater futura praedocetur, moxque divinae animadversionis sententiam poenitentia 1113Bmutata denuntiat, cum misericordiam ejus in progenie et progenies futuram proclamat (Luc. II). Sanctus vero Joannes Baptista castitatis filius mente et corpore virgo, quo magis fuit ab hominibus remotus, tanto magis Deo per contemplationem exstitit proximus; fuit enim iu deserto praedicans baptismum poenitentiae (Matth. III), et clamans gemebunda turturis voce: Facite fructus dignos poenitentiae (ibid.).

VERS. 13.-- Ficus protulit grossos suos, vineae florentes dederunt odorem suum. Surge, propera, amica mea, speciosa mea, et veni.

Ficus, inquit, protulit grossos suos, hoc est Judaea hactenus sterilis carnalis coepit intelligere caeremonias 1113Cet corde credendo ad justitiam, ore autem confitendo ad salutem (Rom. X), quod carnaliter sapiebat, hoc jam spiritualiter sapit et fide atque opere ostendere gestit.

Vineae etiam florentes odorem dederunt, quia gentes audito verbo fidei jam incipiunt boni operis ubique spargere odorem.

Non ergo ordo locutionis hujus sine ratione attenditur, in qua tria ista fides, spes et charitas; sive alia tria, intentio, operatio, contemplatio considerantur, cum ista horum sint consequentia, ut qui credit, speret et diligat; et nemo sperare et diligere possit, nisi qui crediderit; nemo etiam operatur nisi prius intendat quid, et quomodo, et quando, et quare operatur, subtilitatem vero contemplandi 1113Dnemo consequi possit, nisi ad hanc bonorum operum sublimitate profecerit.

Non autem erit, ut credimus, ineptum notare septenum causae numerum, ut ostendamus ipsius causae effectum septiformis Spiritus semper fuisse dignationem et beneplacitum: Nam hiemis, id est infidelitatis transitio; imbris, id est persecutionis transitio; florum, id est bonorum operum apparitio; vitiorum amputatio; turturis, id est Evangelii proclamatio; grossorum ficus prolatio, id est legalium observationum in veritatem mysteriorum revelatio; vinearum, id est gentium ad fidem conversarum suaviter redolens operatio, quid sunt nisi septiformis Spiritus beneplacitum et dignatio?

Causas enim hujusmodi, et quod ex his efficiebatur, 1114Asive efficitur causas, hoc est credere, sperare, diligere, operabatur ab initio, et adhuc operatur quotidie Spiritus Dei, quia omnis infidelitatis et malitiae remotio, fideique et salutis collatio constant ipsius dono qui omnem 107 in sancta Ecclesia aequitatis, honestatis et utilitatis providet, componit et ordinat statum. Unde etiam sponsus cum loquitur sponsae: Vox turturis audita est, subdit, in terra nostra, ut videlicet insinuat nullum effectum sacramentorum, nullam spem salutis esse extra catholicam Ecclesiam: sed omnem evangelicae praedicationis vocem, in observatione praeceptorum, in ordine et reverentia sacramentorum infra sanctam Ecclesiam tenendam, in qua datur et accipitur ipse Spiritus sanctus. In principio enim, ut scriptum 1114Best, terra erat inanis et vacua, quia antequam mens humana spiritu fecundaretur divino, nullo virtutum flore vel germine componebatur, sed postquam spiritus Dei ferebatur super aquas (Gen. I), hoc est super fluentia et instabilia hominum corda, dum demum lux veritatis et fructus justitiae per totum effunditur mundum, ut terra illa primo inanis et vacua Dei fieret Ecclesia, in qua ipse per gratiam suam inhabitaret, et suam faceret terram jam florentem et fructificantem, et quoddam vitale et rationale honestatis et disciplinae quasi hominis specimen praeferentem per gratiam inhabitantem.

Igitur cum propriae salutis dilectus dilectam fecerit sollicitam, proximorum quoque salutis negligentem 1114Cnon esse admonet, ut hanc insinuet charitatem, quae proximis sicut et sibi studio pietatis providet, quatenus merito amica, columba, formosa, gratiae vocantis et justificantis appellatione honoretur.

Sequitur enim cum dilectus repetito superiori appellationis numero, surge, propera, amica mea, speciosa mea, et veni. Quia, inquit, ad hoc mea gratia profecisti, ut tuimet curam gerere possis, mundum contemnendo, et meae dilectioni per contemplativae vitae studium inhaerendo, debes quoque interdum per activae vitae laborem proximis prodesse verbo et exemplo, quia cum te talem effecerim, ut habeas gratiam docendi et operandi, non sine tui periculo de infosso reddes rationem talento. Sed surge ad laborem 1114Distum aliquando de illo quietis tuae dulcissimo somno pro causa fraternae necessitatis, et propera docendo, et ab hujus mundi amore proximos retrahendo, ut ipsos quoque tecum in illud solitarium quietis tuae deducas domicilium. Hoc autem facies velut amica mea per fidem, speciosa mea per operationem, columba mea per Spiritus sancti infusionem.

VERS. 14.-- Columba mea in foraminibus petrae, in caverna maceriae, ostende mihi faciem tuam; sonet vox tua in auribus meis, vox enim tua dulcis et facies tua decora.

Quia te columbae comparavi 108. Columba autem refugia sua habet in foraminibus petrae, in caverna maceriae; quaenam quoque tua erunt refugia 1115Ain quibus omnem salutis tuae spem constituas, ut ab hujus mundi multimoda tentatione confugias? nimirum in foraminibus petrae, de qua scriptum est: Petra autem erat Christus (I Cor. X); foramina enim ista sunt passionis meae vulnera, quae sunt omni Christiano quasi quaedam in cunctis adversitatibus refugia. Quinque enim mea vulnera sunt quinque tuorum sensuum tuta refugia, ut cum hoc numero signum passionis meae praetenderis, in omnium sensuum tuorum integritate secura persistere possis. Haec namque integritas sensuum necessaria tibi erit docenti et operanti, quia si ea quae doces et operaris in nomine meo cum honestate et utilitate, rationabiliter ordinate et moderate protuleris, audientium sive inspicientium animos magis attrahere 1115Bvalebis. Plerumque enim honestum genus causae, si indigne profertur, offendit sicut et humile genus causae interdum si rationabiliter profertur, partem honestatis obtinebit.

In passione ergo mea amica, speciosa, columba effecta es quia ad hoc animam meam pro te posui, sanguinem fudi, ut te mihi exhiberem sponsam gloriosam non habentem maculam, neque rugam (Ephes. V). Nam cum foeda ejus per te ipsam, pro te ipsa non suffecisti neque tota pro te sufficere potuit creatura, mea vero passio cui totus non adaequatur mundus pro te satisfecit Deo, ut inde reconciliata mihique conjuncta, dicaris amica, speciosa, columba.

1115CSive foramina petrae sunt quatuor Evangelia, in quibus mea perspiciuntur gesta et dicta, sive etiam virtutum studia, videlicet humilitatis, patientiae, obedientiae, orationum, vigiliarum, lectionum sanctarum, caeterarumque quae sunt quasi quidam aditus ad me veniendi, et regna coelorum introeundi, de quibus omnibus proximis praedicare debes et ostendere, quia sine his salutem consequi non possunt.

Columba mea in foraminibus petrae, in caverna maceriae. Christus petra (I Cor. X), Christus et maceria. Maceria quidem ante passionem, quia adhuc ex humana infirmitate fragilis et passibilis erat; petra vero post resurrectionem, quando deposita omni corruptione impassibilis ex firmitate glorificati 1115Dcorporis factus est. Columba vero in foraminibus petrae, in caverna maceriae dilecta esse debet, quia cum multa virtutum, operationum et virtutum insignia, quae ex fortitudine divinitatis erant in Christo, considerat; specialiter tamen debet considerare, illud charitatis insigne, quod in sua exhibuit carne, quam pro ejus morti tradidit salute: nam magnae hujus dilectionis erga hominem 109 ostendit judicium cum pro eo redimendo, non aliud quam seipsum, valuit offerre.

Caverna ergo maceriae charitas est Christi in carne morientis, in qua videlicet charitate Ecclesiae quidem generaliter, specialiter vero quaevis sancta anima columba est, quia per charitatem invenit locum manendi in Christo, ubi spiritualiter bonorum 1116Aoperum pullos nutriat et antiqui serpentis insidias effugiat: scriptum est enim, quia Deus charitas est et qui manet in charitate, in Deo manet, et Deus in eo (I Joan. IV).

Columba quoque est in foraminibus petrae, in caverna maceriae. Columba autem pro cantu gemitum habet; et gemere debet anima fidelis quando recolit passionem Redemptoris, perpendens quid pro ea Deus fecerit, quando ille qui peccatum non fecit, nec inventus est dolus in ore ejus (I Petr. II), pro peccatoribus mori voluit et quod homo debuit, Deus homo exsolvit. Gemat quoque pro suis excessibus, in foraminibus petrae, in caverna maceriae, quia advocatum habet apud Patrem Jesum Christum justum: et ipse est propitiatio pro peccatis ejus 1116B(I Joan. II), qui quotidie salutem confert omni poenitenti, passionis suae sacramento et singulari charitatis hujus exemplo. Quotidie namque nobis Redemptor noster sua renovat foramina, hoc est passionis signa, in corporis et sanguinis sui immolatione; et cavernam in qua protegamur ab hostium insidiis, ostendit in tantae charitatis assignatione.

Potest etiam maceria accipi doctrina apostolorum, sive apostolicorum virorum, quia sicut maceria ex multis construitur lapidibus, ita doctrina sanctorum ex plurimis virtutum constituitur documentis. In qua est cuique fideli animae caverna, id est vitae custodia, quia ex eorum dictis et scriptis discit, qualiter peccata fugiendo et bonorum operum 1116Cpullos nutriendo malignorum spirituum insidias effugere possit.

Monetur ergo dilecta quietem contemplationis interdum relinquere et ad activae vitae laborem causa proximorum exire, ut quod ipsa per quietem ex divinis praeceptis, et sanctorum exemplis didicit, hoc proximorum mentibus praedicando inferat, et sicut ipsa horum suavitate contemplationis assiduitatem affecta est, ita quoque proximorum animos ipsorum desiderio per virtutem praedicationis afficiat.

Unde et dilectus eam admonendo subdit: Ostende mihi faciem tuam. Quae est enim facies dilectae, nisi ex consortio dilecti quaedam refulgens imago sanctitatis? Nam quanto divinae contemplationi quisque 1116Dsedulus inhaeret, tanto pulchrior ex sanctitatis jubare facies mentis resplendet. Hinc est, quod Moyses in monte cum Domino quadraginta diebus 100 conversatus splendidam faciem scribitur protulisse ex consortio sermonis Domini (Exod. XXXIV). Qui enim in monte supernae contemplationis commoratus fuerit, ab ipso Spiritu Dei cum quo unum sit, quamdam sanctitatis faciem producit; unde Apostolus: Revelata, inquit, facie Domini gloriam speculantes in eamdem imaginem transformamur, a claritate in claritatem, tanquam a Domini Spiritu (II Cor. III). Qui ergo Spiritu Dei aguntur, ab ipso Spiritu transformantur in imaginem Christi secundum interiorem hominem, a claritate in claritatem, ut qui aliquid claritatis ex eo in faciem interioris hominis 1117Atraxerint, qua eum lucidius agnoscant, quanto ei plus appropinquant, contemplatoria claritate, tanto plus claritatis sibi ex eo contrahant, per quam eum semper clarius et verius agnoscant. Unde et Ezechiel, cum sanctorum animalium visionem describeret, dixit: Similitudo hominis in eis (Ezech. I). Quidquid enim justitiae et mansuetudinis, quidquid modestiae et humilitatis, quidquid patientiae et pietatis, quidquid postremo unquam sanctitatis habere potuerunt vel possunt electi Dei, ab illo singulari homine Domino Jesu Christo traxerunt, et ab illa principali sanctitatis facie illustratam, ipsi quoque quamdam suo modo sanctitatis faciem conceperunt.

Talem, inquit, dilectus faciem tuam a mea gratia spiritualiter deductam, o dilecta, ostende mihi, hoc 1117Best ad laudem mei nominis in publicum procede, pulchra actionis et sermonis specie, ut proximi tui videntes opera tua, glorificent Patrem tuum qui in coelis est (Matth. V), ipsique ex recte composito actionis et sermonis tui vultu suae quoque mentis et intentionis vultum componant.

Sonet vox tua in auribus meis, tum in auribus Domini vox praedicantis sonat quando voci meae concordat, ut quod foris ad aures hominis per vocem sonat; hoc in Dei auribus per fidem loquatur. Et pulchre cum praemisisset, ostende mihi faciem tuam, subdit, sonet vox tua in auribus meis, ut ostendat quod corde creditur ad justitiam, ore autem confessio sit ad salutem (Rom. X); per faciem 1117Cenim notitia fidei, per vocem vero sonus praedicationis exprimi [potest].

Amplius: Ostende, inquit, mihi faciem tuam, sonet vox tua in auribus meis, hoc est tali intentione ex illo angelico sanctae solitudinis tuae dormitorio in publicum procede actione et praedicatione, ut me solum conscientiae tuae testem admittas, non ut humanis te exponas favoribus, sed ut meis tantum placeas conspectibus. Vox enim tua dulcis, et facies tua decora. Ideo enim, procedere debes, quia hoc in pulchritudine morum et sermonum tuorum dulcedine proximi tui attendere possunt, unde et suorum pravitatem morum corrigant, et rectae fidei integritatem capiant.

111 Plerumque autem et ipsa vultus et habitus 1117Dostensio vox quaedam mentis est et ut quidam dicit: Saepe tacens vocem verbaque vultus habet.

Unde de illa quae tristitiam mentis vultus diversitate praetendebat, post ablatum sterilitatis opprobrium scribitur, quia: Vultus ejus non sunt amplius in diversa mutati (I Reg. I). Diversitas quippe vultus diversitatem animi ostendebat, sed ablata causa diversitatis hujus, rectum et compositum animum rectus quoque et compositus loquebatur vultus. Sed haec vox honestatis in exterioris hominis vultu et habitu constituta, tunc in Dei auribus sonat, quando hanc pro sola aeternae vitae gloria promerenda immutabiliter servat. Vox, inquit, tua dulcis et facies tua decora: vox, inquit tua quae interpres animi est et vel moribus, vel lingua loquitur, 1118Apraedicat enim et docet, sive bene agendo, sive bene loquendo; haec, inquit, vox quae est dulcis, sonet in auribus meis, quia valde mihi placet illa vita, quae et agit et docet bona, hoc in se dilectione Dei et proximi agente ut et Deo placeat, et proximum aedificet. Et facies tua decora, quia hoc ex intentione et fide tua quae utraque mihi soli cognita est, perficit, ut quod agis vel dicis dignum sit laude meae approbationis. Hac ergo specie et pulchritudine tua intende, prospere procede et regna, ut quia tali mihi virtutum dote conjungeris, sponsi tui qui Rex est, non incongrue Regina dicaris, cum me regente et instruente, et te ipsam rationabiliter regere, et aliis regimen animarum noveris impendere.

1118BSed quia hanc suavitatem et pulchritudinem rectae fidei et rectae praedicationis plerumque haeretici perversa doctrina depravant, ut simplicium corda pervertant, vox dilecti facit apostropham ad ipsius fidei et praedicationis hujus magistros cum subdit, capite nobis vulpes purvulas.

VERS. 15.-- Capite nobis vulpes parvulas quae demoliuntur vineas; nam vinea nostra floruit.

Vulpes sunt haeretici, propter dolositatem et astutiam qua decipiunt incautos argumentis verborum, qui semper quaerunt latebras in quibus doceant, eaque perverse sentiunt, facientes seorsum conventicula, ne eorum pravitatem sancta et catholica deprehendat Ecclesia. Dicuntur autem vulpes parvulae, 1118Csive propter ipsorum haereticorum fictam humilitatem, sive propter argutissime exquisitarum sententiarum subtilitatem, quibus maxime mentes demirantium sed minus intelligentium, pravis suis cogunt favere doctrinis. Capite, inquit, nobis; tunc enim haeretici Deo capiuntur quando a Catholicis doctoribus per rectae rationis assertionem, quam nullis argumentis destruere possunt, divina praecurrente gratia ad matris suae sanctae Ecclesiae sinum de 112 quo errando recesserant reducuntur, et fidem quam prius impugnabant, verbis et exemplis confirmant. Capite, inquit, nobis vulpes parvulas, ac si aliis verbis dicat subtiles et callidos rectae fidei corruptores, propriis convincite sententiis, et probabili ratione quam non possint omnino refellere, in 1118Dnostrae partis compellite transire conturbernium: Comprehendam enim sapientes in astutia sua, perdamque sapientiam sapientium, et prudentiam prudentium reprobabo (I Cor. I, III), ut cum rationem recte vivendi sive docendi agnoverint, sua eis sapientia displiceat, et quod per eam prius astruere nitebantur, agnita veritate destruant, atque cum meis fidelibus unum fiant.

Vinea enim nostra floruit, hoc est vel Ecclesia universalis vel particularis, vel aliquis fidelis individuus et singularis initium recte vivendi vel credendi arripuit, et ideo removendi vel capiendi sunt, si qui inter eos non recte viventes, vel credentes surrexerint, ne teneram fidem pietatis opera, et pravi dogmate et pravis exemplis suffocent.

1119ANeque absurdum est, ut credimus, si unam quamque fidelem animam, vineam Domini dicimus, sicut universalem vel particularem Ecclesiam propter consimilem virtutum propaginem, et vinum spirituale quod laetificat cor hominis (Psal. CIII), quae in unoquoque individuo fideli possunt exuberare per gratiam Spiritus sancti, sicut et in universali vel particulari Ecclesia. Debet enim unusquisque cultro spiritualis exercitii sacramenta vitiorum praecidere, terram cordis sui sarculo intimae considerationis evertere, et si quod terrenum vel sordidum cogitatione, vel opere admiserit, radici cordis in memoria habendo circumponere, crebrisque lacrymarum fontibus poenitendo irrigare, omnem boni propositi sui intentionem, ad Christum, qui est lignum vitae, 1119Bne iterum ad terrena defluat, alligare, atque in ejus semper adjutorio et sustentatione sperare, sive in ligno crucis Christi haerere, mortificationem ejus in corpore suo circumferendo, talique modo, Spiritus sancti gratia mens assidue culta et curata semper fructuosior fiat, dicaturque juxta prophetam vinea Sorec, quod electam et pulchram sonat. Unde Domini in Evangelio sententia est de vinea sterili, et vinea fructum faciente, ubi se vineam, et discipulos palmitem, Patrem vero agricolam vocat: Omnem, inquit, palmitem in me non ferentem fructum, tollet eum Pater, et omnem qui fert fructum purgabit eum, ut fructum plus afferat (Joan. XV). Si ergo Salvator vitis est et nos palmites, et Deus Pater agricola, quandiu praecepta Dei servamus semper 1119Cexcolimus et cultura nostra purgatio est, ut fructum plus afferamus: Non enim est volentis, neque currentis, sed miserentis Dei (Rom. IX), cujus adjutorio semper indigemus, ut ad finem boni propositi perveniamus.

113 VERS. 16, 17.-- Dilectus meus mihi, et ego illi, qui pascitur inter lilia donec aspiret dies, et inclinentur umbrae.

Non simili modo neque pari ratione constituitur dilectio divina et humana, quae quamvis aequivoce dicatur, diffinitionis tamen ratione valde diversa est, dum inter hujusmodi affectiones carnis et spiritus nulla prorsus sit comparatio. Habet enim dilectio divina semper quoddam relativum, porro dilectio 1119Dhumana non semper, quia plerumque diligens non diligitur, nec est eadem utrobique consequentia. Consequitur enim ut homo diligens Deum diligatur a Deo, dum non sit aliud Deum diligere, quam juste et pie vivere, sitque consequens ut justos et pios Deus justus et pius diligat, quando talis affectio ex ipsius gratiae proveniat dono: non autem consequitur ut homo diligens semper ab homine diligatur, quia licet plerumque non tamen semper istud relativum carnalis affectio operatur; semper autem hoc operatur divinitatis affectio, juxta Salvatoris sententiam qui dicit, qui diligit me, diligetur a Patre meo et ego diligam eum et manifestabo ei me ipsum (Joan. XIV). Nam hujus dilectionis relativum convertitur, ut quia diligit diligatur, 1120Aet quia diligitur diligat, hoc operante in electorum cordibus praecedente gratia, ut videant dilectione divina quae et in unoquoque sua diligit dona. Unde hic dilecta loquitur de dilecto, dilectus meus mihi et ego illi. Proprium est enim relativorum ad convertentiam dici, quod enim praedicatur de dilecto e converso praedicatur de dilecta: nam dilectus alicujus dilectus est et dilecta alicujus dilecta. Fit ergo hoc modo ista relatio ut dicatur dilectus dilectae, dilectus et dilecta, dilecti dilecta: dicat ergo dilectus meus mihi et ego illi; ac si dicat: Quia hoc mihi dilectus suam contulit gratiam ut ei placeam recta fide et operatione, idcirco mihi dilectus est et quia cum mihi liberum dederit arbitrium vocanti gratiae obedio praecepta ejus servando, ideo sum ei dilecta: 1120Bnisi enim me diligeret ex misericordia, ego eum diligere non possem ex gratia, ipse me non diligeret ex misericordia. Siquidem quidquid boni mihi adjacet velle, posse agere, perficere totum ex ejus habeo munere (Rom. IV).

Qui pascitur inter lilia. Ecce causa cur ei sim dilecta, pascitur enim, id est delectatur candore, hoc est munditia et castitate mentis et corporis et suavissimo odore virtutum, quae quoniam per gratiam suam ex meo respirant amore, ideo me dignam sua fecit dilectione.

Donec aspiret dies et inclinentur umbrae, hoc est donec die illo vero et aeternali futurae beatitudinis clarescente, et hujus mundanae miseriae et tribulationis nocte recedente 114.

1120CCum erit Deus omnia in omnibus (I Cor. XV) plenam et perfectam et incommutabilem suae visionis mihi dabit remunerationem ubi ipse in me suorum pulchritudine donorum et ego in eo aeterna corporis et animae incorruptione pascantur.

Quia vero haec mutua quam posuimus dilectio semper convenit cuique patri et filio, hoc proprium est eorum quae dicuntur ad aliquid, ut hoc ipsum quod sunt aliorum dicautur, vel quomodolibet aliquid ad aliud. Quidquid enim in natura relationis agnoscitur, id cum alio necesse est consideretur: nam cum dicitur pater, necesse est ut sit filius cujus pater dicatur, eodemque modo per conversionem dicendum de filio. Si ergo sancti filii sunt Dei, 1120Dper dilectionem et mandatorum ejus observationem, necesse est ut ipse Deus pater eorum dicatur per gratiam, per conditionem et per gubernationem, et e converso, si Deus pater, ipsi filii. Unde et hic non absurdum est dicere, dilectus meus mihi in patrem, et ego illi in filium vel filiam; dicit enim ipse Deus quodam loco de suis: Ego ero illis in patrem et ipsi erunt mihi in filios et filias (II Reg. VII).

Sive alio modo dicamus, prope consimilem videtur habere sensum relationis, ut cum dicitur dilectus meus mihi, subaudiatur adjutor et protector est; et ego illi, subaudiatur obediens sum. Haec quoque sibi conferuntur ut quia mihi adjutor et protector est, ideo illi obediens sim, et quia illi obediens sum, ille mihi suum impendat adjutorium.

1121AQui pascitur inter lilia, quia delectatur candore virtutum et munditia cogitationum et operum, sicut dicit quodam loco: Et ego mundis intersum cogitationibus (Prov. VIII); et sicut scriptum est: Beati mundo corde, quoniam ipsi Deum videbunt (Matth. V), tandiu gratiae suae in me operatur effectum, donec dies intelligentiae et scientiae spiritualis elucescat fugato caligine ignorantiae, vel carnalis intelligentiae. Quo enim magis mens Deo in virtutum profectibus jungitur, eo altius in divinae contemplationis subtilitate elevatur.

Sive donec dies est, hoc est lux et splendor bonorum operum qui in mea mente per divinae gratiae inhabitationem effulsit, ad aliorum corda verbo et exemplo resplendeat, et ab eis omnem pravitatis et 1121Bmalitiae umbram sive noctem removeat: fructus enim lucis est in omni bonitate et justitia et veritate.

Revertere: similis esto, dilecte mi, capreae, hinnuloque cervorum super montes Bethel.

Dum pasceretur dilectus inter lilia candentis et virtutibus redolentis animae, tantum ipsam animam charitatis suae dulcedine reficit, ut terrena despiciens tota in coelestibus suspenderetur, nec tamen sicuti est incircumscriptam divinitatem 115 comprehendere posset. Unde cum omnem sensum excedentem et quasi quodammodo fugientem dilectum persequitur toto mentis conatu, quia incomprehensibilis et ineffabilis est, tam immensae claritatis 1121Cjubare repercutitur, nec ultra eum persequendum existimat, quem nullo modo comprehendi posse considerat. Huic enim de sanctis animalibus scriptum est, quia cum fieret vox supra firmamentum, stabant et submittebant alas suas (Ezech. I). Firmamenti quippe nomine virtutes supernae designantur, quae aliis angelorum coetibus de coelo cadentibus ipsae in amore Dei firmiter perstiterunt. Vox vero in mente est quidam sonus intelligentiae; sed vox alia fit sub firmamento, alia de firmamento, atque alia super firmamentum. Sanctis quippe mentibus de terrenis ad superna se sublevantibus vox fit sub firmamento, quando aliqua de visibilium natura, ordine, qualitate, subtiliter intelligunt, vox autem fit de firmamento, quando illorum supernorum 1121Dspirituum ineffabilia et aeterna gaudia pensant; vox vero super firmamentum fit, quando aliquid de Divinitatis celsitudine contemplando cogitant, de qua quia nihil ad plenum sicuti est, comprehendere possunt, stantes et ultra progredi non valentes, humiliter alas contemplationis deponunt et eum quem incomprehensibilem esse intelligunt obstupescunt, obstupescentes venerantur et expavescunt, expavescentes diligunt, diligentes quandoque sicuti est conspiciunt.

Quia ergo in Divinitatis contemplatione dilecta deficit, quasi jam avolantem dilectum diu consequi non potest, revocat et ut saltem humanitatis suae sacramenta, quoquo modo revelare dignetur, implorat 1122Adicens: Revertere, dilecte mi, similis esto capreae aut hinnulo cervorum super montes Bethel; ac si aliis verbis dicat: Quoniam divinitatis tuae sublimitatem perfecte capere non valeo, videmus enim nunc per speculum in aenigmate (I Cor. XIII), saltem concede mihi humanitatis tuae scrutari et intelligere veritatem, veritatis rationem, rationis utilitatem; veritatem in fide, rationem in causa, utilitatem in causae fine. Credimus enim te hominem factum hac ratione ut salvares genus humanum, cujus finis vita aeterna est.

Sed in hujusmodi causae actione similis fuisti capreae aut hinnulo cervorum, quia de stirpe patriarcharum natus, veluti servorum hinnulus velociter humanae salutis ordinem dispensasti; nam 1122Bpostquam praedicare coepisti, tribus et semis annis tam celebris et mirabilis negotii universale bonum peregisti, passus vero cito post triduum surrexisti; et post quadraginta dies coelos ascendisti, talisque excursus et recursus fuit quasi capreae aut hinnuli cervorum salientis in montibus.

116 Sed iste excursus sive recursus tuus fuit super montes Bethel, id est domus Dei quae est Ecclesia, cujus profectus et institutio agebatur in excursu et recursu isto, super cujus montes, hoc est apostolos caeterosque sanctos praedicatores quasi velox hinnulus prompto tuae gratiae munere concurristi, quando eos repentino Spiritus sancti adventu docuisti, ut quod alii per longa temporum spatia vix capere possunt, isti uno momento attingerent. 1122CQuo enim velocior potuit saltus tuus super hos montes esse, quam una hora omnium linguarum scientiam dare.

Harum ergo rerum omnium sacramenta concede ut intelligam, intelligens in his meditare valeam, ab his fide et opere non recedam, fide credendo, opere pro posse imitando. Similis enim es capreae aut hinnulo cervorum in corde meo, quando ista dispensationis tuae sacramenta revolvo, quomodo scilicet ad haec instituenda de coelo in uterum virginis, de utero in crucem, de cruce in sepulcrum de sepulcro denuo in coelum quasi quibusdam saltibus cucurristi. Similitudo autem ista mihi apparet super montes Bethel, hoc est in Scripturis quas tenet 1122Det veneratur sancta Ecclesia, quae videlicet Scripturae montes sunt propter altitudinem sensuum qui continentur in eis, ex utilitatibus praeceptorum divinorum sive ex sacramentis et rebus sacramentorum.

Sed quia tota vis dilectionis hujus inter dilectum et dilectam pendet ex fide sacramentorum et observantia divinorum mandatorum omissa intentione illa quaerendi, qua Deum in sua natura comprehendere voluit, sed minime potuit, coepit intendere qualiter Deum per fidem et justitiam comprehendere posset. Si enim juxta Joannis vocem Deus charitas est (I Joan. IV), fidem vero et justitiam habere Deum est diligere, profecto charitatem istam habere est Deum habere.

1123AQuid autem charitatem istam dicimus, nisi omne illud bonum, quod potest animo concipi, corde credi, ore confiteri, opere exerceri? nempe omne istud nemo consequitur bonum, nisi qui perfecte diligit Deum, et nemo diligit Deum, nisi qui hoc consequitur bonum, sicut paulo superius positum est, dilectus meus mihi et ego illi.

Hoc etenim bonum quaedam est via, quae ducit ad meliora comprehendenda, cujus vitae terminus et clausula est vita aeterna. Verum quoniam non parva difficultas est hujusmodi bonum inveniendi, dum sint perpauci qui perfectam Dei charitatem habeant, subdit dilecta, enarrans ordinem inquisitionis et inventionis hujus non facile provenientis:

CHAPTER II FOLLOWS.

VERSE 7.-- I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes and the harts of the fields, that you stir not up nor make the beloved to awake, till she herself please.

The beloved, therefore, delighted by the sleep of his beloved, under whose head, that is, her mind, he had placed his left hand, that is, temporal profit, but whom with his right, that is, with the love of eternal life, he had embraced, addresses the daughters of Jerusalem, that is, faithful souls, 1104Din this manner, saying: I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes and the harts of the fields, that you stir not up nor make the beloved to awake, till she herself please.

What is this sleep, so sweet and so wholesome, that for its sake such an adjuration of the beloved is made! Is it not that in which the beloved, resting in sweet and desirable quiet, had said above, his left hand under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me?

97 For she had set all temporal things behind her, 1105Abut with that contemplative eye of the desiring soul she was intent on the eternal and unfailing goods, and in this desirable vision of the mind she was delightfully as it were sleeping. For a sleep of this kind cannot come about lightly in a mind already disengaged from all doings and laid down for itself in great quiet in the love of God. Whence the Lord, admonishing through the Psalmist: Be free, he says, and see that I am God (Psal. XLV). These two words are inseparable in this purpose, because no one at all will be able with the eye of inmost contemplation to see the essence of the Godhead unless he has first been careful to be free from every exterior hindrance: having set be free first, then, he adds see, so as to intimate that one must first be free in mind from all thought of worldly things, so that thence 1105Bit may become possible, the eye being as it were closed upon earthly things, to sleep in the love of the Divinity with a keener and subtler vision.

But since the grace of this sleep does not come and remain equally, as it is established that one is raised up by a greater, another by a lesser power of contemplation (for Mary advanced further in the divine vision than Peter or John, but these further than any other saint): it is certain that all the saints have the holiness of this sleep in diverse manner, manifold because of the disparity of quiet, so that each in his own place, according to the grace of quiet conferred on him, has his special sleep in the contemplative life. Whence the prophet, in the person of every faithful one who sleeps in this manner, says: I will take my rest, and consider 1105Cin my place (Isa. XVIII): as if he said openly: Because this is the order of sleep, that it is not permitted to sleep before having quiet, I will take my rest, that is, I will take away from me the causes of all earthly care, and then at last, sleeping in mind from these things, I will cleave to divine contemplation in the place of the grace specially conferred on me. While the beloved, then, sleeps in whatever manner or place, the daughters of Jerusalem are adjured by the beloved that they stir her not up nor make her awake, till she herself please.

But what are the daughters of Jerusalem but souls tending towards the vision of heavenly peace, yet, the infirmity of the mind still hindering praepudiente, less able to arrive?

And what is it of the beloved to help [adjuvare; read adjurare, "to adjure"], but to bind by the decretal writ of his 1105Dprecepts? Further, what are the precepts themselves, but, like roes and harts of the fields, lifting up to heavenly things and making eager and strong in good work, the doctrines of the Holy Scriptures.

Or by the roes and the harts we can understand the Fathers of the Old and New Testament, whose talents, virtues and pursuits are denoted by natural behaviour. For it is said that roes have four notable marks of nature: that when she has been wounded she is healed by tasting 98 dittany; that she discerns wholesome herbs by the keenness of her sight; that she ruminates; that she feeds in mountainous places and always seeks the higher. And this is the life and doctrine of the saints: to heal their excesses by humble 1106Aconfession, to discern the better sentences of the Holy Scriptures by the keenness of their understanding, to take the food of the divine commandments by reading and to take it up again by committing it to a retentive memory, to rise up from virtues to virtues by daily progress.

In the hart also three commendable marks of nature are observed: namely, that swallowing a serpent, it drinks from a spring and puts off all the venom together with the hairs of its whole body; that, chased by dogs in the densest woods, it opens a way of flight for itself with its horns; that in changing pastures, forming a column, one setting its head on the back of another, they bear one another up because of the weight of their horns.

These things too it befits the faithful to do and to teach: that he who has been infected by some venom of sin should run back to Christ, the fountain 1106Bof mercy, by the infusion of whose kindness and grace he may be free both of that sin and of the other vices of the soul. If in his mind he is chased by malignant spirits, as by certain dogs, in the woods of worldly affairs, which are full of sins and vices, let him make himself a way of escaping them by a strong repulse of the spirit, or, having renounced all occupations of this kind, let him be careful to be free for God alone in the love of the contemplative life, which is also to open for oneself with the horns a way of salvation. For the horn, though it is born of the flesh, goes beyond the flesh; and he who cleaves to the contemplative life, though he be in the flesh, is yet raised up in mind outside the flesh. Let them be careful to bear one another's infirmities of manners or of bodies with equanimity, and to serve one another with dutiful charity; as 1106Cthe Apostle says: Bear one another's burdens and so you shall fulfil the law of Christ (Gal. VI).

The daughters of Jerusalem, then, are adjured by the bridegroom, that is, souls desiring to follow peace are bound, by the roes and the harts of the fields, that is, by the precepts and teachings of the holy Fathers, lest they stir up or make to awake the beloved, that is, lest they disquiet her from the purpose of this inmost quiet and sleep; till she herself please, that is, till that inmost indweller of hers inspires her, to whom she is bound by love, so that she may be willing at times to condescend to the infirmity of her neighbours and to provide for their necessary profits. For this willing lies in the disposition of him who provides all things, who by a hidden inspiration makes known to her 1106Dwhen it is useful and honourable to cleave to contemplation and when to provide for the necessities of neighbours 99 according to place and time.

Finally, the force of this admiration [admirationis; read adjurationis, "adjuration"] is such, by which the sons of obedience are constrained, that they show their prelates the honour of reverence, because it is written: Obey those set over you and be subject to them, for they watch as those who will render an account for your souls (Hebr. XIII). Hence it is that they do not dare to rouse them, as vicars of Christ in office, but as spouses sponsus in the zeal of holy conversation, lest they disturb them, if they compel them by some shamelessness or importunity of their own to be torn away from the secret of inner quiet and more often to be occupied with outward things. The subjects themselves also ought to receive the word of this admiration [admirationis; read adjurationis, "adjuration"] among one another 1107A, lest they disquiet the pious pursuits of the brethren, whether in reading, or in prayer, or in some spiritual office, so long as the inspiration of the Divinity holds them in it.

But the beloved, ever burning for the quiet of this contemplative sleep, may rejoice that she is confirmed and defended by such an adjuration of the beloved and as it were by right ought not to be disquieted, made more secure she proclaims: The voice of my beloved.

VERSE 8.-- The voice of my beloved, behold he cometh leaping upon the mountains, skipping over the hills.

The voice, she says, of the aforesaid admiration [admirationis; read adjurationis, "adjuration"] is not the voice of some prophet, not of a lawgiver, not of a teacher, as of one announcing or teaching something of himself; but rather of the beloved himself, both through himself, and 1107Bthrough them establishing the decrees of his mysteries and commandments; because all Scripture is the voice of my beloved, uttered by the spirit of his mouth and written in our hearts by the finger of his divinity. And therefore you ought not to hold this voice of small account, daughters of Jerusalem, so as to rouse me for the sake of outward things and compel me to wake more often.

For this too is a certain kind of the voice of the beloved, a voice adjuring and as it were juridical: Seek first the kingdom of God and his justice and all these things shall be added unto you (Matth. VI), so that this ought to be fair, the beloved himself dictating it, that for those who cleave to God the necessary use of the creature should consequently serve. The beloved himself plainly taught and confirmed it by his own testimony, when he extolled the partner of this my pursuit 1107Cwith such praise, Mary, he said, hath chosen the best part, which shall not be taken away from her (Luc. X). This surely is also the voice of the beloved, so that I ought rightly to set this pursuit of my sleep before the watchings of all affairs. But what is it that I heard and learned from this voice of my beloved, that is, from Holy Scripture, when through the quiet of the mind I slept in his contemplation? This, assuredly, which I will now tell you, O daughters of Jerusalem, of the power of my beloved himself. Behold he cometh leaping upon 100 the mountains, skipping over the hills. Behold, she says, he cometh. His coming is spoken of not according to the divinity but according to the humanity. For he who according to the divinity is uncircumscribed and not in a place 1107D, how should he be said to come, who, existing immovable and unchangeable, as he remains ever one and the same in himself, so that he is neither changed in place nor borne into diverse states by any variation. But as often as he shall be said to come into the hearts of the saints, this is not according to any movableness of his, but according to their aptitude, by which they apply themselves less or more to his love, that he will be alleged to come through his inspiration. According to the humanity, then, he came, when, made passible for us, he willed to suffer the local translation of human custom: for that he might become visible he came from heaven and assumed human nature, in which he suffered and died and rose again; and he ascended into heaven, all of which he did, to be moved and as it were to come from one thing to another. In this manner of coming, then, 1108Athe beloved cometh, leaping upon the mountains, when in the time of the dispensation he shone forth with many and magnificent leaps upon the mountains of the sublime virtues.

For certain mountains are the chief and eminent virtues, upon which this beloved made his leaps when he made certain progressions from virtue to virtue: for God, high above the heavens, came to earth humble by being born; from which mountain of humility he ascended to another mountain, of obedience, for he was made obedient to God the Father unto death, but the death of the cross (Philip. II); by taking which upon him he made a leap onto the mountain of patience; from which at last he climbed onto the mountain of glory, where by rising again and ascending into heaven he set up the triumph of his victorious death.

1108BThis beloved, then, cometh leaping upon the mountains, skipping over the hills; because whatever of wisdom and understanding, whatever of counsel and fortitude, whatever of knowledge and piety, whatever of divine fear, whatever finally of any honesty, justice and holiness ever could be or can be, shone forth more sublimely and more brightly in this beloved, as in the head, before all his members, that is, the saints, who are called hills. Anyone of understanding can see this in part in the books of the Gospels: how this beloved leaped upon the mountains, that is, upon the virtues, by word and example, skipping over the examples and teachings of all the saints by his singular and incomparable pre-eminence of working and doctrine; he hath rejoiced 1108Cas a giant to run the way, because from the highest heaven is his going out, and his circuit even to the highest of it (Psal. XVIII).

101 VERSE 9.-- My beloved is like a roe, and to a young hart: lo, this one standeth behind our wall, looking through the windows, looking forth through the lattices.

Hence he is said to be like a roe and to a young hart: for it is natural to the roe always to seek ascents; and while to the saints the distribution of graces is allotted in diverse manner: Some indeed thus, and others thus, to the only-begotten alone sol God giveth not the spirit by measure, because in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead corporeally (I Cor. VII; Joan. III; Coloss. II). For the saints 1108Din the pursuit of the virtues now ascend, now do not ascend, because in their merits that grace which they have now works, now rests, so that this may serve them for the keeping of humility, that they do not always have ready to hand the grace of the virtue conferred. But in this beloved the grace of the virtues abides not for a time, nor by intervals, but without intermission, as it is written of him that the Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove and remained upon him (Luc. III; Joan. I).

He is likened also to a young hart for swiftness, because, as the young hart, through the lightness of its youthful body, is much swifter than the hart, so this beloved, as it were the young one of the harts, that is, the son of the patriarchs, from whose stock he came forth, is far 1109Amore excellent and more agile in the efficacy of the virtues and the wisdom of his words than even the pursuits and teachings of the ancient Fathers themselves.

Since, then, this beloved by exhorting and by leaping on before calls all to the pursuits of the virtues, and some follow according to their power, some, their frailty standing in the way, despair of being able to follow, some, weighed down by the mass of their sins, distrust that they can rise again to them, [she] takes away from them every occasion of distrusting, holding out to the beloved the ineffable kindness of this beloved, mercifully inviting all to his grace, and adds: Lo, he himself standeth behind our wall, etc. There is one general wall, namely that of original sin; but this wall is spread out into many special walls 1109Bof actual sin. For from original sin, as from a certain mass, have come forth many and diverse actual sins, because after they fell through the original sin of the first parent, the kind of this infirmity is poured over into their posterity, namely to be always prone to sins. But this general wall began to be destroyed when the Son of God came through the flesh, by whose blood it was at length removed and scattered, when, dissolving the enmities between God and man, he reconciled us to God (Eph. II); and lest it be able to be built again, it is destroyed daily in the Church through the grace of baptism.

But the special wall is set up in diverse men in diverse manner, because in one it is the vice of pride, in 1109Canother that of avarice, 102 in this one that of lust, in that one that of unchastity, in some one that of obedience [obedientiae; read inobedientiae, "of disobedience"], in some other that of impatience, or whatever other vice, which according to the quality, and the manner and the number, of the vice itself makes a wall of whatever kind between man and God also [quoque; read quo, "by as much as"] the vice is greater or more frequent or more numerous and in man, by so much the heavier and more immovable is the weight in the wall.

But behind this wall, whether the general one of original sin or the special one of actual sin, this beloved stands, because he is ready mercifully to receive whoever, some such wall being removed, have been zealous to draw near to him again by destroying it through penance. For to stand is the part of one who helps, to sit of one who judges. He standeth behind the wall, because while he disposes through his grace to come to us 1109D, the wall of sin standing in the way, he is as it were compelled to stand. For at first he stood long so as not to come to remove that wall of original sin, on account of many things, by hindering his coming, by many afflictions and adversities by which those were pursued who desired and awaited his coming, at whose coming they knew that this wall was to be destroyed through his blood and that they were to be reconciled to God.

He stood, then, for this cause and put off coming, looking meanwhile through the windows, looking forth through the lattices. For what were the windows in the wall but the prophets and other teachers of the divine law, by whose doctrine and preaching God might find as it were certain outlets for looking, through which he might pour out some 1110Alight of his grace, by which the human race, enlightened and admonished, might cease to delay the coming of this beloved, which was to profit its salvation, by the interposing of so great malice as of a certain wall

But the lattices, that is, the front part of the building, were the ancient fathers who went before, namely the patriarchs before the law announcing Christ, through whom he who was to come long after looked forth in part by signs and portents and certain teachings of reasons; admonishing that they should not hinder by the wall of their evils the future times of his so great salvation.

So long, then, did he stand behind our wall, looking forth mercifully and taking counsel by word, law, signs and prodigies, until at last, moved per motus 1110Bby the affliction of his own, who cried out often: Come, O Lord, and do not delay, loose the crimes of thy people, the commotions of all lands being quelled under Caesar Augustus, and a most firm and most true peace being disposed by the ordinance of God, as though the wall of the resisting malice were now shaken, this beloved began to show by being born the face long desired, 103 and thereafter by preaching, dying, rising again, ascending into heaven, and so spreading the law of his Gospel through the whole world, to destroy daily through the grace of baptism the wall of original sin long set against him.

Further, the windows and lattices in the wall of actual sin, through which this beloved is daily looked out upon, 1110Care the examples and teachings of the Gospels and of the apostles and of the other holy fathers; windows indeed there, where they pour the light of knowledge and understanding into our hearts, that we may be able to see how we may remove the wall of each sin set between us and God; but lattices in that place where, from their writings, through the power of contemplation, we know in part and we prophesy in part (I Cor. XIII) God looking upon us, so that while we attend to the glory or the punishment of the future life, we may labour daily to destroy the wall of sin that separates us from God.

Moreover. The Son of God, coming in the flesh, stood behind the wall of our mortality, looking forth upon us through the windows and lattices of his divinity; who 1110Dalso shone out as God from the power of the miracles and yet lay hidden from the nature of human passibility. For he who looks forth through windows and lattices is neither wholly seen nor wholly not seen: so, surely, our Redeemer too, coming in the flesh, showed himself God by the miracles, but hid it by the sufferings. He stood, then, behind the wall of human passibility, because, hidden among men by his humanity, he did not come as God; but he looked forth through the windows and lattices, because by divine compassion he dictated to the whole human race the everlasting gifts of salvation. And because the beloved whom he drew inwardly by the regard of his mercy he instructed outwardly too by the word of preaching, he shows it by adding:

VERSE 10-- Behold my beloved speaketh to me: Arise, make haste, my love, my dove, my beautiful formo sa one, and come. 1111A

This speech of the beloved is distinguished in a threefold manner, by the beauty of the address, of the exhortation, and of the cause: of the address indeed, when he says: my love, my dove, my beautiful one, but of the exhortation when he says: Arise, make haste, come; of the cause when he says: For winter is now past, the rain is over and gone, the flowers have appeared, the time of pruning is come. For the beauty of the address is to say: Love, dove, beautiful one; the beauty of the exhortation, arise, make haste, come; the beauty of the cause, that the winter and the rain have gone back, that the flowers appear, that the time of pruning is here, that the voice of the turtle has been heard, that the fig tree has put forth her green figs, that the flowering vines have given their fragrance.

1111B104 But the order in this address, exhortation and cause is not disposed without consideration. In the address indeed, when first he says love, then dove, lastly beautiful one; but in the exhortation first arise, then make haste, lastly come. Further, in the cause, in the first place winter is past, in the second the rain is gone, in the third the flowers have appeared, in the fourth the time of pruning is come, in the fifth the voice of the turtle is heard in our land, in the sixth the fig tree hath put forth her green figs, in the seventh the flowering vines have given their fragrance. The cause of this exhortation, by which the beloved is admonished to arise, to make haste, to come, is the going back of the winter and the rain, the appearing of the flowers, and the time of pruning; the voice of the turtle and the fig trees putting forth their green figs, and the flowering vines.

1111CBut it must be seen whence this speech proceeds: she had said above, the voice of my beloved, which voice we said is Holy Scripture, for the whole divine page is the voice of God, through which by reading the beloved the leaps of him clothed with the wall of our mortality, and speaking to her through the windows and lattices of miracles and doctrines; for as often as we see or read the Holy Scriptures, God speaks to us or with us. In this manner, then, the beloved, that is, the Church or any faithful soul, perceives the beloved speaking to her, when she hears, reads and understands the order of the divine dispensation, the religion of the sacraments, the profit of the divine precepts.

But the beloved himself, as it were solicitous out of the salvation of his beloved, 1111Din a speech of this kind takes on assumunt himself the office of a good orator, so as to draw the hearer in three ways, that is, so as to make her attentive, teachable, well-disposed: for while he calls out not once but three times, saying, arise, make haste, come, as if he said, Offer thyself not sluggishly but swiftly and zealously, he makes her attentive, as one about to hear something settled and unwonted; but when he often addresses her with a word of love and of grace, saying: My love, my dove, my beautiful one, he renders her well-disposed, so that she may bring forth a greater will to prepare herself and to hear.

Further, he teaches him the cause of this calling distinctly by number, saying: For winter is now past, the rain is over and gone, the flowers have appeared, the time of pruning is come, the voice of the turtle is heard, 1112Athe flowering vines have given their fragrance, he makes her teachable, so that she may recognize the time of great salvation and grace, which she ought to receive with great veneration and joy.

And this is the sign of great kindness, by which this beloved often looks toward us through the windows and lattices of his infinite clemency, standing behind the wall of our evils, set against us as a cloud, that prayer may not pass through (Thren. III), speaking daily and admonishing us to scatter this wall or this cloud with the battering-ram of the virtues and the breath of the Holy Spirit.

What, then, does the beloved speak to the beloved? Arise, he says, make haste, my love 105 my dove, my beautiful one, and come: arise through faith, make haste through hope, 1112Bcome through charity: or, arise through intention, make haste through working, come through contemplation: for this is the perfection of thy whole worship and religion, to believe, to hope, to love: for the other three, namely intention, working, contemplation, are constituted from these. For if thou believest rightly, thou also aimest rightly at doing good things; but thou workest for the hope of obtaining the reward, and thou contemplatest the more subtly, the more thou art raised up to God through charity.

And this thou wilt be able to do if thou be a love, that is, if, the error of unbelief being cast away, to be reconciled to me through faith; if thou be a dove, that is, if thou live simply, harm no one and be content with thine own alone, in the hope of the future reward; or if, some frailty 1112Ccompelling thee, thou go out of the ark, that is, out of the Church, by doing ill, thou remain not in the world, but return quickly bearing an olive branch in thy mouth, that is, having hope of mercy through confession and the measure of penance.

If thou be beautiful, that is, keeping by the love of God alone, thou set behind thee all the cares of the world, or whatever things can infect the beauty of thy mind, so that, having not the bleared eyes of Lia but the beautiful and fair face of Rachel, thou mayest be able with the eye of the mind purged to gaze into that majesty of heavenly beatitude which is God.

VERSE 11, 12.-- For winter is now past, the rain is over and gone.

1112DThe flowers have appeared in our land, the time of pruning is come: the voice of the turtle is heard in our land.

But why do I so greatly invite thee se to these things? Because the cold of unbelief and the storm of blindness and ignorance, which had overcast the whole face of the world, have gone back; and the flowers have appeared, that is, the beginnings of good works have now begun to spring up, and the time of pruning is come, that is, the counsel and rule of cutting away vices and sins are now had in the time of grace. The voice also of the turtle is heard, that is, the sound of preaching, from which resound the counsels, precepts and examples of chastity, of solitary conversation, of heavenly speculation and of penance, all of which the turtle expresses, chaste and moaning, a lover of solitude and 1113Anesting on high. For in the very beginning of the Gospel voice the turtle cries out by words and by manners, whether the Lord Jesus Christ himself, the son of virginity, or his mother herself, the blessed Virgin Mary, or his forerunner, blessed John the Baptist. Finally, the Lord himself, born of the Virgin, is the herald of chastity; led into the desert, he consecrates solitude; praying on the mountain, he admonishes that contemplation be pursued; he exhorts to penance, proclaiming as with a moaning voice: 106 Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand (Matth. X). The blessed Mother of God also is a singular mirror of chastity, who, solitary solidaria and set in divine contemplation, is greeted by the angel and taught beforehand that she is to be the mother of Christ, and soon announces the sentence of divine punishment changed by penance 1113B, when she proclaims that his mercy in generation and generations is to be (Luc. II). But Saint John the Baptist, the son of chastity, a virgin in mind and body, the more he was removed from men, the nearer he stood to God through contemplation; for he was in iu the desert preaching the baptism of penance (Matth. III), and crying with the moaning voice of the turtle: Bring forth fruits worthy of penance (ibid.).

VERSE 13.-- The fig tree hath put forth her green figs, the flowering vines have given their fragrance. Arise, make haste, my love, my fair one, and come. [Vulg. Ct 2:13 Surge, amica mea, without propera, "make haste"]

The fig tree, he says, hath put forth her green figs, that is, Judaea, hitherto barren, carnal, has begun to understand the ceremonies 1113Cand, by believing with the heart unto justice, but by confessing with the mouth unto salvation (Rom. X), what it savoured carnally, this it now savours spiritually and longs to show by faith and by work.

The flowering vines also have given their fragrance, because the gentiles, having heard the word of faith, now begin to spread everywhere the fragrance of good work.

Not without reason, then, is the order of this speech attended to, in which these three, faith, hope and charity; or the other three, intention, working, contemplation, are considered, since these are the consequences of those: that he who believes should hope and love; and no one can hope and love except he who has believed; no one also works unless he first intends what, and how, and when, and why he works; but the subtlety of contemplating 1113Dno one can attain unless he has advanced to it by the sublimity of good works.

But it will not be, as we believe, unfitting to note the sevenfold number of the cause, so that we may show that the effect of the cause itself was always the condescension and good pleasure of the sevenfold Spirit: For the passing of the winter, that is, of unbelief; the passing of the rain, that is, of persecution; the appearing of the flowers, that is, of good works; the cutting away of vices; the proclaiming of the turtle, that is, of the Gospel; the putting forth of the green figs of the fig tree, that is, the revealing of the legal observances into the truth of the mysteries; the sweetly fragrant working of the vines, that is, of the gentiles converted to the faith: what are they but the good pleasure and condescension of the sevenfold Spirit?

For causes of this kind, and what was effected from them, 1114Aor is effected, causes, that is, to believe, to hope, to love, the Spirit of God worked from the beginning and works still daily; because all removal of unbelief and malice, and the bestowal of faith and salvation, stand by the gift of him who provides, composes and orders every 107 state of equity, honesty and profit in holy Church. Whence also the bridegroom, when he speaks to the bride: The voice of the turtle is heard, adds, in our land, namely so as to intimate that there is no effect of the sacraments, no hope of salvation, outside the Catholic Church: but that every voice of the Gospel preaching, in the observance of the precepts, in the order and reverence of the sacraments, is to be held within holy Church, in which the Holy Spirit himself is given and received. For in the beginning, as it is written, 1114Bthe earth was void and empty, because before the human mind was made fruitful by the divine spirit, it was composed with no flower or bud of the virtues; but after the spirit of God moved over the waters (Gen. I), that is, over the flowing and unstable hearts of men, while at length the light of truth and the fruit of justice is poured out through the whole world, so that that earth, at first void and empty, became the Church of God, in which he himself might dwell through his grace, and might make it his land, now flowering and fruitful, and showing forth a certain living and rational pattern of honesty and discipline, as it were of a man, through the indwelling grace.

Since, therefore, the beloved has made the beloved solicitous for her own salvation, he admonishes her not to be negligent 1114Cof the salvation of her neighbours too, so as to intimate this charity, which provides for neighbours as for itself with the zeal of kindness, so that she may deservedly be honoured with the address of the grace that calls and justifies, love, dove, beautiful one.

For it follows, when the beloved, the former number of the address being repeated, [says] arise, make haste, my love, my fair one, and come. Because, he says, thou hast advanced by my grace to this, that thou art able to take care of thyself, by despising the world and by cleaving to my love through the pursuit of the contemplative life, thou oughtest also at times to profit thy neighbours by word and example through the labour of the active life; because, since I have made thee such that thou hast the grace of teaching and of working, not without peril to thyself wilt thou render account for the buried talent. But arise at some time to this labour 1114Dfrom that most sweet sleep of thy quiet, for the sake of a brother's need, and make haste by teaching and by drawing back thy neighbours from the love of this world, that thou mayest lead them too with thee into that solitary dwelling of thy quiet. And this thou shalt do as my love through faith, my fair one through working, my dove through the infusion of the Holy Spirit.

VERSE 14.-- My dove in the clefts of the rock, in the hollow of the stone wall, show me thy face; let thy voice sound in my ears, for thy voice is sweet and thy face comely.

Because I have compared thee to a dove 108. But the dove has her refuges in the clefts of the rock, in the hollow of the stone wall; what also will be thy refuges 1115A, in which thou mayest set all the hope of thy salvation, so as to flee from the manifold temptation of this world? surely in the clefts of the rock, of which it is written: And the rock was Christ (I Cor. X); for these clefts are the wounds of my passion, which are to every Christian as it were certain refuges in all adversities. For my five wounds are the safe refuges of thy five senses, so that when thou hast held out the sign of my passion in this number, thou mayest be able to persist secure in the integrity of all thy senses. For this integrity of the senses will be necessary to thee as thou teachest and workest, because if thou bring forth the things thou teachest and workest in my name with honesty and profit, reasonably, orderly and moderately, thou wilt be able the more to draw the minds of those who hear or look on 1115B. For generally an honourable kind of case, if it is brought forth unworthily, gives offence, just as a lowly kind of case too, if it is at times brought forth reasonably, will obtain a share of honour.

In my passion, then, thou hast been made love, fair one, dove, because to this end I laid down my life for thee, I shed my blood, that I might present thee to myself a bride glorious, not having spot, nor wrinkle (Ephes. V). For when, foul of it through thyself, thou didst not suffice for thyself, nor could the whole creation suffice for thee, my passion, to which the whole world is not equal, made satisfaction to God for thee, so that thence, reconciled and joined to me, thou mayest be called love, fair one, dove.

1115COr the clefts of the rock are the four Gospels, in which my deeds and words are looked into; or else the pursuits of the virtues, namely of humility, patience, obedience, prayers, vigils, holy readings, and the rest, which are as it were certain approaches for coming to me and for entering the kingdoms of heaven, of all of which thou oughtest to preach to thy neighbours and to show them, because without these they cannot attain salvation.

My dove in the clefts of the rock, in the hollow of the stone wall. Christ the rock (I Cor. X), Christ also the stone wall. The stone wall indeed before the passion, because he was still frail and passible from human infirmity; but the rock after the resurrection, when, all corruption laid aside, he was made impassible from the firmness of his glorified 1115Dbody. But the beloved ought to be a dove in the clefts of the rock, in the hollow of the stone wall, because while she considers the many marks of powers, of works and of virtues which were in Christ from the strength of the divinity, yet she ought specially to consider that mark of charity which he showed in his flesh, which he delivered to death for her salvation: for he showed the judgment of this great love towards man 109 when for his redeeming he was able to offer nothing other than himself.

The hollow of the stone wall, then, is the charity of Christ dying in the flesh, in which charity, of the Church indeed generally, but specially any holy soul is a dove, because through charity she finds a place of abiding in Christ, where spiritually she may nourish the young of good 1116Aworks and escape the snares of the ancient serpent: for it is written that God is charity, and he who abideth in charity abideth in God, and God in him (I Joan. IV).

The dove is also in the clefts of the rock, in the hollow of the stone wall. But the dove has a moaning instead of a song; and the faithful soul ought to moan when she recalls the passion of the Redeemer, weighing what God has done for her, when he who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth (I Petr. II), willed to die for sinners, and what man owed, God made man paid. Let her moan also for her excesses, in the clefts of the rock, in the hollow of the stone wall, because she has an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the just: and he is the propitiation for her sins 1116B(I Joan. II), who daily confers salvation on every penitent by the sacrament of his passion and the singular example of this charity. For daily our Redeemer renews his clefts for us, that is, the signs of his passion, in the immolation of his body and blood; and he shows the hollow in which we may be protected from the snares of the enemies in the assigning of so great a charity.

The stone wall can also be taken as the doctrine of the apostles, or of apostolic men, because as a stone wall is built of many stones, so the doctrine of the saints is constituted of very many teachings of the virtues. In it there is for every faithful soul a hollow, that is, a keeping of life, because from their sayings and writings she learns how, by fleeing sins and by nourishing the young of good works 1116C, she may escape the snares of malignant spirits.

The beloved, then, is admonished at times to leave the quiet of contemplation and to go out to the labour of the active life for the sake of her neighbours, so that what she herself learned through quiet from the divine precepts and the examples of the saints, this she may bring into the minds of her neighbours by preaching; and as she herself by the sweetness of these was affected as to the assiduity of contemplation, so also she may affect the minds of her neighbours with desire of them through the power of preaching.

Whence the beloved too, admonishing her, adds: Show me thy face. For what is the face of the beloved but a certain image of holiness shining out from fellowship with the beloved? For the more sedulously each one 1116Dcleaves to divine contemplation, the more beautiful the face of the mind shines out from the radiance of holiness. Hence it is that Moses, having conversed forty days with the Lord on the mountain, 100 is written to have brought forth a shining face from fellowship with the speech of the Lord (Exod. XXXIV). For he who has tarried on the mountain of heavenly contemplation brings forth a certain face of holiness from the very Spirit of God, with whom he is one; whence the Apostle: With open, he says, face beholding the glory of the Lord, we are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord (II Cor. III). Those, then, who are led by the Spirit of God are transformed by the Spirit himself into the image of Christ according to the inner man, from glory to glory, so that those who have drawn from him something of glory into the face of the inner man 1117A, by which they may know him more clearly, the nearer they draw to him by contemplative glory, the more glory they may gather to themselves from him, through which they may know him ever more clearly and more truly. Whence also Ezechiel, when he described the vision of the holy living creatures, said: The likeness of a man in them (Ezech. I). For whatever of justice and meekness, whatever of modesty and humility, whatever of patience and piety, whatever finally of holiness the elect of God ever could have or can have, they drew from that singular man, the Lord Jesus Christ; and, illumined by that principal face of holiness, they too conceived in their own manner a certain face of holiness.

Such, says the beloved, thy face, drawn out spiritually from my grace, O beloved, show me, that 1117Bis, go forth in public to the praise of my name with a fair appearance of action and speech, so that thy neighbours, seeing thy works, may glorify thy Father who is in heaven (Matth. V), and themselves, from the rightly composed countenance of thy action and speech, may compose the countenance of their own mind and intention too.

Let thy voice sound in my ears: the voice of one preaching sounds in the ears of the Lord then, when it accords with my voice, so that what sounds outwardly to the ears of man through the voice, this may speak in the ears of God through faith. And, having set first, show me thy face, he fittingly adds, let thy voice sound in my ears, to show that with the heart it is believed unto justice, but with the mouth confession is unto salvation (Rom. X); for by the face 1117Cthe knowledge of faith, but by the voice the sound of preaching [can] be expressed.

Further: Show, he says, me thy face, let thy voice sound in my ears, that is, go forth in public in action and preaching from that angelic dormitory of thy holy solitude with such an intention that thou admit me alone as witness of thy conscience, not so as to expose thyself to human favours, but so as to please my sight alone. For thy voice is sweet, and thy face comely. For this reason thou oughtest to go forth, because thy neighbours can attend to this in the beauty of thy manners and the sweetness of thy speeches, whence they may both correct the depravity of their own manners and take hold of the integrity of right faith.

111 But often also the very showing of the countenance and bearing 1117Dis a certain voice of the mind, and as a certain one says: Often the countenance, though silent, has a voice and words.

Whence of her who showed the sadness of her mind by the change of her countenance, after the reproach of barrenness was taken away, it is written that: Her countenance was no more changed to divers ways (I Reg. I). For the diversity of the countenance showed the diversity of the soul; but the cause of this diversity being taken away, a right and composed countenance too spoke a right and composed soul. But this voice of honesty, set in the countenance and bearing of the outward man, sounds in the ears of God then, when one keeps it unchangeably for meriting the glory of eternal life alone. Thy voice, he says, is sweet and thy face comely: thy voice, he says, which is the interpreter of the soul and speaks either by manners or by tongue, 1118Afor it preaches and teaches, whether by doing well or by speaking well; this voice, he says, which is sweet, let it sound in my ears, because that life pleases me greatly which both does and teaches good things, the love of God and of neighbour so acting in it that it both pleases God and edifies the neighbour. And thy face comely, because it brings this to pass from thy intention and faith, both of which are known to me alone, that what thou doest or sayest may be worthy of the praise of my approval. With this comeliness, then, and thy beauty set out, proceed prosperously and reign, so that, since thou art joined to me by such a dowry of virtues, thou mayest not unfittingly be called Queen of thy bridegroom who is King, since, with me ruling and instructing, thou knowest both to rule thyself reasonably and to bestow on others the rule of souls.

1118BBut because heretics often deprave this sweetness and beauty of right faith and right preaching by perverse doctrine, so as to pervert the hearts of the simple, the voice of the beloved makes an apostrophe to the masters of this very faith and preaching when it adds, catch us the little purvulas foxes.

VERSE 15.-- Catch us the little foxes that destroy the vines; for our vineyard hath flourished.

The foxes are the heretics, because of the craftiness and cunning with which they deceive the unwary by the arguments of words; who always seek hiding places in which to teach, and think those things perversely, making conventicles apart, lest the holy and Catholic Church detect their depravity. And they are called little foxes, 1118Cwhether because of the feigned humility of the heretics themselves, or because of the subtlety of their most keenly sought-out sentences, by which they force chiefly the minds of those who marvel but understand less to favour their depraved doctrines. Catch, he says, us; for the heretics are then caught for God when by Catholic doctors, through the assertion of right reason, which they can destroy by no arguments, divine grace going before, they are led back to the bosom of their mother, holy Church, from 112 which they had departed by erring, and confirm by words and examples the faith which before they attacked.
