Qui lilia sunt distillantia myrrham primam, id est optimam, quia, dum pro integritate et munditia cordis et corporis servanda vitia atque peccata in semetipsis mortificant, aliisque eadem facienda verbo et exemplo incessanter praedicant, profecto ostendunt quantam erga Deum et proximum charitatem habeant.

Charitas enim dici potest myrrha prima, id est optima et probata, quia, ubi vera et perfecta est, omnia exstinguit in homine vitiorum incentiva; sicut enim myrrha mortuorum corpora condiuntur, ne putrescant, ita charitate divina animae roborantur, ne putredinem vitiorum incurrant.

1196CEt in hoc quoque corporis sui membro, dilectus candidus est et rubicundus, quia in sanctis praedicatoribus suis pro lilio castitatis candidus dicitur, per myrrham vero passionis, Omnes enim qui in Christo pie volunt vivere, persecutionem patientur, (II Tim. III), rubicundus praedicatur.

VERS. 14.-- Manus illius tornatiles aureae, plenae hyacinthis. Venter ejus eburneus distinctus sapphiris.

Si ipsum caput respiciamus, manus ejus profecto tornatiles et aureae sunt, quia de eo scriptum est: Quam magnificata sunt opera tua, Domine, omnia in sapientia fecisti (Psal. CIII): qui enim torno operatur, citius et perfectius atque planius operatur. Qui 1196Dvero unquam citius, et perfectius, sive planius est operatus, quam ipse Deus? Valde enim cito fecit quae facere disposuit, quia solummodo dixit, et facta sunt (Psal. XXXII), atque uno eodemque tempore, licet diverso modo, diversa quoque forma ejus dixisse fecisse fuit. Perfectius eo nemo operatus est, quia non diminuta, vel per partes, et quae adhuc melioranda essent, sed omnia perfecta fecit, et semel fecisse totum et integrum fecisse fuit. Porro planius nihil ejus opere fuit, quia nullo impedimento natura rerum retardari potuit, sed quem semel accipit cursum modumque, pro perpetua lege servavit: nihil in ejus operibus distortum et inaequale, diminutum vel superfluum, quia omnia in mensura, et numero, et pondere 1197Aconstituit (Sap. II). Bene ergo manus ejus tornatiles fuerunt, quia tanta, ut dictum est, velocitate, 195 perfectione et pulchritudine omnia operatus est, ut ex ipsis operibus consideranti clarescat quantae pulchritudinis, quantaeve majestatis ipse conditor existat, non quod ista consideratio deitatis ipsius sit plenaria comprehensio, sed quod sit quaedam a creaturae dignitate proficiscens et quantum humanae menti possibile est sublucens Creatoris speculatio.

Unde et ipsae manus dicuntur aureae, quia hoc quod sunt, quod vivant, quod vigent et florent ex divinitatis constat dispositione: auro quippe quod omnibus metallis pretiosius, divinitas qua nihil supra designatur.

1197BSed quid est quod plenae hyacinthis dicuntur, cum et alii sint lapides valde etiam competentes ad ornatum manuum sive digitorum? Omnia quidem visibilia, quaedam mira et pulchra operum divinorum sunt ornamenta, sed in his magis sunt miranda, quia et subtiliora coelestium mirabilium secreta; quorum consideratio primo loco est in incorporea creatura, supernorum videlicet spirituum sive sanctarum mentium solis coelestibus semper intendentium, quarum conversatio divina bonitatis est operatio; secundo loco incorporea creatura rerum superiorum, quae sunt quaedam nutrimenta inferiorum quarum rationabilis dispositio divinae quoque sapientiae est mirabilis operatio. Hyacinthus 1197Cenim aerii coloris est, atque ideo manus dilecti hyacinthis plenae dicuntur, quia opera Creatoris magis in coelestium decore et ornatu praedicantur.

Porro si ad membra capitis respicias, manus ejus tornatiles aureae et plenae hyacinthis sunt, quia bonis operibus intenti et semper futuram requiem ingredi festinantes, non tarde neque pigre, sed velociter et studiose viam mandatorum currunt, quidquid in suis moribus pravum et inaequale cernunt, rectae operationis tornatura repellunt et planum faciunt et in oculis sui Conditoris, ipso tamen opifice, perfectum reddunt, cujus efficientiae causa est sensus in eis auro sapientiae divinitus collatae respondens et semper coelestium bonorum felicitatibus contemplativae vitae dulcedine intendens.

1197DQui ideo manus ejus dicuntur, quia quidquid boni faciunt, non propriae virtutis, sed Dei gratiae est, cujus et hoc quoque quod tornatiles morum perfectione, quod aureae sensuum claritate, quod plenae hyacinthis angelicae conversationis sublimitate.

Sane et in hujus membris consideratione duplex color in corpore dilecti speciali laude praedicatus apparet, quia in eo quod tornatiles sunt manus, laboris sive passionis est signum quo ab omni morum superfluitate et inaequalitate, in vas 196 honoris et divinis spectabile oculis sunt tornatae. Quod vero aureae et hyacinthis plenae, fulgida virtus caelibis vitae, qua castitatis et pudicitiae claritate rutilant, designatur; hocque modo et in ista parte dilectus candidus et rubicundus decantatur.

1198AVenter ejus eburneus, distinctus sapphiris. Si personam ipsius dilecti distincte inspiciamus, humanitatem ipsius ventris nomine designari non absurde accipimus, quia fragilior pars corporis venter est, et humanitas illa omnem humani corporis fragilitatem praeter peccatum experta est. Sed quid est quod iste venter eburneus dicitur? Ebur quippe os elephantis est, quod animal castissimum esse perhibetur: quid autem castius humanitate Christi, quae ex castissima Virgine absque ullo virili opere, per solam Spiritus sancti operationem assumpta sit? Venter ergo dilecti eburneus, quia cum omnes homines in iniquitatibus et peccatis concipiuntur, solus ipse in humanitate, singulariter sine peccato de castissima, ut dictum est, Virgine conceptus 1198Best.

Quid porro est quod ipse venter sapphiris distinctus esse memoratur? Sapphirus quippe caerulei coloris est; sapphiris autem venter dilecti distinctus dicitur, quia, etsi ex humanitate terrena pertulit esuriem, sitim, lassitudinem caeteraque secundum quod homo pati potuit, patiendo tamen coelestia ex divinitate ostendit miracula faciendo.

Ac si multitudinem fidelium quae ipsi personae velut capiti membra per fidem adhaerent, consideremus, quae pro majore sui fragilitate ventri comparari potest: sunt enim in Ecclesia aliqui vinculo conjugali dediti, sunt aliqui mire se continentes in sexu fragili: sed qui uxores habent, tanquam non habentes (I Cor. VII), recte venter eburneus 1198Cdici possunt, quia, etsi foris fragiles videntur, tamen fortes sunt per sanctae et castae vitae honestatem. Unde et de sanctis conjugatis scriptum est, quia erant incedentes in omnibus mandatis et justificationibus Domini sine querela (Luc. III): hoc est enim ventrem distinctum esse sapphiris, quia inter curas rerum mundanarum, quas conjugalis fragilitas exposcit, coelestium praeceptorum devota observatione refulgent. Porro mire se continentes in sexu fragili laudabiliorem in hoc propositi sui ostendunt conservationem, quia, cum sint infirmi et fragiles corpore, fortiter tamen ad sanctitatis merita assurgunt animi virtute. Unde et in his venter eburneus dicitur, quia magis in sexu fragili virtus 1198Dcastitatis praedicatur.

Distinctus vero sapphiris memoratur, quia virtus castitatis aliarum quoque virtutum ornamentis decoratur: aliter namque castitas corporis virtus esse non potest, nisi 197 ornetur castitate mentis, quae constat humilitate, patientia, sobrietate et contemptu saecularis vitae, caeterorumque coelestium praeceptorum observatione. Nam, ut de corpore hujus dilecti esse possit, venter eburneus, sapphiris debet esse distinctus, quia nihil prodest castitas corporis sine bono opere, nec opus bonum sine castitate (GREGORIUS). » Quia ergo fragilis sexus castitatis virtutem forti animo tenet, venter dilecti eburneus est, quia vero et aliis virtutibus pro coelesti gloria studet, sapphiris distinctus est, quia in 1199Aventre eburneo color castitatis nitet, in sapphiro quamvis caeruleo, tamen pro labore virtutum color passionis rubet. Ipsa quoque castitas quae exterius in corpore mundo candet, interius per mentis martyrium rubet: nam naturali carnis motui repugnare, quaedam nimirum passio mentis est.

Praesentis sane decantatio particulae ad vestrae professionis normam non modice spectat, sorores dilectissimae, quia, cum revera de corpore hujus dilecti sitis, tale ejus membrum decentissimum esse potestis. Nam, cum in tam fragili corporis vestri vasculo, candido castitatis et pudicitiae indumento resplendetis, profecto venter dilecti hujus eburneus dici et esse potestis; quia vero cum ista castitate, aliis quoque virtutum ornatibus refulgetis, nimirum 1199Bsapphiris distinctae relucetis. Sed summopere vobis attendendum est, ne per solam castitatem Deo vos placere posse putetis, si alia bona opera non habueritis, atque idcirco semper et castitatem bono operi, et opus bonum castitati jungere debetis, ut Deo perfecte placere possitis.

VERS. 15.-- Crura illius columnae marmoreae, quae fundatae sunt super bases aureas. Species ejus ut libani, electus ut cedri.

Octavo loco quasi octavam tangit chordam decachordi psalterii attenta spectatrix dilecti, veluti symphoniam illam διαπασον reddens, cui proprium est eamdem habere vocem octavam quam primam. Nam, cum supra prima chorda sonuerit caput dilecti aurum esse optimum, nunc dicit crura super bases 1199Caureas posita, ut sit eadem vox gravis et acuta, resonans supremum et infimum dilecti aureum ornamentum. Sed considerandum quaenam sint hujus dilecti crura, curve ipsa comparentur columnis marmoreis super bases aureas aedificatis.

Cum Deus in sui natura immobilis atque incommutabilis sit, quippe qui est illocalis, omnia enim complet et continet, ipse autem a nullo continetur qui totus semper ubique est; cumque localis sit qui de loco ad locum movetur, Deus autem non moveatur, atque ideo illocalis sit, quia immobilis, moveri tamen dicitur, 198 non in se, sed in his quos suo nutu et voluntate movet per virtutem omnia disponentem, sive secundum justitiam, sive secundum misericordiam, cujus enim vult miseretur et quem vult indurat 1199D(Rom. IX), quorum unum est misericordiae, alterum justitiae. Cum ergo omnem creaturam suam quasi praeambulet hac gemina suae dispositionis via, videlicet justitia et misericordia, recte possunt dici ejus crura, justitia et misericordia: universae enim viae ejus, sicut dicit Psalmista, misericordia et veritas (Psal. XXIV). Veritas autem et justitia idem est: quod enim verum est, justum est; et quod justum est, verum est.

Cur autem crura ista dicuntur columnae marmoreae, nisi quia recta sunt et fortia? nam in columna est rectitudo, in marmore duritia; justitia enim Dei occulta, nunquam tamen injusta. Quis enim scire potest quare hunc misericorditer eligat, illum 1200Ajudicialiter repellat? ideo clamat Apostolus: O altitudo divitiarum sapientiae et scientiae Dei: quam incomprehensibilia sunt judicia ejus, et investigabiles viae ejus! (Rom. II.)

Porro quaenam sunt bases aureae, super quas columnae istae, quae crura illa intelliguntur, sunt fundatae? nimirum si recte perpendas, sunt sapientia ejus et bonitas, quia omnia quae facit, sapienter et bene ordinat et disponit: bases nempe sunt quia omnia continent et sustentant, aureae, quia in ipsis rerum efficientiis mirabiliter clarescunt. Crura ergo dilecti, si ad ipsum caput intendas, sunt, ut dictum est, misericordia et veritas, quae super bases, id est pedes sapientiae et bonitatis illius fundata, aut stant, aut ambulant, secundum mensuram et qualitatem 1200Beorum quae facta sunt: omnia enim quae facta sunt, aut aeterna sunt, aut temporalia. Stant autem in his quae aeternaliter mansura secundum gratiam et misericordiam suis ipse Deus praefinivit, ambulant in his quae temporaliter aut confert, aut aufert, sive misericorditer, sive judicialiter.

Porro si ad membra ipsius capitis respicias, quid putas crura dilecti hujus dicenda sunt? In illo antiquo Dei populo, in quo tunc tantum notus erat Deus, duas praecipue dignitates posuit Deus, quibus ipse populus muniretur et ornaretur, regnum videlicet et secerdotium, in exterioribus quidem regia fortitudine armabatur contra eos qui auctore diabolo laborabant destruere propositum Dei, quod pro totius mundi salute habebat, et eidem populo 1200Cin typo praemonstrabat, quatenus in tota sua republica cum pace et honore praecurrerent in figura divinae promissionis fideliter adimplenda negotia. Porro in interioribus sacerdotali officio erudiebatur, ad ipsa negotia prudenter per figuram intelligenda et reverenter tractanda, ut ipsi proposito Dei quandoque adimplendo allaboraret fide et dilectione, in spe futurae salutis.

199 In quibus videlicet dignitatibus tantum erat ejusdem populi firmamentum, ut postmodum cum eidem populo peccanti iratus Deus multas comminaretur poenas, postremo minime se corrigenti hanc finalem proponeret poenam ut, ablato et destructo regno et sacerdotio, omnis eorum funditus migraret honor et religio. Dicitur enim sic per Jeremiam 1200Dprophetam: Oblivioni tradidit Dominus in Sion festivitatem et sabbatum; et in opprobrium, in indignationem furoris sui regem et sacerdotem (Thren. II). Regem quippe et sacerdotem non esse, hoc fuit omnem ritum caeremoniarum defecisse.

Nonne et in hoc tempore, quo promissio illa jam impleta est, hujusmodi duabus dignitatibus sancta subsistit Ecclesia? Pugnat enim contra infideles et incredulos materiali gladio exterius regalis judicii potestas, pugnat etiam interius contra eosdem spirituali gladio sacerdotalis officii majestas. Vide cum Dominus pro defendenda hujus novae, quae nunc est, reipublicae universali salute, gladium permitteret, duosque paratos esse audiret, sat esse respondit 1201A(Luc II), quia duas in Ecclesia sententias peremptorias constituit, unam gladio materiali, alteram gladio spirituali. Etenim hoc exterius agitur regni timore, ut Ecclesia serviat Deo cum pace et honore, interius eruditur sacerdotio, ut sciat servire Deo cum reverentia et amore. Quid ergo? Nunquid cum hae duae dignitates sint Ecclesiae Dei omni religione propaganda quasi quoddam firmamentum et, ut recte dicam, totius corporis dilecti hujus fortissimum sustentaculum, non recte possunt dici crura ejusdem dilecti regnum et sacerdotium?

Et haec propter sui fortitudinem et eminentiam columnae dicuntur marmoreae, quando et ipsae virtute et potestate eriguntur et in eis tota domus sanctae Ecclesiae sustentatur. Quid vero sunt bases 1201Baureae super quas istae columnae sunt aedificatae? Plane oportet ut in ipso regno sive sacerdotio, quia causa debet esse communis utilitatis et honestatis, magna resplendeat vis rationis et virtus discretionis, ut in omni sua dispensatione et judicio semper sit ratio et discretio. Sed cum haec ex magna debeant sensus et sapientiae claritate procedere, nonne recte dici possunt harum columnarum bases aureae?

Crura ergo ista dilecti hujus columnae sunt marmoreae super bases aureas collocatae, quia in sancta Ecclesia regnum et sacerdotium vigent dispensationis et judicii ratione et discretione.

Hujus quoque octavae chordae cantui succinit praecentus ille juxta introitum ipsius decachordi carminis positus, quo dilectus decantatur candidus et 1201Crubicundus, quando hoc agit pars ista regni cum labore et periculo vitae ut in se dilectus iste rubicundus praedicetur: porro 200 altera pars sacerdotii in pace et tranquil itate hoc agat, ut in se dilectus candidus pronuntietur, in sanctitate et castitate, conversatione, mandatorum Dei observatione et praedicatione. Species ejus ut Libani, electus ut cedri. Sicut, inquit, mons Libani montibus caeteris praestantior est, decore et pulchritudine, miroque ordine arborum inibi positarum, sic dilectus meus omnibus sanctis eminentior, et longe pulchrior est potentia virtutum, sapientia quoque et scientia, atque omni decore mundanarum actionum, omnique plenitudine divinarum gratiarum. Non enim ei ad mensuram 1201Ddat Deus Spiritum (Joan. III). Sed habitat in eo omnis plenitudo divinitatis corporaliter (Coloss. II); et de hac ejus plenitudine sancti accipiunt gratiam pro gratia (Joan. I); quodque ipse universaliter habet, isti particulariter consequuntur, et hoc non semper pro cujusque voluntate, quia et interdum prompta est, et interdum quasi sopita segniter jacet in eis eadem particula gratiae, quam suscitare oportet non sine aliquo labore Unde Paulus ad Timotheum: Propter quam causam, inquit, admoneo te ut resuscites gratiam quae in te est per impositionem manuum mearum (II Tim. I). Suscitatur autem multis modis, maxime tamen orando et psallendo; exempli gratia, cum diceret rex Israel ad Eliseum: Quare congregavit Deus tres reges istos, ut tradat eos in manus 1202AMoab? respondit: Vivit Dominus in cujus conspectu sto, quia nisi vultum Josaphat regis Judae erubescerem, nec attendissem utique, nec respexissem; nunc autem adducite mihi psalten: et factum est dum caneret psaltes, facta est super eum manus Domini, et reliqua. (IV Reg. III.)

Excepto ergo dilecto isto de quo scriptum est: Super quem videris Spiritum descendentem et manentem super eum, hic est qui baptizat in Spiritu (Joan. I): caeteri omnes sancti divisam vel particularem accipiunt gratiam Spiritus sancti prout ipsi Spiritui sancto placet, qui ubi et quando vult spirat (Joan. III). Merito ergo hujus dilecti species ut Libani dicitur, quia speciosus forma prae filiis hominum (Psal. XLIV), et nulla species ejus speciei, nulla 1202Bvirtus ejus virtuti, nulla gratia ejus gratiae comparari potest.

Electus ut cedri: cur prae caeteris arboribus Libani electi sunt cedri, nisi quia quaedam speciales naturae suae habent virtutes? Est enim cedrus imputribilis, est odorifera, est serpentibus contraria; quis autem sine corruptione esse potuit, nisi solus ipse dilectus, qui peccatum non facit, nec inventus est dolus in ore ejus? (I Petr. II.) Nullus unquam tam sanctus, tam innocens esse potuit, quin aliquid corruptionis contraxerit, cum scriptum sit, quia et in angelis suis Deus iniquitatem reperit (Job IV). Peccatum nempe quaedam putredo, quaedam corruptio est, et cum in alio major, in alio minor sit, in nullo tamen quamvis valde sancto, valde justo, 1202Cpotest non esse, licet etiam parvissima; porro in solo isto dilecto, nulla prorsus hujusmodi putredinis sive corruptionis 201 vel tenuissima existere potuit macula.

Bene ergo dicitur electus ut cedri, quia hoc unus specialiter habet ex natura, quod nullis sanctorum concessum est ex gratia. Haec quidem de solo capite dicta sint.

Caeterum, si ad corpus respicias, quod capiti conjunctum unum sit secundum incorporationem, quia ipsi capiti per gratiam ipsius incorporatur, congrue species ejus Libano comparatur, quando totus dilectus iste in se et in corpore suo discrete attenditur. Quid enim in facie sive specie Ecclesiae considerari 1202Dpotest, nisi praesentia divinitatis in exsecutione sacramentorum, in enuntiatione divinorum eloquiorum, in dispositione et ordinatione convenientium et rationabilium causarum? Quis vero iste Libanus est, cui species hujus dilecti in toto suo corpore assimilatur? Si ipsam rem sicuti est attendas, Libanus mons Phoenicis est, abundans cedris et in ipso radicatis et in altum porrectis: sicut autem iste mons cedrorum multitudine decoratur, ac per hoc magnam sui pulchritudinem aspicientibus offert, ita dilectus iste in corpore suo multitudine electorum suorum sibi in fide radicantium et in charitate cohaerentium decoratus mirabile profecto toti mundo praebet sanctitatis et honestatis spectaculum.

1203ASi autem metaphorice intelligas, Libanus iste est de quo propheticus sermo clamat: Aperi, inquiens, Libane, portas tuas et comedat ignis cedros tuas (Zach. II). Templum enim Dei, quod in illa terrestri Jerusalem constructum fuerat et habebat tabulata intrinsecus per circuitum de lignis Libani, lignis cedrinis, idcirco Libani nomine appellatum est, quia in eo fuit Sanctum sanctorum, quod erat decus quoddam, et eminens pulchritudo non tantum illius civitatis, sed et totius populi ejusdem per multos terminos dilatati. Species ergo dilecti ut species Libani, quia sicut hoc templum fuit quondam caput et singulare monumentum religionis illi antiquo Dei populo; ita nunc conventus Ecclesiae ubi Christus honoratur in suo corpore caput quoddam 1203Bet eminentia quaedam sanctitatis est omni populo Christiano, quia in eo attenditur via quaedam et perventio ad illius summi boni sublimitatem et futurae salutis aeternitatem. Adhuc nunc conventum quasi ad quemdam montem Dei, currit quotidie fidelis populus prospicere in spe terram promissionis illius, quam Deus suis dabit electis, in qua est templum supernae illius Jerusalem, quod inhabitat ipse Sanctus sanctorum, in quo multiplicantur sancti ut cedri Libani, imputribiles facti participatione illius aeternae beatitudinis et summi boni quod est Deus.

Electus ut cedri: quomodo dilectus iste in corpore suo, hoc est 202 Ecclesia, electus dicitur 1203Cut cedri? Si naturas cedri quas supra memoravimus attendas, videlicet quod imputribilis est, quod odorifera, quod serpentes fugat, nimirum perpendere potes quanta sit utilitas sanctae Ecclesiae unitas, et quantum omni animae eligenda, quantumque rebus caeteris sit praeferenda. Nam ibi incorruptio animi adipiscitur, odor virtutum sentitur, vitia et peccata, quasi serpentes venenati fugantur. Quid hac re praestantius? Merito ergo Christus in corpore suo electus ut cedri dicitur, quia in omni ejus actione sive dispositione canonica, vel dispensativa, ipse est omnis spiritualis efficientiae causa.

Hoc autem loco dilectus qui supra, ut saepe diximus, dupliciter coloratus inducitur, candidus videlicet et rubicundus, sola corporis pulchritudine 1203Din corporis sui, hoc est Ecclesiae, splendet facie, quam sibi elegit non habentem maculam neque rugam (Ephes. V), quod ipsius partis probat decantatio de specie Libani, qui interpretatur candidutio.

VERS. 16.-- Guttur ejus suavissimum et totus desiderabilis: talis est dilectus meus, et ipse est amicus meus, filiae Jerusalem.

In gutture vox, in voce sonus est, in sono si vox articulata est, alicujus rei certa expressio. Quid per guttur, nisi sanctae Scripturae sonus accipitur? Totam vero Scripturam sacram, aut ipsius Domini voce, aut sanctorum quibus ipse Deus quasi quibusdam organis utebatur constitutum novimus. Quid enim divinae Scripturae sonant, nisi aut per seipsum aut per suos loquentem Deum? Quid porro loquentem? 1204Animirum futurae promissionis qualitatem, juxta propositum ipsius praedestinantis, vocantis, justificantis et glorificantis electos suos, cujus glorificationis dulcedinem et suavitatem concedit eis praegustare nunc per spem sublevantem, et ad ipsam toto desiderio anhelantem, et quasi quoddam jam experimentum suavitatis ejusdem quodammodo capientem.

Ipsum nempe experimentum guttur quoque dilecti hujus dici potest, quia in mente cujusque sanctae animae, divinae bonitatis dulcedinem praegustantis, delectabiliter sapit suavitas illa quam ex sacrae Scripturae praedicatione intelligit, de qua dicitur, quod nec oculus vidit, nec auris audivit, nec in cor hominis ascendit, quae praeparavit Deus 1204Bdiligentibus se (Isa. LIV; I Cor. II). Unde et ipsius suavitatis experimento proficientibus dicit Psalmista: Gustate et videte quoniam suavis est Dominus! beatus vir qui sperat in eo (Psal. XXXIII). Guttur ergo dilecti, vel vox est sacrae Scripturae, divinae pietatis suavitatem enarrantis, vel experimentum ejusdem pietatis animum cujusque fidelis suaviter reficientis. 203 Quod guttur suavissimum est, quia tantae memoriam abundantiae divinae sanctitatis eructat, ut attento adjutori nihil dulcius in aure cordis videatur sonare, quam futurae beatitudinis perennia bona non tantum sperare, sed et firma certitudine tenere, ideoque toto ea animo desiderare.

Unde cum superius singulae partes alicui comparentur 1204Crei, utpote caput auro, comae elatis palmarum, oculi columbis, genae aromatum areolis, caeteraeque, sicut supra digestum est, rebus sibi competentibus, haec ultima sola nulli comparatur, quia bonum illud supremum et generalissimum, sicut indicibile ita et incomparabile.

Enumeratis autem per partes hujus dilecti praeconiis, sive in se ipso sive in corpore suo, quasi singulis in hujusmodi decachordo expensis nervis, finalem quodammodo decantatae laudis reponit vocem, dicens: Et totus desiderabilis: ac si dicat: Quid est quod per partes pulchritudinem et dignitatem ejus praedico? Nihil est in eo quod excipere possim: nam totus est desiderabilis, sive divinitatis ejus celsitudinem attendas, sive humanitatis humilitatem 1204Drespicias. Haec est enim summa totius laudis, quae in fine canitur et quemdam in se colorem totius cantionis exprimit.

Quid enim brevius et magis definite ad summam laudis dici potest de Christo Deo et homine, quam ut dicatur, totus desiderabilis! Si enim totum quod in eo est, vel de eo dici potest, desiderabile est, ab omni parte beatum est, profecto concluditur supremum et finalem modum laudis esse, totum desiderabilem dicere.

Talis est dilectus meus, et ipse est amicus meus, filiae Jerusalem. Quaesistis, inquit, a me qualis esset dilectus meus, pro quo vos tantopere adjuraverim, ecce ostendi vobis qualis sit dilectus meus, cujus habitum per singula membra expressi. Sed quid 1205Adicendum de habitu isto? Nunquid dilectus iste per dispositionem sive affectionem sortitus est habitum istum et susceptibilis est intentionis et remissionis? In sui quidem natura minime, qui essentialiter bonus, sapiens, pulcher, sanctus est et justus; porro in corpore suo, hoc est Ecclesia, per dispositionem sive affectionem transit in habitum istum, suscipiens magis et minus, secundum quod suae placet gratiae in singulo suo, membro disponere. Ista qualitas sive iste habitus natura ejus est, quia ipse est bonitas, sapientia, pulchritudo, sanctitas et justitia.

Et iste dignus meo quaesitu est, non quod ego sim ei necessaria, sed quod ipse mihi valde sit necessarius. Quare? quia ipse est amicus 204 meus, o filiae Jerusalem; mei quippe interioris hominis 1205Bhabitus ex illo informatur, quasi ex imagine in imaginem, per participationem gratiae habitantis in corde meo, cujus illuminatione aperiuntur mihi arcana illa invisibilium rerum, quae continentur in sublimitate et significatione praeceptorum et sacramentorum divinorum, juxta quod me instruunt et ducunt intellectus et ratio, quae sunt ipsius mei interioris habitus maxima pulchritudo. Iste amicus meus custodit me in hujusmodi scientiam per humilitatis gratiam: nam ipse Patri dicit: Confiteor tibi, Pater, quia abscondisti haec a sapientibus et prudentibus, et revelasti ea parvulis (Matth. XI): humilitas nempe custos virtutum est. Dicitur autem amicus quasi animi custos; ut enim istum amicum 1205Cnon perdam, debeo eum per humilitatem habere quasi animi mei custodiam. Si enim animus ad divinam scientiam affectus sive dispositus, quandoque per cooperantem gratiam suscipit habitum, hoc est permanentem in se hujusmodi scientiam, quasi unum cum Deo efficitur ipse animus participatione ipsius, ut et ipse quoque ex Dei consortio dicatur Deus. Unde quidam sapiens dicit ad filium: Si Deus est animus, nobis ut carmina dicunt, Hic tibi praecipue sit pura mente colendus. Ac si aperte dicat: Cum animus sit nobis Deus, hoc est vera et spiritualis vita, hunc praecipue bene vivendo glorifica. Auribus quippe per insitam sibi vim rationis et intellectus, recte discernendo et bene vitam suam agendo Deum in se retinens, Deus 1205Dest, non quidem essentialiter, sed nuncupative, sicut de sanctis dicit Propheta: Ego dixi: Dii estis et filii Excelsi omnes (Psal. LXXXI), talisque enuntiationis virtus magnae est amicitiae foedus; sed hujus amicitiae bonum attendentes, non filii sed filiae Jerusalem, hoc est infirmae adhuc animae et nondum perfectionem virtutum assequi valentes, et hoc in dilecta, dilecti hujus magnam pulchritudinem spiritus constituisse, amore sancti desiderii et ipsae accensae, cupiunt etiam hujus amicitiae bono perfrui, quo et eamdem spiritus pulchritudinem valeant ad ipisci. Dicunt enim: Quo abiit dilectus tuus, etc.

VERS. 17.-- Quo abiit dilectus tuus, o pulcherrima mulierum! quo declinavit dilectus tuus? et quaeremus eum tecum.

1206AQuid abire Dei, vel declinare est, qui loco non capitur, et apud quem non est transmutatio nec vicissitudinis obumbratio? (Jac. II.) Dupliciter dicitur Deus abire vel declinare, scilicet et per appropinquationem et per recessionem gratiae suae juxta perfectum, sive defectum animi cujuscunque, vel ad Deum appropinquantis, 205 vel ab eo recedentis. Sed in hoc loco dilecti hujus abire, est misericordia bonitatis suae quempiam moveri, declinare quoque ejus est gratiae suae munere menti cujuslibet illabi.

Dic, inquiunt, nobis, o pulcherrima mulierum, quonam dilectus tuus abeundo et declinando per misericordiam et gratiam suam exemplum nobis bene vivendi sive in qualibet virtute amplius studendi, 1206Bin aliquo fidelium suorum proposuit. Dic, hoc est ostende vel lectione qua eorum vitam quotidie pronuntias, vel actione qua eos quotidie in tui consortium annumeras, et nos quoque eorum exemplo inducti, quaeremus tecum dilectum istum, orando, jejunando, aliisque bonis operibus eum vocando, quatenus ad nos etiam declinare dignetur, suae nos gratiae munere visitando. Ipse enim dicit: Si quaesieritis me in toto corde vestro, inveniar a vobis (Jerem. XXIX): nam eum quaerere non est sola oratione, sed etiam bona actione, sicut et alibi de se quaerentibus dicit: Me etenim de die in diem quaerunt et scire vias meas volunt (Isa. XXXVIII). Quos enim dicit vias ejus scire velle, profecto ostendit 1206Cbona eos actione quaerere.

Quaeremus ergo tecum dilectum hoc modo, o pulcherrima mulierum. Qualium vero mulierum? Nimirum vel in seipsis Deo boni operis fructus, veluti sanctitatis filios fide et dilectione gignentium, vel alios quasi lucis filios verbo et exemplo ad aeternae vitae diem generantium. Quia ergo tantam in te pulchritudinem miramur, o pulcherrima mulierum, quam tibi attraxisti quaerendo et inveniendo dilectum tuum, idcirco et nos tantae et tam generosae pulchritudinis tuae aliquod vestigium adipisci cupientes, ad quos moveatur vel ad quos declinet dilectus tuus per misericordiam et gratiam scire cupimus, ut eum quoque tuo exemplo quaerentes, postquam invenerimus et si non pulcherrimae, aliquatenus 1206Dtamen pulchrae existimemur. Ad haec Ecclesia sive dilecta Deo anima locum motionis sive declinationis dilecti hujus demonstrans, actum quoque simul in ipsa declinatione ejus insinuat dicens: Dilectus meus descendit in hortum suum, etc.

172 CHAPTER V.

VERSE 1.-- Let my beloved come into his garden, and eat the fruit of his apples. Come into my garden, my sister, bride, I have reaped my myrrh with my spices: I have eaten the honeycomb with my honey, I have drunk the wine with my milk: eat and drink, friends, and be inebriated, dearest.

Well does she say that the beloved comes into his garden, because the cause of his coming is that he is beloved, that his 1177Bis the garden; for unless he were loved he would not come. If any one love me, he will keep my commandments, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him, and will make our abode with him (Joan. XIV) [Vulg. sermonem meum servabit, "he will keep my word"]. But he who says that he loves God ought to prove it by work, for this is to be his garden: for where diverse flowers of the virtues bloom, and fruits abound, it is not undeservedly called spiritually the garden of the Lord, and to be such a garden is to love God. Comes, then, the beloved into his garden, when he illumines with the grace of his visitation a mind given to good actions. In which garden he eats the fruit of his apples, because he is delighted and fed by the odour and sweetness of the virtues in the mind which his grace has filled. Whence the beloved himself, as if congratulating, answers his beloved: Come into my 1177Cgarden, my sister, bride, I have reaped my myrrh with my spices. What is taken by myrrh but the mortification of the flesh? But because, as by the delight of the flesh vices are nourished, so by mortification virtues are generated, rightly he puts myrrh first specially, and afterwards subjoins the spices generally: for unless the flesh be subjected to the spirit through the mortification of the vices, the mind does not rise to the virtues, because in its suggestion the spirit does not contradict the flesh; but when the spirit always resists the flesh, 173 to the summits of the virtues, the flesh being now at length subjected, the mind advances: and when through the daily progress of good work it has come to a certain ripeness of perfection, it is as if the time of harvest has now come to it.

1177DHer good works, therefore, the beloved reaps, when he gathers her, cut off by the sickle of death from the field of earthly habitation, into the barns of the heavenly kingdom, to be rewarded: this harvest indeed is either the separation of the soul from the flesh, or of the elect from the reprobate: now he who reaps takes up a part, and leaves a part; and in the separation of the soul from the body the soul is taken up and the body is left. Further, the elect, when they are separated from the reprobate, are themselves taken up to life as good corn, as the reprobate, as remaining stubble, are left to the eternal fire. But the beloved reaps myrrh when he says: Come to me all you that labour and are burdened, and I will make you to rest (Matth. XI) [Vulg. reficiam vos, "I will refresh you"]; he reaps spices when he says: Come, you blessed of my Father, 1178Areceive the kingdom which is prepared for you from the beginning of the world (Matth. XXV) [Vulg. possidete paratum vobis regnum a constitutione mundi, "possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world"]. He reaps myrrh, then, with spices, when he divides from the company of the wicked those who through contempt of the world and affliction of the flesh have advanced to the works of the virtues, and lays them up in the storehouse of his kingdom.

Whom he well calls his myrrh and his spices, because whatever good they have they possess from the gift of his grace: and this harvest is made, as has been said, by the sickle of judicial sentence in this time, both through dissolution and through predestination. Through dissolution indeed, when the soul, as the superior and worthier part, is taken up to heaven, but the body, as the inferior and viler part, is left in the earth. Through predestination, however, because those whom in his foreknowledge he holds as going to persevere 1178Bin good he chooses as corn by predestining them to eternal life; but those going to remain in evil, as stubble fixed in earthly acts, he leaves by predestining them to eternal death. Let the beloved therefore say: Come into my garden, I have reaped my myrrh with my spices, because after, by my grace, visiting the Church or the faithful soul, I made it bud with virtues, I fitted specially to myself those dead to the world and given to pious actions, whom, because I separated them from the reprobate by election, I numbered into the fellowship of my kingdom. Whence he presently subjoins: I have eaten the honeycomb with my honey, I have drunk my wine with my milk. Yet further the beloved rejoices at the progress of his budding garden, in the pursuits and virtues of the elect wonderfully adorning that same garden. In 1178Cthe honeycomb there is honey and wax, the honey indeed sweet, the wax soft and pliant, and a minister of light: further, in wine there is austerity, but in milk whiteness and smoothness. What, then, can be signified by these kinds of things, but the diverse quality of speech in holy preachers, on account of the diverse qualities of minds in hearers? For as the Apostle says to one of them corum, whom he was instructing for preaching: Reprove, entreat, rebuke (II Tim. IV), the holy doctors 174 temper the force of their preaching, when they consider person, place, time, and profitably weigh where and when, or whom they ought to reprove, entreat, rebuke.

For according to the diversities of minds, there are some who 1178Dwillingly receive the word of holy preaching, as soon as they have heard it; and there are some who will neither hear nor receive it; further, there are many who what they will not or cannot receive and hear in this place or time, hear and receive in another place and time. Again, there are some minds which are amended by soft and gentle preaching. But some which are restrained by nothing but hard rebuke, while some are exercised to greater works of the virtues by pious entreaty. On account of these diverse qualities of souls, therefore, the doctors of souls ought to be very discreet in their preaching, because they ought subtly to weigh what, and when, and where, or to whom they preach, lest they seem to throw words away in vain. When, therefore, they correct delinquents whom they see soft and pliant, they ought to reprove them with gentle and 1179Asweet admonition, according to the saying of the wise man: A softer answer breaketh wrath (Prov. XV) [Vulg. Responsio mollis, "a mild answer"]: but those whom they see hard and intractable they ought to strike with harsh rebuke, and with the terror of divine punishment; while those given to good acts they ought to entreat, that they may always advance to better.

Since, therefore, prelates ought to instruct their subjects in these three ways, surely when they cherish the good with the sweetness of pious exhortation, and console them by preaching the sweetness of the heavenly kingdom, they are the honeycomb with honey; but when they now restrain delinquents with modest speech, now reprove them with hard rebuke, announcing the pains of hell, they are wine with milk.

The beloved, therefore, eats the honeycomb with his honey, drinks wine 1179Bwith his milk; because the rulers of holy Church, whom by his grace he composes for preaching in the manner said above, he makes his members by incorporating them into himself, in whose pursuits and progress he is delighted, and as it were refreshed. And because he has proved them to be of his body, by the conformation and unity by which he has incorporated them into himself, he makes an apostrophe to those who can be instructed by their doctrines and examples, saying:

Eat and drink, friends, and be inebriated, dearest: as if he should say openly: Because I have prepared for you the refreshment of souls in the deeds and words of the doctors, whom I have filled with my Spirit, you who ought to be instructed by their doctrines, what you hear and see from them lay up in the belly of memory, and fill your mind 1179Cwith such sweetness of the virtues, that you may remain insensible to every motion of the vices: friends indeed to me through faith and working, dearest through intimate love. For this eating and drinking, the 175 full perception of the divine precepts: whence the Psalmist says of those who are inebriated with this fullness: We are inebriated with the plenty of thy house (Psal. XXXV) [Vulg. Inebriabuntur, "they shall be inebriated"]. For what is the house of God, but the Church, or the mind of any just man? And what is the plenty of this house, but a certain fullness of the divine precepts and sacraments, with which holy Church, or the soul of some saint, is filled and grows rich? But with this plenty they are filled and inebriated, whoever, from the institution of the Church or the teaching of any saint, 1179Dreceive full knowledge in the necessary utility and honourableness of those precepts and sacraments. With this plenty was he filled who said: Though rude in speech, yet not in knowledge (II Cor. II): the fullness of this plenty the Psalmist desired when he said: Let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness (Psal. LXII).

But because the bride had heard the voice of the exhorting bridegroom, and had tasted the sweetness of his precepts with the palate of the heart, and had been inebriated with the fullness of this good by hearing, reading, believing and working. what effect this plenary outpouring had, or what of utility she obtained from it, she declares, saying: I sleep, etc.

VERSE 2.-- I sleep and my heart watcheth. The voice 1180Aof my beloved knocking: Open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my undefiled; for my head is full of dew and my locks of the drops of the nights.

The act of this sleeping and watching, if thou look to outward things, can by no means be at once in one and the same, at one and the same time, because no one can at once both sleep and think something by watching, at one and the same moment or time: but if thou look to inward things, and attend to the manner of this sleeping and watching, these two so inseparably cleave to each other that at one and the same time they must either not be, or be together.

For what is this sleep, but a disengagement from all the cares and actions of the world, and as it were a certain 1180Brest and pause of the mind? And what is the watching of the heart, but a contemplative love tending continually to God with sincerity, or an amatory contemplation? But since it is certain that no one can have the virtue of holy contemplation unless he has striven to be free and disengaged from all the business of the world; and conversely that no one can disengage himself from the business of the world unless he begin to love and desire God with pure and simple intention, it is established that these two, as has been said, so cleave to each other, that at one and the same time, in one and the same, 176 they must either ab altogether not be, or be together. In this manner, therefore, it is possible to sleep and to watch at once, nor is there any contrariety there, where there is this identity of habit in the affected mind, for to watch in this manner is the same 1180Cas to sleep, and to sleep is the same as to watch; because to cleave to contemplation and to sleep to the world, and to watch to God, and unless he sleeps to the world he does not watch, and unless he watches to God, he does not sleep to the world.

But it can be asked why the bride says: I sleep, and my heart watcheth, as if the whole man were said to sleep, and a part of the man, that is, the heart, to watch. To which it must be said that the whole man is said to be body and soul, while a certain part of the whole is the heart; and this part looks to the inner man alone, that is, the soul; but the whole man tends to the outer and at the same time the inner man. Now the whole man ought to sleep when this part, namely the heart, is zealous to watch in contemplation, that is, in body and mind, 1180Dwhich is, in will and in action, to cease from all exterior things, and as it were to rest, that he may be able more freely to be at leisure for interior things; because, therefore, the bride considered that she could not perfectly cleave to the vision of the heavenly bridegroom unless she had all her senses, interior and exterior, free and disengaged, rightly does she say: I sleep, and my heart watcheth: as if she should say powerfully in other words: Because I rest utterly from the din of earthly things, in thought and in work, therefore I watch in mind more subtly in divine contemplation.

But to what precedes it must be joined thus, that because the bridegroom had said of his preachings that he had filled them with such sweetness and authority of sound doctrine that no one ought to doubt that they were incorporated into him, and that therefore to be inebriated in their preaching 1181Awas both very useful and honourable; the bride, as if roused by this admonition, and having greatly profited by the preaching, words and examples of the saints, answers: Since, she says, O beloved, I have obeyed thy admonitions, thou preventing me by inspiring and following me by helping, and the doctrines of thy preachers; I have so applied my mind through faith, hope and charity, that I have not only as it were eaten and drunk, but am wholly inebriated, so my carnal senses have been lulled by this inebriation that behold I now sleep utterly from all the cares and desires of the present life, and in the sole contemplation of the Godhead I watch in heart through intimate love.

I indeed, she says, although taught by the sayings, writings and deeds of the holy Fathers how I ought to advance both in the active 1181Band in the contemplative life, have yet chosen the better part; since I determined to be at leisure for God alone in the contemplative life with whole heart and body; but because the beloved through his grace hath fed me with the bread of life and understanding, and given me the water of wholesome wisdom to drink (Eccli. XV), that I may be fit 177 for the office of preaching, he knocks and rouses, and commands that I take care not only of myself alone by resting in contemplation, but also of my neighbours by labouring in preaching. Open, he says, to me, for the foxes have holes and the birds of the air nests, but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head (Matth. VIII; Luc. IX): for save a few, by whose faith I have been received, almost the whole world repels me either by unbelief or by depravity of faith, the Jews 1181Cand pagans not believing, the heretics depraving the orthodox faith. Whence my head, placed under the open sky, is drenched with dew, because my Godhead is dishonoured by the perverse opinions of heretics, falling as it were from heaven on account of the elegance of their speech, but warm [calentibus; read carentibus, "lacking"] with the heat of truth and of right faith. My locks also are full of the drops of the nights, because the faithful, who ought to cleave to me as to their head through faith and working, are infected by their perverse dogmas, falling in the nights of depraved senses, and are made cold from the love of truth.

Or: My head is full of dew and my locks of the drops of the nights, because from the love of God and of neighbour cold 1181Dare the hearts of unbelievers: for by the head God, by the locks neighbours can be understood. Open therefore to me, because unless thou preach and teach I shall not be able to enter into their hearts: wherefore rise at times from that sweet dormitory of thy inner solitude and take up the office of preaching, that after they, taught by thy preaching, have renounced their former errors, and have prepared for me the lodging of their mind by right faith and working; I may gladly enter and bestow on them the saving gift of my grace.

Sister, he says, mine, my love, my dove, my undefiled: what means the proving of these four appellations? Does the Holy Spirit attend to nothing in so distinct a placing of these four words? by no means. For if thou apply the eyes of the inner man, 1182Athou wilt perceive in this number of appellations a reason not to be despised, and the utility of the reason: for the form of spiritual squareness is necessary to every soul wishing to stand on the summit of perfection; for a square, whichever way it is turned, will stand. And this ought to be the constancy of the perfect, that they be neither lifted up by prosperity nor cast down by adversity, but persist always in one manner in the order and place of their holy purpose

But what is this spiritual squareness? Surely faith, hope, charity and working. For faith, as the Apostle says, worketh by love (Gal. V), and, Faith, if it have not works, is dead in itself (Jac. II); and the proof of charity is working: but he who does not believe does not hope either; and he who does not hope, 1182Bhas not what he may love: further, he who does not believe neither hopes nor loves what there is 178 for which he should work. This is the intention of all good work in each one, that what he believes, hopes, and loves, he may at some time merit to obtain. In the measure of a square, however, not one side is greater and another less, but all four sides together are stretched out with equal extent, because also in these same virtues which we have mentioned, namely faith, hope, charity and working, as long as we live in this life, we shall find that they are equal in ourselves. For each one who is engaged in the exercise of the active life believes as much as he hopes; as much as he believes, he works, and loves; he loves as much as he believes, hopes and works; he works as much as he believes, hopes and loves.

1182CBut let us say that this squareness of the soul also consists in four principal virtues, namely prudence, fortitude, justice, temperance; for these virtues are so in a square that one does not exceed another. For prudence is great; but if it is less brave in dangers, less just in operations, less temperate from pleasures, surely it is less prudent.

Fortitude is great, but if it understands less what goods it should guard, what evils it should resist, if it holds less to the works of justice, and at times is overcome by the domination of injustice; if it tempers the appetite less from pleasures, but is conquered by delight, it is less brave. Justice is great, but if it discerns less than it desires 1182Dbetween just and unjust works, if it strengthens itself less against adversities, if it tempers the flesh less in delight, it is less just. Temperance is great, but if it understands less whence it should temper itself, if it is less able to endure adversities through fortitude, and casts down the mind in fear, if by its precipitation it sometimes breaks out into works of injustice, it is less temperate.

If, then, the life of the perfect faithful is measured by the square, one side has as much as the single sides; because each one is as much prudent as he is brave, just and temperate; as much brave as just, prudent and temperate; as much just as prudent, brave, temperate; as much temperate as he shall have been prudent, brave and just. 1183ABut because the Doctor of the Gentiles says: I chastise my body, and bring it into subjection, lest perhaps, when I have preached to others, I myself should become reprobate (I Cor. IX), the preacher ought always to study this, that the right things which he preaches with the mouth he himself also shows in his acts.

There is necessary, therefore, to every preacher the squareness of these virtues which we have set down, namely that he himself have in himself faith, hope, charity and working, and preach them to others to be had; that he also shine with prudence, fortitude, justice, temperance, and train others also to these by teaching.

179 Since, then, this beloved rouses his beloved, resting securely in contemplation, to the office of preaching, he calls her by the name of fourfold grace, so that by this he may intimate to her that he who is sent to 1183Bpreach ought always to be squared by these four virtues. For he calls her sister on account of faith, love on account of hope, dove on account of charity, undefiled on account of working. For holy Church, or any holy soul, which has obtained the name of bride and beloved by believing in the Almighty, attains the eternal inheritance, that she may become an heir of God, and a joint heir with Christ, because she merits by grace the sonship of God which he has by nature.

This heavenly Bridegroom, therefore, calls the soul beloved by him, redeemed by the price of his blood, sister, because what he is essentially, this she can be called by name; for John says in his Gospel that as many as received him, he gave them 1183Cpower to be made the sons of God, to them that believe in his name, who are born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God (Joan. I): of whom the Lord himself also says: Whosoever shall do the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother and sister and mother (Matth. XII).

He calls her love, because while he manifests to her certain secrets of his knowledge, and the immensity of his ineffable goodness, he raises her up into great hope of future beatitude; for it is a sign of true friendship to make someone privy to one's secret; whence the Lord to the disciples, to whom he had revealed the mysteries of the divine will: Now I will not call you, he says, servants, but friends, because all things which I have heard from my Father 1183DI have made known to you (Joan. XV).

He names her dove, because he approves her as simple, innocent and peaceable, endowed also with the love of God and of neighbour, as the dove is a simple and innocent animal, abstaining from all tearing, and sometimes cherishing others' young as her own.

For he who is truly innocent is known to have the charity of God and of neighbour, because true innocence is that which is thus defined: True innocence is that which harms neither itself nor others: for it harms itself when it offends God by acting ill; it harms others when it offers examples of evil action; he, then, who avoids working ill proves that he loves God, because thereby he also keeps himself, whereby he labours lest he lose God; he proves that he loves his neighbour, because thereby he invites him to act well, 1184Awhereby he guards himself lest he offend God. Right, therefore, is the true definition of innocence, which harms neither itself nor others, because through it the love of God and neighbour is expressed, in which the whole fullness of the law consists.

180 For what the fullness of the law is, is beautifully declared by the fifth kind of definition, which in Greek is called κατα αντιλεχιν, in Latin "ad verbum", word for word, when that which is asked is shown by one word, in this manner: The fullness of the law, love (Rom. XIII). If, then, the fullness of the law is charity, but charity dealeth not perversely (I Cor. XIII), surely he who is known to have charity is proved to keep the whole law: and since that charity is poured forth in the hearts of the elect through the Holy Spirit (Rom. V), it follows that he who possesses the gift of charity confirms himself illumined with the gifts of the Holy 1184BSpirit. For if no virtue avails without charity, and charity is conferred through the Holy Spirit, surely he who has charity is proved to have the Holy Spirit, in whom the gifts of all the virtues are bestowed. Whence now rightly the bridegroom calls the bride whom he invites to preaching a dove, that he intimates to her that she ought to have charity, which is given through the Holy Spirit, who is asserted to have been seen in the form of a dove.

He calls her undefiled, that whatever she shows in working she may remember to do it with pure intention, not that she may receive human praise from it, but that she may please the Godhead alone, because before God those works are foul which have been displayed for the favour of the world.

Or he calls her undefiled for this, that he may intimate that cleanness 1184Cof mind and of body is to be loved, or that he may forewarn her to avoid diligently in her preaching every stain of heretical depravity.

Further, on account of the four principal virtues in which the most beautiful squareness of the mind consists, the beloved calls his beloved by these four names, that he may show that she whom he exhorts to rise to preaching ought to be prudent, brave, just and temperate, as being sister, love, dove and undefiled.

For he who through the integrity of faith hastens to the inheritance of the supreme Father surely understands prudently what, or of what kind, is that which he believes: but he who, God revealing, knows the mysteries of the divine precepts and sacraments, 1184Dwhile he bravely endures adversities for God, while he also bravely despises the flattering joys of the world, surely shows what he hopes; but he who, full of the grace of the Holy Spirit, embraces the good of simplicity and innocence, because he is zealous to be just, surely his very justice speaks that he loves God. Further, he who has so ordered for himself his manner of living, that in all his acts he knows how to hold the governance of holy discretion, while he both tempers himself from the pleasures of the world through the pursuits of the virtues, and does not handle the good of justice indiscreetly, shows how clean and right he is in all his working.

181 Well, therefore, does the bridegroom call the bride, whom he rouses to the office of preaching, sister, love, 1185Adove and undefiled, that he may intimate to her with how squared a mind she ought to stand in all her offices and acts. But she answers him knocking, and refuses to rise from that deliberate leisure of inner quiet, saying: To be stripped Exspoliari of my tunic, etc.

VERSE 3.-- I have stripped myself of my tunic, how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet, how shall I defile them?

The hindrances, she says, of the world, and the cares of the active life, in which I was till now entangled, I have cast from my mind, that I may be able more freely to be at leisure in divine contemplation; how now dost thou exhort me to rise again from this quiet through the office of preaching, and to serve the pursuits of the active life? I have washed my feet, that is, the negligences of my works, which I contracted from the dust 1185Bof thoughts and of worldly things, I have washed thoroughly with the water of compunction rising from divine charity; how shall I contract them again from the filth of earthly din? For it is very difficult to converse among the men of this world and to be stained by no contagion of human frailty. For matter applied outwardly to the bodily senses easily infects the beauty of the soul within.

But while I was turning these things over with myself, and did not wholly purpose to depart from my resolve, I will tell, O daughters of Jerusalem, what my beloved did.

VERSE 4.-- My beloved put his hand through the opening, and my belly trembled at his touch.

For what is his hand, what the opening, what his belly? Surely you ought to understand the hand of the beloved 1185Cas the power of his omnipotence and of his hidden inspiration. When, however, the mind of man, given to the pleasures of the world, thinks nothing of God, nothing of the salvation of the soul, being as it were shut round and beset by a certain mute, and a wall of perversity, it has now no access or opening through which the light of divine grace may deign to enter.

But because divine power sometimes prevents such men by inspiring, so that they are pricked with compunction for their sins, the wall of the pre-damned mind being as it were broken, an opening and a certain rent is opened, whence may flow the tears of compunction, stirred up by the grief of a penitent and as it were rent heart. Of such a rending the prophet warns: Rend, he says, your hearts and not your 1185Dgarments (Joel. II).

And since there are two kinds of compunction, 182 because the mind turned to God is pricked first by fear, afterwards by love, when anyone, dreading the torments of hell, having renounced the desires of the world, bewails the sins which he had committed, it is as if divine grace made an opening and a rent in his heart. But in the progress of good conversation, after he has conceived some security from the divine mercy, he burns with so great love toward God, that he who before wept lest he should be led to punishment, afterwards begins to weep most bitterly because he is delayed from the kingdom.

Then, therefore, through the opening which grief has made in the penitent's heart, the most loving Lord puts in the hand of soothing grace and mercy, and with so very sweet a 1186Atouch refreshes the mind, that, wholly kindled in the love of God, it seeks and desires nothing earthly, sets even all visible things at little, and strives with all its mind to attain only heavenly and eternal things.

At the sweetness of whose touch the belly trembles, because the mind, drinking the sweetness of the contemplative life, is moved by the power of inspiring grace, so that it understands that the love of God cannot be without the love of neighbour, but that this is the fullness of perfect love, that he who loves God for his own sake should also love his neighbour for God's sake. In this manner, therefore, O daughters of Jerusalem, my beloved put his hand, that is, the help of his power and grace, through the opening, of my pricked heart, intimating and admonishing that, 1186Bbecause I have made entry for him in my heart by cleaving to his love, I should not hesitate also to prepare an entrance for him into the hearts of my neighbours through the office of preaching, since he himself is always at hand through helping grace, and is wont both to bestow on me what, or how, I should teach, and to open the ears of the minds of the hearers.

Whence also this same sentence which I have referred to myself I can, not absurdly, refer also to my hearers, so that the beloved may be said to put his hand through the opening as often as, by sounding through the voice of preaching at the outer ears of the hearers, by putting the hand of helping grace into the inner ears, he enters. At whose touch my belly trembles, because all the weaker ones of mine, what 1186Cthey before did not understand for weakness of wit, understand, and when, hearing the terror of divine judgment, they tremble, they learn to be moved also to the fruit of good work.

VERSE 5.-- I arose therefore to open to my beloved: my hands dropped myrrh, and my fingers full of the most approved myrrh.

For since he promised me his help, by which I might obtain the 183 fruit of my labour, it was fitting that I should not flee the office of preaching, but that, as I had opened my heart to him by his grace, so also I should open the hearts of my neighbours to him by the same grace through preaching

My hands, however, distilled myrrh, because, 1186Daccording to the voice of the Doctor of the Gentiles, I chastised my body and subjected it to servitude, lest perhaps while I preached to others I myself should become reprobate (I Cor. IX). For my hands are my works, which ought always to distil myrrh, because they ought always to be fragrant of the mortification of the flesh, of abstinence from the vices and of the affluence of the virtues.

My fingers, moreover, full of the most approved myrrh, because those very works of mine, of the virtues, if there are any, ought indeed to have great governance of discretion, but that discretion itself ought to overflow with charity divine and fraternal. For what is the most approved myrrh, but charity, the most choice of all the virtues? But why myrrh, unless because love is strong as death, and jealousy hard as hell inferrus? (Cant. VIII.) For no one 1187Ahath greater charity than that a man lay down his life for his friends (Joan. XV).

Fingers, then, mine, that is, the acts distinguished in one mind, as in one body, by the ten precepts, are full of myrrh of charity, because when I love my beloved strongly, I do not refuse to labour even unto death for keeping and preaching his laws.

For the salvation also, or the need, of the brethren I am zealous to have this discretion, that while I desire rather to be suspended in divine contemplation, fraternal charity nevertheless at times compels me to descend, and to gather the myrrh of labour for their utility.

When therefore at the exhortation of my beloved I had now risen, that by preaching the word of life to my neighbours I might open to him their shut hearts also, with my hands 1187Bdistilling myrrh, my fingers also full of the most approved myrrh, I girded myself for the office of preaching.

VERSE 6.-- I opened the bolt of my door to my beloved: but he had turned aside and had gone by. The soul melted when the beloved spoke: I sought and found him not; I called and he answered me not.

I loosened, I say, for a time the rigour of my purpose, or the enclosure of my silence, and going forth into public, I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit (Psal. CXVIII). Having cast from myself also every obstacle of the mind, I began more diligently to search out the wonderful testimonies of the beloved, which I might both show in work and declare in speech. But when I wished that he would enter wholly to me, and said to him with Moses: Lord, show me 1187Cthy face (Exod. XXXIII), he had now turned aside and had gone by and had left only his back parts to be seen in some measure.

184 For what was his turning aside and going by? Surely his turning aside was to lower himself from that sublimity of the heavens to our infirm things by being born and by dying, and because he did it with time, this was his going by: for all those things were in passing, for Christ rising again now dieth no more, death shall no more have dominion over him (Rom. VI). When therefore I strove to comprehend him as he is, in some measure, and to show him in whatever way to others desiring to hear, he withdrew, turned aside, and went by, because he is incomprehensible, and in this life no one can perfectly grasp that divine 1187Dsubstance by sense. And when he had gone by, I saw his back parts only, because I could understand something of his humanity, and preach it.

And when I thus preached the sayings and deeds of my beloved, and provoked the minds of the hearers to keep his precepts and to follow his footsteps, a greater force of compunction dissolved me, so that I wholly flowed out in his love, because he who spoke from me outwardly to others through the voice of preaching was speaking also to me inwardly through the grace of inspiration. For as often as we preach him, he himself speaks in us and through us, as he also says in the Gospel: For it is not you that speak, but the Spirit of your Father that speaketh in you (Matth. X). But where the Spirit speaks to the Father [Patri; read Patris, "of the Father"], 1188Athe Son also speaks, because those whose substance is one, one also is their operation. And I was taken with such sweetness of his speech, that my soul, hearing him within, not only softened from all hardness, but even melted, and, growing strong by deliberate counsel for the daily exercises of good works, said with the Psalmist: I will hear what the Lord God will speak in me (Psal. LXXXIV). For he well attends to God speaking in himself, who obeys with ready will the grace that inspires and goes before free will: he also hears God speaking in himself, whoever understands, by its own revealing, what he reads in Holy Scripture. And when by meditating more frequently in it he seeks God, the more subtly he searches him out, the higher is God exalted in his heart; whence the Psalmist: Man shall come 1188Bto a high heart, and God shall be exalted (Psal. LXIII); and in Ezekiel it is written that when the living creatures were lifted up from the earth, the wheels also were lifted up together beside them (Ezech. I): for the more attentively Holy Scripture is attended to, the more sublimely is it raised up into the spiritual sense for him who subtly considers it.

When, therefore, at such speech of the beloved my soul was melting through the fire of charity, I sought him the more vehemently by reading, by meditating, by preaching, and I desired to know what manner of one he was; I sought him by praying, by fasting, by keeping vigil, by macerating the flesh, but in this life I could not find 185 him as he is. I sought therefore him, and found him not, because I myself could neither know him perfectly by reading. nor show him to others by preaching; for we see through a 1188Cglass in a dark manner (II Cor. XIII). I called, and he answered me not: when I thought him now as it were present to me, although placed in some manner a little far off, and as though I were soon to lay hold of him, and called with some voice of subtle understanding, he answered me not, because, as I went back over the things which I thought I had understood perfectly, he did not open them to the full through the answering voice of his grace. For it is written in the vision of Ezekiel the prophet that when a voice came above the firmament, the living creatures stood, and let down their wings (Ezech. I.) For they had already spread the wings of inmost contemplation, already they had conceived, by flying with the mind, some knowledge, however great, of the Godhead, though yet in a dark manner; but when the voice came not beneath the firmament 1188Dnor from the firmament, but above the firmament, they stood still, not able to go further, and, the wings of the contemplation they had begun being let down, they perceived that to comprehend the incomprehensible was above them. For, deeming him so present that they could comprehend him, they called, but he did not answer them, because what they thought they had understood of God, he did not show by the voice of inner address to be so. I called therefore and he answered me not, because, while I wished to attempt something above me, I recognized how far beneath it I was, since I could attain no perfect knowledge of the incomprehensible substance.

VERSE 7.-- The watchmen that go about the city found me: they struck me and wounded me; the watchmen of the walls took away my cloak from me.

1189AWhat then? I laid down the wings which I had spread in vain beyond my power, and, turned to the writings or sayings of the holy Fathers, I heard: Advance not the bounds which thy fathers have set (Prov. XXII) [Vulg. Ne transgrediaris terminos antiquos, "pass not beyond the ancient bounds"], who indeed spoke inspired by the Holy Spirit (II Petr. I) and showed the way and manner of believing, or of disputing about God. They, assuredly, are the watchmen of the city, that is, of holy Church, of which it is written: Glorious things are said of thee, city of God (Psal. LXXXVI), because they guard her from the onset of evil spirits and men by words and examples and by the defences of their prayers.

These, then, found me, because they proved me drawing back from my former intention and willing to be 1189B186 content with their sayings and writings: they found, I say, because they so drew me by the sweetness of their discourses that, every other intention set aside, I would attend to the sole final and supernal cause, namely life eternal, which is God himself; the vision of him is the full and perfect rest and consummation of all our labour. They, then, while I read or heard their writings, struck me with the dart of divine love, and not only struck, but also wounded, because they so pierced my mind with the compunction of heavenly desire that a fountain of tears flowed from it, as it were a kind of blood of the soul.

The watchmen of the walls also took away my cloak. Now by the walls in this place the Holy Scriptures can, not unfittingly, be 1189Cunderstood, because, just as a wall is built of many and diverse stones, so Holy Scripture is made up of many and diverse sentences and teachings of the holy Fathers. And as walls fortify a city, so the Holy Scriptures guard holy Church, because all her fortification or adornment is the knowledge and observance of the Holy Scriptures. Further, the watchmen of these walls can be understood as all the simple in the Church, of whom it is written: The simplicity of the just shall direct them (Prov. XI), who, although they have either little or no knowledge of the Scriptures, yet, while they preach by their works the precepts of those same Scriptures that are to be observed, edify their neighbours 1189Dtoo in no mean degree. These watchmen, then, of the spiritual walls took away my cloak, because by the example of good works they took from me the hindrances of superfluous thought, which veiled my mind with the enfolding of undiscerning inquiry, and they persuaded me not to be wise in high things, but to consent to the humble (Rom. XII), and to serve God in simplicity.

VERSE 8.-- I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, that you tell him that I languish with love

Wherefore I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, that you announce to him that I languish with love. But what is my adjuring? Surely to bind by the sacrament of faith and of working; otherwise 1190Ayou are not daughters of Jerusalem, because you do not belong to the vision of supernal peace, unless you please God by faith and work. If, therefore, you find the beloved, that is, if you have so far profited by my preaching that by believing rightly and working well you have him, then I adjure you, that is, as I have said, I bind you by the sacrament of faith and of working, which to violate is to lose salvation; that you announce to him, namely, by showing forth the signs and as it were a certain stamp of my zeal and labour, with which in preaching 187 I have toiled for the sake of your salvation, as the Apostle says to his disciples: But the signs of my apostleship are you among the gentiles (II Cor. XII).

And what ought you to announce to him? Namely, that I languish with love, that is, I am so held by his charity and love that toward every pleasure 1190Band beauty of the world I remain weak and languid and as it were already without feeling. Do you, therefore, announce by your life and manners how true, right and profitable my preaching has been, so that your progress may become the fruit of my labour also.

At this voice of the beloved obeying the beloved, and rising up to preach, and setting forth the zeal and profit of that same preaching, the daughters of Jerusalem, that is, holy souls belonging to the vision of supernal peace, inquiring the causes of so great an adjuration, address the beloved also in this manner: What manner of one is thy beloved of the beloved, etc.

VERSE 9.-- What manner of one is thy beloved of the beloved, O most beautiful among women! what manner of one is thy beloved of the beloved, that thou hast so adjured us?

1190CWe attend, they say, to no small force in this adjuration, in which we have learned that the whole sum of our salvation hangs, and therefore we desire to know the power and dignity of this beloved, for whose sake thou hast so adjured us.

What manner of one is, then, the beloved of the beloved, that is, the Son of the Father, God of God, light of light? For it is a great thing to know him whom thou art at such pains to commend, and of the highest prudence to understand him for love of whom thou languishest so greatly. But since the beloved of the beloved, that is, the Son of the substance of the Father, of one essence, of one power, of one will, and of one operation, cannot be perfectly comprehended, for we know in part and we prophesy in part 1190D(I Cor. XIII), yet whatever that is which can be thought, understood, or said of God, thou, O most beautiful among women, that is, among souls that bring forth spiritual sons to God, canst teach, because this thy special prerogative of beauty has merited, that since thou art called the beloved of this beloved, thou canst draw nearer to him with the eye of the mind. For all thy glory and adornment is from within (Psal. XLIV), and the pure God, to whose purity nothing can be compared, is not discerned except by pure hearts, because blessed are the clean of heart, for they shall see God (Matth. V).

Beautiful indeed are the other women, that is, the faithful souls which in their own manner and place and time beget spiritual sons to God, but thou art the most beautiful of all, the Church universal, who daily 1191Abeget sons in the spirit through the sacrament of baptism and the teaching of holy preaching. Do thou, therefore, make known to us what manner of one is the beloved of the beloved, that 188 is, what is to be understood and believed concerning his divinity, according to human possibility. Or again, what manner of one is the beloved of the beloved, that is, how he who was once made beloved to thee by being born and dying for thee is now beloved, by pouring into thee the abundance of his grace and drawing thee into the divine sweetness of his love. Or, how he who formerly, in an earlier time, was beloved in the ancient fathers by showing the majesty of his divinity through figures and dark sayings with very many signs of miracles, is now beloved in the last time by assuming flesh and working the salvation of the whole world. And that 1191Bthe same words are repeated is the eager inquiry of a mind striving to know.

Further, the beloved, that she may kindle the souls of those inquiring to greater love and reverence for her beloved, sets forth his quality tropologically, while she sings the singable beauty of his divinity and humanity with ten proclamations, as it were on a psaltery of ten strings (Psal. XCI). For the number ten is perfect, and is contained in the sacrament either of the Decalogue or of the four Gospels; which, beginning from one, so arrives at four as to complete the number ten; for if upon unity you add the three following numbers, that is, two, three and four, you will have ten, and so through four 1191Cyou will complete the number ten.

Now the psaltery is a musical instrument formed after the fashion of the letter Delta, which in Greek expresses four. Beautifully, then, does the beloved sing the dignity and beauty of the beloved as it were on a psaltery of ten strings, by the testimony of ten proclamations, to show that every sacrament flowing to her from the grace of the beloved sounds forth the Old and the New Testament, the one singing beforehand in figure that it was to be shown, the other now singing that it has been shown in truth. She says, therefore: My beloved is white and ruddy.

VERSE 10.-- My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen out of thousands.

If we draw near diligently with the ear of the heart, we shall be able to perceive with the inner hearing that the chief matter of such a harmony 1191Das the beloved intends to measure out on this ten-stringed instrument is the grace, worthy to be preached, of a twin beauty, namely of chastity and of martyrdom, which, first considered in the head itself, is afterwards diffused through his members, now alternately, now with a sweetness intermingled.

My beloved, she says, is white and ruddy: this twin colour, 189 namely whiteness and ruddiness, appears chiefly indeed and singularly and fully in the head of the Church, that is, Christ, because to the whiteness of his most chaste and most holy flesh, which he took from the most chaste Virgin by the ineffable operation of the Holy Spirit, no whiteness can be compared. And of the wisdom of God the Father, which he himself is, it is written: Above all the beauty of the stars, 1192Abeing compared with the light, she is found before it; for she is the brightness of eternal light, and the unspotted mirror of the majesty of God (Sap. VII) [Vulg. Sap 7:29 super omnem dispositionem stellarum, "above all the order of the stars"].

He is white, then, in divinity, because of the unspeakable splendour of the divine nature, by which he enlighteneth every man that cometh into this world (Joan. I): and white also from humanity, because of the assumption of flesh, immaculate, as we have said, and free of all sin. Further, he was ruddy specially from the passion, because no charity can be equalled to his charity, since he so loved his own handiwork that he chose to die for it, not disdaining to be made the sin of the flesh and the curse of the cross (Rom. VIII; Gal. III) Of which singular passion of his he himself speaks in the prophet: I have trodden the winepress alone, and of the gentiles there is not a man with me (Isa. LXIII).

1192BFor no passion is compared with this passion, which alone has wrought the salvation of the whole world, alone has led the captive servant out of the servitude of sin into the true liberty of the glory of the sons of God (Rom. VIII).

Whence, when she had first said, my beloved is white and ruddy, she added, chosen out of thousands: for the number a thousand, because it is set for perfection, signifies universality. Chosen, therefore, out of thousands he is said to be, because he alone is set before the whole company of the faithful by the singularity of his virtues and graces: for of him it is written that God anointed him with the oil of exultation above his partakers (Psal.
