XLIV). And whereas all the elect receive a divided grace, one indeed after this manner, and another after that (I Cor. VII), to the Only-begotten alone God giveth not the Holy Spirit by measure (Joan. 1192CIII), and of his fulness all receive (Joan. I), in whom dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily (Coloss II), because he is the head above all principality, and power, and virtue, and dominion (Ephes. I).

This beloved, then, the Lord Jesus Christ, is singularly white and ruddy in the personal matter of his own divinity and humanity; chosen he is out of thousands: but in those thousands themselves, that is, in the whole company of the elect, the whiteness of holiness and the ruddiness of the passion do not shine in one manner nor in equal measure; because in some both, in some not both, but now to this one the whiteness of purity and the ruddiness of martyrdom together, now to that one either whiteness alone or ruddiness alone is allotted, so that in the 190 1192Dsight of God this one is white and ruddy, that one either wholly white or wholly ruddy; the one goes before with the greater, the other with the lesser, sometimes with an equal share of those virtues. In his body, therefore, that is, the Church, Christ also is white and ruddy, according to the measure which it pleases his kindness and grace to allot to each of the elect.

VERSE 11.-- His head is as the finest gold. His locks are as the high branches of palm trees, black as a raven. [Vulg. Caput ejus aurum optimum, without sicut: "his head is the finest gold"]

Whence presently, in what follows, the gifts of his twin beauty are enumerated part by part, now together, now alone, shining forth in the same body of Christ, so that after the singular dignity above all the saints first set forth in the head, there may be added the colours of the diverse 1193Adignities in his body, advancing in their own manner and place through the grace that unites them and incorporates them to himself. For she says: His head is as the finest gold. What is understood by the gold but his divinity? For as gold is more precious than all metals, so the divinity of Christ surpasses all creatures; and whatever glory of its dignity there can be in those creatures is nothing in comparison with the divinity. The head, then, of the beloved, that is, his divinity, is as gold, and not gold absolutely, but the finest gold, because the substance of the divinity is good, and not only good, but also the supreme and most general good, and, so to speak, becomes the good of goods, because he himself is the fountain and origin of all good, from whom all good things proceed. Or 1193Bbecause in Holy Scripture the principal part of the mind is called the head, and Christ is the power and wisdom of God the Father (I Cor. I), and the Word begotten from the heart of the Father, by which Word and by which wisdom all things were made, and without which nothing is made. The gold, then, that is finest is that power and wisdom itself, which is the brightness of the glory of God and the figure of his substance (Hebr. I).

And whatever of beauty and comeliness is diffused into the body of this head flows forth from that divinity and wisdom itself, so that the grace of the locks, of the eyes, of the cheeks, and of the other members, which will presently be numbered in what follows, may worthily be proclaimed of this body.

The first of which is, his locks are as the high branches of palm trees, 1193Cblack as a raven: the locks of this head can be understood in two ways, namely as the holy prophets and apostles, or as the Holy Scriptures which flowed forth through them by the inspiration of God. For they clung to God as to their head by the sweetness of contemplative charity, and therefore they received from that very power and wisdom of God great subtlety of mind in beholding that divine Word.

191 Whence they are called As the high branches of palm trees, because, since their conversation was in heaven (Philip. III), they were also lifted up in mind by contemplation into heaven, every trouble of earthly delight being overcome and trodden down; the glory of which spiritual triumph is signified by the palm, which is the sign 1193Dof victory. But because for the gaining of this victory they were afflicted with no small evils, whether by bearing adversities from wicked men, or by crucifying in themselves their flesh with its vices and concupiscences (Gal. V), they are rightly called black as a raven. For the despisers of worldly glory were reputed by the lovers of the world as base and obscure, but they were fitted as fine locks to the glory and comeliness of the divine head all the more, the more they were despised by the worldly for the love of the Godhead.

Further, the Holy Scriptures which were brought forth through them can for this reason be called the locks of the divine head, because, as locks spring from the head, so the Holy Scriptures are produced from the divine wisdom; and as those adorn the head, so the Holy Scriptures adorn the 1194Aeminence and principality of the Church of God. And they are said to be as palms lifted high, because qui a the minds of the faithful are lifted up by their admonition or consolation from earthly things to the loving and seeking of heavenly things, and ub they proclaim the spiritual armour against vices and sins, and promise also the palm of eternal blessedness to those who strive well unto the end. But these locks are said to be black as a raven, because the Holy Scriptures are wrapped in many obscurities, for dark is the water in the clouds of the air (Psal. XVII), because the knowledge in the Holy Scriptures is deep. But because this blackness signifies affliction, whether voluntary or compelled, therefore, while some suffering of mind or body is attended to in it, the beloved in this part is proclaimed wine-coloured, that is, ruddy 1194Bonly, in his body.

VERSE 12.-- His eyes are as doves upon the brooks of waters, which are washed with milk, and sit beside the plentiful streams.

What is understood by the eyes of the beloved but the prelates or angels of the Churches, who are set as it were as watchmen over the house of God, that is, holy Church: whence God says to one of them: I have made thee a watchman to the house of Israel, and thou shalt hear the word out of my mouth, and shalt tell it them from me (Ezech. III). For the watchman looks out from on high, so that he may announce the coming of enemies the better to be guarded against, the further off it is; whence the Lord says through the prophet to a watchman of this kind: Let there be a trumpet in thy throat, as an 1194Ceagle upon the house of God (Ose. VIII). For the watchman has a trumpet in his throat when he preaches the word of God openly and publicly, far and wide, and announces with lofty voice and mind what end 192 there is for virtues and vices, who is as an eagle upon the house of God, because, attending to the Godhead with the keenness of subtle understanding, he calls forth those committed to him to the subtlety of the contemplative life, spreading over them the wings of his protection, with which, by zeal for doctrine and by the support of prayers, he may keep them from the snares of the malignant spirits.

But these eyes of the beloved are as doves, which are washed with milk, because the holy watchmen, attending over the house of God, if they are truly the eyes of God, have works of simplicity and innocence, with chastity of heart and 1194Dof body, by which they nourish both themselves and those subject to them unto life eternal. And whence this? Because they dwell upon the brooks of waters, and sit beside the plentiful streams. For this is the natural custom of doves, that, sitting upon the streams of waters, they guard against the coming of hawks: because, then, these watchmen abide upon the brooks of waters, that is, the sentences of the Scriptures, therefore they know how to provide both for themselves and for their subjects, by composing or correcting manners, and by guarding against the snares of the ancient enemy. They sit also beside the plentiful streams, because daily they have before their eyes the teachings of both Testaments, which are in truth not only full but most full of the knowledge of all sacraments, which in the one are set forth through figures and dark sayings, 1195Aand in the other are preached as shown in truth. And in this third member one of the twin colour in the body of the beloved proclaimed above is to be considered, namely whiteness, so that souls washed with the milky colour may bear the ensign of chastity and purity.

VERSE 13.-- His cheeks are as beds of aromatical spices set by the perfumers. His lips are lilies dropping choice myrrh.

By the cheeks of the beloved the continent can, not unfittingly, be understood, adorning their purpose by a plurality of diverse virtues, as by a multitude of hairs showing forth manliness of soul, who, while for God they abstain from the pleasure of the eyes or of the ears and of the other senses, of foods also and garments, and of the other delightful things of this world, 1195Bbuild as many beds of spices as the scents of continence they spread from themselves.

For, for example, the reverent restraint of the eyes, or their turning away, is a certain beautiful bed, in which as many merits of continence shine forth, so many fragrances do the spices breathe. The ear 193 also, and the mouth and the nostrils and the hands can be called certain beds, which because they are perceptive of good or evil things, while certain things, though good in their own nature, very often become evil by the abuse of those who partake of them. As often as the irrational appetites for those things are broken by the love of virtue, those beds breathe with the kinds of spiritual spices with which they are sown, so that each spice breathes according to that which the quality of continence begets, because 1195Cthe more it delights by it, the more does the continence of that thing commend it to God.

But because these continences ought to have a fitting state by the virtue of discretion, so that neither natural necessity be turned into vice, nor the rigour of virtue exceed the honest measure, rightly are these beds said, by the perfumers, to be set, because not at random, not without discretion and as it were confusedly, but in order and composedly and with reason are continences of this kind set in their beds, by those, namely, who are proved to have had the knowledge of this setting. For these perfumers are the holy apostles and holy doctors, who in their sayings and writings show forth the kinds of virtues as certain perfumes, out of which 1195Dthey compound against vices and sins, as against diseases of the soul, a certain most wholesome antidote. The cheeks, then, of the beloved are as beds of spices, which are set by the perfumers, because assuredly those who give out from themselves the diverse odours of continence gather from the sayings and deeds of the holy Fathers whatever of diligence and comeliness they fashion in their manners.

And it is to be considered that in this member too the twin colour of the beauty foretasted above, namely ruddiness and whiteness, shines forth, so that by the outward bearing the inward is denoted, because, while these cheeks are ruddy and white, they give testimony both to the modesty of chastity and to the labour of continence, where it cannot easily be judged which colour is the more eminent, whether ruddiness in martyrdom or whiteness in virginity, because both virginity 1196Ais found in martyrs and itself makes martyrs. For in these cheeks two things are regarded in one, because in the virtue of each one both the merit of continence and chastity shines forth, and for the labour the reward of martyrdom is hoped for.

His lips are lilies dropping choice myrrh. Behold the perfumers by whose industry the grace of modesty shines forth in the cheeks, namely the holy preachers, who are therefore designated by the lips, because by their preaching they 194 compound the diverse perfumes of the virtues. They are as lilies, because they both give a secundam precept for integrity and purity of life, and give counsel for the wounds of souls, and they can say with the Apostle: We are the good odour of Christ unto God in them that are saved (II Cor. II). For the nature of the lily shows forth whiteness 1196Band odour together, and yields very much healing for the curing of wounds.

They are lilies dropping choice myrrh, that is, the best, because, while for the keeping of integrity and purity of heart and body they mortify vices and sins in themselves, and unceasingly preach to others by word and example that they should do the same, they assuredly show how great a charity they have toward God and their neighbour.

For charity can be called choice myrrh, that is, the best and proved, because, where it is true and perfect, it extinguishes in man all the incentives of vices; for as the bodies of the dead are embalmed with myrrh, lest they putrefy, so souls are strengthened by divine charity, lest they incur the putrefaction of vices.

1196CAnd in this member of his body also the beloved is white and ruddy, because in his holy preachers he is called white for the lily of chastity, but through the myrrh of the passion, For all that will live godly in Christ shall suffer persecution, (II Tim. III), he is proclaimed ruddy.

VERSE 14.-- His hands are turned and of gold, full of hyacinths. His belly is of ivory, set with sapphires.

If we look to the head itself, his hands are assuredly turned and of gold, because of him it is written: How great are thy works, O Lord, thou hast made all things in wisdom (Psal. CIII): for he who works with the lathe works more quickly and more perfectly and more smoothly. But 1196Dwho ever worked more quickly and more perfectly or more smoothly than God himself? For very quickly he made what he disposed to make, because he only spoke, and they were made (Psal. XXXII), and at one and the same time, though in a diverse manner, in a diverse form also, his having spoken was his having made. No one has worked more perfectly than he, because he made not things diminished, or by parts, and such as were yet to be bettered, but made all things perfect, and his having made once was his having made the whole and entire. Further, nothing was smoother than his work, because the nature of things could be retarded by no hindrance, but the course and measure which it once received it kept as a perpetual law: nothing in his works is distorted and unequal, diminished or superfluous, because he appointed all things in measure, and number, and 1197Aweight (Sap. II) [Vulg. Sap 11:21 omnia in mensura, et numero et pondere disposuisti, "thou hast ordered all things"]. Well, therefore, were his hands turned, because he wrought all things with such, as has been said, swiftness, 195 perfection and beauty, that from the works themselves it becomes clear to one who considers them of how great beauty, or of how great majesty, the founder himself is, not that this consideration is a full comprehension of his deity, but that it is a certain beholding of the Creator, setting out from the dignity of the creature and shining through as far as is possible to the human mind.

Whence also the hands themselves are called of gold, because this, that they are, that they live, that they thrive and flourish, stands by the disposition of the divinity: for by gold, which is more precious than all metals, the divinity is designated, than which there is nothing above.

1197BBut what is it that they are called full of hyacinths, when there are also other stones very suitable too for the adornment of the hands or fingers? All visible things indeed are certain wonderful and beautiful adornments of the divine works, but in these they are more to be wondered at, because they are also the subtler secrets of heavenly wonders; the consideration of which is, in the first place, in the incorporeal creation, namely of the supernal spirits or of holy minds always attending to heavenly things alone, whose conversation is the working of the divine goodness; in the second place, in the incorporeal creation of the superior things, which are certain nourishments of the inferior, whose rational disposition is also the wonderful working of the divine wisdom. For the hyacinth 1197Cis of the colour of the air, and therefore the hands of the beloved are called full of hyacinths, because the works of the Creator are proclaimed rather in the comeliness and adornment of heavenly things.

Further, if you look to the members of the head, his hands are turned and of gold and full of hyacinths, because, intent on good works and always hastening to enter into the rest to come, not slowly nor sluggishly, but swiftly and zealously, they run the way of the commandments; whatever they discern crooked and unequal in their manners they drive out with the turning of right working, and make it smooth, and render it perfect in the eyes of their Maker, yet with him as the craftsman; the cause of which effectiveness is the understanding in them, answering to the gold of wisdom divinely conferred, and always attending with the sweetness of the contemplative life to the felicities of heavenly goods.

1197DAnd they are therefore called his hands, because whatever good they do is not of their own virtue but of the grace of God, whose also is this, that they are turned by the perfection of manners, that they are of gold by the clearness of the understanding, that they are full of hyacinths by the sublimity of the angelic conversation.

Truly, in the consideration of this member also a twofold colour, proclaimed with special praise, appears in the body of the beloved, because in this, that the hands are turned, there is the sign of labour or of passion, by which they have been turned from all superfluity and inequality of manners into a vessel 196 of honour and worthy to be looked upon by the divine eyes. But in that they are of gold and full of hyacinths, the shining virtue of the celibate life is designated, by which they glow with the clearness of chastity and modesty; and in this manner in this part also the beloved is sung white and ruddy.

1198AHis belly is of ivory, set with sapphires: If we look distinctly upon the person of the beloved himself, we accept not absurdly that his humanity is designated by the name of the belly, because the belly is the frailer part of the body, and that humanity experienced all the frailty of the human body except sin. But what is it that this belly is called of ivory? For ivory is the bone of the elephant, which animal is held to be most chaste: and what is more chaste than the humanity of Christ, which was assumed from the most chaste Virgin without any work of man, through the sole operation of the Holy Spirit? The belly, then, of the beloved is of ivory, because, whereas all men are conceived in iniquities and sins, he alone in his humanity was conceived singularly without sin of the most chaste Virgin, as has been said 1198B.

Further, what is it that this belly is recorded to be set with sapphires? For the sapphire is of the colour of the sky; and the belly of the beloved is said to be set with sapphires because, although from his earthly humanity he bore hunger, thirst, weariness and the other things which he could suffer according as he was man, yet while suffering he showed heavenly miracles from his divinity by working them.

And if we consider the multitude of the faithful who cleave to that person as members to a head through faith, which for its greater frailty can be compared to a belly: for there are in the Church some given to the bond of marriage, there are some wonderfully continent in the frail sex: but they that have wives, as though they had none (I Cor. VII), can rightly be called a belly of ivory 1198C, because, although outwardly they seem frail, yet they are strong through the comeliness of a holy and chaste life. Whence also of holy married persons it is written that they were walking in all the commandments and justifications of the Lord without blame (Luc. III): for this is for the belly to be set with sapphires, because amid the cares of worldly things, which the frailty of marriage requires, they shine forth by the devout observance of the heavenly precepts. Further, those wonderfully continent in the frail sex show in this a more praiseworthy keeping of their purpose, because, though they are weak and frail in body, yet they rise bravely by virtue of soul to the merits of holiness. Whence in these also a belly of ivory is spoken of, because the virtue 1198Dof chastity is more proclaimed in the frail sex.

And it is recorded set with sapphires, because the virtue of chastity is adorned also with the ornaments of the other virtues: for otherwise chastity of body cannot be a virtue, unless 197 it be adorned with chastity of mind, which consists in humility, patience, sobriety and contempt of the worldly life, and the observance of the other heavenly precepts. For, that it may be of the body of this beloved, the belly of ivory ought to be set with sapphires, because chastity of body profits nothing without good work, nor good work without chastity (GREGORIUS). » Because, then, the frail sex holds the virtue of chastity with a strong mind, the belly of the beloved is of ivory; but because it also strives after other virtues for heavenly glory, it is set with sapphires, because in 1199Athe ivory belly the colour of chastity gleams, in the sapphire, although sky-coloured, yet for the labour of the virtues the colour of the passion is ruddy. Chastity itself also, which outwardly is white in a pure body, inwardly is ruddy through the martyrdom of the mind: for to fight against the natural motion of the flesh is assuredly a certain suffering of the mind.

Truly the singing of the present portion has regard in no small measure to the rule of your profession, most beloved sisters, because, since you are in truth of the body of this beloved, you can be a most comely member of his of this kind. For when, in so frail a little vessel of your body, you shine with the white garment of chastity and modesty, assuredly you can be called and be the belly of this beloved of ivory; but because together with that chastity you shine also with other adornments of virtues, you assuredly 1199Bgleam set with sapphires. But you must take very great heed lest you think you can please God by chastity alone, if you have not other good works, and therefore you ought always to join both chastity to good work and good work to chastity, that you may be able to please God perfectly.

VERSE 15.-- His legs are pillars of marble, that are set upon bases of gold. His form is as of Libanus, chosen as the cedars.

In the eighth place, as it were, the attentive beholder of the beloved touches the eighth string of the ten-stringed psaltery, as though rendering that symphony διαπασον, whose property it is to have the same voice in the eighth as in the first. For, whereas above, on the first string, it sounded that the head of the beloved is the finest gold, now she says that the legs are set upon bases 1199Cof gold, so that the same voice may be low and high, sounding the highest and the lowest golden adornment of the beloved. But it is to be considered what are the legs of this beloved, or why they are compared to pillars of marble built upon bases of gold.

Since God in his nature is immovable and unchangeable, inasmuch as he is not in a place, for he fills and contains all things, while he himself is contained by nothing, who is always wholly everywhere; and since he is in a place who is moved from place to place, but God is not moved, and therefore is not in a place, because immovable, yet he is said to be moved, 198 not in himself, but in those whom he moves by his nod and will through the power that disposes all things, whether according to justice or according to mercy, for he hath mercy on whom he will, and whom he will he hardeneth 1199D(Rom. IX), of which the one is of mercy, the other of justice. Since, therefore, he goes before all his creation as it were by this twin way of his disposition, namely justice and mercy, justice and mercy can rightly be called his legs: for all his ways, as the Psalmist says, are mercy and truth (Psal. XXIV). But truth and justice are the same: for what is true is just; and what is just is true.

But why are these legs called pillars of marble, unless because they are straight and strong? For in a pillar there is straightness, in marble hardness; for the justice of God is hidden, yet never unjust. For who can know why he chooses this man mercifully, and 1200Arepels that man judicially? Therefore the Apostle cries: O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God: how incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways! (Rom. II.)

Further, what are the bases of gold upon which these pillars, which are understood as those legs, are set? Assuredly, if you weigh it rightly, they are his wisdom and goodness, because all things that he makes he orders and disposes wisely and well: they are bases, namely, because they contain and sustain all things, of gold, because they shine forth wonderfully in the very effecting of things. The legs, then, of the beloved, if you attend to the head itself, are, as has been said, mercy and truth, which, set upon bases, that is, the feet of his wisdom and goodness, either stand or walk, according to the measure and quality 1200Bof the things that have been made: for all things that have been made are either eternal or temporal. And they stand in those things which God himself has foreordained for his own to abide eternally according to grace and mercy; they walk in those things which he either confers or takes away temporally, whether mercifully or judicially.

Further, if you look to the members of that head, what do you think are to be called the legs of this beloved? In that ancient people of God, in which alone God was then known, God set chiefly two dignities, by which that people might be fortified and adorned, namely the kingship and the priesthood secerdotium; outwardly indeed it was armed with royal strength against those who, at the devil's prompting, laboured to destroy the purpose of God, which he held for the salvation of the whole world, and which he showed beforehand to that same people 1200Cin type, so that in their whole commonwealth, with peace and honour, they might run beforehand, in figure, through the business of the divine promise that was faithfully to be fulfilled. Further, inwardly it was instructed by the priestly office, to understand prudently through figure and to handle reverently that same business, so that it might labour toward that purpose of God, one day to be fulfilled, by faith and love, in hope of the salvation to come.

199 In which dignities, namely, lay so much of the strength of that same people, that afterwards, when God, angered at that same people sinning, threatened many punishments, at last, as it did not correct itself at all, he set forth this final punishment, that, the kingship and the priesthood being taken away and destroyed, all their honour and religion should depart utterly. For it is said thus through Jeremiah 1200Dthe prophet: The Lord hath delivered up to oblivion in Sion the festival and the sabbath; and to reproach, into the indignation of his wrath, the king and the priest (Thren. II). For there to be no king and priest, this was for all the rite of the ceremonies to have failed.

Does not holy Church also in this time, in which that promise is now fulfilled, stand by two dignities of this kind? For the power of royal judgment fights outwardly with the material sword against the unbelieving and incredulous, and the majesty of the priestly office fights inwardly also against the same with the spiritual sword. See, when the Lord, for defending the universal salvation of this new commonwealth which now is, permitted the sword, and heard that two were ready, he answered that it was enough 1201A(Luc II), because he established in the Church two peremptory sentences, one by the material sword, the other by the spiritual sword. For outwardly this is brought about by the fear of the kingdom, that the Church may serve God with peace and honour; inwardly she is instructed by the priesthood, that she may know how to serve God with reverence and love. What then? Since these two dignities are to the Church of God, which is to be propagated with all religion, as it were a certain strength and, if I may rightly say so, the strongest support of the whole body of this beloved, can not the kingship and the priesthood rightly be called the legs of that same beloved?

And these, for their strength and eminence, are called pillars of marble, since they too are raised up by virtue and power, and in them the whole house of holy Church is sustained. And what are the bases 1201Bof gold upon which these pillars are built? Plainly it is fitting that in that kingship or priesthood, because their cause ought to be that of common utility and comeliness, a great force of reason and virtue of discretion should shine forth, so that in all their dispensation and judgment there may always be reason and discretion. But since these ought to proceed from a great clearness of understanding and wisdom, can they not rightly be called the golden bases of these pillars?

These legs, then, of this beloved are pillars of marble placed upon bases of gold, because in holy Church the kingship and the priesthood flourish by the reason and discretion of dispensation and of judgment.

To the song of this eighth string also that prelude answers, set beside the entry of the ten-stringed song itself, by which the beloved is sung white and 1201Cruddy, when this part of the kingship so acts, with labour and peril of life, that in it this beloved may be proclaimed ruddy: further, 200 the other part, of the priesthood, may so act in peace and tranquillity tranquil itate that in it the beloved may be pronounced white, in holiness and chastity, in conversation, in the observance and preaching of the commandments of God. His form is as of Libanus, chosen as the cedars. As, she says, mount Libanus is more excellent than the other mountains, in comeliness and beauty, and in the wonderful order of the trees set there, so my beloved is more eminent than all the saints, and far more beautiful, in power of virtues, in wisdom also and knowledge, and in all comeliness of worldly actions, and in all fulness of divine graces. For God doth not give him the Spirit by 1201Dmeasure (Joan. III). But in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily (Coloss. II); and of this his fulness the saints receive grace for grace (Joan. I); and what he himself has universally, these obtain particularly, and this not always according to each one's will, because that same particle of grace in them is at times ready, and at times lies sluggishly as though asleep, which must be stirred up not without some labour Whence Paul says to Timothy: For which cause, he says, I admonish thee that thou stir up the grace which is in thee by the imposition of my hands (II Tim. I). And it is stirred up in many ways, but most of all by praying and by singing psalms; for example, when the king of Israel said to Elisha: Why hath God gathered these three kings together, to deliver them into the hands 1202Aof Moab? he answered: As the Lord liveth, in whose sight I stand, that unless I reverenced the face of Josaphat king of Juda, I would not indeed have hearkened, nor looked; but now bring me a minstrel: and it came to pass, while the minstrel was playing, the hand of the Lord came upon him, and the rest. (IV Reg. III.)

Except, then, this beloved, of whom it is written: He upon whom thou shalt see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, he it is that baptizeth in the Spirit (Joan. I): all the other saints receive a divided or particular grace of the Holy Spirit as it pleases the Holy Spirit himself, who breatheth where and when he will (Joan. III). Rightly, therefore, is the form of this beloved said to be as of Libanus, because he is beautiful in form above the sons of men (Psal. XLIV), and no form can be compared to his form, no 1202Bvirtue to his virtue, no grace to his grace.

Chosen as the cedars: why are the cedars chosen before the other trees of Libanus, unless because they have certain special virtues of their nature? For the cedar is incorruptible, it is fragrant, it is hostile to serpents; and who could be without corruption, save only this beloved himself, who doeth not sin, neither was guile found in his mouth? (I Petr. II.) No one was ever able to be so holy, so innocent, that he did not contract something of corruption, since it is written that God found iniquity even in his angels (Job IV). For sin is a certain rottenness, a certain corruption, and though in one it is greater, in another less, yet in no one, however very holy, very just, 1202Ccan it not be, though it be even the very least; but in this beloved alone no stain at all of rottenness or corruption of this kind, 201 not even the slightest, could exist.

Well, therefore, is he called chosen as the cedars, because this one has specially by nature what has been granted to none of the saints by grace. These things indeed are to be said of the head alone.

But if you look to the body, which, joined to the head, is one according to incorporation, because it is incorporated to that head through his grace, fittingly is his form compared to Libanus, when this whole beloved is attended to distinctly in himself and in his body. For what can be considered in the face or form of the Church 1202Dbut the presence of the divinity in the performing of the sacraments, in the utterance of the divine oracles, in the disposing and ordering of fitting and reasonable causes? And who is this Libanus, to which the form of this beloved in his whole body is likened? If you attend to the thing itself as it is, Libanus is a mountain of Phoenicia, abounding in cedars both rooted in it and stretched up on high: and as this mountain is adorned with a multitude of cedars, and thereby offers great beauty of itself to those who behold it, so this beloved, adorned in his body with the multitude of his elect who are rooted in him by faith and cleave to him in charity, assuredly offers to the whole world a wonderful spectacle of holiness and comeliness.

1203ABut if you understand it metaphorically, this Libanus is that of which the prophetic word cries: Open, it says, Libanus, thy gates, and let fire devour thy cedars (Zach. II). For the temple of God, which had been built in that earthly Jerusalem and had boards within round about of the woods of Libanus, of cedar woods, was therefore called by the name of Libanus, because in it was the Holy of holies, which was a certain glory and an eminent beauty not only of that city, but also of the whole people itself, spread through many borders. The form, then, of the beloved is as the form of Libanus, because, as this temple was formerly the head and singular monument of religion to that ancient people of God, so now the assembly of the Church, where Christ is honoured in his body, is a certain head 1203Band a certain eminence of holiness to all the Christian people, because in it is regarded a certain way and arrival at the sublimity of that highest good and at the eternity of the salvation to come. Still now, to the assembly, as it were to a certain mountain of God, the faithful people runs daily, to look forth in hope upon that land of promise which God will give to his elect, in which is the temple of that supernal Jerusalem, which the Holy of holies himself inhabits, in which the saints are multiplied like the cedars of Libanus, made incorruptible by participation in that eternal beatitude and in the highest good, which is God.

Chosen as the cedars: how is this beloved, in his body, that is, the 202 Church, said to be chosen 1203Cas the cedars? If you attend to the natures of the cedar which we recounted above, namely that it is incorruptible, that it is fragrant, that it puts serpents to flight, assuredly you can weigh how great is the utility of the unity of holy Church, and how much it is to be chosen by every soul, and how much it is to be preferred to all other things. For there incorruption of soul is attained, the odour of virtues is perceived, vices and sins, as venomous serpents, are put to flight. What is more excellent than this thing? Rightly, therefore, is Christ in his body said to be chosen as the cedars, because in all its action or disposition, canonical or dispensatory, he is the cause of all spiritual effecting.

But in this place the beloved who above, as we have often said, is brought in coloured in two ways, namely white and ruddy, by the beauty of the body alone 1203Dshines in the face of his body, that is, of the Church, which he chose for himself not having spot nor wrinkle (Ephes. V), which the singing of that part concerning the form of Libanus proves, which is interpreted whitening candidutio.

VERSE 16.-- His throat is most sweet, and he is all lovely: such is my beloved, and he is my friend, daughters of Jerusalem.

In the throat is the voice, in the voice is sound, in sound, if the voice is articulate, the sure expression of some thing. What is understood by the throat but the sound of Holy Scripture? And we know that the whole of Holy Scripture was established either by the voice of the Lord himself, or by that of the saints, whom God himself used as certain instruments. For what do the Holy Scriptures sound but God speaking either through himself or through his own? And speaking what? 1204AAssuredly the quality of the promise to come, according to the purpose of him who predestines, calls, justifies and glorifies his elect, the sweetness and suavity of which glorification he grants them to foretaste now through hope that lifts up, and pants after it with all desire, and as it were already in some manner takes a certain trial of that same suavity.

That very trial, namely, can also be called the throat of this beloved, because in the mind of every holy soul that foretastes the sweetness of the divine goodness there savours delightfully that suavity which it understands from the preaching of Holy Scripture, of which it is said that neither hath eye seen, nor ear heard, neither hath it entered into the heart of man, what things God hath prepared 1204Bfor them that love him (Isa. LIV; I Cor. II). Whence also the Psalmist says to those who profit by the trial of that suavity: O taste and see that the Lord is sweet! blessed is the man that hopeth in him (Psal. XXXIII). The throat, then, of the beloved is either the voice of Holy Scripture telling forth the suavity of the divine loving-kindness, or the trial of that same loving-kindness sweetly refreshing the soul of each of the faithful. 203 It is a throat most sweet, because it utters the memory of so great an abundance of the divine holiness, that to the attentive helper nothing seems to sound sweeter in the ear of the heart than not only to hope for, but also to hold with firm certainty, the everlasting goods of the beatitude to come, and therefore to desire them with the whole soul.

Whence, whereas above the several parts are compared each to some 1204Cthing, as the head to gold, the locks to the high branches of palm trees, the eyes to doves, the cheeks to beds of spices, and the rest, as has been set out above, to things befitting them, this last alone is compared to nothing, because that supreme and most general good, as it is unspeakable, so is it incomparable.

And the proclamations of this beloved having been enumerated part by part, whether in himself or in his body, as though each string of this kind of ten-stringed instrument had been played out, she sets down in some manner the final note of the praise that has been sung, saying: And he is all lovely: as if she said: Why is it that I proclaim his beauty and dignity part by part? There is nothing in him that I can except: for he is all lovely, whether you attend to the loftiness of his divinity, or regard the lowliness of his humanity 1204D. For this is the sum of the whole praise, which is sung at the end and expresses in itself a certain colour of the whole song.

For what can be said more briefly and more definitely of Christ, God and man, for the sum of praise, than that it be said, all lovely! For if all that is in him, or can be said of him, is lovely, is blessed on every side, assuredly it is concluded that to call him all lovely is the supreme and final measure of praise.

Such is my beloved, and he is my friend, daughters of Jerusalem. You have asked of me, she says, what manner of one my beloved was, for whom I so greatly adjured you; behold, I have shown you what manner of one my beloved is, whose bearing I have expressed through each of his members. But what 1205Ais to be said of this bearing? Has this beloved obtained this bearing through disposition or affection, and is he susceptible of intensification and remission? In his own nature, by no means, who is essentially good, wise, fair, holy and just; but in his body, that is, the Church, he passes through disposition or affection into this bearing, receiving more and less, according as it pleases his grace to dispose in each, his member. This quality or this bearing is his nature, because he himself is goodness, wisdom, beauty, holiness and justice.

And he is worthy of my seeking, not that I am necessary to him, but that he is very necessary to me. Why? Because he is my 204 friend, O daughters of Jerusalem; for the bearing of my inner man 1205Bis formed from him, as from image into image, through participation in the grace dwelling in my heart, by whose illumination are opened to me those secrets of invisible things which are contained in the sublimity and signification of the divine precepts and sacraments, according as understanding and reason instruct and lead me, which are the greatest beauty of that inner bearing of mine. This my friend guards me into knowledge of this kind through the grace of humility: for he himself says to the Father: I confess to thee, Father, because thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them to little ones (Matth. XI): for humility is the guardian of the virtues. And he is called amicus, friend, as it were animi custos, guardian of the mind; for that I may 1205Cnot lose this friend, I ought to have him through humility as the guard of my mind. For if the mind, affected or disposed toward divine knowledge, at some time through co-operating grace receives a bearing, that is, knowledge of this kind abiding in itself, the mind itself becomes as it were one with God by participation in him, so that it too, from fellowship with God, is called God. Whence a certain wise man says to his son: If God is the mind, as the songs tell us, Let him be chiefly worshipped by thee with a pure mind. As if he openly said: Since the mind is God to us, that is, the true and spiritual life, glorify this chiefly by living well. For by the ears, through the power of reason and understanding implanted in it, by discerning rightly and leading its life well, retaining God in itself, it is God 1205D, not indeed essentially, but by appellation, as the Prophet says of the saints: I have said: You are gods, and all of you the sons of the Most High (Psal. LXXXI), and the power of such an utterance is the covenant of a great friendship; but, attending to the good of this friendship, not the sons but the daughters of Jerusalem, that is, souls still weak and not yet able to attain the perfection of the virtues, and this, in the beloved, to have established the great beauty of spirit of this beloved, they too being kindled with the love of holy desire, desire also to enjoy the good of this friendship, by which they may be able to attain ad ipisci that same beauty of spirit. For they say: Whither is thy beloved gone, etc.

VERSE 17.-- Whither is thy beloved gone, O most beautiful among women! whither is thy beloved turned aside? and we will seek him with thee.

1206AWhat is it for God, who is not contained by place, and with whom there is no change nor shadow of alteration, to go away, or to turn aside? (Jac. II.) God is said in two ways to go away or to turn aside, namely both by the approach and by the withdrawal of his grace, according to the perfection or the defect of any mind, either drawing near to God, 205 or withdrawing from him. But in this place the going away of this beloved is for someone to be moved by the mercy of his goodness, and his turning aside also is to glide into the mind of anyone by the gift of his grace.

Tell us, they say, O most beautiful among women, whither thy beloved, by going away and turning aside through his mercy and grace, has set forth to us an example of living well, or of striving more fully in any virtue, 1206Bin any of his faithful. Tell, that is, show, either by the reading in which thou daily recitest their life, or by the action by which thou daily numberest them into thy fellowship, and we too, led on by their example, will seek with thee this beloved, by praying, fasting, and calling him by other good works, that he may deign to turn aside to us also, visiting us with the gift of his grace. For he himself says: If you shall seek me with all your heart, I shall be found by you (Jerem. XXIX): for to seek him is not by prayer alone, but also by good action, as also elsewhere he says of those who seek him: For they seek me from day to day, and desire to know my ways (Isa. XXXVIII). For in saying that they wish to know his ways, he assuredly shows 1206Cthat they seek him by good action.

We will seek, then, with thee the beloved in this manner, O most beautiful among women. But of what women? Assuredly either of those who in themselves bring forth to God the fruits of good work, as sons of holiness, by faith and love, or of those who beget others, as sons of light, by word and example unto the day of eternal life. Because, then, we marvel at so great a beauty in thee, O most beautiful among women, which thou hast drawn to thyself by seeking and finding thy beloved, therefore we too, desiring to attain some trace of thy so great and so noble beauty, desire to know to whom thy beloved is moved, or to whom he turns aside, through his mercy and grace, so that, seeking him too by thy example, after we have found him, even if not most beautiful, we may yet in some measure 1206Dbe accounted beautiful. To these things the Church, or the soul beloved of God, showing the place of the moving or turning aside of this beloved, suggests at the same time also the act in that turning aside of his, saying: My beloved is gone down into his garden, etc.

CAPUT VI.

206 VERS. 1.-- Dilectus meus descendit in hortum suum ad areolam aromatum, ut pascatur in hortis, et lilia colligat.

Quid nempe fuit dilectum quaerere, nisi ad eum per contemplationis virtutem ascendere? quia enim in sanctorum cordibus fides per dilectionem operatur (Gal. V), dilectio vero mentem semper ad superna trahit, bonum ergo operari est ad Deum mente descendere. Sed cum omne bonum a Deo sit, sine 1207Aquo nihil boni existit, ab illo quempiam in bono adjuvari, profecto est ejus ad eum descendere; scriptum quippe est in Exodo, quia Moyses in montem ascendit, et Dominus ad eum descendit (Exod. XIX). Quantum enim quisque ad Deum ascendit cogitatione, et actione illum quaerendo, tantum ad illum Deus descendit, sive sua ei mysteria per intellectum aperiendo, sive adjutorium suae gratiae per virtutem animi conferendo. Ubi enim per liberum arbitrium voluntate et opere quilibet ad Deum ascendit, ibi ad eum Deus per auxiliatricem gratiam misericordia et dignatione sua descendit

Unde et hic dilecta dilectum quaerere cupientibus congrue respondit, quia dilectus meus descendit in 1207Bhortum suum: ac si diceret: Quia scire desideratis quonam abierit, vel declinaverit dilectus meus, ecce dico tibi quia dilectus meus descendit in hortum suum. Quis est hortus dilecti, nisi aut sancta Ecclesia aut sancta quaevis anima diversa virtutum specie germinans? in quam dilectus descendit, quia bonis actibus germinanti suae adjutorium gratiae impendit. Sed postquam in hortum descendit, quonam se inclinavit? ad areolam, inquit, aromatum. Quae est areola aromatum, 207 nisi mens variis virtutum suaviter redolentium speciebus consita, sive diversarum gratiarum opinione quasi bono odore respersa? qui enim possunt dicere cum Apostolo: Christi bonus odor sumus Deo in omni loco (II Cor. II), isti profecto 1207Cin horto Domini, hoc est in sancta Ecclesia, singuli quique suo modo possunt dici areola aromatum, quia mentibus proximorum spargunt odorem bonae opinionis per exempla bonorum operum.

Cur vero non aream, sed per diminutionem, dicit areolam, nisi quia mens sancta quae virtutum sublimitate fulget, parva debet esse in oculis suis et magnopere ostendere, quia excelsus Dominus et humilia respicit et humiles spiritu salvabit? (Psal. CXII, XXXIII.) Ad hanc ergo areolam dilectus in hortum suum descendens declinat, quia sanctae menti per incrementa sanctitatis et scientiae facilem se et quasi tractabilem praestat. Omne enim studium inchoanti difficile, assuescenti facile videtur: et viam mandatorum Dei, sive sanctae Scripturae scientiam ingredienti 1207Dangusta videtur porta et difficilis introitus, longa vero exercitatione terenti, et quasi frequentes obices repellenti lata et spatiosa panditur via sanctitatis et intellectus atque ideo facilis deinceps patet ingressus et egressus.

Subdit vero causam cur descenderit: Ut pascatur, inquit, in hortis, et lilia colligat: pascitur quippe in hortis, quia delectatur odore illo qui spargitur ex areola spiritualium aromatum, id est operum bonorum. Ipse enim in Evangelio dicit: Meus cibus est, ut faciam voluntatem Patris mei (Joan. IV); voluntas quippe Patris est, omnes homines salvos fieri (I Tim. II). Porro homines salutem appetere et ad eam pervenire, opus est illius. Quae autem Pater operatur, haec eadem operatur et Filius, quia quod 1208Avult Pater, vult et Filius, et una et amborum voluntas et operatio. Lilia vero colligit, quia magis eos qui integritate et munditia cordis et corporis candent, eligit, sive fide et opere perfectos in aeternam beatitudinem remunerandos assumit.

VERS. 2.-- Ego dilecto meo et dilectus meus mihi, qui pascitur inter lilia.

Dilectus, inquit, meus supra mihi praeceperat dicens: Surge, aperi mihi, soror mea, amica mea, columba mea, immaculata mea, cui ego obediens pessulum ostii mei aperui (Cant. V), cunctis eum praedicando et quantus qualisve sit rationabiliter ostendendo. Sed quid ad haec dilectus meus? nimirum vicem rependit obedientiae meae gratulabundae mihi decantans laudem dignationis suae, non meam sed 1208Bsuam in me beatificans gratiam. Ejus enim fuit quod volui, quod potui, quod perfeci, atque ideo sua in me ipse dona praedicat, ut mihi et omnibus gratiae suae obedientibus 208 quanti sit apud Deum meriti vita sanctitati et honestati obediens ostendat.

Qualis vero dilectus? Qui pascitur, inquit, inter lilia, hoc est munda cogitatione et operatione delectatur, non quod in aliquid ex accidenti accrescat, qui nullum unquam recipit augmentum vel detrimentum. Cum semper in una eademque essentia et proprietate incommutabilis permaneat, sed quod per aliquem modum locutionis a creatura translatum, affectus bonitatis ejus exprimatur erga eos 1208Cquos sua dilectione et gratia dignatus fuerit. Pasci namque dicitur quando in mente cujusque quam sua gratia inhabitat, virtutum profectus augetur.

Quali vero cantico vel cantici modo insonuit mihi vox hujus dilecti? cantico certe suavi, cantico non mediocriter attendendo, modo quidem octochordo, sed in singulis chordis propter vim cujusque soni proprio theoremate insigniter hoc modo disposito.

VERS. 3.-- Pulchra es, amica mea, suavis et decora sicut Jerusalem: terribilis ut castrorum acies ordinata.

Spectabiliter hic intueri libet qualiter praesentis cantici modulatio octo partibus veluti octo decurrit vocibus, ut proprietas ejus symphoniae quam διαπασον 1208Dmusici dicunt, hic attendatur, cujus ultima vox eadem est quae prima, sicut et in harum dispositione partium videre licet ubi cum prima pars hoc modo deponatur, terribilis ut castrorum acies ordinata, ultima pars nihilominus eodem modo terminetur, scilicet terribilis ut castrorum acies ordinata.

Sed singulae partes singulas deposcunt rationes, quae hoc modo distinguuntur. Prima est, pulchra es, amica mea, suavis et decora sicut Jerusalem, terribilis ut castrorum acies ordinata.

Pulchra es, inquit, amica mea, suavis et decora sicut Jerusalem: pulchra, intentione, suavis locutione, decora operatione ac ideo mihi sanctae amicitiae inviolabili foedere copulanda. Et quomodo ista 1209Apulchritudo, vel suavitas, sive decor apparent? Sicut Jerusalem. Quid autem Jerusalem interpretatur, nisi visio pacis? Tres autem qualitates hujus visionis sub nomine Jerusalem denotantur: una terrestris, altera spiritualis, tertia coelestus; et media quidem ad similitudinem extremorum constituitur, cum tamen ipsa sit primae supergressio, ultimae vero praeparatio. Quomodo autem media ad similitudinem extremarum constituitur? in mente cujusque sunt virtutes, quasi animae cives et domestici, quibus opponuntur vitia et peccata, quasi 209 ipsius animae hostis amarissimi. Datur autem ei similitudo a terrenae pacis visione, ut quomodo civitas de victis et expulsis hostibus in pace floret, laetatur et proficit, ita mens superatis vitiis et peccatis in delectatione 1209Bvirtutum suaviter quiescit et in Dei gratia pacifice crescit subjecta carne spiritui, eoque magis ad divinitatis contemplationem erigitur, quo minus a terrenis desideriis impugnatur.

Porro alteram similitudinem accipit a supernae pacis visione, sed non omnino comparabilem, quia haec in aenigmate, illa autem in veritate, ut sicut ibi anima ab omni miseria et labore libera jugiter Deum contemplatoria aspicit charitate; ita hic mens ab omni carnis impugnatione liberata ad ejusdem contemplativae vitae dulcedinem quotidiano proficit incremento. Unde ista media recte, ut dictum est, illius ultimae et aeternae potest esse praeparatio, quia per istam pervenitur ad illam: porro primae est supergressio, quia licet aliqua in eis sit ex ratione 1209Csimilitudo, nulla tamen est in dignitate comparatio, dum illa sit mundanae pacis momentanea susceptio, ista supernae aeterna speculatio, quae hic quidem incipit sed ibi perficitur.

Cui ergo istarum trium visionum pacis pulchritudo dilectae comparatur? Si dicamus primae, quae erit comparatio carnis ad spiritum, lucis ad tenebras, temporis ad aeternitatem? Si vero dicamus ultimae, quae comparatio ejus quae adhuc cum timore tenetur, et illius quae ab omni timore libera et secura sine fine conceditur? Mediae ergo comparari potest, ut ista pulchritudo, ista suavitas, iste decor ex intimae pacis visione colligantur, et haec ibi oriantur, proficiant et maneant, ubi nullae animum delectationes 1209Drerum temporalium fatigant, sed cessante pugna carnis et Spiritus, secundum Apostolum: Pax Christi quae exsuperat omnem sensum, custodiat corda et intelligentias (Philip. IV), in amore contemplativae vitae quiescentis. Pulchra es ergo, dilecta, suavis et decora sicut Jerusalem, quemadmodum visio pacatae mentis, quam nulla inquietudinis injuria, nulla adversitatis molestia in sanctae contemplationis jucunditate disturbat.

Quem vero effectum partitur hujus contemplationis jucunditas? profecto magnum, quia totam mentem in Dei et proximi charitate succendit, et malignis spiritibus, animae videlicet suae hostibus, nam subdit, terribilis ut castrorum acies ordinata; acies namque castrorum quando ita ordinatur, 210 ut 1210Aex unanimitate et concordia exercitus insimul dispositi, nullus hosti aditus irrumpendi parere possit, tunc profecto ipsi hosti terribilem se ostendit. Ubi autem hosti aditus irrumpendi ex inordinatione exercitus tribuitur, ibi certe nullo modo terribilis videtur.

Sancta ergo Ecclesia, sive dilecta Deo anima, dum contra malignos spiritus spiritualis certaminis aciem ponit, summopere necesse est ut per charitatem semper unita atque constricta, et nunquam per discordiam interrupta inveniatur, quia, etsi quaelibet bona habuerit, si charitas desit, per malum discordiae locus aperitur in acie, unde ad feriendum hostis valeat intrare. Antiquus enim hostis, neque castitatem, neque abstinentiam, neque 1210Bdistributionem terrenarum rerum, si sine charitate fuerint, timet, quia ipse carne non premitur, ut vel ejus luxuria dissolvatur, vel necessitate ipsius in sumendo cibo, sive divitiarum subsidiis acquirendis urgeatur.

Valde autem charitatem veram, id est amorem humilem, quem sibi fideles vicissim impendunt, timet: et nimis concordiae eorum invidet, quia hanc ipsi tenent in terra, quam ipse tenere nolens amisit in coelo.

Bene ergo dicitur terribilis ut castrorum acies ordinata, quia electorum multitudinem eo maligni spiritus amplius pertimescunt, quo magis eos per charitatis concordiam unitos contra se et conglobatos aspiciunt.

1210CVERS. 4.-- Averte oculos tuos a me, quia ipsi me avolare fecerunt. Capilli tui, sicut grex caprarum, quae apparuerunt de Galaad.

Secunda et tertia pars hoc versu continentur. Dicit ergo, averte oculos tuos a me, quia ipsi me avolare fecerunt; quia, inquit, aedificium tuae mentis a fundamento fraternae charitatis honeste et utiliter surgit intra Jerusalem, id est visionem pacis, pulchritudinem suam longe ostendens, cogitatione, locutione et opere; hoc nimirum ejusdem aedificii summum et supremum, et quasi quaedam conclusio est, ut in uno consummetur cubito, videlicet totam intentionem tuam in Dei solius amore constituendo: unde et istud, o amica, adhuc abundantius mea habes 1210Dex gratia, ut aliquid de mei potentia et claritate purgatae mentis penetrare possis subtilitate. Attamen quantum coneris, quantum animi tui acumen praetendas, labor tuus frustratur, quia incomprehensibilem et incircumscriptum impossibile est aliquo ingenio vel ratione definire.

Qua de re averte oculos tuos a me, hoc est noli divinitatis meae substantiam velle perfecte cognoscere, quod nulli in hac vita conceditur, quin potius ad te ipsam convertere, et memor esto fragilitatis humanae: 211 nam oculi tui, hoc est sensus mentis tuae, in me nimis defixi, ipsi me avolare fecerunt, quia quanto plus in me tenderis, tanto amplius incomprehensibilem probabis, juxta quod scriptum est: Accedet homo ad cor altum et exaltabitur Deus 1211A(Psal. LXIII): quanto quippe ad me accesseris altius atque subtilius substantiae meae proprietatem discutiendo, tanto sublimius avolo, omnem sensus tui considerationem et subtilitatem excedendo. Quapropter averte oculos tuos a me, quia valde quidem perspicaces sunt sensus tui meae gratiae largitate in mentis contemplatione, sed me quasi avolantem prae rei profunditate, prorsus deficiunt in mei consideratione. Sed cum tanta sit gratia oculorum tuorum, quaenam quoque est gratia capillorum?

Capilli, inquit, tui sicut grex caprarum quae apparuerunt de Galaad. Paulo superius laus dilectae iisdem decantata est modis, quos ideo nunc repetit, vel ut ostendat eamdem debere eam habere habitus et animi decorem et pulchritudinem in verbi 1211BDei praedicatione, pro auditorum eruditione, quam habuit in contemplationis solitudine pro suimet utilitate; vel quod commendabilior est sancta Ecclesia sive universalis sive particularis in suo gemino ordine ex quo constituitur, videlicet praepositorum et subjectorum, in quibus omnis ejus pulchritudo, decus et honestas consideratur, ex illorum quidem vita et doctrina, ex istorum vero obedientia et disciplinae reverentia.

Nam quemadmodum capilli de capite nascentes capiti adhaerent, ita subjecti praelatis, qui eos verbo vitae genuerunt, fide et moribus adhaerent; quasi de Galaad ascendentes, quia, dum eis docentibus acervum testimonii, hoc est sacrae Scripturae ferunt, vitam suam ad coelum bene conversando sustollunt.

1211CVERS. 5.-- Dentes tui sicut grex ovium quae ascenderunt de lavacro, omnes gemellis fetibus, et sterilis non est in eis.

Hic quarta pars attingitur. Quid vero per dentes nisi doctores intelliguntur, grossitudinem litterae in subtilitatem spiritualis sensus traducentes et simplicitate candidi, tanquam lavacro sanctae compunctionis loti, unde et ipsi gemina sunt charitate fecundi, sive duplici testamento instructi, et sibi subjectos eadem charitate eodemque testamento reddunt fecundos, ita instruendo ut nullus inter eos, hoc est praepositos vel subjectos, virtutum sterilitate detorpeat.

Particularis vero animae capilli de principalitate mentis quasi de 212 capite nati, sunt cogitationum 1211Dsubtilitates acervum divinarum sententiarum intendentes: porro dentes ejusdem mentis tractantis et retractantis vehementes cum studio applicationes duras et fortes Scripturarum propositiones sive oppositiones infringentes, et plurima earum involucra expedientes. In quibus nulla est sterilitas, quia quanto studiosius animum et diutius applicant Scripturis, tanto vehementius ad amorem Dei et proximi compunguntur, tantoque plenius utriusque Testamenti scientiam assequuntur, sive custodientes praeceptum superaddunt consilium: praeceptum quippe est aliena non rapere, consilium sua tribuere.

Isti nempe sunt gemelli fetus, quibus anima fecundatur, amor videlicet Dei et proximi, scientia 1212AVeteris et Novi Testamenti, observatio praecepti cum superadditione consilii. Horum profecto intentione et studio omnis interior sterilitas propulsatur, ut merito in cogitatione, operatione, praedicatione pulchra, suavis et decora dilecta pronuntietur.

VERS. 6.-- Sicut cortex mali punici, sic genae tuae, absque occultis tuis.

Si universaliter ad totam Ecclesiam referamus, genae ejus possunt dici spiritualiter in ea conversantes, qui dum verbis et factis memorabilibus et mirandis nitens, miraculis quoque stupendis fulgent, quasi in facie Ecclesiae venerabiles apparent; pulchritudo namque genarum in rubore consideratur earum. Sed si tanta est decoris ejus gloria in his quae apparent, quae pura gloria ejus erit in his quae nondum apparent? de quibus scriptum est: quia 1212Bnec oculus vidit, nec auris audivit, quae praeparavit Deus diligentibus se (I Cor. II).

Genae ergo Ecclesiae, cortici mali punici comparantur, sed occulta ejus quia ineffabilia, ideo et incomparabilia sunt.

At si specialiter ad sanctae animae referamus honestatem, plerumque pulchritudo ipsius interior signis quibusdam exterioribus declaratur; nam dum pudor virginalis pudicitiae rubet in facie, hoc foris ostenditur, quod intus in animo tenetur. Genae ergo ejus sunt sicut cortex mali punici absque occultis ejus, quia foris quidem ex verecundia signum quoddam sanctitatis profert, sed quantum in occulto mentis ejus ipsa sanctitas vigeat, illi soli patet, 1212Cquem nihil latere potest. Atque hoc genarum.

213 VERS. 7.-- Sexaginta sunt reginae et octoginta concubinae et adolescentularum non est numerus.

Sexta et septima pars praesenti describitur versu. Nam cum in praecedentibus pulchritudinem Ecclesiae per partes in praelatis et subjectis et spiritualiter conversantibus, qui per capillos, dentes et genas designati sunt, praedicasset, nunc a toto perfectum ejus decorem in unitate fidei celebri laude prosequitur: nam cum sancta Ecclesia aliquo modo pro diversitate meritorum diversa videntur, tamen propter unam eamdemque fidem diversa non invenitur; tres quippe qualitates conversantium in ea considerari possunt, quia sunt in illa et perfecti et minus perfecti et imperfecti: perfecti quidem 1212Dsunt illi, qui omnia sua reliquerunt, et Deo soli tota mente adhaeserunt; minus perfecti, qui non quidem omnia sua reliquerunt, sed de his quae habere possunt, Deo in suis membris ministrare satagunt; imperfecti, qui fide quidem superioribus adhaerent, sed quasi in tenera adhuc conversatione, nondum perfectae bonum discretionis sunt assecuti.

Unde hic non inconvenienter trium numerorum summa inducitur? videlicet senarii, octonarii atque denarii. Denarius quippe per senarium multiplicatus, in sexagenarium surgit, octonarius vero per denarium ductus, octogenarium efficit. Senarius autem perfectus arithmetica lege dicitur, quia cum omnibus suis partibus, quae sunt tres, duo, et unum, 1213Aaltera quippe pars ejus sunt tres, tertia duo, sexta unum insimul aggregatur, in priorem summam absque aliquo augmento, vel detrimento reparatur. Porro octonarius diminutus nuncupatur, quia cum ejus altera pars sint quatuor, quarta duo, octava unum, eisdem partibus aggregatis septenarius conficitur, minor scilicet summo priori quantitate. Denarius vero qui Decalogum legis insinuat, quia ex septenario et trinario constat, septiformem Spiritus sancti gratiam et fidem sanctae Trinitatis confessio, qui numerus perfecti, qui imperfecti demonstrant Deest aliquid.. Ipse enim Spiritus sanctus in donorum suorum effectibus ostendit qui Deum perfecte, qui minus diligant, qui adhuc neque timorem neque amorem Dei habeant.

1213BDuo quippe sunt quae nos omnino Deo subjectos efficiunt, timor videlicet et amor: cujus potentia quidem et sapientia maxime timorem 214 incutiunt, cum eum quem esse scimus, et cuncta quae voluerit punire posse, et nihil latere cognoscimus; begninitas autem ejus specialiter ad amorem pertinet, ut quem benignissimum habemus potissimum diligamus. Ex qua etiam certum est eum ulcisci impietatem velle, quia quo plus ei placet aequitas, magis displicet iniquitas, sicut scriptum est: Dilexisti justitiam et odisti iniquitatem (Psal. XLIV).

Sexagenario ergo numero qui per senarium, perfectus, denario multiplicatum conficitur, perfectorum vita exprimitur, qui perfecte praecepta 1213Cdivina non observarent, nisi primo timorem initialem, postea amorem filialem ipsum timorem excludentem haberent. Et tales animae bene reginae nuncupantur, quia divina cooperante gratia sciunt et possunt se per rationem et intellectum regere, quando discernunt utilitatem, gloriam, et honorem in boni exsecutione, porro damnum, miseriam, et horrorem in mali perpetratione, ideoque bonum fortiter affectant, malum fortiter declinant.

Octogenario vero numero, qui denario per octonarium, qui diminutus dicitur, ducto completur, minus perfectorum vita denotatur, qui praecepta quidem divina observant, sed non ita perfecte Deum amant, ut omnia terrena relinquere valeant. Istae vero animae concubinarum nomine designantur, quia, 1213Dquamvis per bona opera Deo jungantur, nondum tamen jus illud divinum adepti sunt de quo dicitur, Qui adhaeret Deo unus cum eo Spiritus efficitur (I Cor. VI): haec est enim plenaria spiritualis dotis conscriptio, ut qui funditus renuntiant saeculo, nunquam a divino separentur consortio. Adolescentularum vero numerus non definitur, quia infinitus est numerus imperfectorum, qui adhuc sub primitiis fidei constituti, majorum eruditione indigent ad concipiendum timorem Dei, per quem quandoque ad ipsius proficiant amorem.

In quibus nonnulli sunt de quibus plerumque dubia est aestimatio, dum non omnes ad electorum 1214Asortem pertineant, juxta vocem Dominicam quae dicit: Multi sunt vocati pauci vero electi (Matth. XX).

VERS. 8.-- Una est columba mea, perfecta mea: una est matri suae, electa genitrici suae. Viderunt eam filiae et beatissimam praedicaverunt: reginae et concubinae laudaverunt eam.

Cum vero tam diversae sint qualitates meritorum in Ecclesia; num ideo diversa esse dicitur? minime; sed sicut sequitur, una est columba mea, perfecta mea, una est matri suae, electa genitrici suae. Unde una? videlicet 215 propter unam eamdemque fidei et sacramentorum susceptionem, et propter unius Dei cultum, similemque religionis ritum: una est enim fides, sicut dicit Apostolus, unum baptisma, unus Deus et Pater omnium, qui super omnes est 1214Bin omnibus nobis (Ephes. IV).

Una est, inquit, columba mea, perfecta mea: nam aliter non est columba mea nisi pacis et misericordiae signum ferens in ore unitatem spiritus servet in corde et virtutem misericordiae exerceat in opere: Misericordia enim et veritas obviaverunt sibi, justitia et pax osculatae sunt (Psal. LXXXIV), misericordiam quippe et judicium semper cantare debet (Psal. C), in concessa sibi a me potestate ligandi atque solvendi. Neque aliter perfecta mea erit nisi plenam habeat scientiam discretionis, ut sciat quis juste et digne ligandus sit sive solvendus. Una est autem columba et una perfecta mea, quia extra illam non datur remissio peccatorum, neque distributio donorum, ideoque excluduntur, qui unam, 1214Csanctam, catholicam et universalem Ecclesiam non confitentur. In una enim domo agnus comeditur et ejus carnes extra non efferuntur, quia nulla est sacramentorum efficacia, nisi in una catholica Ecclesia.

Una est matri suae, id est Jerusalem supernae, quia quae hic in terris una est in fide et sacramentorum dignitate, ibi in coelis una erit in aeternae vitae beatitudine: una enim est beatitudo sanctorum, quamvis non uno modo ea fruantur, propter diversorum meritorum qualitates. Electa genitrici suae, id est Ecclesiae antiquorum Patrum, videlicet patriarcharum et prophetarum, quorum imitata fidem haereditavit promissionem: 1214Dnam ipsa electa est, cui exhiberetur illa promissio propositi Dei quae in primis diebus facta ad Patres in novissimis diebus impleta est, eadem fide eam justificante de praeteritis et futuris, quae Patres antiquos justificavit solummodo de futuris. Fides enim est tam de praesentibus et futuris quam de praeteritis; licet abusive et non proprie dicatur fides de praesentibus: cum enim Apostolus fidem definiens dicit: Fides et substantia sperandarum rerum, argumentum non apparentium (Hebr. XI), profecto liquet, quia fides illarum rerum est argumentum, quae apparere non possunt, quae enim sunt apparentia fidem non habent, sed agnitionem.

Sed quia agimus de Canticis canticorum, num 1215Aaliquid ad ea attinet duorum numerorum supra positorum, sexagenarii scilicet et octogenarii, musica speculatio? Non sane extra rem videtur esse, si ubi de canticis agitur, modos canendi interdum speculemur. Etenim cum tota animae corporisque nostri compago musica coaptatione conjuncta sit, perspicuum est et exemplis probatum, ex auctoritate divinae et humanae Scripturae ad componendos, 216 vel ad commovendos, sive ad pacandos animos multum valuisse vim musicae harmoniae. Nunquid et in hoc Cantico canticorum, quod totum intendit ad amorem coelestis sponsi animos accendere, non debet valere ad compositionem vel commotionem animae aliqua speculatio musicae consonantiae? Certe et in hoc loco ad modicum suffragari 1215Bpoterit imperfectioni concubinarum et adolescentularum, quatenus incitentur aliquo modo ad assequendam perfectionem, quam eas nondum constat habere.

Sed quia omnis concinna dispositio numerorum proportionibus assignatur, videndum quae consonantia in horum duorum numerorum sexagenarii et octogenarii proportionalitate consistat. Est ergo octogenarii ad sexagenarium habitudo ἐπιτριτα sive sesquitertia, quia octogenarius totum in se habet sexagenarium, et ejus tertiam partem, id est viginti, qua proportio in musica διατέσσερον consonat; dicitur διατέσσερον de quatuor, eo quod quatuor vocibus resonet, constans duobus tonis et semitono.

1215CSi quaeritur quid ad rem hoc in loco per istorum numerorum proportionem hujus symphoniae consideratio? respondemus satis competentem in hujusmodi consideratione esse rationem, quia tota universalis Ecclesia per quatuor mundi partes diffusa, quae, ut dictum est, tribus qualitatibus in ea conversantium, hoc est perfectorum, minus perfectorum, imperfectorum distinguitur, per fidem et sacramenta Novi Testamenti, quod quatuor Evangeliorum perfectione institutum est, omnem suae salutis summam consequitur, ut quasi quidam suavis concentus διατέσσερον symphoniae evangelistarum consonantia quatuor libris velut quatuor constans vocibus quibus omnium Christianonorum animus ad sacrae religionis commovetur et 1215Dcomponitur cultus.

Viderunt eam filiae Sion et beatissimam praedicaverunt, reginae et concubinae laudaverunt eam. Talem, inquit, Ecclesiam, ut dictum est, meritorum qualitate distantem, sed fidei et sacramentorum unitate similem, viderunt filiae Sion, hoc est animae mentis speculatione non carnali visione intendentes et compensantes totius Ecclesiae pulchritudinem et honestatem, in spiritualium dignitatum excellentia, et virtutum gratia, ipsius quoque pulchritudinis necessariam utilitatem, dum in ea consistant et temporalium largior et salubrior concessio, ut aeternorum incomparabilis et nunquam terminabilis attributio: proinde eam beatissimam praedicaverunt, quia nihil beatius quam Deum semper habere, 1216Ahic temporaliter eo in suis donis utendo, ibi aeternaliter fruendo.

217 Reginae quoque et concubinae laudaverunt eam, quia sanctis animabus quae sciunt ratione sensus suos interiores et exteriores regere, valde placet ista sanctae Ecclesiae honestas et honestatis utilitas, multumque laudant, hoc est approbant operationum ejus spiritualia insignia et rerum sacramentalium pia suffragia.

VERS. 9.-- Quae est ista quae progreditur quasi aurora consurgens, pulchra ut luna, electa ut sol, terribilis ut castrorum acies ordinata?

Unde et istae filiae Sion, sive ipse dilectus, hanc ejus pulchritudinem praedicantes, non interrogative quasi ignorantes, sed affirmative quasi demirantes, 1216Bquam bene quidem agnoscunt, tali praeconio, quasi octava attollunt voce et dicunt:

Quae est ista, quae progreditur quasi aurora consurgens, pulchra ut luna, electa ut sol, terribilis ut castrorum acies ordinata? Non transeunter sed diligenter hic inspicientibus in hujusmodi laudis modulo offertur praelibatae symphoniae, quam διατέσσερον diximus, non contemnenda modulatio, qua subinnuitur fidei, spei, charitatis, et sacramentorum confirmatio et per quatuor partes mundi Evangelii praedicatio, quatuor quoque virtutum principalium utilis et necessaria assecutio. Cur enim hic non attendatur quasi quatuor vocum distinctio, rerum diversarum quatuor comparatio, videlicet aurorae progressio, lunae pulchritudo, solis electio, 1216Caciei ordinatae fortitudo. Nam quid amplius est in decore totius Ecclesiae? Denique si desint fides, spes, charitas et sacramenta, si non recipitur Evangelii praedicatio, si non adsint quatuor virtutum fundamenta, de quibus omnium aliarum virtutum surgunt aedificia, quae erit Ecclesiae, sive cujusque sanctae animae pulchritudo?

Sed videndum quid insinuent istae similitudines rerum, qualiter competant ad supra dicta, videlicet fidem, spem, charitatem et sacramenta. Aurora initium est diei, porro fides initium est sanctitatis et religionis veluti cujusdem diei, quia nomine diei et luminis sanctitas accipitur sicut et nomine noctis ac tenebrarum peccatum. Ecclesia 1216Dergo sive quaelibet sancta anima quasi aurora progreditur, quia divina vocante gratia primo ad fidem venit et per eamdem gratiam quotidie ejusdem fidei incrementa capit. Luna vero a sole semper lumen accipit, atque in alia parte hemispherii contra solem posita plenum sui orbis lumen terris infundit; sed cum deficere incipit, ad solem revertitur, ut iterum ab eo reaccendatur, demumque sui luminis 218 plenitudine mundo suffragetur. Unde autem sancta Ecclesia, sive sancta quaelibet anima lumen scientiae, lumen quoque sanctitatis et justitiae, et sanctae spei accipit, nisi ab illo vero sole justitiae Domino Jesu Christo, qui illuminat omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum? (Joan. I.) Sed quia valde differt pulchritudo ejus ab illius 1217Apulchritudine, a quo accipit ut pulchra sit, non absolute pulchra, sed per comparationem pulchra dicitur ut luna: nam quemadmodum luna soli comparata, sive cum sole lucens non lucet: quidquid tamen luminis habet a sole habet, ita et sancti Sancto sanctorum comparati non sunt, quidquid tamen sanctitatis habent, ab ipso habent. Quid autem est Ecclesia, nisi sanctorum collectio? cumque a divina contemplatione causa fraternae dilectionis, vel objectu propriae fragilitatis, plerumque recedens a lumine subtilis intelligentiae paululum defecerunt, se ad se quandoque recolligentes, ad illum tota mente recurrunt, de quo scriptum est: Accedite ad eum et illuminamini (Psal. XXXIII), ut illum quasi per quoddam mentis oppositum respicientes, 1217Bsuam qualemcunque plenitudinem recipiant ab eo, de quo dicitur: Et de plenitudine ejus omnes nos accepimus (Joan. I).

Quid ergo isti fide fideique operibus progredientes nisi spem concipiunt? Qui enim non sperent futura bona, quorum opera sunt luminis plena; ut merito in eis Ecclesia dicatur pulchra ut luna?

Sed cum fides sit quasi aurora progrediens, hoc est primum religionis et sanctitatis suae lumen effundens, per fidem utique ad spem acceditur, quia quod credimus, quandoque nos adepturos speramus. Unde Apostolus (Rom. V): Accessum, inquit, habemus per fidem in gratiam istam in qua stamus, et gloriam in spe gloriae filiorum Dei; ac si aliis verbis dicat: Per fidem quae est principium et 1217Cquasi quidam introitus totius boni operis, quemadmodum aurora diei accedimus et proficimus in gratiam pleni luminis, id est sanctitatis, juxta modum quem ipsa nobis gratia concesserit, in cujus luminis gratia stamus, hoc est perseveramus, quia spem habemus per hanc associari futurae gloriae filiorum Dei: statimque subinfert: Non solum autem, subauditur in hac spe gloriamur, sed et gloriamur in tribulationibus, scientes quod tribulatio patientiam operatur, patientia autem probationem, probatio vero spem, spes autem non confundit. Et ut ostenderet causam efficientem hujus spei certitudinem, subdit, quia charitas diffusa est in cordibus nostris per sanctum qui datus est nobis. Haec est enim anchora 1217Dtotius bonae intentionis et operationis, quia, ut idem dicit Apostolus: Charitas nunquam excidet (I Cor. XIII).

219 Hoc est autem quod sequitur, electa ut sol, videlicet propter charitatem, quia sicut sol omnibus astris clarior est, ita charitas omnibus virtutibus excellentior est, quamvis secundum divinitatem prorsus incomparabilis. Sancta vero Ecclesia in his qui perfecta charitate ardent et operatione lucent, electa ut sol dicitur, quia, cum stella ab stella differat in claritate (I Cor. XV), ea pars sanctorum soli comparatur quae caeteris sanctitate clarior invenitur, nempe in his qui adhuc debiles et teneri sunt in fide et opere, quasi aurora progreditur; in illis vero qui processu conversationis jam aliquantulum 1218Aprofecerunt, pulchra ut luna dicitur: porro in illis qui perfecti sunt, et per charitatem quae perfecta foras mittit timorem, in summorum spirituum, qui seraphim, id est ardentes nuncupantur, transeuntes vero soli vicinius conjunguntur, recte electa ut sol memoratur, sive electa ut sol, id est, praedestinata in adoptionem, ut ipsa hoc sit per gratiam, quod ille verus sol est per naturam, qui dedit potestatem filios Dei fieri his qui credunt in nomine ejus (Joan. I).

Quid vero ad sacramenta pertinet, dicet aliquis, quartum hoc membrum quasi quarta vox praescriptae δια τεσσερον symphoniae: terribilis ut castrorum acies ordinata? Plane, inquam, satis pertinet et hoc ex ipsorum sacramentorum effectibus constat, nam quid 1218Bterribilius est hostibus animae, hoc est malignis spiritibus, quam virtutes sacramentorum, quibus eorum virtus debilitatur, omnisque potestas et audacia fugatur?
