Ubi enim quodcunque sacramentum ita peragitur, ut res quoque sacramenti adesse possit, hoc est in pace et unitate Ecclesiae, extra quam non est locus salutarium sacramentorum, ibi profecto valde terribilis et importabilis est ipsis malis spiritibus ejusdem sacramenti effectus, sive hoc sit in baptismate, sive in Dominico corpore, sive in ordinum distributione, sive in quarumcunque rerum ordinatione, quae ecclesiasticis peraguntur institutis; hoc enim insinuare videtur 1218Ccomparatio ista, qua dicitur terribilis ut castrorum acies ordinata: quia sicut bene vincta acies, et ordinatim constipata nullam sui irruptionem patitur, ita Ecclesia unitatis sacramento colligata nulla malignorum spirituum incursione dissipatur. Haeretici vero qui se ab hac unitate praeciderunt, quia in hac acie non continentur, foris positi nullas ipsorum spirituum adversitates repellere valent, quando quidem sacramenta Ecclesiae quae videntur habere, non habent in re, sed tantum in specie. Ipsa tamen sacramenta recte ab eis celebrata, si fideles accipiunt, et 220 sacramentum et rem sacramenti, hoc est virtutem interius operantem accipiunt: dum ipsi haeretici sacramentum quidem, non autem rem sacramenti sumere comprobentur, 1218Dideoque illorum collectio non est terribilis ut castrorum acies ordinata, quia quantum ad eos non hoc operantur sacramenta, quae nulla eis conferunt remedia.

VERS. 10.-- Descendi in hortum nucum ut viderem poma convallium, et inspicerem si floruissent vineae, et germinassent mala punica.

Postquam dilectus pulchritudinem dilectae sanctae, videlicet Ecclesiae, gratiosa prosecutus est laude, cujus tamen eadem laus ex ipso est, qui sua gratia illam sibi exhibuit, non habentem maculam aut rugam (Ephes. V), ostendit in sequentibus, propter incredulitatem Judaici populi istam promeruisse donum et meritum fidei, sicut dicit Apostolus: Illorum delicto salus gentibus, et delictum eorum deliciae 1219Amundi, et diminutio illorum divitiae gentium (Rom. XI). Qui enim istam admirativo modo extulit, eodem modo illam deprimit, quia ista credente et verbum Dei suscipiente, illa neque credere neque ipsum verbum suscipere voluit: unde scriptum est de ea in Evangelio: Et mirabatur, haud dubium quin Jesus, super incredulitate illorum (Marc. VI). Dicit ergo, descendi in hortum nucum. Quid fuit ejus descendere, nisi de divinitatis suae celsitudine in mundum istum nascendo venire, deinde omnia humanitatis infirma tolerare? Nonne haec omnia suo ordine completa quidam descensus fuerunt? Ubi autem descensus isti celebrati sunt? Nonne in Judaea? Denique ipse Dominus dicit: Non sum missus nisi ad oves quae perierunt domus Israel (Matth. XV), hoc 1219Best enim quod hic dicit, descendi in hortum nucum; hortus enim nucum non inconvenienter dici potest gens Judaeorum: sicut enim in nuce sub cortice et testa nucleus tegitur, ita apud Judaeos spiritualis intelligentiae dulcedo sub duritia litteralis superficiei absconditur. Illa ergo gens hortus nucum dicitur, quia quamvis propter legalium utilitatem praeceptorum et observationum, quae suo tempore florebant, suisque observatoribus usque ad tempus gratiae proderant, hortus dicatur, omnia tamen futura Ecclesiae sacramenta, in eo sub figura, quasi sub nucis cortice latebant. In hunc itaque hortum Dominus descendit, quia in primis Judaico populo suae carnis praesentiam praedicando et miracula faciendo exhibuit.

1219CQuare autem in hunc hortum descendit? Ut viderem, inquit, poma convallium, hoc est, ut cognoscerem utrum aliquae fructum fidei et injustitiae fecissent, atque ratione ostendente intelligerent quod ex 221 operibus legis justificari non possint, sed ex fide quam proposui credentibus per gratiam Novi Testamenti. Dico autem ut cognoscerem, non quod hoc vel aliud quid in praesentia mea ab aeterno non habuerim, qui ubique sum, et cui omnia praeterita et futura praesentia sunt, sed humano more loquens, eorum opera mundo ostenderem utrum sequenda essent an non. Cur vero dico convallium? Propter humilitatem litterae quam carnaliter exsequuntur, sive propter umbram legis qua circumdatur, 1219Dne veritatis suae luce illustrentur.

Et inspicerem si floruissent vineae, hoc est si saltem aliquem saporem spiritualis intelligentiae concepissent, si aliquo initio boni operis fidei se applicuissent: vineae enim dicuntur domus Israel, quae per tribus duodecim distinctae sunt; quae cum vineae dicantur propter distinctionem tribuum, una tamen dicuntur vinea, propter unam legis observantiam; sicut cum multae nunc dicantur Ecclesiae propter diversitatem locorum, una tamen dicitur Ecclesia propter unitatem fidei. Quod vero universitas illius populi vinea Domini dicatur, Propheta testatur. Vinea, inquit, Domini domus Israel est (Isa. V); de qua dicit et Psalmista: Vineam de Aegypto transtulisti (Psal. LXIX); sed cum exspectarem ut haec vinea 1220Afloreret et uvam faceret, fecit labruscas (Isa. V). nam postquam gentes crediderunt, ipsi in incredulitate permanserunt.

Descendi etiam, ut inspicerem si germinassent mala punica, hoc est, ut non tantum in me crederent, sed etiam pro me patiendi voluntatem haberent: at illi neque credere, neque aliquid propter me pati voluerunt, quin imo me eis praedicantem, et viam salutis ostendentem occiderunt.

Alio quoque modo per similitudinem nucis hanc particulam praesentis cantici exponere non videtur onerosum, quatenus lector eligat quod in his melius et rectius pensat. Hortum nucum universitatem generis humani accipere non videtur absurdum, in nuce enim tria considerantur, cortex, testa et nucleus; 1220Bin humano autem genere constat homo carne, osse et anima; carnis namque materies est quasi cortex, virtus vero ossea est quasi testa, porro animae dulcedo est quasi nucleus: et sicut nucleus cortice et testa tegitur, ita anima carne et ossibus vestitur. Unde his tribus hominem constare Job considerans dicit: Pelle et carne vestisti me, ossibus et nervis compegisti me (Job X). Et ut tertium quod duo illa vivificat et vegetat, hoc est animam, ostenderet, subdit: Vitam et misericordiam tribuisti mihi (ibid.). In hortum ergo nucum Christus descendit, quando humanam naturam in hunc mundum veniendo suscepit.

Et quare? Ut videret poma convallium 222, hoc est, ut visitaret humiles fructum justitiae habentes, 1220Ceosque sibi eligeret, videre quippe ejus eligere est, quatenus humilis veniens, insinuaret se humiles et obedientes suscipere, sicut scriptum est: Et humiles spiritu salvabit (Psal. XXXIII). Descendit quoque ut inspiceret si floruissent vineae, et germinassent mala punica, hoc est, si fidelium Ecclesiae recte vivendi sive docendi studium inchoassent, et usque ad mortem in ejus dilectione perseverare contenderent, quatenus suum eis adjutorium impendendo ipse et inspirator et cooperator exsisteret, quemadmodum eis promittens dicit: Ecce ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus usque ad consummationem saeculi (Matth. XXVIII).

1220DVERS. 11.-- Nescivi: anima mea conturbavit me, propter quadrigas Aminadab.

Causam ignorantiae et caecitatis suae praetendit populus Judaeorum, quod postquam lex data fuerat, quae eos justificaret et salvaret, et hanc Deus multis signis et magnis sanctorum Patrum auctoritatibus confirmasset, impossibile foret hanc aliqua novitate evacuari cum Deus sit immutabilis, nec humano more aliquid in uno tempore dicat, praecipiat et instituat, quod alio tempore prohibeat et destruat. Si enim, inquiunt, hoc in futuro displicet quod nunc placet, mutabilis est, quod absurdissimum est dicere, nec aliqua ratione potest constare, Deum mutabilem esse. Si autem ipse incommutabilis est, verba quoque ejus atque praecepta incommutabilia sunt: sed quia ipse est omnino incommutabilis, quidquid 1221Adixit vel constituit, fixum et incommutabile esse necesse est, nullam ergo legem secundam et novam posuit, ut primam et antiquam destrueret.

Quibus respondetur, concedendum esse quid proposuerint, videlicet Deum incommutabilem esse, unde in nova lege nihil constituisse quod priori derogarit, quin potius eamdem esse legem novam et antiquam, sed illam in littera, hanc in spiritu; illam in figura, istam in veritate. Quod ita esse, olim in visione Ezechielis prophetae praemonstratum est, ubi rota in medio rotae (Ezech. X) visa esse memoratur. Rota quippe in medio rotae est Testamentum Novum inter Testamentum Vetus, quia quod Vetus Testamentum designavit, hoc Novum exhibuit: nihil ergo Deus incommutabilis in hoc mutavit, qui alterum 1221Baltero ita supposuit, ut unum esset significans, aliud significatum.

Hoc ergo primo populus iste nescivit, quia significans legit, sed significatum non intellexit: postquam vero divina visitatus gratia coepit cognoscere et credere litteram esse occidentem, spiritum vero 223 vivificantem, poenitens erroris sui expavit dicens: Nescivi: anima mea turbavit me propter quadrigas Aminadab. Ac si diceret: Ideo credere non potui, quia gratiam Evangeiii minime adhuc intellexi, nam turbavit me anima mea, quia mirabar quidnam esset, quod quatuor libros Evangeliorum nunc deberem recipere qui prius quinque libros Moysi receperam, quasi haec mutatio in Deum caderet, ut ei hoc modo non placeret quod prius placuerat, 1221Cqui novam conderet legem vetere translata. At postquam mirabilem Dei providentiam intellexi, qui me per carnalia ad spiritualia erudiebat, ut non prius spirituale, sed quod animale, deinde quod spirituale, facilius et veracius comprehenderem, deposita omni dubietate veritatem quam prius impugnabam, postea defendebam, non tantum ipsam veritatem credendo et docendo, sed etiam pro ea moriendo.

Cur autem dico quadrigas Aminadab? nimirum propter quatuor libros Evangelii, in quibus praedicantur quatuor sacramenta ejusdem Aminabad, qui interpretatur spontaneus populi mei. Quis est autem iste Aminabad, nisi Christus qui sponte posuit 1221Danimam suam, ut me sibi faceret populum spontaneum Deoque acceptabilem? Quae porro ejus sunt quatuor sacramenta nisi incarnatio, passio, resurrectio et ascensio illius? Quadriga ergo Aminabad hujus liber est quatuor Evangeliorum continens et conferens quatuor praedictorum sacramentorum cognitionem, aurigante Spiritu sancto, cujus inspiratione compositae et ordinatae sunt hujusmodi quadrigae.

Cumque eumdem populum qui ex circumcisione crediderat, tetra ignorantiae caligine excussa, ad se revertentem benignus Pater susciperet, quasi consolatoria et exhortatoria voce ei occurrens, ad poenitentiam provocat dicens: Revertere, revertere, Sunamitis, etc.

1222AVERS. 12.-- Revertere, revertere, Sunamitis; revertere, revertere, ut intueamur te.

Ecce, inquit, occurrit sibi vox quadrigae meae, quae resonat causam et ordinem atque necessariam utilitatem sacramentorum meorum, videlicet nativitatis, passionis, resurrectionis et ascensionis meae, quam vocem quidem prius ignorans neque audire, neque recipere voluisti, sed nunc, o Sunamitis, id est captiva quae adhuc captiva teneris eo quod nondum per baptismi ablutionem corporisque et sanguinis mei, participationem originalis sive actualis peccati nexus deposuisti, revertere, quia spem habes veniae. Recessisti enim a me per incredulitatem et ingratitudinem, oblitus beneficiorum quae erga te operatus fui, quando te de Aegypti 1222Bservitute liberavi, quando te 224 coelesti pane pavi, quando tibi legem meam dedi, et prae omnibus gentibus te mihi in populum peculiarem elegi. Sed nunc revertere ad me per vocem quadrigae meae, per quatuor Evangelia, quasi per quatuor rotas ad te clamantis et te ad poenitentiam quater adhortantis, revertere, revertere, revertere, revertere. Revertere per fidem, revertere per operationem, revertere per rectam intentionem, revertere per dilectionem: primo namque debes credere, deinde operari, quia fides sine operibus mortua est (Jac. II); porro operatio tua debet ex bona intentione procedere, ea videlicet, ut fides per dilectionem operetur; nam operatio tua si non est ex dilectione divina, vanae 1222Cgloriae subjacet, atque ideo mercede caret, quia meritum sanctitatis non habet.

Revertere autem ut intueamur te, hoc est, ut decorem animae tuae quem per fidem accepisti, approbemus, et aliis te sequendam pro exemplo ponamus: haec est enim tua laudabilis pulchritudo quae placet oculis nostris, ut errore deposito veritatem sequaris, et quae per errorem et umbram legis, deformis et obscura videbaris, per reversionem, per veritatem et lucem Evangelii formosa et clara conspiciaris. Quandiu enim sub umbra latebas, despicabilis eras, postquam vero ad veritatis lucem existi conspicabilis apparuisti, et nunc concupivit rex decorem tuum (Psal. XLIV), ille videlicet Rex coelestis 1222Dqui te fecit sponsam per Spiritus sancti gratiam, postquam ad eum reversa es fide, operatione, recta intentione, dilectione; haec quidem dicta sunt specialiter, quantum ad illum antiquum Dei populum, qui Aminadab nostri quadrigam, quanto minus primo intellexit, tanto amplius postquam intellexit venerata suscepit.

Ut autem ad moralitatem revertamur, potest non inutiliter referri ad humani generis universitatem hujus quadrigae significatio, ita ut de toto duas constituamus partes, quarum uni eam demus quadrigam cujus auriga sit diabolus. Homo namque constans ex quatuor elementis, et quatuor humoribus, quatuor quoque aetatum incrementis, quasi quamdam materialem videtur habere quadrigam 1223Aex parte corporis: porro ex parte animae dum constat quatuor affectionibus, quatuor etiam virtutibus quibus ad bonum ducitur, ipsius animae vis et profectus videntur spiritualem habere quadrigam.

Videamus ergo primo quantulaecunque animo occurrerint per quaternarium dispositas in homine secundum corpus complexiones, deinde secundum animam etiam quadriformiter designatas affectuum qualitates, ut ex his, sicut diximus, 225 duas constituamus quadrigas, materialem scilicet et affectualem, quae utraeque ad duos respicientes quadrigas, Christum videlicet et diabolum, alteri eorum subjiciantur, dum non possint duobus servire dominis (Matth. VI), et aut per Dei gratiam spiritualis recte ac feliciter currens dicatur quadriga Christi, 1223Baut per privationem ejusdem gratiae carnalis perverse ac infeliciter currens dicatur quadriga diaboli.

Quatuor itaque ut diximus sunt elementa, quibus constat homo, ignis, aer, aqua, terra; quae quatuor intermiscentur qualitatibus, videlicet calore, frigiditate, humiditate, siccitate. Ignis quippe calidus est et siccus, aer calidus et humidus, aqua frigida et humida, terra frigida et sicca: ipse autem homo his quatuor constans elementis, elementorumque qualitatibus, dum habet calorem ex igne, spiritum ex aere, sanguinem ex aqua, carnem ex terra, in quatuor temporibus, quatuor permutatur humoribus per quatuor aetatum incrementa.

1223CVer quippe qui est quasi primus flos et principium anni: tunc enim terra florere incipit et germinare, et est calidus et humidus; pueritiam praetendit quae est calida et humida, quia in puero sanguis est calidus et humidus; aestas vero quae est calida et sicca adolescentiam ostendit, quae est calida et sicca, colera habens rubea quae abundant in adolescentibus sicca et calida. Porro autumnus qui est frigidus et siccus juventutem denuntiat, quae est frigida et sicca, habens melancolica, id est colera nigra, quae sunt in juvenibus frigida et sicca. Hiems autem quae est frigida et humida senectutem insinuat, quae est frigida et humida, labens flegma, quod in senibus abundat frigidum et humidum.

Hujusmodi nempe complexiones quando in homine 1223Dbene et ordinate vigent, hominem sanum ostendunt, quando vero inordinate vagantur, hominem perturbant et infirmum efficiunt: sed quia haec quadriformis constitutio materialiter in corpore hominis est, ex qua trahitur ipse homo ad amorem carnis et mundi hujus desideria, quae contraxit ex traduce peccati originalis, nascuntur quoque ex hac materiali constitutione quatuor affectuales qualitates, quae principaliter vim et naturam trahunt ex quatuor membris intrinsecis, videlicet felle, splene, jecore et corde. Denique homo habet ex felle ut sit irascibilis, ex splene ut sit risibilis, ex jecore ut sit concupiscibilis, ex corde ut sit rationabilis: porro ex ipso corde sive mente seu animo procedunt quasi quaedam quatuor conceptiones, quae 1224Aomnem praecedunt actionem, videlicet cogitatio, intentio, voluntas, deliberatio. 226 Nam aliquid acturi prius cogitamus, deinde intendimus quare et qualiter id faciamus, post in voluntate faciendum disponimus, postremo perficere deliberamus. At vero ipsa vis rationis quadrifariam diffunditur: qui habet ingenium, memoriam, intellectum, discretionem, habet quippe per ingenium ignota et abscondita quaerendo et investigando invenire, per memoriam inventa retinere, per intellectum retenta prudenter, viriliter et honeste disponere, per discretionem bene disposita modeste locis sibi competentibus assignare.

Quatuor quoque affectiones habet sibi insitas ipsa anima rationalis: hoc est timorem, spem, gaudium 1224Batque tristitiam, de quibus dicit poeta: . . . Hi metuunt, cupiunt, gaudentque, dolentque. Et philosophus cuidam suo alumno quem ab istarum passionum affectionibus relevare cupiebat, dicit: Gaudia pelle, Pelle timorem, Spemque fugato, Nec dolor adsit. Et hae quidem affectiones ab eis qui de physica tractant, dicuntur secundum complexiones materialium qualitatum, quae supra posuimus, in quibusdam magis, in quibusdam minus dominari: sed 1224Cpraeest omnibus his animus ratione vigens, qui ea cum se inordinate ingerunt, componat et ad aliquem modum honestatis vel utilitatis Spiritu regente divino deflectat. Ad hujusmodi vero studium vel disciplinam necessario adhibendae, et a Deo flagitandae sunt quatuor virtutes principales, hoc est prudentia, fortitudo, justitia, temperantia, quae quia in omni spiritualis aedificii structura, quasi quidam angulares ponuntur lapides quibus caeterae virtutes includuntur et retinentur, majora in eis divinae gratiae dona considerantur.

Quia ergo duas constituimus quadrigas, materialem scilicet et affectualem, ponamus quoque quasi duos utrique praesidentes spiritum et carnem, aurigantes vero Deum et diabolum: nam illa affectualis 1224Dtantum plus vel minus movetur ad rationem et honestatem, quantum plus minusve impellitur ab illa materiali per carnis curam ad temporalis vitae amorem; et quantum utrique praesidens superior fuerit vel inferior, spiritus scilicet et caro, quae duo semper sibi invicem adversantur; quia caro concupiscit adversus spiritum, spiritus autem adversus carnem (Gal. V). Etenim idcirco utrique praesidere dicimus spiritum et carnem, quia sunt in eis quaedam partes, quae de carne tendunt ad spiritum, vel de spiritu labuntur ad carnem.

Namque in illa materiali quadriga plerumque aliqui qui naturali 227 carnis calore et humore incitantur tanta per Dei gratiam spiritus fortitudine decertant, ut omnem illum naturalem carnis impetum 1225Aper ignem divini amoris et impetu spiritus frangunt, et funditus quandoque excoquant, atque ita ad Deum incalescunt, ut ad saeculum omnino frigidi remaneant. Econtra aliqui frigidae naturae sicut ad omnem actionem intrinsecus in Dei amore frigent, ideoque ad nullum opus bonum laborando student. In illa quoque affectuali quadriga sunt qui irascuntur pro temporali incommodo, sunt et qui irascuntur pro justitia; sunt quoque, qui concupiscunt bona, sunt qui concupiscunt mala; sunt qui rident et gaudent propter hujus vitae miseram prosperitatem, sunt etiam qui gaudent et rident in adversitatibus propter spem et securitatem futurae beatitudinis; sunt etiam qui bono rationis bene utuntur, et recte agunt et sapiunt; sunt qui male 1225Butuntur et perverse sapiunt et agunt. Sunt nihilominus aliqui qui ingenio naturali ad bonum utuntur, sunt qui ad malum; sunt qui bonum recte, sunt qui male intelligunt, sunt qui recte offerunt, sed non recte dividunt, hoc est discernunt; et sunt qui et recte offerunt et recte dividunt, hoc est discernunt; sicut econtra quidam neque recte offerunt neque recte dividunt, hoc est discernunt.

Unde ambabus quadrigis istis quatuor cohaerent species quae utrasque in plenos proprii studii deducunt motus, videlicet suggestio, delectatio, consensus, consuetudo. Deducitur quippe animus cujusque sive ad bonum sive ad malum, istis quatuor modis, ad bonum quidem suggestione Spiritus sancti, sicut de eo dicitur: Ipse enim suggeret vobis 1225Comnia quaecunque dixero vobis (Joan. XIV); delectatione animae, consensu spiritus, et consuetudine boni ipsius: ad malum vero suggestione diaboli, delectatione carnis consensu spiritus, consuetudine mali ipsius.

In medio ergo istarum quadrigarum, quae ex materia carnis et affectu mentis formantur, quatuor virtutes principales, quas supra posuimus, scilicet prudentia, fortitudo, justitia, temperantia constituantur necesse est, ut ex earum quadam quasi circumpositione tota concretio introrsus positi corporis regatur et ad aliquem modum rationabilis formae componatur. Nam sicut quidam dicit: Virtus est medium vitiorum, et utrinque reductum, 1225D(HOR., Ep. I, XVIII, 9.) hoc est ab utroque parte remotum: verbi gratia hebetem esse vel male callidum vitiosum esse, sed horum in medio vitiorum, scilicet hebetudinis et male calliditatis, prudentiae virtus constituitur, cujus moderamine ista inaequalitas corrigatur: fortitudo quoque inter timiditatem et audaciam ponitur, ut hoc sit vere fortem esse 228 qui nec timidus in bono nec audax in malo invenitur. Similiter et in caeteris videri potest virtutibus, ex quarum consideratione juxta se positarum intelligitur qualitas vitiorum.

Ex tota ergo materia hujusmodi, carnali scilicet et spirituali, quadrifariam distincta, unum quoddam fit materiatum, quod in se quasi geminam praefert quadrigam carnis et spiritus, cui praesit 1226Aaurigans vel Deus vel diabolus: sed Deus regens, salvans et vivificans; diabolus subvertens, damnans et occidens.

Nomen quidem aequivocum est, quod cum utrobique quadriga appelletur, definitione tamen diversum est: nam per suggestionem diaboli et delectationem carnis, consensum quoque spiritus, et consuetudinem mali operis a Deo deficere, est quadrigam diaboli esse; et e converso per suggestionem Dei, et delectationem animae, consensum quoque spiritus, et consuetudinem boni operis ad Deum proficere, est quadrigam Dei esse: et e converso quadriga quoque Dei est mens, quatuor virtutibus quas supra posuimus, hoc est prudentia, justitia, temperantia, fortitudine quadrata; cui opponitur 1226Bquadriga diaboli, mens scilicet quatuor vitiis ipsis virtutibus contrariis, hoc est, stultitia, iniquitate, luxuria, formidine enervata.

Clamat ergo Ecclesia, sive ipse sponsus per Ecclesiam Sunamiti, Revertere, revertere, revertere, revertere, ut quae quatuor his modis deliquerat, quatuor quoque poenitentiae fructus ad Deum revertendo, et haec in se per Dei gratiam et virtutem animi mortificando offerat. Revertere, inquit, per poenitentiam et satisfactionem praeteritorum malorum, revertere per contemptum saeculi, revertere per mortificationem carnis, revertere per virtutum constantiam. Revertere autem ut intueamur te, hoc est ut postquam poenitentiam egeris misereamur tui. Videre enim Dei est misereri: unde Psalmista ad 1226CDeum: Respice, inquit, in me et miserere mei (Psal. LXXXV); et contra aversio vultus ejus, ira est illius, sicut idem Psalmista dicit: Avertisti faciem tuam a me, et factus sum conturbatus (Psal. XXIX).

Quod autem pluraliter dicit: Ut intueamur te, modus ille locutionis est in Deo, quo alibi dicit. Faciamus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram (Gen. III), qui modus inducitur propter pluralitatem personarum in sancta Trinitate,

CHAPTER VI.

206 VERSE 1.-- My beloved is gone down into his garden, to the little bed of spices, that he may feed in the gardens, and gather lilies.

What indeed was it to seek the beloved, but to ascend to him through the power of contemplation? for since in the hearts of the saints faith worketh by love (Gal. V), and love always draws the mind to the things above, to work good is therefore to descend [descendere; read ascendere, "to ascend"] to God in mind. But since all good is from God, without 1207Awhom nothing of good exists, for anyone to be helped by him in good is surely his descending to him; for it is written in Exodus that Moses ascended into the mountain, and the Lord descended to him (Exod. XIX). For as much as each one ascends to God in thought, and in action by seeking him, so much does God descend to him, whether by opening his mysteries to him through the understanding, or by conferring the help of his grace through strength of soul. For where anyone ascends to God by free will, in will and in work, there God descends to him through helping grace, by his mercy and condescension

Whence also here the beloved fittingly answered those desiring to seek the beloved, that my beloved is gone down into his 1207Bgarden: as if she said: Since you desire to know whither my beloved is gone, or whither he has turned aside, behold, I tell thee that my beloved is gone down into his garden. What is the garden of the beloved, but either holy Church or any holy soul sprouting with the diverse beauty of the virtues? into which the beloved descends, because to it as it sprouts with good acts he bestows the help of his grace. But after he has gone down into the garden, whither has he turned himself? to the little bed, she says, of spices. What is the little bed of spices, 207 but a mind planted with various kinds of sweetly fragrant virtues, or sprinkled with the repute of diverse graces as with a good odour? for those who can say with the Apostle: We are the good odour of Christ unto God in every place (II Cor. II), these surely 1207Cin the garden of the Lord, that is, in holy Church, each one in his own manner can be called a little bed of spices, because they spread on the minds of their neighbours the odour of good repute through the examples of good works.

But why does she say not "bed" but, by diminution, little bed, unless because the holy mind which shines with the sublimity of the virtues ought to be little in its own eyes and greatly to show that the Lord is high and looketh on the low things and will save the humble of spirit? (Psal. CXII, XXXIII.) To this little bed, then, the beloved, going down into his garden, turns aside, because to the holy mind, through increases of holiness and knowledge, he shows himself easy and as it were tractable. For every pursuit seems difficult to the beginner, easy to the one grown used to it: and to one entering the way of the commandments of God, or the knowledge of Holy Scripture, 1207Dthe gate seems narrow and the entry difficult, but to one who wears it by long exercise, and as it were thrusts back frequent obstacles, the way of holiness and understanding is opened broad and spacious, and therefore easy ingress and egress thereafter lie open.

She adds, however, the cause why he descended: That he may feed, she says, in the gardens, and gather lilies: he feeds in the gardens because he delights in that odour which is spread from the little bed of spiritual spices, that is, of good works. For he himself says in the Gospel: My meat is to do the will of my Father (Joan. IV); for the will of the Father is that all men be saved (I Tim. II). Further, that men desire salvation and attain to it is his work. And what things the Father works, these same the Son also works, because what 1208Athe Father wills, the Son also wills, and one is the will and operation of both. And he gathers lilies, because he chooses rather those who are white with integrity and cleanness of heart and body, or takes up those perfect in faith and work to be rewarded in eternal beatitude.

VERSE 2.-- I to my beloved, and my beloved to me, who feedeth among the lilies.

My beloved, she says, had above commanded me, saying: Arise, open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my undefiled, and I, obeying him, opened the bolt of my door (Cant. V), by preaching him to all and showing reasonably how great and of what kind he is. But what did my beloved to these things? truly he repays the return of my joyful obedience, chanting to me the praise of his condescension, beatifying not my grace but 1208Bhis own in me. For his was it that I willed, that I was able, that I accomplished, and therefore he himself proclaims his gifts in me, that to me and to all obedient to his grace 208 he may show of how great merit before God is a life obedient to holiness and uprightness.

But of what kind is the beloved? Who feedeth, she says, among the lilies, that is, he delights in clean thought and working, not that he grows into anything by accident, who never receives any increase or loss. Since he remains always unchangeable in one and the same essence and property, but that, by some manner of speech transferred from the creature, the affection of his goodness is expressed toward those 1208Cwhom he has deigned to count worthy of his love and grace. For he is said to feed when, in the mind of anyone which he inhabits by his grace, the progress of the virtues is increased.

With what song, then, or in what mode of song, did the voice of this beloved sound to me? with a sweet song surely, a song to be attended to not moderately, in an eight-stringed mode indeed, but on the several strings, because of the force of each sound, notably disposed with its own theorem in this manner.

VERSE 3.-- Thou art beautiful, my love, sweet and comely as Jerusalem: terrible as an army of a camp set in array.

Here it is pleasing to behold, as a spectacle, how the modulation of the present song runs through eight parts as through eight voices, so that the property of that symphony which 1208Dmusicians call διαπασον may here be attended to, whose last voice is the same as the first, as can be seen also in the disposition of these parts, where, while the first part is set down in this manner, terrible as an army of a camp set in array, the last part is nonetheless ended in the same manner, namely terrible as an army of a camp set in array.

But the several parts demand several reasons, which are distinguished in this manner. The first is, thou art beautiful, my love, sweet and comely as Jerusalem, terrible as an army of a camp set in array.

Thou art beautiful, he says, my love, sweet and comely as Jerusalem: beautiful, in intention, sweet in speech, comely in working, and therefore to be joined to me in the inviolable covenant of holy friendship. And how do this 1209Abeauty, or sweetness, or comeliness appear? As Jerusalem. And what is Jerusalem interpreted, but vision of peace? Now three qualities of this vision are denoted under the name of Jerusalem: one earthly, another spiritual, the third heavenly coelestus; and the middle one indeed is constituted after the likeness of the extremes, while yet it is itself the surpassing of the first and the preparation of the last. And how is the middle one constituted after the likeness of the extremes? in the mind of each one are the virtues, as the citizens and household of the soul, to which are opposed vices and sins, as 209 the most bitter enemies of that soul. And a likeness is given to it from the vision of earthly peace, that as a city, its enemies conquered and driven out, flourishes in peace, rejoices and prospers, so the mind, vices and sins overcome, rests sweetly in the delight 1209Bof the virtues and grows peaceably in the grace of God, the flesh subject to the spirit, and is raised the more to the contemplation of the Godhead, the less it is assailed by earthly desires.

Further, it receives the other likeness from the vision of peace above, but not wholly comparable, because this is in a riddle, but that in truth, so that as there the soul, free from all misery and labour, beholds God continually with contemplative charity, so here the mind, freed from every assault of the flesh, advances by daily increase to the sweetness of that same contemplative life. Whence this middle one rightly, as has been said, can be the preparation of that last and eternal one, because through this one that one is reached: further, it is the surpassing of the first, because although there is some likeness in them in reason, 1209Cyet there is no comparison in dignity, since that is the momentary reception of worldly peace, this the eternal beholding of the peace above, which here indeed begins but there is perfected.

To which, then, of these three visions of peace is the beauty of the beloved compared? If we say to the first, what comparison will there be of flesh to spirit, of light to darkness, of time to eternity? But if we say to the last, what comparison is there of that which is still held with fear, and of that which, free and secure from all fear, is granted without end? To the middle one, then, it can be compared, so that this beauty, this sweetness, this comeliness are gathered from the vision of inward peace, and these things arise there, advance and abide, where no delights 1209Dof temporal things weary the soul, but, the fight of flesh and Spirit ceasing, according to the Apostle: The peace of Christ which passeth all understanding keep the hearts and understandings (Philip. IV) [Vulg. pax Dei, "the peace of God"], of one resting in the love of the contemplative life. Thou art beautiful, then, beloved, sweet and comely as Jerusalem, like the vision of a pacified mind, which no injury of disquiet, no trouble of adversity disturbs in the joyfulness of holy contemplation.

And what effect does the joyfulness of this contemplation impart? surely a great one, because it kindles the whole mind in the charity of God and neighbour, and to the malignant spirits, that is, the enemies of its soul, for she adds, terrible as an army of a camp set in array; for the army of a camp, when it is so set in array 210 that, 1210Afrom the unanimity and concord of the host disposed together, no access of breaking in can open to the enemy, then surely shows itself terrible to that enemy. But where access of breaking in is granted to the enemy through the disorder of the host, there certainly it seems in no way terrible.

Holy Church, therefore, or the soul beloved of God, when it sets the battle line of spiritual combat against the malignant spirits, must of utmost necessity be found always united and bound close through charity, and never broken through by discord, because, even if it should have whatever goods, if charity be lacking, a place is opened in the line through the evil of discord, whence the enemy may be able to enter to strike. For the ancient enemy fears neither chastity, nor abstinence, nor 1210Bthe distribution of earthly things, if they should be without charity, because he himself is not pressed by flesh, so that either he should be undone by its lust, or be urged by its necessity in taking food, or in acquiring the supports of riches.

But he greatly fears true charity, that is, humble love, which the faithful bestow on one another in turn: and he envies their concord exceedingly, because they hold this on earth which he, being unwilling to hold it, lost in heaven.

Well, therefore, is it said terrible as an army of a camp set in array, because the malignant spirits fear the multitude of the elect the more, the more they see them united and massed together against themselves through the concord of charity.

1210CVERSE 4.-- Turn away thy eyes from me, for they have made me flee away. Thy hair is as a flock of goats, which have appeared from Galaad.

The second and third parts are contained in this verse. He says, therefore, turn away thy eyes from me, for they have made me flee away; because, he says, the building of thy mind rises honourably and profitably from the foundation of fraternal charity within Jerusalem, that is, the vision of peace, showing its beauty far off, in thought, speech and work; this truly is the summit and the top of that same building, and as it were a certain conclusion, that it be finished in one cubit, namely by setting thy whole intention on the love of God alone: whence thou hast this also, O love, still more abundantly 1210Dfrom my grace, that thou canst penetrate with the subtlety of a purged mind something of my power and brightness. Yet however much thou strivest, however much thou puttest forward the sharpness of thy soul, thy labour is frustrated, because it is impossible by any wit or reason to define the incomprehensible and uncircumscribed.

Wherefore turn away thy eyes from me, that is, do not wish to know perfectly the substance of my Godhead, which is granted to no one in this life, but rather turn back to thyself, and be mindful of human frailty: 211 for thy eyes, that is, the senses of thy mind, fixed too much on me, have themselves made me flee away, because the more thou stretchest toward me, the more thou wilt prove me incomprehensible, according to what is written: Man shall approach to a deep heart and God shall be exalted 1211A(Psal. LXIII): for the higher and more subtly thou approachest me by examining the property of my substance, the more sublimely do I fly away, by exceeding all the consideration and subtlety of thy sense. Wherefore turn away thy eyes from me, because thy senses are indeed very keen in the contemplation of the mind, by the largess of my grace, but they fail utterly in the consideration of me, as I flee away for the depth of the matter. But since so great is the grace of thy eyes, what too is the grace of the hair?

Thy hair, he says, is as a flock of goats which have appeared from Galaad. A little above, the praise of the beloved was sung in the same modes, which he therefore now repeats, either to show that she ought to have the same comeliness and beauty of bearing and of soul in the preaching of the word 1211Bof God, for the instruction of the hearers, which she had in the solitude of contemplation for her own profit; or because holy Church, whether universal or particular, is more commendable in her twin order from which she is constituted, namely of those set over and of subjects, in whom all her beauty, grace and honour is considered, from the life and doctrine of the former, and from the obedience and reverence for discipline of the latter.

For as the hairs, springing from the head, cleave to the head, so subjects cleave to the prelates who begot them by the word of life, in faith and morals; as it were going up from Galaad, because, while at their teaching they bear the heap of testimony, that is, of Holy Scripture, they lift their life up to heaven by living well.

1211CVERSE 5.-- Thy teeth are as a flock of sheep which have come up from the washing, all with twin offspring, and there is none barren among them.

Here the fourth part is touched. What indeed is understood by the teeth but the doctors, carrying the grossness of the letter over into the subtlety of the spiritual sense, and white with simplicity, as washed in the washing of holy compunction, whence they themselves also are fruitful with twin charity, or instructed in the double testament, and render those subject to them fruitful with the same charity and the same testament, so instructing them that none among them, that is, those set over or subjects, grows sluggish with barrenness of the virtues.

But the hairs of the particular soul, born from the principal part of the mind as from the 212 head, are the 1211Dsubtleties of the thoughts, attending to the heap of divine sentences: further, the teeth of that same mind, as it handles and handles again, are the vehement applications with zeal, breaking the hard and strong propositions or oppositions of the Scriptures, and unfolding very many of their wrappings. In these there is no barrenness, because the more zealously and the longer they apply the soul to the Scriptures, the more vehemently are they pricked to the love of God and neighbour, and the more fully do they attain the knowledge of each Testament, or, keeping the precept, they add the counsel over it: for the precept is not to seize what is another's, the counsel to give away one's own.

These surely are the twin offspring, by which the soul is made fruitful, namely the love of God and of neighbour, the knowledge 1212Aof the Old and New Testament, the observance of the precept with the adding of the counsel. By the intent and zeal of these, surely, all inward barrenness is driven off, so that deservedly in thought, working, preaching the beloved is pronounced beautiful, sweet and comely.

VERSE 6.-- As the rind of a pomegranate, so are thy cheeks, besides thy hidden things.

If we refer it universally to the whole Church, her cheeks can be called those who live spiritually in her, who, while shining in memorable and wonderful words and deeds, gleam also with stupendous miracles, appear venerable as it were in the face of the Church; for the beauty of cheeks is considered in their redness. But if so great is the glory of her comeliness in those things which appear, what pure glory of hers will there be in those things which do not yet appear? of which it is written: that 1212Bneither eye hath seen, nor ear heard, what things God hath prepared for those who love him (I Cor. II).

The cheeks, then, of the Church are compared to the rind of a pomegranate, but her hidden things, because they are ineffable, are therefore also incomparable.

But if we refer it specially to the honour of the holy soul, very often its inward beauty is declared by certain outward signs; for while the modesty of virginal chastity blushes in the face, that is shown outwardly which is held inwardly in the soul. Her cheeks, then, are as the rind of a pomegranate besides her hidden things, because outwardly indeed she puts forth from bashfulness a certain sign of holiness, but how much that holiness itself flourishes in the hidden place of her mind lies open to him alone 1212Cfrom whom nothing can be hidden. And this of the cheeks.

213 VERSE 7.-- There are threescore queens and fourscore concubines, and of young maidens there is no number.

The sixth and seventh parts are described in the present verse. For since in the foregoing he had proclaimed the beauty of the Church by parts, in the prelates and subjects and those living spiritually, who are designated by the hair, teeth and cheeks, now he follows up with renowned praise her comeliness, perfect as a whole, in the unity of faith: for although holy Church in some manner seem diverse by the diversity of merits, yet because of one and the same faith she is not found diverse; for three qualities of those living in her can be considered, because there are in her both the perfect and the less perfect and the imperfect: the perfect indeed 1212Dare those who have left all their things, and have cleaved to God alone with their whole mind; the less perfect, those who have not indeed left all their things, but out of those things which they can have are busy to minister to God in his members; the imperfect, those who in faith indeed cleave to the higher ones, but, as it were in a still tender manner of life, have not yet attained the good of perfect discretion.

Whence here not unfittingly the sum of three numbers is brought in? namely of six, of eight and of ten. For ten, multiplied by six, rises to sixty, while eight, led through ten, makes eighty. Six, moreover, is called perfect by arithmetic law, because when with all its parts, which are three, two, and one, 1213Afor its half part is three, its third two, its sixth one, it is gathered together, it is restored into the prior sum without any increase or decrease. Further, eight is named diminished, because since its half part is four, its fourth two, its eighth one, when these same parts are gathered together seven is made, less, that is, in quantity than the prior sum. And ten, which intimates the Decalogue of the law, because it consists of seven and three, the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit and the faith of the holy Trinity confession, which numbers show who are perfect, who imperfect. For the Holy Spirit himself shows in the effects of his gifts who love God perfectly, who less, who as yet have neither the fear nor the love of God.

1213BFor there are two things which make us wholly subject to God, namely fear and love: his power indeed and his wisdom chiefly 214 strike fear, when we know that he whom we know to exist is both able to punish all things he will, and that nothing is hidden from him; but his kindness begninitas pertains specially to love, that we may love most him whom we hold most kind. From which also it is certain that he wills to punish impiety, because the more equity pleases him, the more iniquity displeases him, as it is written: Thou hast loved justice and hated iniquity (Psal. XLIV).

By the number sixty, therefore, which is made by six, perfect, multiplied by ten, the life of the perfect is expressed, who would not perfectly observe the divine precepts 1213Cunless they had first the initial fear, afterwards the filial love that shuts out that very fear. And such souls are well named queens, because, divine grace working with them, they know how and are able to rule themselves by reason and understanding, when they discern profit, glory, and honour in the performing of good, and on the other hand loss, misery, and horror in the committing of evil, and therefore they strongly strive after good and strongly turn aside from evil.

But by the number eighty, which is completed by ten led through eight, which is called diminished, the life of the less perfect is denoted, who observe indeed the divine precepts, but do not love God so perfectly that they are able to leave all earthly things. And these souls are designated by the name of concubines, because, 1213Dalthough they are joined to God through good works, yet they have not yet obtained that divine right of which it is said, He who cleaveth to God is made one Spirit with him (I Cor. VI): for this is the full writing of the spiritual dowry, that those who renounce the world utterly are never separated from the divine fellowship. But of the young maidens the number is not defined, because infinite is the number of the imperfect, who, set as yet under the first-fruits of faith, need the instruction of their elders for conceiving the fear of God, through which they may at some time advance to his love.

Among whom there are some concerning whom very often the estimate is doubtful, since not all belong to the lot of the elect, 1214Aaccording to the voice of the Lord which says: Many are called but few chosen (Matth. XX).

VERSE 8.-- One is my dove, my perfect one: she is one to her mother, the chosen of her that bore her. The daughters saw her and declared her most blessed: the queens and concubines praised her. [Vulg. matris suae, "of her mother"]

But since the qualities of merits in the Church are so diverse, is she therefore said to be diverse? by no means; but as follows, one is my dove, my perfect one, she is one to her mother, the chosen of her that bore her. Whence one? namely 215 because of the one and the same receiving of faith and of the sacraments, and because of the worship of one God, and a like rite of religion: for one is the faith, as the Apostle says, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is above all 1214Bin us all (Ephes. IV).

One is, he says, my dove, my perfect one: for otherwise she is not my dove unless, bearing in her mouth the sign of peace and mercy, she keep the unity of the spirit in her heart and exercise the virtue of mercy in work: For mercy and truth have met each other, justice and peace have kissed (Psal. LXXXIV), for she ought always to sing mercy and judgment (Psal. C), in the power of binding and loosing granted her by me. Nor otherwise will she be my perfect one unless she have full knowledge of discretion, that she may know who is justly and worthily to be bound or loosed. One is moreover the dove and one my perfect one, because outside her there is given no remission of sins, nor distribution of gifts, and therefore those are shut out who do not confess one, 1214Choly, catholic and universal Church. For in one house the lamb is eaten and its flesh is not carried out, because there is no efficacy of the sacraments except in the one catholic Church.

She is one to her mother, that is, to the Jerusalem above, because she who here on earth is one in faith and in the dignity of the sacraments, there in heaven will be one in the beatitude of eternal life: for one is the beatitude of the saints, although they do not enjoy it in one manner, because of the qualities of diverse merits. The chosen of her that bore her, that is, of the Church of the ancient Fathers, namely of the patriarchs and prophets, whose faith she imitated and inherited the promise: 1214Dfor she is chosen, to whom should be shown that promise of the purpose of God which, made to the Fathers in the first days, was fulfilled in the last days, the same faith justifying her concerning things past and future which justified the ancient Fathers concerning things future only. For faith is as much concerning things present and future as concerning things past; although faith concerning things present is said improperly and not properly: for when the Apostle, defining faith, says: Faith and the substance of things to be hoped for, the evidence of things not appearing (Hebr. XI) [Vulg. Est autem fides sperandarum substantia rerum, "now faith is the substance of things to be hoped for"], it is surely clear that faith is the evidence of those things which cannot appear, for things which are apparent have not faith, but acknowledgment.

But since we are treating of the Canticles of canticles, does 1215Aany musical speculation of the two numbers set above, namely sixty and eighty, pertain to them? It does not seem at all beside the matter, if, where canticles are treated, we sometimes speculate on the modes of singing. For since the whole frame of our soul and body is joined by musical fitting together, it is plain, and proved by examples, on the authority of divine and human Scripture, that the force of musical harmony has had great power for composing, 216 or for stirring, or for pacifying souls. Ought not some speculation of musical consonance to have power also in this Canticle of canticles, which wholly aims at kindling souls to the love of the heavenly bridegroom, for the composing or stirring of the soul? Surely in this place too it will be able to lend a little 1215Bsupport to the imperfection of the concubines and young maidens, so that they may be incited in some way to attaining the perfection which it is agreed they do not yet have.

But since every well-ordered disposition is assigned to the proportions of numbers, it must be seen what consonance consists in the proportionality of these two numbers, sixty and eighty. The relation of eighty to sixty, then, is ἐπιτριτα or sesquitertian, because eighty has within itself the whole of sixty, and its third part, that is, twenty, in which proportion διατέσσερον sounds together in music; it is called διατέσσερον from four, because it resounds with four voices, consisting of two tones and a semitone.

1215CIf it is asked what is to the point in this place, by the proportion of these numbers, the consideration of this symphony? we answer that there is a reason sufficiently fitting in a consideration of this kind, because the whole universal Church spread through the four parts of the world, which, as has been said, is distinguished by three qualities of those living in her, that is, of the perfect, the less perfect, the imperfect, attains the whole sum of her salvation through the faith and sacraments of the New Testament, which was instituted by the perfection of the four Gospels, so that as it were a certain sweet concord of the διατέσσερον symphony, the consonance of the evangelists, consisting in four books as in four voices, by which the soul of all Christians Christianonorum is stirred to the worship of holy religion and 1215Dis composed.

The daughters of Sion saw her and declared her most blessed, the queens and concubines praised her. Such a Church, he says, as has been said, differing in the quality of merits, but alike in the unity of faith and sacraments, the daughters of Sion saw, that is, souls attending by the speculation of the mind, not by carnal vision, and weighing the beauty and honour of the whole Church, in the excellence of spiritual dignities, and the grace of the virtues, and also the necessary profit of that beauty, since there consist in her both the more generous and more wholesome granting of temporal things, as the incomparable and never-ending bestowal of eternal things: accordingly they declared her most blessed, because nothing is more blessed than always to have God, 1216Ahere temporally by using him in his gifts, there eternally by enjoying him.

217 The queens also and concubines praised her, because to holy souls who know how to rule their inner and outer senses by reason this honour of holy Church and the profit of that honour is very pleasing, and they praise much, that is, they approve, the spiritual insignia of her workings and the pious supports of sacramental things.

VERSE 9.-- Who is she that cometh forth as the dawn rising, fair as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army of a camp set in array?

Whence also these daughters of Sion, or the beloved himself, proclaiming this beauty of hers, not interrogatively as those who do not know, but affirmatively as those who marvel, 1216Bwhom indeed they know well, with such a proclamation, as it were with the eighth voice, raise and say:

Who is she that cometh forth as the dawn rising, fair as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army of a camp set in array? To those looking here not in passing but diligently there is offered, in the measure of praise of this kind, a modulation not to be despised of the symphony tasted beforehand, which we have called διατέσσερον, by which is hinted the confirmation of faith, hope, charity, and the sacraments, and the preaching of the Gospel through the four parts of the world, and also the useful and necessary attaining of the four principal virtues. For why should there not be attended to here, as it were, the distinction of four voices, the comparison of four diverse things, namely the coming forth of the dawn, the beauty of the moon, the choosing of the sun, 1216Cthe strength of the army set in array. For what more is there in the comeliness of the whole Church? In short, if faith, hope, charity and the sacraments be lacking, if the preaching of the Gospel is not received, if the foundations of the four virtues be not present, from which the buildings of all the other virtues rise, what will be the beauty of the Church, or of each holy soul?

But it must be seen what these likenesses of things intimate, how they fit the things said above, namely faith, hope, charity and the sacraments. The dawn is the beginning of the day, further faith is the beginning of holiness and religion as of a certain day, because by the name of day and light holiness is understood, as also by the name of night and darkness sin. The Church, 1216Dthen, or any holy soul cometh forth as the dawn, because, divine grace calling, she comes first to faith and through the same grace daily takes the increases of that same faith. The moon, moreover, always receives light from the sun, and, set in the other part of the hemisphere over against the sun, pours the full light of her orb upon the lands; but when she begins to wane, she returns to the sun, that she may be kindled again by it, and at length with the 218 fullness of her light may aid the world. And whence does holy Church, or any holy soul, receive the light of knowledge, the light also of holiness and justice, and of holy hope, but from that true sun of justice, the Lord Jesus Christ, who enlighteneth every man that cometh into this world? (Joan. I.) But because her beauty differs greatly from the 1217Abeauty of him from whom she receives that she be fair, she is called not absolutely fair, but by comparison fair is she called as the moon: for as the moon compared to the sun, or shining with the sun, does not shine: yet whatever of light she has she has from the sun, so also the saints compared to the Holy of holies are not, yet whatever of holiness they have, they have from him. And what is the Church but the gathering of the saints? and when, often withdrawing from divine contemplation for the sake of fraternal love, or by the obstacle of their own frailty, they have waned a little from the light of subtle understanding, gathering themselves again to themselves at some time, they run back with their whole mind to him of whom it is written: Come ye to him and be enlightened (Psal. XXXIII), that, looking back upon him as through a certain opposition of the mind, 1217Bthey may receive their fullness, such as it is, from him of whom it is said: And of his fullness we all have received (Joan. I).

What then do these, coming forth by faith and the works of faith, conceive but hope? For who would not hope for good things to come, whose works are full of light; so that deservedly the Church is called in them fair as the moon?

But since faith is as the dawn coming forth, that is, pouring forth the first light of religion and of its holiness, through faith certainly one approaches hope, because what we believe we hope that we shall at some time obtain. Whence the Apostle (Rom. V): Access, he says, we have through faith into this grace in which we stand, and glory in the hope of the glory of the sons of God; [Vulg. et gloriamur, "and we glory"] as if he said in other words: Through faith, which is the beginning and 1217Cas it were a certain entrance of every good work, as the dawn of the day, we approach and advance into the grace of full light, that is, of holiness, according to the measure which grace itself shall have granted us, in the grace of which light we stand, that is, we persevere, because we have hope of being joined through this to the future glory of the sons of God: and at once he adds: And not only so, it is understood, we glory in this hope, but we glory also in tribulations, knowing that tribulation worketh patience, and patience trial, and trial hope, and hope confoundeth not. And to show the efficient cause of this hope, its certainty, he adds, because charity is poured forth in our hearts by the holy one who is given to us. [Vulg. caritas Dei … per Spiritum Sanctum, "the charity of God … by the Holy Spirit"] For this is the anchor 1217Dof all good intention and working, because, as the same Apostle says: Charity shall never fall away (I Cor. XIII).

219 And this is what follows, chosen as the sun, namely because of charity, because as the sun is brighter than all the stars, so charity is more excellent than all the virtues, although according to the Godhead it is altogether incomparable. And holy Church, in those who burn with perfect charity and shine in working, is called chosen as the sun, because, since star differeth from star in brightness (I Cor. XV), that part of the saints is compared to the sun which is found brighter than the rest in holiness, namely in those who are still weak and tender in faith and work, she cometh forth as the dawn; but in those who by the progress of their manner of life have already somewhat 1218Aadvanced, she is called fair as the moon: further, in those who are perfect, and through the charity which, being perfect, casteth out fear, in of the highest spirits, which are named seraphim, that is, burning, but passing over are joined more nearly to the sun, she is rightly spoken of as chosen as the sun, or chosen as the sun, that is, predestined unto adoption, that she herself may be this by grace, which he is by nature, the true sun, who gave power to become sons of God to those who believe in his name (Joan. I).

But what, someone will say, does this fourth member, as it were the fourth voice of the δια τεσσερον symphony described above, pertain to the sacraments: terrible as an army of a camp set in array? Plainly, I say, this too pertains well enough, and this is established from the effects of the sacraments themselves, for what 1218Bis more terrible to the enemies of the soul, that is, to the malignant spirits, than the powers of the sacraments, by which their power is weakened, and all their might and daring put to flight?

For where any sacrament is so performed that the thing of the sacrament also can be present, that is, in the peace and unity of the Church, outside which there is no place for the saving sacraments, there surely the effect of that same sacrament is very terrible and unbearable to the evil spirits themselves, whether this be in baptism, or in the Lord's body, or in the distribution of orders, or in the ordering of whatever things are performed by ecclesiastical institutions; for this 1218Ccomparison seems to intimate this, by which it is said terrible as an army of a camp set in array: because as a well-bound battle line, and packed close in order, suffers no breaking in upon itself, so the Church, bound together by the sacrament of unity, is scattered by no incursion of the malignant spirits. But the heretics who have cut themselves off from this unity, because they are not contained in this battle line, being set outside, are able to repel none of the assaults of those spirits, since indeed the sacraments of the Church which they seem to have, they have not in reality, but only in appearance. Yet those same sacraments, rightly celebrated by them, if the faithful receive them, they receive both 220 the sacrament and the thing of the sacrament, that is, the power working within: while the heretics themselves are proved to take the sacrament indeed, but not the thing of the sacrament, 1218Dand therefore their gathering is not terrible as an army of a camp set in array, because as far as they are concerned the sacraments do not work this, which confer no remedies on them.

VERSE 10.-- I went down into the garden of nuts to see the fruits of the valleys, and to look if the vineyards had flourished, and the pomegranates budded. [Vulg. floruisset vinea, "the vineyard had flourished"]

After the beloved has followed up with gracious praise the beauty of the holy beloved, namely the Church, whose praise however is from him who by his grace presented her to himself not having spot or wrinkle (Ephes. V), he shows in what follows that, because of the unbelief of the Jewish people, she earned the gift and merit of faith, as the Apostle says: By their offence salvation to the Gentiles, and their offence the delight 1219Aof the world, and their diminution the riches of the Gentiles (Rom. XI) [Vulg. divitiae mundi, "the riches of the world"]. For he who extolled the one in the manner of admiration, in the same manner presses down the other, because while the one believed and received the word of God, the other would neither believe nor receive that word: whence it is written of her in the Gospel: And he wondered, no doubt Jesus, at their unbelief (Marc. VI). He says therefore, I went down into the garden of nuts. What was his going down, but to come down from the height of his Godhead into this world by being born, then to endure all the weak things of humanity? Were not all these things, fulfilled in their order, a certain descent? And where were these descents celebrated? Was it not in Judaea? In short, the Lord himself says: I was not sent but to the sheep that are lost of the house of Israel (Matth. XV), for this 1219Bis what he says here, I went down into the garden of nuts; for the nation of the Jews can, not unfittingly, be called the garden of nuts: for as in a nut the kernel is covered under the rind and shell, so among the Jews the sweetness of spiritual understanding is hidden under the hardness of the literal surface. That nation, then, is called the garden of nuts, because although it is called a garden because of the profit of the legal precepts and observances, which flourished in their time and profited their observers up to the time of grace, yet all the future sacraments of the Church lay hidden in it under a figure, as under the rind of a nut. Into this garden, therefore, the Lord went down, because first of all he showed the presence of his flesh to the Jewish people by preaching and doing miracles.

1219CBut why did he go down into this garden? To see, he says, the fruits of the valleys, that is, to know whether any had made fruit of faith and of injustice [injustitiae; read justitiae, "of justice"], and, reason showing it, might understand that they cannot be justified by the 221 works of the law, but by the faith which I have set before those who believe through the grace of the New Testament. But I say "to know," not that I have not had this or anything else present to me from eternity, who am everywhere, and to whom all things past and future are present, but, speaking in human fashion, that I might show their works to the world, whether they were to be followed or not. But why do I say of the valleys? Because of the lowliness of the letter which they follow carnally, or because of the shadow of the law by which it is surrounded, 1219Dlest they be enlightened by the light of its truth.

And to look if the vineyards had flourished, that is, whether they had conceived at least some savour of spiritual understanding, whether they had applied themselves to the faith by some beginning of good work: for the houses of Israel are called vineyards, which are distinguished by twelve tribes; which, although they are called vineyards because of the distinction of the tribes, yet are called one vineyard, because of the one observance of the law; as, although there are now said to be many Churches because of the diversity of places, yet there is said to be one Church because of the unity of faith. And that the whole of that people is called the vineyard of the Lord the Prophet testifies. The vineyard, he says, of the Lord is the house of Israel (Isa. V); of which the Psalmist also says: Thou hast brought a vineyard out of Egypt (Psal. LXIX); but when I looked that this vineyard 1220Ashould flourish and make grapes, it made wild grapes (Isa. V). for after the Gentiles believed, they remained in unbelief.

I went down also to look if the pomegranates had budded, that is, that they might not only believe in me, but also have the will of suffering for me: but they would neither believe, nor suffer anything for me, but rather they killed me as I preached to them and showed the way of salvation.

In another way also it does not seem burdensome to expound this particle of the present song by the likeness of the nut, so that the reader may choose what in these he weighs better and more rightly. It does not seem absurd to take the garden of nuts as the whole of the human race, for in the nut three things are considered, rind, shell and kernel; 1220Band in the human race man consists of flesh, bone and soul; for the matter of the flesh is as the rind, the bony strength is as the shell, further the sweetness of the soul is as the kernel: and as the kernel is covered by rind and shell, so the soul is clothed with flesh and bones. Whence Job, considering that man consists of these three, says: Thou hast clothed me with skin and flesh, thou hast put me together with bones and sinews (Job X). And to show the third, which quickens and enlivens those two, that is, the soul, he adds: Thou hast granted me life and mercy (ibid.). Into the garden of nuts, then, Christ went down when, by coming into this world, he took up human nature.

And why? To see the fruits of the valleys 222, that is, to visit the humble having the fruit of justice, 1220Cand to choose them for himself, for his seeing is choosing, so that, coming humble, he might intimate that he takes up the humble and obedient, as it is written: And he will save the humble of spirit (Psal. XXXIII). He went down also to look if the vineyards had flourished, and the pomegranates budded, that is, whether the Churches of the faithful had begun the pursuit of living or teaching rightly, and were striving to persevere in his love even unto death, so that by bestowing his help on them he himself might be both inspirer and fellow worker, as he says, promising them: Behold, I am with you all days even to the consummation of the world (Matth. XXVIII).

1220DVERSE 11.-- I knew not: my soul troubled me, because of the chariots of Aminadab.

The people of the Jews puts forward the cause of its ignorance and blindness, that since the law had been given which should justify and save them, and God had confirmed it by many signs and by the great authorities of the holy Fathers, it would be impossible for it to be made void by any novelty, since God is unchangeable, nor does he, in human fashion, say, command and institute anything at one time which at another time he forbids and destroys. For if, they say, that displeases in the future which now pleases, he is changeable, which is most absurd to say, nor can it stand by any reason that God is changeable. But if he himself is unchangeable, his words also and precepts are unchangeable: but because he is wholly unchangeable, whatever 1221Ahe has said or established must be fixed and unchangeable, therefore he has laid down no second and new law to destroy the first and old one.

To whom it is answered that what they have proposed must be granted, namely that God is unchangeable, whence in the new law he has established nothing which derogated from the former, but rather that the new law and the old are the same, but that one in the letter, this in the spirit; that one in figure, this in truth. That this is so was shown beforehand of old in the vision of Ezechiel the prophet, where a wheel in the midst of a wheel (Ezech. X) is recorded to have been seen. For the wheel in the midst of the wheel is the New Testament within the Old Testament, because what the Old Testament designated, this the New displayed: God, then, being unchangeable, changed nothing in this, who 1221Bso placed the one under the other that the one should be the signifying, the other the signified.

This, then, that people at first knew not, because it read the signifying, but did not understand the signified: but after, visited by divine grace, it began to know and believe that the letter killeth, but the spirit 223 quickeneth, repenting of its error, it was sore afraid, saying: I knew not: my soul troubled me because of the chariots of Aminadab. As if it said: Therefore I could not believe, because I did not yet at all understand the grace of the Gospel Evangeiii, for my soul troubled me, because I wondered what it could be, that I should now have to receive the four books of the Gospels who before had received the five books of Moses, as if this change could befall God, that in this way that should not please him which had pleased him before, 1221Cwho should found a new law, the old one transferred. But after I understood the wonderful providence of God, who instructed me through carnal things toward spiritual things, so that I might comprehend more easily and more truly not first the spiritual, but that which is animal, afterwards that which is spiritual, having laid aside all doubt I afterwards defended the truth which I had before assailed, not only by believing and teaching that truth, but also by dying for it.

But why do I say the chariots of Aminadab? truly because of the four books of the Gospel, in which are preached the four sacraments of that same Aminabad, who is interpreted the willing one of my people. And who is this Aminabad, but Christ who willingly laid down 1221Dhis life, that he might make me for himself a willing people and acceptable to God? And what are his four sacraments but his incarnation, passion, resurrection and ascension? The chariot, then, of this Aminabad is the book of the four Gospels, containing and conferring the knowledge of the four sacraments aforesaid, the Holy Spirit driving, by whose inspiration chariots of this kind were composed and ordered.

And when the kind Father received that same people which had believed out of the circumcision, returning to him, the black darkness of ignorance shaken off, running to meet it as it were with a consoling and exhorting voice, he calls it to penitence, saying: Return, return, Sunamitis, etc.

1222AVERSE 12.-- Return, return, Sunamitis; return, return, that we may behold thee. [Vulg. Sulamitis]

Behold, he says, there runs to meet it the voice of my chariot, which sounds forth the cause and order and necessary profit of my sacraments, namely of my nativity, passion, resurrection and ascension, which voice indeed thou, formerly ignorant, wouldst neither hear nor receive, but now, O Sunamitis, that is, captive, who art still held captive because thou hast not yet laid down the bond of original or actual sin through the washing of baptism and the participation of my body and blood, return, because thou hast hope of pardon. For thou didst withdraw from me through unbelief and ingratitude, forgetful of the benefits which I wrought toward thee, when I freed thee from the 1222Bbondage of Egypt, when I 224 fed thee with heavenly bread, when I gave thee my law, and chose thee before all nations for myself as a peculiar people. But now return to me through the voice of my chariot, through the four Gospels, [the chariot] crying out to thee as through four wheels and four times exhorting thee to penitence, return, return, return, return. Return through faith, return through working, return through right intention, return through love: for first thou must believe, then work, because faith without works is dead (Jac. II); further thy working must proceed from good intention, namely that faith may work through love; for thy working, if it is not from divine love, lies subject to vain 1222Cglory, and therefore lacks reward, because it has not the merit of holiness.

Return, moreover, that we may behold thee, that is, that we may approve the comeliness of thy soul which thou hast received through faith, and set thee forth as an example for others to follow: for this is thy praiseworthy beauty which pleases our eyes, that, error laid aside, thou follow the truth, and that thou who through error and the shadow of the law didst seem misshapen and dark, through thy return, through the truth and light of the Gospel, be seen beautiful and bright. For as long as thou didst lie hid under the shadow thou wast despicable, but after thou camest forth to the light of truth thou didst appear worthy to be seen, and now the king hath desired thy comeliness (Psal. XLIV) [Vulg. concupiscet, "shall desire"], that heavenly King namely 1222Dwho made thee his bride through the grace of the Holy Spirit, after thou didst return to him by faith, working, right intention, love; these things indeed have been said specially with regard to that ancient people of God, which, the less it at first understood the chariot of our Aminadab, the more it received it with veneration after it understood.

But to return to the moral sense, the signification of this chariot can, not unprofitably, be referred to the whole of the human race, so that we make two parts of the whole, to one of which we give that chariot whose charioteer is the devil. For man, consisting of four elements, and four humours, and also of the increases of four ages, seems to have as it were a certain material chariot 1223Aon the side of the body: further on the side of the soul, since it consists of four affections, and also four virtues by which it is led to good, the force and progress of that soul seem to have a spiritual chariot.

Let us see therefore first the complexions arranged in man by fours according to the body, such few as have occurred to the mind, then the qualities of the affections, designated also in fourfold manner according to the soul, so that from these, as we have said, 225 we may make two chariots, the material namely and the affectual, which both, looking to two chariots [quadrigas; read aurigas, "charioteers"], namely Christ and the devil, are made subject to one of them, since they cannot serve two masters (Matth. VI), and either, running rightly and happily through the grace of God, the spiritual one is called the chariot of Christ, 1223Bor, running perversely and unhappily through the privation of that same grace, the carnal one is called the chariot of the devil.

There are, then, as we have said, four elements of which man consists, fire, air, water, earth; which are intermingled with four qualities, namely heat, cold, moisture, dryness. For fire is hot and dry, air hot and moist, water cold and moist, earth cold and dry: and man himself, consisting of these four elements and of the qualities of the elements, while he has heat from fire, breath from air, blood from water, flesh from earth, in four seasons is changed by four humours through the increases of four ages.

1223CFor spring, which is as it were the first flower and beginning of the year: for then the earth begins to flower and bud, and it is hot and moist; it shows forth childhood, which is hot and moist, because in the child the blood is hot and moist; summer, which is hot and dry, shows youth, which is hot and dry, having red choler which abound in the young, dry and hot. Further autumn, which is cold and dry, announces manhood, which is cold and dry, having melancholy, that is, black choler, which are in men in their prime cold and dry. And winter, which is cold and moist, intimates old age, which is cold and moist, slipping phlegm, which abounds in the old, cold and moist.

For complexions of this kind, when they flourish well and in order in man, 1223Dshow the man healthy, but when they wander out of order, they disturb the man and make him sick: but because this fourfold constitution is materially in the body of man, by which man himself is drawn to the love of the flesh and the desires of this world, which he contracted from the propagation of original sin, there are born also from this material constitution four affectual qualities, which draw their force and nature chiefly from four inward members, namely the gall, the spleen, the liver and the heart. In short, man has from the gall that he is irascible, from the spleen that he is risible, from the liver that he is concupiscible, from the heart that he is rational: further from that heart, or mind, or soul, there proceed as it were four conceptions, which 1224Aprecede every action, namely thought, intention, will, deliberation. 226 For being about to do something we first think, then we intend why and how we should do it, afterwards we dispose in the will what is to be done, lastly we deliberate to accomplish it. But the very force of reason is spread fourfold: he who has wit, memory, understanding, discretion; for he has through wit to find things unknown and hidden by seeking and investigating, through memory to retain things found, through understanding to dispose things retained prudently, manfully and honourably, through discretion to assign things well disposed modestly to the places fitting them.

The rational soul itself also has four affections implanted in it: that is, fear, hope, joy 1224Band sorrow, of which the poet says: . . . These fear, desire, and rejoice, and grieve. And a philosopher, to a certain pupil of his whom he desired to relieve from the affections of these passions, says: Drive out joys, Drive out fear, And put hope to flight, Nor let sorrow be present.
