And these affections, by those who treat of physics, are said, according to the complexions of the material qualities which we have set down above, to rule more in some, less in others: but 1224Cover all these presides the soul strong in reason, which, when they thrust themselves in out of order, is to compose them and bend them to some measure of honour or profit, the divine Spirit ruling. And for a pursuit or discipline of this kind there must of necessity be applied, and implored from God, the four principal virtues, that is, prudence, fortitude, justice, temperance, which, because in every structure of the spiritual building they are laid as it were as certain corner stones by which the other virtues are enclosed and held, greater gifts of divine grace are considered in them.

Since, then, we have made two chariots, the material namely and the affectual, let us set also as it were two presiding over each, spirit and flesh, and as charioteers God and the devil: for that affectual one 1224Dis moved more or less toward reason and honour just so far as it is more or less driven by that material one, through care of the flesh, to the love of temporal life; and so far as the one presiding over each, namely spirit and flesh, which two are always opposed to one another, shall have been superior or inferior; because the flesh lusteth against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh (Gal. V). For therefore we say that spirit and flesh preside over each, because there are in them certain parts which tend from the flesh to the spirit, or slip from the spirit to the flesh.

For in that material chariot very often some who are stirred by the natural 227 heat and moisture of the flesh contend with such strength of spirit through the grace of God that they break all that natural impulse of the flesh 1225Athrough the fire of divine love and the impulse of the spirit, and at times utterly burn it out, and so grow hot toward God that they remain wholly cold toward the world. On the other hand some of cold nature, as they are cold inwardly toward every action in the love of God, therefore are zealous to labour at no good work. In that affectual chariot also there are those who are angry for temporal inconvenience, and there are those who are angry for justice; there are also those who desire good things, there are those who desire evil things; there are those who laugh and rejoice because of the wretched prosperity of this life, there are also those who rejoice and laugh in adversities because of the hope and security of future beatitude; there are also those who use the good of reason well, and act and savour rightly; there are those who 1225Buse it ill and savour and act perversely. There are nonetheless some who use natural wit for good, there are those who use it for evil; there are those who understand good rightly, there are those who understand it ill; there are those who offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, that is, discern; and there are those who both offer rightly and divide rightly, that is, discern; as on the other hand some neither offer rightly nor divide rightly, that is, discern.

Whence to both these chariots there cleave four species which lead both into the full motions of their own pursuit, namely suggestion, delight, consent, custom. For the soul of each one is led either to good or to evil in these four ways, to good indeed by the suggestion of the Holy Spirit, as it is said of him: For he himself shall suggest to you 1225Call things whatsoever I shall have said to you (Joan. XIV); by the delight of the soul, by the consent of the spirit, and by the custom of good itself: but to evil by the suggestion of the devil, by the delight of the flesh the consent of the spirit, by the custom of evil itself.

In the midst, then, of these chariots, which are formed from the matter of the flesh and the affection of the mind, the four principal virtues which we have set down above, namely prudence, fortitude, justice, temperance, must needs be set, so that by a certain setting of them as it were round about, the whole concretion of the body placed within may be ruled and composed to some measure of rational form. For as a certain one says: Virtue is the mean of vices, and drawn back from both, 1225D(HOR., Ep. I, XVIII, 9.) that is, removed from either part: for example, to be dull or to be evilly cunning is vicious, but in the midst of these vices, namely dullness and evil cunning, the virtue of prudence is set, by whose governing this inequality may be corrected: fortitude also is set between timidity and daring, so that this may truly be to be brave, 228 to be found neither timid in good nor daring in evil. Likewise it can be seen also in the other virtues, from the consideration of which, set beside themselves, the quality of the vices is understood.

From the whole matter, then, of this kind, carnal namely and spiritual, distinguished fourfold, there is made one certain thing formed of matter, which shows in itself as it were a twin chariot of flesh and spirit, over which presides 1226Aas charioteer either God or the devil: but God ruling, saving and quickening; the devil overturning, damning and killing.

The name indeed is equivocal, since though in both cases it is called a chariot, yet in definition it is different: for to fall away from God through the suggestion of the devil and the delight of the flesh, the consent also of the spirit, and the custom of evil working, is to be the chariot of the devil; and conversely, to advance toward God through the suggestion of God, and the delight of the soul, the consent also of the spirit, and the custom of good working, is to be the chariot of God: and conversely the chariot of God is also the mind made four-square by the four virtues which we set down above, that is, by prudence, justice, temperance, fortitude; to which is opposed 1226Bthe chariot of the devil, namely the mind unnerved by the four vices contrary to those very virtues, that is, by folly, iniquity, lust, fear.

The Church therefore cries, or the bridegroom himself through the Church, to the Sunamite: Return, return, return, return, so that she who had transgressed in these four ways, by returning to God may offer four fruits of penance also, mortifying these things in herself through the grace of God and the strength of the mind. Return, he says, through penance and satisfaction for past evils, return through contempt of the world, return through mortification of the flesh, return through constancy in the virtues. Return, moreover, that we may behold thee, that is, that after thou hast done penance we may have mercy on thee. For to see is, in God, to have mercy: whence the Psalmist to 1226CGod: Look, he says, upon me and have mercy on me (Psal. LXXXV); and on the contrary the turning away of his face is his wrath, as the same Psalmist says: Thou turnedst away thy face from me, and I became troubled (Psal. XXIX).

But that he says in the plural, That we may behold thee, that is the manner of speech used of God by which he says elsewhere. Let us make man to our image and likeness (Gen. III), which manner is brought in on account of the plurality of persons in the holy Trinity,

229 CAPUT VII.

VERS. 1.-- Quid videbis in Sulamite, nisi choros castrorum? Quam pulchri sunt gressus tui in calceamentis, filia principis! juncturae femorum tuorum, sicut monilia quae fabricata sunt manu artificis.

1226DQuandiu Judaea erroris sui vinculo sive quaelibet anima peccati jugo tenebatur captiva, nulla in ea jucunditas, sed miseria videri poterat, quia et illa inter pugnam litterae et spiritus et ista inter pugnam carnis et spiritus meliore parte semper inferior erat: nam illa solam litteram sequebatur, ista carnem; at ubi per poenitentiam illa sensum spiritualem agnovit et recepit, ista carnis amore calcato secundum spiritum vivere coepit, benignus pater utrumque misericorditer suscipiens ostendit suum ei adjutorium impensurum ut veram jam et plenam libertatem adepta et quasi victoriam de parte sibi adversa consecuta, devotas ei laudes carne et spiritu laetabunda persolvat. Hoc enim ipse per prophetam promittit dicens: 1227ARevertimini ad me, et ego revertar ad vos. (Malach. V). Unde et eorum conversioni congaudens dicit Ecclesiae: Quid videbis in Sulamite, nisi choros castrorum? In choris quippe concorditer resonantia melodiae alternatio ostenditur; in castris vero bellatorum societas pro tuitione colligitur. Quid ergo sunt chori castrorum, nisi laudes bellatorum? et est sensus: Quia Sulamitis ista de captivitate, sub qua per 230 culpam detinebatur, ad me conversa est, tantam ei libertatis et securitatis gratiam conferam, ut nihil aliud in ea, o dilecta, videre et mirari debeas, quam pro devictis ac depressis vitiorum motibus, et concessis virtutum profectibus laetas gratiarum actiones et quotidiana laudum praeconia.

1227BJam quasi in unum conjunctis duobus parietibus, ex adverso venientibus Judaico videlicet atque gentili populo, quibus ostendit totam universalem constare Ecclesiam, dirigitur rursus in laudem ipsius, ut praedicet in uno corpore tam diversas suae dignationis gratias insigniter constitutas, et ob hoc juste et digne sibi gratiarum actiones persolvendas. Dicit ergo: Quam pulchri sunt gressus tui in calceamentis, filia principis!

Quid per gressus, nisi actionum cursus exprimitur? quid per calceamenta, quae ex mortuorum animalium pellibus fiunt, nisi praecedentium patrum, et ex hac vita subtractorum exempla signantur? sicut enim calceamentis pedes tuentur, ita sanctorum patrum exemplis mores eos sequentium 1227Cdefenduntur.

Quae vero filia principis, nisi aut Ecclesia, aut sancta quaelibet anima illi per adoptionis gratiam dedita, qui est princeps regum terrae? Pulchros ergo gressus habet Ecclesia, sive sancta quaelibet anima in calceamentis, quia pulchros et reverendos habet actus ex sanctorum patrum gestis et documentis. Quare non inconvenienter subjungit: Junctura feminum tuarum sicut monilia quae fabricata sunt manu artificis.

Per juncturam feminum concordia duorum Testamentorum accipitur, quia tam aequaliter junguntur Vetus et Novum Testamentum, ut quod unum annuntiat in figura, hoc aliud repraesentet in veritate. 1227DSed quid est quod haec testamenta monilibus comparantur? Monile enim componitur ex auro et argento pretiosisque lapidibus, et in pectore matronarum ponitur, ut sit eis et pro munimento et pro ornamento. Utrumque autem Testamentum constructum est ex divini sensus fulgore et eloquii nitore quasi ex auro et argento, diversarum quoque virtutum praedicamentis, quasi quibusdam pretiosis gemmis. Et sicut matronarum pectus monile munit et ornat, ita utrumque Testamentum sanctae Ecclesiae, sive cujusque sanctae animae pectus spiritualiter munit et ornat, munit quidem a vitiorum hostilitate, ornat vero virtutum pulchra varietate.

Junctura ergo feminum ejus, sicut monilia, quia 1228Aconcordia duorum Testamentorum, quibus quotidie sancta Ecclesia, vel quaevis sancta anima instruitur, magnum ei conferunt tutamentum et ornamentum; tutamentum 231 quidem contra perversitates haereticorum, ornamentum autem propter decorem et pulchritudinem sensuum et eloquiorum, sive quae in ea celebrantur virtutem sacramentorum, et honestatem ordinum ecclesiasticorum.

Quis vero est iste artifex, cujus manu ista monilia, hoc est Testamenta, fabricata sunt, nisi omnipotens Deus, cujus voluntate, potestate, operatione haec honeste composita, utiliter exposita, feliciter sunt suscepta? Quare dignitas horum Testamentorum valde est commendabilis, quando tali sunt auctore constituta, cujus artificium non est 1228Bhumanum, sed divinum, non inventum, sed voluntarium et potestativum, omnia enim quaecunque voluit fecit (Psal. XIII), semperque ejus velle, fuit etiam ejus fecisse.

Omnem ergo decorem et pulchritudinem interioris hominis sui sancta Ecclesia, sive quaelibet sancta anima ex istorum Testamentorum consideratione colligit, quid credendum, quid sperandum, quid amandum necessaria sibi utilitas proponat. Unde vero junctura feminum ejus, a sponso laudatur? quia concordia duorum Testamentorum, sive duorum populorum, sive geminae charitatis maximam et totam bene vivendi constituunt regulam, et certissimam pro conservata regula reponunt remunerationis gloriam; et bene juncturam 1228Cnon femorum, sed feminum dixit, quia ex his concipitur, nascitur et proficit omnis sanctae Ecclesiae, vel cujuslibet fidelis animae honestas et utilitas.

VERS. 2.-- Umbilicus tuus sicut crater tornatilis; nunquam indigens poculis. Venter tuus sicut acervus tritici vallatus liliis.

Umbilicus ventris meditullium est: quid ergo est umbilicus Ecclesiae, nisi sancti praedicatores et doctores, qui in medio populi versantur eumdem populum sibi colligentes doctrina et operatione? Sicut enim umbilico omnia adhaerent viscera, ita populus suis adhaeret praedicatoribus, ad eorum verba et exempla semper quasi ad quoddam meditullium 1228Dcirca se positum respiciens, ut in eorum moribus et sermonibus firmamentum sibi quoddam bene vivendi constituat.

Sed iste umbilicus sicut crater tornatilis dicitur, quia ut superflua et inaequalia morum resecent, sancti doctores semper ad idem versantur, quando pro hoc adipiscendo quod semper est immutabile et idem in sui qualitate perseverat, currunt, laborant, et alios secum trahere festinant. Qui crater nunquam indigere poculis dicitur, quia iidem praedicatores semper abundant divinorum 232 sententiis eloquiorum, quibus et ipsi per gratiam sancti Spiritus debriantur et sitibunda populorum pectora sufficienter reficere student.

Alio quoque modo, si ad cujusque fidelis animam 1229Aintendimus, spiritualiter umbilicus mentis sancta dici charitas potest, quae veluti in centro quodam posita, omnes quasi per circumferentiam virtutes tangit, quia dum nulla virtus sine charitate esse potest, omnes profecto virtutes ad eam respicientes quasi charitatis appendices esse videntur.

Sed quomodo haec dicitur crater tornatilis? Apostolus dicit, quia finis praecepti charitas ad justitiam omni credenti (I Tim. I), ergo, omnis perfectio in charitate consistit, quia est tornatilis, nihil in se superfluitatis et obstantis vitii retinens, atque ideo perfecta et plana, perfecta quippe charitas foras mittit timorem, quia timor non est in charitate (I Joan. IV). Ista etenim perfectio finis est praecepti, id est consummatio, ut dicit propheta, verbum 1229Bconsummatum quod fecit Dominus super terram (Isa. X; Rom. IX).

Quomodo autem nunquam indigens poculis? musto pleni dicebantur apostoli quando Spiritu sancto, hoc est igne divinae charitatis ardebant: ebrii enim erant poculo illo calicis spiritualis, de quo dicit Psalmista: Et calix meus inebrians quam praeclarus est! (Psal. XXII.) Qui ergo divina charitate replentur, quomodo non semper illo indeficienti Spiritus sancti madent, et calent poculo? Econtra terra siti arere dicitur, quae divinae charitatis infusione non respergitur: unde Dominus hac siti arentibus clamat, dicens: Qui sitit veniat ad me et bibat, et de ventre ejus fluent aquae vivae (Joan. VII). Igitur crater iste tornatilis nunquam indiget poculo, quia perfecta 1229Ccharitas nunquam eget rore coelesti, et illius summi boni desiderio. Quia vero sunt in Ecclesia praelati et subjecti, fortes et infirmi, prudentes et simplices, postquam in praelatorum virtutibus Christus Ecclesiam suam laudavit, subdit quoque laudabile testimonium ex obedientia et disciplina subjectorum, venter tuus, inquiens, sicut acervus tritici. Quia enim venter pars est corporis fragilis et mollis, per ventrem fragilitas subjectorum, qui nondum perfectionem magistrorum consequi possunt, designatur; sed quia et ipsi quoque ad Ecclesiam pertinent, et de sorte sunt electorum, quos ille summus Pater familias triticum suum appellat, et in horreum suum congregari jubet, non incongrue acervo tritici comparatur. Acervus autem inferius 1229Ddilatatur, superius acuitur, tota vero congeries est granorum, quasi invicem se complectentium et portantium collatio.

233 Quid ergo per acervum tritici, nisi multitudo fidelium praelatis obedientium exprimitur, qui quamvis per infirmitatem carnis et curas rerum saecularium, circa latam et spaciosam viam aliquantulum deprimantur, tamen per obedientiam et humilitatem, fraternam quoque charitatem fide et spe ad superna eriguntur? nam invicem se complectentes et adjuvantes, atque infirmitates morum et corporum tolerantes implent illud Apostoli: Alter alterius onera portate, et sic adimplebitis legem Christi (Gal. VI).

1230ASed iste acervus tritici vallatus liliis dicitur, quia per rectae fidei odorem et peccatorum confessionem multum proficit ad aeternae vitae candorem, in liliis enim est et odor et candor et medicina: odor enim est in fide et operatione, medicina in peccatorum confessione, candor in vitae aeternae retributione.

VERS. 3.-- Duo ubera tua sicut duo hinnuli gemelli capreae.

Per duo ubera non absurde accipi possunt duo charitatis praecepta, per quae anima cujusque fidelis per teneritudinem intimi lactis nutritur et in spiritualis exercitii robur perducitur, ut possit cum Apostolo dicere: Omnia possum in eo qui me confortat (Philipp. IV); nam fortis est ut mors dilectio (Cant. VIII); et a charitate nulla sanctos separat tribulatio 1230B(Rom. VIII). Per hanc enim eunt de virtute in virtutem (Psal. LXXXIII): unde et recte ipse charitatis praecepta duobus gemellis hinnulis capreae quae naturaliter semper alta petit comparantur.

Sed quare gemellis? nimirum propter ipsius geminae charitatis, Dei videlicet et proximi, concordiam et unitatem, quia ita insimul in mente sanctorum concipiuntur et crescunt, ut neutra possit esse prior altera, sed cum diligit Deum, diligit et proximum et cum diligit proximum, diligit Deum. Utrumque enim alterius et probativum, quia sicut dicit Joannes: Qui dicit se diligere Deum et non diligit fratrem suum mendax est (I Joan IV): atque ideo ista duo charitatis praecepta quasi duo gemelli sunt capreae, quia et uno geruntur loco et tempore, 1230Cet semper ad altiora quotidiano virtutum proficiunt incremento.

Sive, duo ubera duo sunt Testamenta quibus sancta Ecclesia quotidie ad pietatis enutritur opera, quod etiam sunt quasi duo hinnuli gemelli capreae, quia ita unum sunt significans et significatum, ut quamvis non uno fuerint tempore in exhibitione, uno tamen sint tempore in significatione et tanta est ipsorum Testamentorum majestas, ut de eis disputantibus semper major et altior occurrat subtilitas.

1230D234 VERS. 4.-- Collum tuum sicut turris eburnea: oculi tui sicut piscinae in Hesebon, quae sunt in porta filiae multitudinis. Nasus tuus sicut turris Libani, quae respicit contra Damascum.

Quia per colli fistulam vox egreditur, et cibus ventri ministratur, recte per collum sancti praedicatores designantur, qui per praedicationis officium conservis ministrant cibaria doctrinarum. Sed considerandum quare dicatur turris, et quare eburnea. Turris, inde primo, quia praedicatio sanctorum alta est propter sensus sublimitatem; deinde quia ex alta mentis speculatione, veluti ex quadam turri, adventus hostis prospicitur, ut eorum insidiae praecaveantur, et haec mentis speculatio ex sanctorum sumitur doctrina praedicatorum: eburnea propter candorem interius refulgentis sapientiae; castam vero pronuntiationem exterius resonantis eloquentiae, sicut in Psalmo canitur, quia eloquia 1231ADomini casta et praeceptum Domini lucidum, illuminans oculos (Psal. XVIII).

Collum ergo sanctae Ecclesiae, sive sanctae cujusque animae, est sicut turris eburnea, quia illius praedicatio alta, et firma, et pulchra est, et dum mentem ad Deum erigit, ab hostium insidiis defendit, atque nulla haereticae pravitatis macula corrumpi permittit; econtra Synagoga per prophetam dicitur turris nebulosa (Mich. IV), quia obscura et involuta est carnali Judaeorum scientia, quae quidem turris est, propter sublimium sacramentorum quae in ea teguntur continentiam, sed nebulosa propter carnalem solius intelligentiam litterae. Oculi tui sicut piscinae in Hesebon, quae sunt in porta filiae multitudinis.

Oculi sanctae Ecclesiae, sive potius cujusque fidelis 1231Banimae, non inconvenienter accipi possunt duae in mente quasi in capite considerationes dextra laevaque intendentes, videlicet ad parvitatem et miseriam temporalis vitae, ad aeternitatem et felicitatem perpetuae et incommutabilis vitae.

Quae recte dicuntur quasi piscinae in Hesebon, quod interpretatur cingulum moeroris, quia profecto ex moerore et tristitia peccatorum, sive ex desiderio aeternorum bonorum profluunt per compunctionem veluti piscinae fontes lacrymarum. Istae siquidem piscinae profluunt ex duplici compunctione, quae nascuntur ex istorum duorum oculorum consideratione, quia dum mens futura supplicia pensat, et suorum reminiscitur malorum, ad poenitentiam compungitur, quasi ex altera piscina irrigatur.

1231CSed istae piscinae sunt in Hesebon, quia ex hac gemina compunctione, ex una parte poenitentiae, ex altera dilectionis cingitur moerore, ut et ad priora vitia ex futurorum malorum recordatione non defluat, et ad 235 virtutum studia ex futurorum bonorum desiderio se fortiter stringat, Dominicum praeceptum adimplens: Sint lumbi vestri praecincti (Luc. XII).

Piscinae autem istae dicuntur esse in porta filiae multitudinis. Sed quae est ista porta? nimirum exitus vitae hujus et introitus vitae futurae; unde dicitur in Psalmo de viro beato: Non confundetur cum loquetur inimicis suis in porta (Psal. CXXVI): nulla quippe confusio erit viro sancto in exitu hujus vitae, 1231Dcum ei pars adversa obstare et nocere voluerit, quia illi in vita sua servivit in quo nihil suum princeps mundi hujus invenit.

Quae est autem filia multitudinis, cujus illa porta dicitur esse, nisi sancta cujusque fidelis anima, illius videlicet multitudinis filia, cujus erat cor unum et anima una (Act. IV)? Quae tunc quidem in terris rudis erat et primitiva Ecclesia, sed illius praefigurabat unitatem, quae nunc in coelis vera et perfecta concordia, cum Christo regnat per ineffabilem et immutabilem charitatem.

Hujus nimirum multitudinis filia piscinas illas geminae compunctionis in sua habet porta, quia per poenitentiam praeteritorum malorum, et desiderium futurorum bonorum confidenter et feliciter de hac 1232Avita exiens intrat regna coelorum. Pulchre ergo oculi Ecclesiae sive sanctae animae dicuntur esse veluti piscinae in Hesebon quae sunt in porta filiae multitudinis, quia dum ex peccatorum recordatione, vel ex aeternae vitae amore, per geminam compunctionem madent lacrymarum fonte, introitum sibi regni coelestis aperiunt in exitu vitae.

Aliter oculi Ecclesiae possunt non inconvenienter dici provisores et doctores ejusdem, quibus ista similitudo quoque aptari potest, ut sicut piscinae in Hesebon civitatem cingunt et muniunt, ita isti cingunt et muniunt Ecclesiam cingulo moeroris, quod Hesebon interpretatur, dum sua doctrina et praedicatione quasi quodam salutari fonte provocant ad compunctionem, ad confessionem, ad satisfactionem, 1232Bdicentes illud evangelicum: Poenitentiam agite, appropinquabit enim regnum coelorum (Matth. III). Poenitentia quippe recte dici potest cingulum moeroris, quia sic undique cingi et muniri debet vita poenitentis, ut et commissa lugeat, et lugenda ulterius non admittat. Ea namque vera poenitentia est qua sic retroacta peccata conspiciuntur, ut futura timeantur habeatque moerorem ex praeteritis, timorem ex futuris. Sed quia timor iste poenam habet dum ex recordatione praeteritorum et timore futurorum moerorem animi contrahit, recte poenitens cingulo moeroris vitam constringit.

Sed piscinae istae in Hesebon sunt in 236 porta filiae multitudinis: quae autem est filia multitudinis, vel quae est ista multitudo? Nonne sanctam Ecclesiam 1232Cgenuerunt apostoli, et eorum successores, apostolici viri? Quorum dignitatem intuens Psalmista, Nimis, inquit, honorati sunt amici tui, Deus, nimis confortatus est principatus eorum (Psal. CXXXVIII); quos non paucos, sed multos fuisse considerans, Dinumerabo, inquit, eos et super arenam multiplicabuntur (ibid.) Hujus ergo multitudinis filia est sancta Ecclesia, quam, ut diximus, sua genuerunt doctrina, quae habet portam, discretionis videlicet januam, per quam discernit quos vel quales in suo corpore repellat. Nam cum semper tritico mista sint zizania, bonos quidem sibi quasi dulces cibos incorporat, malos vero veluti malos humores in corpore suo tolerat, haereticos vero quasi venenum 1232Dmortiferum a se prorsus alienat.

In hac ergo discretionis porta stant quotidie provisores sive doctores sanctae Ecclesiae; quasi quidam oculi in capite discernere sciunt per spiritum sapientiae, qui pertineant, vel non pertineant ad corpus Ecclesiae, qui pisces eligendi quive rejiciendi sint in ultimae stationis littore: denique fidelibus apertas vitae januas ostendunt, peccatoribus vero poenitentibus clausas aperiunt, porro impiis et non poenitentibus aeternaliter claudunt.

Sive porta filiae multitudinis fides dicitur, quae est initium et quasi quidam introitus ad viam salutis, sine qua impossibile est placere Deo (Hebr. XI), quam prima fronte proponunt sancti doctores viam vitae quaerentibus, et ad coelestem patriam 1233Apervenire cupientibus; quia primo debet quisque recte credere, ac deinde recte credens bene operari.

Sed quia portam istam filiae multitudinis diximus discretionis gratiam, qua sancti provisores et doctores Ecclesiae vel poenitentes admittere, vel non poenitentes excludere sciunt, qualis ipsa discretio sit vel esse debeat, subditur, cum dicitur: Nasus tuus sicut turris Libani, etc.

Per nasum quippe quo odores foetoresque discernimus, sanctorum discretio designatur per quam norunt discernere odores virtutum, foetoresque vitiorum, ut intelligant quid eligere et quid reprobare debeant. Qui nimirum nasus sicut turris Libani esse 1233Bdicitur, quia videlicet praepositorum discretio et munita semper debet esse ex circumspectione, et in altitudine semper vitae consistere, id est, in valle infirmi operis non jacere. Sicut enim turris in montem idcirco ad speculum ponitur, ut hostes qui veniunt longius videantur, sic praedicatoris vita semper in alto debet fixa permanere, ut more narium discernat foetores 237 vitiorum, odoresque virtutum, incursus malignorum spirituum longe prospiciat, et commissas sibi animas per suam prudentiam cautas reddat. Et quia ipsa discretio mater virtutum esse dicitur, recte turri Libani qui candidationem sonat comparatur, quatenus per eam omnium virtutum pulchritudo custodiri intelligatur.

Sed haec turris contra Damascum respicere dicitur, 1233Cquia sanctorum vita contra vitiorum tentamenta per altam discretionis considerationem forti custodia munitur. Damascus, quippe sanguinem bibens interpretatur, quo mundus iste recte designatur, qui quotidie vitiis et peccatis inebriatur; sanguine enim peccata designari propheta indicat, dicens: Et sanguis sanguinem tetigit (Ose. IV), hoc est peccato peccatum accessit; et Psalmista: Libera me, inquit, de sanguinibus, Deus, Deus salutis meae (Psal. L).

Turris ergo ista contra Damascum dirigitur, quia sanctorum vita virtutibus alta et munita, contra mundi hujus voluptates forti et discreta consideratione praemunitur.

VERS. 5.-- Caput tuum sicut Carmelus: et comae capitis tui sicut purpura regis juncta canalibus.

1233DPer caput principale mentis designatur. Carmelus autem sciens circumcisionem sive mollis fluvius interpretatur.

Recte ergo mens sancta Carmelo comparatur, quia et in divina contemplatione alta est, et a se carnalitatem morum sive cogitationum spirituali circumcisione abscidere novit, atque divini Spiritus infundente gratia, suavi doctrina quasi molli fluvio audientium corda irrigare studet. Et comae capitis tui sicut purpura regis, juncta canalibus.

Comae capitis cogitationes mentis accipi possunt, quae sicut purpura regis juncta canalibus dicuntur, quia quanto magis junguntur, et intendunt Scripturis quasi quibusdam canalibus, tanto magis accenduntur ad imitationem passionis Christi carnem 1234Asuam mortificando, cum vitiis et concupiscentiis, sive ipsam carnem, si necesse fuerit, pro Christo persecutionibus offerendo, pretiosam Deo purpuram cordis et corporis martyrio sacrificantes.

Possumus et alio modo hanc orationis particulam ipsi capiti Ecclesiae, hoc est Domino Jesu Christo, aptare, ut videlicet ex persona sua eidem Ecclesiae sponsae suae seipsum inducat loquentem: Caput tuum sicut Carmelus, et comae capitis tui sicut purpura regis juncta canalibus. Ego, inquit, o sponsa, qui dicor et sum caput tuum, monti Carmelo, propter altitudinem et nominis interpretationem, comparari possum; quia cum sim bonum generalissimum, nihil est quod mea natura excellentius esse possit secundum divinitatem, porro secundum humanitatem 1234B238 nihil vita et conversatione mea sanctius, et in mea doctrina vera et perfecta cordis circumcisio discitur, atque omnis mea praedicatio vere quasi mollis fluvius decurrit, ut audientium mentes sui salubritate reficiat, et ad boni operis studia informet. Hujus capitis tui comae, mei sunt apostoli, caeteri quoque mei sancti, qui mihi charitate, sicut comae capiti adhaerent, quibus purpura bene congruit, quia sicut purpura quae vicinior canalibus est, melius tingitur, ita illorum mens quae magis meis vel meorum prophetarum verbis et institutionibus vicina efficitur, eo magis ad amorem mei virtute accenditur, et in tabernaculo meo, hoc est in Ecclesia mea, pretiosa et regalis purpura, coccus scilicet bis tinctus (Exod. XXVIII) Dei et proximi dilectione refulgere 1234Cconatur.

Igitur quia caput viri Deus (I Cor. II), si hujus capitis sui coma quisque fidelis virtute animi esse desiderat, sacris Scripturarum canalibus necesse est ut sedulius scrutator inhaereat, quia ibi invenit unde tingatur, ut Regis sui coelestis per amorem intimum purpura mortificatione carnalis vitae efficiatur. Notandum autem quod pulchre respondet dilectus dilectae hujusmodi laudis praeconio decem partibus quasi decem chordis, uno resonans spiritualiter decachordo, quod ita superiori decachordo, quod in laude sponsi sponsa decantaverat, decenter opponitur, ut illud a superioribus, istud ab inferioribus modum gratissimae melodiae imponant. Quia enim sponsa ad sponsum recta intentione et perfecto 1234Damore semper ascendere debet, justum est ut de minoribus ad majora assurgat, atque ideo a sponso proficientis et quasi crescentis ad virtutes animi ejus praeconium dignanter decantatur; non quod iste profectus, virtus et potentia sit accipientis, sed potius quia laus est sponsi dantis et hanc ei virtutem atque potentiam suo munere tribuentis.

At vero sponsa intendens venerabiliter immensam sponsi benignitatem de coelo descendentis, et ad nostram se infirmitatem propter nos humiliantis, laudis ejus praeconia a summo corporis praeconio, hoc est a capite, quasi a superiori orditur chorda, ut ostendat se inferius positam, semper se respicere debere ad vitam et doctrinam sui sponsi superius sibi e regione oppositam, et ad illum per imitationem 1235Aascendere, quem cognoscit ad se per compassionis pietatem descendisse.

239 VERS. 6.-- Quam pulchra es, et quam decora, charissima, in deliciis!

Postquam sponsus in sponsa per partes praedicavit varietatem membrorum ex habitu mentis bone et honeste compositorum, unum quiddam totum exinde procrevisse ostendens, universitatem virtutum staturae nomine appellat, doctrinae vero abundantiam uberum significatione declarat. Quae enim pulchritudo morum sive eloquiorum deest in toto corpore sanctae Ecclesiae? nam cum istae ista, ille illa, alius alia virtute resplendeat, quidam plura, quidam pauciora virtutum genera possideat, quid potest esse speciei pulchritudinis et decoris quam 1235Bin suo corpore sancta Ecclesia non habeat? Cumque diversi diversa sanctarum doctrinarum eruditione clarescant, quae potest esse veritatis vel sanctitatis scientia, qua sancta non exuberet Ecclesia? Nam cum secundum Apostolum, alii detur sermo sapientiae, alii sermo scientiae, alteri fides, alii gratia sanitatum, alii operatio virtutum, alii prophetia, alii discretio spirituum; alii genera linguarum, alii interpretatio sermonum (I Cor. XII), omnis profecto pulchritudo atque ornatus operum sive sermonum interiori statura sanctae Ecclesiae spiritualiter refulget.

Unde merito pulchra et decora, et in deliciis charissima pronuntiatur; quia profecto magnae sunt 1235Cdeliciae animae virtutum abundantia, et sapientiae salutaris doctrina; sed quo magis anima his delectatur, tanto amplius divinae dilectionis dulcedine repletur.

VERS. 7.-- Statura tua assimilata est palmae et ubera tua botris.

Cur autem hujusmodi statura assimilata est palmae? Palma namque victoriae signum est; quae autem major et gloriosior victoria quam de vitiis et peccatis triumphare? Unde autem ejusmodi mirabilis et gloriosa succrevit statura, nisi ex victoria virtutum et destructione vitiorum? Non incongrue ergo statura Ecclesiae palmae assimilatur, quia omnis ejus morum honestas et probitas insignes loquitur victorias.

1235DPorro ubera ejus botris assimilantur, quia doctrina et praedicatio ejus dulci et suavi abundat sapore sapientiae et spiritualis intelligentiae, et auditores suos ita inebriat, ut a mundi hujus voluptatibus velut insensibiles faciat. Ut autem ostendat ipse sponsus quod pulchritudo hujus staturae maxime et principaliter proficiat et succrescat ex mortificatione carnalis vitae, passionis suae ei praetendit exemplum et ipsius passionis emolumentum: Dixi, inquiens, ascendam in palmam.

240 VERS. 8.-- Dixi: Ascendam in palmam et apprehendam fructum ejus: et erunt ubera tua sicut botri vineae, et odor oris tui sicut odor malorum.

Ac si eidem sponsae suae patenter dicat: Unde 1236Ahabes vincere, unde habes proficere? Estne tuae virtutis et industriae, quod tantae pulchritudinis decus tibi potes comparare? Si recte consideres, nequaquam tuae fortitudini vel prudentiae alicujus boni meritum ascribes. Ego enim dixi, hoc est ante tempora saecularia decrevi et determinate disposui, quia per signi praevaricationem occubuisti et impotens esse coepisti, et inimicum tibi ipsi peccando invenisti, cui postmodum praevalere non potuisti, sed quasi captiva ejus dominio subjacuisti, ut rursus per ligni oppositionem perditum tibi bonum recuperarem, et ab inimici potentia, et a captivitate qua detinebaris eriperem, redditaque libertate inimicum tibi substernerem et contra ejus insidias providentiam tibi praecavendo et virtutem 1236Bresistendi darem: idcirco dixi: Ascendam in palmam, hoc est in crucem, in quam postquam de hoste triumphavero, et fructus hujus passionis meae apprehendero, atque in signum victoriae resurgendo protulero, omnibus mihi obedientibus et in mea virtute spem habentibus hujus consolationis oraculum proferam: Confidite, ego vici mundum (Joan. XVI). Tu ergo debes pugnare, et quia secura es de victoria me victoriam jam adepto, crucem mecum carnem mortificando ascende ut omnis statura tuae animae assimiletur palmae, et perseverantiae titulo aeternae mancipetur victoriae.

Sed veneranda et adoranda omni animae hujus ascensio palmae. Quare? quia magnus profecto et 1236Cincomparabilis fructus ejus: quid enim? nonne per hunc fructum refectum et reparatum est totum genus humanum? Quis autem aut qualis fructus iste fuit et est? Nimirum generis humani redemptio, inimicitiae erga Deum reconciliatio, quotidiana peccatorum remissio, contra insidias inimici firma defensio, mundanae miseriae exitus, et regni coelestis introitus. Omnis enim profectus Ecclesiae ex tempore passionis et resurrectionis Christi coepit, atque exinde sanctitatis ejus praeconia et Spiritus sancti bona abundantissime profluxerunt. Unde et sequitur: Et erunt ubera tua sicut botri vineae, et odor oris tui sicut odor malorum. Nam praedicatio et doctrina ejus post remotionem umbrae per exhibitionem veritatis suavior et uberior emanavit, et 1236Dpost passionem et resurrectionem Christi, multos 241 divina charitate ita ebrios fecit, ut omnem in eis mundanae voluptatis humorem calore sancti Spiritus excoxerit, et ad coelestis vitae amorem accenderit.

Ex gutture vero vox egreditur, et idcirco per guttur memoria praeceptorum divinorum, per vocem ipsorum praeceptorum praedicatio, non incongrue accipitur; nisi enim primo in mente per memoriam teneantur, minime foras per sermonem proferentur; sed hujusmodi vox sermonis malorum odori comparatur, quia sicut per odorem res non tantum praesens, sed etiam absens sentitur, sic a tempore passionis et resurrectionis Christi per praedicationem Ecclesiae, non tantum praesentia 1237ADomini ipsius sive sanctorum ejus facta et dicta, sed etiam praeterita cognita sunt et quotidie legendo et audiendo cognoscuntur. Futura quoque bona seu mala ex his colliguntur, quando et justorum praemia et peccatorum supplicia longe quasi ex quodam intimi tactus odore pensantur. Non autem ad odorem florum, sed malorum vox ista refertur, quia praedicatio Ecclesiae quae nunc per totum resonat mundum non rudis vel tenera, sed matura et perfecta unam fidem credentibus ostendit.

VERS. 9.-- Guttur tuum sicut vinum optimum, dignum dilecto meo ad potandum, labiisque et dentibus illius ad ruminandum.

Guttur vero sicut vinum optimum dicitur, quia memoria praeceptorum divinorum mentem sui dulcedine 1237Binebriat, et quod suaviter interius meditando bibit, utiliter exterius eloquendo profundit. Dignum dilecto meo ad potandum. Christus in corpore suo, hoc est in Ecclesia, quae cum eo per Spiritum unum efficitur, sicut justitia, fide et sanctitate refici, ita et potari dicitur; quemadmodum e contrario in infidelibus justitiam, fidem et sanctitatem esurire atque sitire praedicatur. Nam in cruce pendens cum diceret: Sitio (Joan. XIX), fidem et sanctitatem infidelis populi sitiebat, quia propter eum quasi quodam aestu laboris fatigatus fuerat, quem de Aegypto multis signis et portentis duxerat, ante quorum faciem gentes contriverat, ad quos testamenti sui et legis pactum confirmaverat, quibus terram repromissionis, urbem templumque delegaverat, 1237Cpro quorum salute postremo ipsam mortem suscipere non dedignatus fuerat.

Cum ergo sancta Ecclesia, sive sancta quaelibet anima, legem Domini die ac nocte meditatur, in mente ipsius Christus quodam dulci meditationis vino potatur, et illius sancta meditatio est quasi suavis et digna Deo potatio. Unde cum sponsus guttur dilectae, hoc est meditationem mandatorum 242 Dei, quasi vinum optimum praedicaret, illa laudantis vocem interrumpens, et cooperatrici gratiae adgaudens, dignum, inquit, dilecto meo ad potandum, hoc est, dignum quod ipse sua gratia provehat, et ad effectum perducat.

Quomodo? Labiis et dentibus ruminando: quod 1237Denim secum frequenter meditando intelligit, debet aliis docendo impendere, exponendo tractare, et discutiendo retractare, quod est quasi mundi animalis proprium ruminare. In uno enim corpore Ecclesiae quod universus Christus intelligitur, guttur est divinae Scripturae meditatio, labia ipsius Scripturae pronuntiatio, dentes ejusdem explanatio veluti grossae litterae confractio, et ad spiritualis intelligentiae subtilitatem diminutio. Quare ipsi sponso dignum dicitur ad potandum sive ruminandum, quia omnis profectus Ecclesiae sive cujuslibet sanctae animae ejus muneris est et gratiae.

VERS. 10.-- Ego dilecto meo, et ad me conversio illius.

Quandoquidem, inquit, praeeunte ipsius dilecti 1238Amei gratia, placeo illi sanctarum Scripturarum meditatione, ergo volo et jure debeo magis ei appropinquare obediendo, bonis actibus studendo, caeterisque praecepta illius annuntiando, ut fiat hoc quod scriptum est: Appropinquate Deo et appropinquabit vobis (Jac. IV). Si enim me ad ipsum convertero, tunc ad me conversio illius, sicut ipse dixit: Convertimini ad me, et ego convertar ad vos (Zach. I): nulla autem mutabilitas in Deo est, ut humano more averti vel converti posse dicatur, sed quidem motus venientis sive recedentis gratiae in homine, quaedam conversio sive adversio Dei appellatur. Conversio illius ad nos, est gratiae vocantis, justificantis et glorificantis miseratio, per quam liberum juvatur arbitrium, et bonae voluntatis intentio ad 1238Bboni propositi perducitur effectum. Unde bene primo dicit: Ego dilecto meo, ac deinde, et ad me conversio illius, quia nostrum est primo bonae voluntatis intentionem ad boni operis studium assumere, illius bona intentione conceptum opus per cooperatricem gratiam ad bonum usque finem perducere. Quodcirca quia promptam in se sentiens voluntatem de cooperantis sibi adjutorio fiduciam assumit, continuo ad operationis studium accingitur dicens: Veni, dilecte mi.

243 VERS. 11.-- Veni, dilecte mi, egrediamur in agrum, commoremur in villis.

Egrediamur, inquit, quia postquam ad me conversio tua facta fuerit per cooperantem gratiam libere et secure possum exire, et ad praedicationis 1238Cofficium et ad bonae actionis studium, ut omnis mea operatio et a te semper incipiat et per te coepta finiatur: nihil enim boni sine te possumus facere.

Sed quo primo egrediemur? in agrum videlicet, hoc est gentem Judaeorum quae jam habilis est ad suscipiendum semen verbi Dei, quia jam exarata habet corda per legem scriptam et etiam naturalem, atque ideo magis intelligere potest ex lege et prophetis divinae bonitatis propositum quo decrevit restituere genus humanum. Illis enim primo oportet loqui verbum Dei (Act. XIII), quorum adoptio filiorum est gloria, et testamentum et legislatio, et obsequium, et promissa; quorum patres ex quibus 1238DChristus secundum carnem, qui est Deus benedictus in saecula (Rom. IX). In hunc ergo agrum divini verbi semine conspergendum, egrediamur per praedicationis officium, et quia primo credita sunt eis eloquia Dei (Rom. III), prima quoque in eis fidei et divinorum sacramentorum seminaria jaciamus.

Deinde progredientes, in villis commoremur, hoc est in gentibus, quae a civitate Dei, id est Ecclesia, remotae sunt, in quibus quia tardiores sunt ad credendum propter insolitam et inauditam fidei praedicationem, necesse erit moram facere et frequentius verbum vitae annuntiando ad urbanae consuetudinis elegantiam, hoc est ecclesiasticae legis observantiam reducere. Commoremur ergo inter eas, tu, o dilecte, per gratiam inspirans, ego per praedicationem 1239Aadjuvans, ut ingenitam eis ignorantiam, et rudis animi simplicitatem crebra eruditione atterentes, nostram civilem honestatem et veram sapientiam infundamus, per quam illius supernae civitatis felices accolae ascribi mereantur.

Cum autem hos duos parietes e diverso venientes, Judaeos scilicet et gentiles, in una fide conjunxerimus; non duo, sed unus erit populus, una Domini Sabaoth vinea, quae Spiritus sancti opere exculta, non jam labruscas, sed dulces faciet uvas.

VERS. 12.-- Mane surgamus ad vineas, videamus si vinea floruit, si flores fructus parturiunt, si floruerunt mala punica: ibi dabo tibi ubera mea.

244 Ad has autem vineas ex circumcisione et 1239Bpraeputio plantatas, mane surgamus, in exortu scilicet fidei, quando verus sol in cordibus credentium oriri coeperit et suae sapientiae charitate irradiare ea et virtutis calore accendere: videamus si vinea floruit, hoc est si jam unus christianorum populus factus initia bonorum operum protulit; si flores fructus parturiunt, hoc est si ipsa initia ad integritatem et perfectionem aliquam assurgere conantur; si floruerunt mala punica, hoc est si tanto Dei amore flagrent, ut non solum mente sed et corpore pro eo pati desiderent.

Ibi dabo tibi ubera mea: postquam enim hos duos populos per unitatem fidei unum fecerimus, et ad boni operis studium promoverimus, tunc ad laudem tui nominis, o dilecte, sacramenta quae ex 1239Csubtilitate duorum Testamentorum tuo munere cognovimus, eis quoque committemus, quatenus in eis semper et ad majora virtutum opera nutriantur, et contra mundi tentamenta roborentur, et ad futura beatudinis bona appetenda magis accendantur. Confidenter quippe praedicabo, et praeceptorum tuorum praecepta ( sic ) reserabo, quoniam habeo spem fructificandi, et effectum boni operis consequendi. Unde? quia mandragorae dederunt odorem.

VERS. 12.-- Mandragorae dederunt odorem in portis nostris. Omnia poma nova et vetera, dilecte mi, servavi tibi.

Ipse nempe odor spem mihi affert praedicandi, quia credo ex odore illo consequenter provenire 1239Dutilitatem fructus percipiendi. Sed considerandum diligenter quae sit ista mandragora, quive hujus mandragorae odor. Si ad litteram respicias, mandragora est herba aromatica quae ad similitudinem humanorum membrorum formata solo capite caret, cujus virtus est ut in potum data his quos vigiliae premunt, somnum adducat et requiem; porro steriles si ea utantur, concipere faciat.

Si vero spiritualem sensum attendas, mandragora non absurde accipi potest gentilitatis conversio, quae quandiu in sui erroris pravitate agebatur, non inani tantum, sed etiam exitiabili labore fatigabatur; sed postquam conversa Deum agnoscere coepit, et curis et voluptatibus rerum saecularium minus vigilare imo magis quam dormire, et a pravo 1240Alabore hujus mundi quiescere didicit; et quae prius a bono opere sterilis erat, postmodum fecunda virtutibus exstitit, impleta prophetia quae dicit: Laetare, sterilis, quae non paris: erumpe et clama, quae non parturis, quia multi filii desertae, magis quam ejus quae habet virum (Isa. LIV; Gal. IV).

245 Mandragora vero ut diximus cum habeat humani corporis similitudinem, capite caret, quia gentilis populus cum naturaliter ratione vigeret ad discretionem boni et mali, tamen ipsa vis rationis hac in parte in eo hebetata erat, qua Creatorem suum cognoscere non valebat, quem quia in sui cognitione non habebat, quasi capite carebat. Judaicus quoque populus per mandragoram significari potest, qui dum ratione per observantiam legis 1240Buteretur, caput tamen non habebat, quia Christum suscipere recusabat; sed mandragora ista postmodum odorem dedit, quia quae prius per infidelitatem sterilis fuerat, postea credens multos Deo filios generabat. Mandragorae ergo odorem dederunt in portis nostris, quia Judaicus et gentilis populus, te, o dilecte, in coelum ascendente, per tuam gratiam et meam praedicationem fidei sacramenta susceperunt. Quaenam autem sunt istae portae, in quibus credentem populum dicit dilecta odorem dedisse? Nimirum si diligenter consideres, agnoscere poteris per quas portas anima Deum invenire cupiens paulatim usque ad ipsa cubilis secreta progrediatur: primo namque in homine est animi conceptio, qua concipit id cujus summam 1240Cadipisci desiderat, quo concepto quid vel quale sit investigat, donec ipsius cognitionem habeat. Cognito autem eo amplectitur, et sic eo ad utilitatem sui utitur, ut omnem ejus integritatem ad se quandoque convertere conetur. Est ergo in unoquoque credituro quaedam porta et quasi primus ad Deum introitus, prima fidei in animo conceptio qua voluntatem credendi accipit, deinde ipsius fidei investigatio ut cognoscat quid vel qualiter credere debeat; post quam secundam investigationis portam aperitur ei tertia porta, fidei scilicet cognitio, post cognitionem sequitur operatio, sine qua fides otiosa esse decernitur, bene autem operantem Deo conjungit mundi cordis contemplatio.

1240DPer has ergo portas ad Deum venire contendentes, in ipsarum portarum introitu, bonae voluntatis odorem spargunt; sed iste odor per secundam portam investigatae fidei transiens, tertiam quoque cognitae fidei jam portam attingens, ac deinde quartam operationis portam percurrens, per quintam demum contemplativae dulcedinis portam ad ipsa interiora coelestis sponsi secreta illabitur. Cum ergo mandragorae dant odorem in his portis, evidens est quod Deum quaerentes animae ad fructum boni operis jam maturescunt. Digna ergo gratulatione sponsa 246 dilecto alludit dicens: Mandragorae dederunt odorem in portis nostris, quia dum Ecclesia filiorum suorum profectum intendit, competentes Deo gratiarum actiones persolvit. Unde magis ad 1241Apraedicationem accingitur, quia in eorum cordibus proficere se sperat, quos ad Deum toto corde conversos esse considerat. Ipsum vero profectum suum non suo labori et industriae, sed divinae gratiae imputat dicens: Omnia poma nova et vetera, etc., dilecte mi, servavi tibi. Ad tuum, inquit, honorem servavi, o dilecte, omnem fructum sanctitatis, quem ex Veteris vel Novi Testamenti institutione cognovi, sive quem ex praeceptorum informatione didici, sive quem ex Patrum vita et floribus informando collegi. Tui enim hoc est muneris, non mei laboris, vel quod ipsa bene vivendo et docendo profeci, vel quod alii meo exemplo sive doctrina proficere potuerunt. Sive, ut alio modo dicam, Omnia poma nova et vetera servavi tibi, quia omnia quae in 1241BVeteri Testamento mysterialiter facta et dicta, in Novo autem realiter exhibita leguntur, de tua nativitate, passione, resurrectione, et ascensione, scripta docui et exposui, cunctisque legentibus et audientibus fructum in eis fidei et bonae operationis ostendi.

229 CHAPTER VII.

VERSE 1.-- What shalt thou see in the Sulamite, but the choirs of camps? How beautiful are thy steps in shoes, O daughter of the prince! the joints of thy thighs are as necklaces which are made by the hand of a craftsman.

1226DSo long as Judaea was held captive by the chain of her error, or any soul whatever by the yoke of sin, no gladness could be seen in her, but misery, because both the former, in the fight between the letter and the spirit, and the latter, in the fight between the flesh and the spirit, was ever inferior in her better part: for the former followed the letter alone, the latter the flesh; but when through penance the former acknowledged and received the spiritual sense, and the latter, the love of the flesh trodden down, began to live according to the spirit, the kindly Father, receiving each mercifully, showed that he would bestow his help upon her, so that, having now obtained true and full liberty, and having as it were won the victory over the part adverse to her, she might, rejoicing in flesh and spirit, pay him devout praises. For this he himself promises through the prophet, saying: 1227AReturn ye to me, and I will return to you. (Malach. V). Whence also, rejoicing together at their conversion, he says to the Church: What shalt thou see in the Sulamite, but the choirs of camps? For in choirs is shown the alternation of melody sounding in concord; but in camps a fellowship of warriors is gathered for defence. What then are the choirs of camps, but the praises of warriors? and the sense is: Because this Sulamite has turned to me from the captivity under which she was held through 230 guilt, I will confer on her so great a grace of liberty and security that thou, O beloved, oughtest to see and wonder at nothing else in her than joyful thanksgivings and daily proclamations of praise for the motions of the vices overcome and cast down, and the advances in the virtues granted.

1227BNow, the two walls coming from opposite sides being as it were joined into one, namely the Jewish and the gentile people, of which he shows the whole universal Church to consist, he is directed again to her praise, that he may proclaim the so diverse graces of his condescension notably set in one body, and that for this reason thanksgivings are justly and worthily to be paid to him. He says therefore: How beautiful are thy steps in shoes, O daughter of the prince!

What is expressed by steps, but the courses of actions? what is signified by shoes, which are made from the skins of dead animals, but the examples of the fathers who went before and have been withdrawn from this life? for as the feet are protected by shoes, so by the examples of the holy fathers the manners of those who follow them 1227Care defended.

But who is the daughter of the prince, but either the Church, or any holy soul whatever, given over through the grace of adoption to him who is the prince of the kings of the earth? The Church therefore, or any holy soul whatever, has beautiful steps in shoes, because she has beautiful and reverend acts from the deeds and teachings of the holy fathers. Wherefore not unfittingly he adds: The joining of thy thighs as necklaces which are made by the hand of a craftsman. [Vulg. Juncturae femorum tuorum, "the joints of thy thighs"]

By the joining of the thighs the concord of the two Testaments is understood, because the Old and the New Testament are so evenly joined that what the one announces in figure, this the other represents in truth. 1227DBut what is it that these testaments are compared to necklaces? For a necklace is composed of gold and silver and precious stones, and is placed on the breast of matrons, that it may be to them both for a defence and for an ornament. But each Testament is built from the brightness of the divine sense and the lustre of the utterance, as it were from gold and silver, and also from the predications of the diverse virtues, as it were from certain precious gems. And as a necklace defends and adorns the breast of matrons, so each Testament spiritually defends and adorns the breast of holy Church, or of each holy soul: defends it indeed from the hostility of the vices, adorns it with the beautiful variety of the virtues.

The joining therefore of her thighs, as necklaces, because 1228Athe concord of the two Testaments, by which holy Church, or any holy soul, is daily instructed, confers on her a great protection and ornament; a protection 231 indeed against the perversities of heretics, an ornament on account of the comeliness and beauty of the senses and utterances, or of the power of the sacraments which are celebrated in her, and the honourableness of the ecclesiastical orders.

But who is this craftsman, by whose hand these necklaces, that is, the Testaments, have been made, but almighty God, by whose will, power, working these things have been honourably composed, profitably set forth, happily received? Wherefore the dignity of these Testaments is greatly to be commended, since they have been established by such an author, whose workmanship is not 1228Bhuman, but divine, not devised, but willed and of his power, for all things, indeed, whatsoever he would he hath done (Psal. XIII), and ever his willing was also his having done.

Holy Church therefore, or any holy soul whatever, gathers all the comeliness and beauty of her inner man from the consideration of these Testaments, [as to] what her needful profit sets before her to be believed, what to be hoped, what to be loved. But why is her joining of the thighs praised by the bridegroom? because the concord of the two Testaments, or of the two peoples, or of the twofold charity, constitutes the greatest and whole rule of living well, and lays up the most certain glory of reward for the rule kept; and well did he say the joining 1228Cnot femorum, but feminum, because from these is conceived, born and advanced all the honourableness and profit of holy Church, or of any faithful soul.

VERSE 2.-- Thy navel is like a turned bowl; never wanting cups. Thy belly is like a heap of wheat set about with lilies.

The navel is the middle point of the belly: what then is the navel of the Church, but the holy preachers and teachers, who move in the midst of the people, gathering that same people to themselves by teaching and working? For as all the entrails adhere to the navel, so the people adheres to its preachers, ever looking to their words and examples as to a certain middle point 1228Dset about it, that it may establish for itself in their manners and discourses a certain firm foundation of living well.

But this navel is said to be like a turned bowl, because, that they may cut away the superfluous and uneven things of manners, the holy teachers ever turn about the same thing, when for the attaining of that which is ever unchangeable and persists the same in its quality they run, labour, and hasten to draw others with them. Which bowl is said never to want cups, because these same preachers ever abound in the 232 sentences of the divine utterances, with which they themselves too are made drunk through the grace of the Holy Spirit, and are zealous sufficiently to refresh the thirsting breasts of the peoples.

In another way also, if we look to the soul of each faithful man, 1229Aholy charity can spiritually be called the navel of the mind, which, set as it were in a certain centre, touches all the virtues as it were through the circumference, because, since no virtue can be without charity, all the virtues, looking toward it, assuredly seem to be as it were appendages of charity.

But how is this called a turned bowl? The Apostle says that the end of the commandment is charity unto justice to every one that believeth (I Tim. I); therefore all perfection consists in charity, because it is turned, retaining in itself nothing of superfluity and of obstructing vice, and therefore perfect and smooth; for perfect charity casteth out fear, because fear is not in charity (I Joan. IV). For this perfection is the end of the commandment, that is, the consummation, as the prophet says, the word 1229Bconsummated which the Lord hath made upon the earth (Isa. X; Rom. IX).

But how never wanting cups? the apostles were said to be full of new wine when they burned with the Holy Spirit, that is, with the fire of divine charity: for they were drunk with that cup of the spiritual chalice of which the Psalmist says: And my chalice which inebriateth me, how goodly is it! (Psal. XXII.) They then who are filled with divine charity, how are they not ever moist and warm with that unfailing cup of the Holy Spirit? On the other hand, that land is said to be parched with thirst which is not sprinkled with the infusion of divine charity: whence the Lord cries to those parched with this thirst, saying: He that thirsteth, let him come to me and drink, and out of his belly shall flow living waters (Joan. VII). Therefore this turned bowl never wanteth a cup, because perfect 1229Ccharity never lacks the heavenly dew, and the desire of that highest good. But because there are in the Church prelates and subjects, strong and weak, prudent and simple, after Christ has praised his Church in the virtues of the prelates, he adds also a praiseworthy testimony from the obedience and discipline of the subjects, thy belly, saying, is like a heap of wheat. For because the belly is a frail and soft part of the body, by the belly is designated the frailty of the subjects, who cannot yet attain the perfection of the masters; but because they too belong to the Church, and are of the lot of the elect, whom that highest Householder calls his wheat, and commands to be gathered into his barn, it is not unfittingly compared to a heap of wheat. Now a heap is broadened below, 1229Dsharpened above, and the whole pile is a gathering of grains as it were embracing and bearing one another.

233 What then is expressed by the heap of wheat, but the multitude of the faithful obeying their prelates, who, although through the infirmity of the flesh and the cares of worldly things they are somewhat pressed down about the broad and spacious way, yet through obedience and humility, and brotherly charity also, are raised up by faith and hope to the things above? for embracing and helping one another, and bearing with the infirmities of manners and of bodies, they fulfil that saying of the Apostle: Bear ye one another's burdens, and so you shall fulfil the law of Christ (Gal. VI).

1230ABut this is said to be a heap of wheat set about with lilies, because through the odour of right faith and the confession of sins it advances much toward the whiteness of eternal life; for in lilies there is both odour and whiteness and medicine: the odour is in faith and working, the medicine in the confession of sins, the whiteness in the recompense of eternal life.

VERSE 3.-- Thy two breasts are like two young roes that are twins of the she-goat.

By the two breasts may not absurdly be understood the two precepts of charity, through which the soul of each faithful man is nourished by the tenderness of inward milk and is brought to the strength of spiritual exercise, so that it can say with the Apostle: I can do all things in him who strengtheneth me (Philipp. IV); for love is strong as death (Cant. VIII); and no tribulation separates the saints from charity 1230B(Rom. VIII). For through this they go from virtue to virtue (Psal. LXXXIII): whence also rightly the precepts of charity themselves are compared to two twin young roes of the she-goat, which by nature ever seeks the heights.

But why twins? surely on account of the concord and unity of that twofold charity, namely of God and of the neighbour, because they are so conceived and grow together in the mind of the saints that neither can be prior to the other, but when one loves God, one loves the neighbour also, and when one loves the neighbour, one loves God. For each is also a proof of the other, because, as John says: He that saith he loveth God and loveth not his brother is a liar (I Joan IV): and therefore these two precepts of charity are as it were two twins of the she-goat, because they are both carried on in one place and time, 1230Cand ever advance to higher things by the daily increase of the virtues.

Or, the two breasts are the two Testaments by which holy Church is daily nourished to works of piety, which also are as two young roes that are twins of the she-goat, because they are so one, the signifying and the signified, that although they were not of one time in their showing forth, yet they are of one time in their signification, and so great is the majesty of these Testaments that to those disputing of them an ever greater and loftier subtlety presents itself.

1230D234 VERSE 4.-- Thy neck is as a tower of ivory: thy eyes like the fishpools in Hesebon, which are in the gate of the daughter of the multitude. Thy nose is as the tower of Libanus, which looketh toward Damascus.

Because the voice goes out through the pipe of the neck, and food is ministered to the belly, rightly are the holy preachers designated by the neck, who through the office of preaching minister the victuals of doctrine to their fellow servants. But it is to be considered why it is called a tower, and why of ivory. A tower, first on this account, because the preaching of the saints is lofty on account of the sublimity of its sense; next because from the lofty contemplation of the mind, as from a certain tower, the coming of the enemy is foreseen, so that their snares may be guarded against, and this contemplation of the mind is taken from the teaching of the holy preachers: of ivory on account of the whiteness of the wisdom shining within; but the chaste utterance of the eloquence sounding without, as is sung in the Psalm, that the words 1231Aof the Lord are chaste and the commandment of the Lord is lightsome, enlightening the eyes (Psal. XVIII).

The neck therefore of holy Church, or of each holy soul, is as a tower of ivory, because its preaching is lofty, and firm, and beautiful, and while it raises the mind to God, it defends it from the snares of enemies, and suffers it to be corrupted by no stain of heretical depravity; on the other hand the Synagogue is called through the prophet a cloudy tower (Mich. IV), because the carnal knowledge of the Jews is dark and involved, which is indeed a tower, on account of the containing of the sublime sacraments which are hidden in it, but cloudy on account of the carnal understanding of the letter alone. Thy eyes like the fishpools in Hesebon, which are in the gate of the daughter of the multitude.

The eyes of holy Church, or rather of each faithful 1231Bsoul, may not unfittingly be understood as two considerations in the mind, as it were in the head, directed to right and to left, namely to the smallness and misery of the temporal life, and to the eternity and felicity of the perpetual and unchangeable life.

Which are rightly called as fishpools in Hesebon, which is interpreted the girdle of mourning, because assuredly from mourning and sorrow for sins, or from desire of the eternal goods, fountains of tears flow forth like fishpools through compunction. These fishpools indeed flow forth from a twofold compunction, which springs from the consideration of these two eyes, because while the mind weighs the punishments to come, and remembers its own evils, it is pricked to penance, as it were watered from one of the two fishpools.

1231CBut these fishpools are in Hesebon, because by this twofold compunction it is girded on the one side with the mourning of penance, on the other with that of love, so that it both may not slip back to its former vices, from the remembrance of the evils to come, and may bind itself strongly to the 235 pursuits of the virtues from desire of the goods to come, fulfilling the Lord's precept: Let your loins be girt (Luc. XII).

The fishpools moreover are said to be in the gate of the daughter of the multitude. But what is this gate? surely the going out of this life and the entering in of the life to come; whence it is said in the Psalm of the blessed man: He shall not be confounded when he shall speak to his enemies in the gate (Psal. CXXVI): for there shall be no confusion to the holy man in the going out of this life, 1231Dwhen the adverse party would withstand and harm him, because in his life he served him in whom the prince of this world found nothing of his own.

But who is the daughter of the multitude, whose that gate is said to be, but the holy soul of each faithful man, the daughter namely of that multitude of which there was one heart and one soul (Act. IV)? Which then indeed on earth was the rude and primitive Church, but it prefigured the unity of that which now in heaven, true and perfect concord, reigns with Christ through ineffable and unchangeable charity.

The daughter of this multitude surely has those fishpools of twofold compunction in her gate, because through penance for past evils, and desire of the goods to come, going out of this 1232Alife confidently and happily she enters the kingdoms of heaven. Beautifully therefore the eyes of the Church or of the holy soul are said to be as fishpools in Hesebon which are in the gate of the daughter of the multitude, because while from the remembrance of sins, or from love of eternal life, they are moist with the fountain of tears through twofold compunction, they open to themselves the entrance of the heavenly kingdom in the going out of life.

Otherwise the eyes of the Church may not unfittingly be called its overseers and teachers, to whom also this likeness can be fitted, that as the fishpools in Hesebon gird and fortify the city, so these gird and fortify the Church with the girdle of mourning, which Hesebon is interpreted, while by their teaching and preaching, as by a certain saving fountain, they call forth to compunction, to confession, to satisfaction, 1232Bsaying that word of the Gospel: Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven will draw near (Matth. III). For penance can rightly be called the girdle of mourning, because the life of the penitent ought so to be girded and fortified on every side that he both mourns what he has committed, and does not further commit what is to be mourned. For that is true penance by which past sins are so looked upon that future ones are feared, and it has mourning from the past, fear from the future. But because this fear hath punishment, while from the remembrance of the past and fear of the future it draws on mourning of mind, rightly does the penitent bind his life with the girdle of mourning.

But these fishpools in Hesebon are in the 236 gate of the daughter of the multitude: but who is the daughter of the multitude, or what is this multitude? Did not the apostles, and their successors, apostolic men, 1232Cbeget holy Church? Beholding whose dignity the Psalmist says: Exceedingly, he says, are thy friends honoured, O God, exceedingly is their principality strengthened (Psal. CXXXVIII); considering that they were not few but many, I will number, he says, them, and they shall be multiplied above the sand (ibid.) The daughter of this multitude therefore is holy Church, whom, as we have said, they begot by their teaching, who has a gate, namely the door of discretion, through which she discerns whom or what sort she should repel from her body. For since tares are always mixed with the wheat, the good indeed she incorporates into herself as sweet foods, the bad she tolerates in her body like bad humours, but heretics she utterly estranges from herself as deadly 1232Dpoison.

In this gate of discretion, therefore, the overseers or teachers of holy Church stand daily; as certain eyes in the head they know how to discern through the spirit of wisdom who belong, or do not belong, to the body of the Church, which fishes are to be chosen or which rejected on the shore of the last station: in fine, to the faithful they show the doors of life open, for sinners who do penance they open them when closed, but for the impious and those who do not do penance they close them eternally.

Or, the gate of the daughter of the multitude is called faith, which is the beginning and as it were a certain entrance to the way of salvation, without which it is impossible to please God (Hebr. XI), which the holy teachers set forth in the forefront to those seeking the way of life, and desiring to come 1233Ato the heavenly fatherland; because each ought first to believe rightly, and then, believing rightly, to work well.

But because we have said that this gate of the daughter of the multitude is the grace of discretion, by which the holy overseers and teachers of the Church know how either to admit the penitent or to exclude those who do not do penance, what sort that discretion is or ought to be is added, when it is said: Thy nose is as the tower of Libanus, etc.

For by the nose, by which we discern odours and stenches, is designated the discretion of the saints, through which they know how to discern the odours of the virtues and the stenches of the vices, that they may understand what they ought to choose and what to reject. Which surely is said to be a nose as the tower of Libanus, 1233Bbecause, namely, the discretion of those set over others ought both always to be fortified by circumspection, and always to stand in the height of life, that is, not to lie in the valley of infirm working. For as a tower is set on a mountain for a watch-post, that enemies who come may be seen from farther off, so the life of the preacher ought always to remain fixed on high, that after the manner of the nostrils it may discern the stenches 237 of the vices, and the odours of the virtues, may foresee from afar the onsets of the malignant spirits, and make the souls committed to it wary through its own prudence. And because discretion itself is said to be the mother of the virtues, it is rightly compared to the tower of Libanus, which sounds whitening, inasmuch as through it the beauty of all the virtues is understood to be guarded.

But this tower is said to look toward Damascus, 1233Cbecause the life of the saints is fortified with a strong guard against the temptations of the vices through the lofty consideration of discretion. For Damascus is interpreted drinking blood, by which this world is rightly designated, which is daily made drunk with vices and sins; for the prophet shows that sins are designated by blood, saying: And blood hath touched blood (Ose. IV), that is, sin has come to sin; and the Psalmist: Deliver me, he says, from bloods, O God, God of my salvation (Psal. L).

This tower therefore is directed toward Damascus, because the life of the saints, lofty and fortified with virtues, is fortified beforehand against the pleasures of this world by strong and discreet consideration.

VERSE 5.-- Thy head is like Carmelus: and the locks of thy head as the purple of the king joined to the channels. [Vulg. vincta canalibus, "bound in the channels"]

1233DBy the head the principal part of the mind is designated. But Carmelus is interpreted knowing circumcision or soft river.

Rightly therefore is the holy mind compared to Carmelus, because it is both lofty in divine contemplation, and knows how to cut off from itself the carnality of manners or of thoughts by spiritual circumcision, and, the grace of the divine Spirit pouring it in, is zealous to water the hearts of the hearers with sweet teaching as with a soft river. And the locks of thy head as the purple of the king, joined to the channels.

The locks of the head may be understood as the thoughts of the mind, which are said to be as the purple of the king joined to the channels, because the more they are joined to and intent upon the Scriptures as upon certain channels, the more they are kindled to the imitation of the passion of Christ by mortifying 1234Atheir flesh with its vices and concupiscences, or by offering the flesh itself, if need be, to persecutions for Christ, sacrificing to God the precious purple of heart and body in martyrdom.

We can also in another way fit this little portion of the speech to the head itself of the Church, that is, to the Lord Jesus Christ, namely so that in his own person he brings himself in speaking to that same Church, his bride: Thy head is like Carmelus, and the locks of thy head as the purple of the king joined to the channels. I, he says, O bride, who am called and am thy head, can be compared to Mount Carmel on account of its height and the interpretation of its name; because since I am the most general good, there is nothing that could be more excellent than my nature according to the divinity, and further according to the humanity 1234B238 nothing holier than my life and conversation, and in my teaching true and perfect circumcision of heart is learned, and all my preaching runs down truly as a soft river, that it may refresh the minds of the hearers by its wholesomeness, and form them to the pursuits of good work. The locks of this thy head are my apostles, my other saints also, who cleave to me by charity as locks to the head, to whom purple well agrees, because as the purple which is nearer the channels is better dyed, so their mind which is made nearer to my words and institutions or those of my prophets is the more kindled by power to the love of me, and in my tabernacle, that is, in my Church, as precious and royal purple, namely scarlet twice dyed (Exod. XXVIII), to shine forth with the love of God and of the neighbour it 1234Cstrives.

Therefore, because the head of man is God (I Cor. II) [Vulg. omnis viri caput Christus est, "the head of every man is Christ"], if any faithful man desires by virtue of mind to be a lock of this his head, it is needful that as a searcher he should cleave more diligently to the sacred channels of the Scriptures, because there he finds wherewith he may be dyed, that he may be made the purple of his heavenly King through inward love by the mortification of the carnal life. But it is to be noted that the beloved beautifully answers his beloved with a proclamation of praise of this kind in ten parts as it were on ten strings, sounding spiritually on one ten-stringed instrument, which is so fittingly set over against the ten-stringed instrument above, which the bride had sung in praise of the bridegroom, that the one from the higher parts, the other from the lower, impose the measure of a most pleasing melody. For because the bride ought always to ascend to the bridegroom with right intention and perfect 1234Dlove, it is just that she should rise from lesser things to greater, and therefore the proclamation of her advancing and as it were growing toward the virtues of the mind is sung by the bridegroom condescendingly; not that this advance, virtue and power belongs to the one receiving, but rather because it is the praise of the bridegroom who gives and bestows on her this virtue and power by his gift.

But the bride, reverently attending to the immense kindness of the bridegroom descending from heaven, and humbling himself to our infirmity for our sake, begins the proclamations of his praise from the highest proclamation of the body, that is, from the head, as it were from the higher string, that she may show that she, set lower, always ought to look back toward the life and teaching of her bridegroom set over against her above, and to ascend 1235Aby imitation to him whom she knows to have descended to her through the tenderness of compassion.

239 VERSE 6.-- How beautiful art thou, and how comely, dearest, in delights!

After the bridegroom has proclaimed in the bride, part by part, the variety of the members composed from the habit of a mind well bone and honourably ordered, showing that one certain whole had grown up thence, he calls the whole of the virtues by the name of stature, but declares the abundance of doctrine by the signification of breasts. For what beauty of manners or of utterances is lacking in the whole body of holy Church? for since this one shines with this virtue, that one with that, another with another, some possess more kinds of virtues, some fewer, what of form, of beauty and of comeliness can there be which 1235Bholy Church does not have in her body? And since diverse men are renowned for diverse learning in holy doctrines, what knowledge of truth or of holiness can there be in which holy Church does not abound? For since according to the Apostle to one may be given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, to another faith, to another the grace of healings, to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another the discerning of spirits; to another kinds of tongues, to another interpretation of speeches (I Cor. XII), assuredly all the beauty and adornment of works or of speeches shines forth spiritually in the inner stature of holy Church.

Whence she is deservedly pronounced beautiful and comely, and dearest in delights; because assuredly the abundance of the virtues and the saving teaching of wisdom are great 1235Cdelights of the soul; but the more the soul is delighted by these, the more fully is it filled with the sweetness of divine love.

VERSE 7.-- Thy stature is likened to a palm tree, and thy breasts to clusters of grapes.

But why is a stature of this kind likened to a palm tree? For the palm is a sign of victory; and what victory is greater and more glorious than to triumph over vices and sins? And whence has a stature of such a kind, wonderful and glorious, grown up, but from the victory of the virtues and the destruction of the vices? Not unfittingly therefore the stature of the Church is likened to a palm, because all the honourableness and probity of her manners tells of notable victories.

1235DFurther, her breasts are likened to clusters of grapes, because her doctrine and preaching abounds in the sweet and pleasant savour of wisdom and of spiritual understanding, and so inebriates her hearers that it makes them as it were insensible to the pleasures of this world. And that the bridegroom himself may show that the beauty of this stature advances and grows chiefly and principally from the mortification of the carnal life, he holds out to her the example of his passion and the gain of that same passion: I said, saying, I will go up into the palm tree.

240 VERSE 8.-- I said: I will go up into the palm tree and take hold of its fruit: and thy breasts shall be as the clusters of the vine, and the odour of thy mouth like the odour of apples.

As if he should say openly to that same bride of his: Whence 1236Ahast thou to conquer, whence hast thou to advance? Is it of thy own strength and industry that thou canst procure for thyself the glory of so great beauty? If thou considerest rightly, thou wilt by no means ascribe the merit of any good to thy fortitude or prudence.
