XXI), ne scilicet suam praecipitent sententiam, sed sapientes adhibeant in testimonium; nam scire debent, quia prima generis nostri quam omnes luimus culpa est inobedientia, et quia contumacibus et protervis nullam justitia Dei reponit veniam, sed, sicut scriptum est: Deus superbis resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam (I Petr. V).

Semper enim tales ad portam judicii examinandi sunt, ut si in sua contumacia vel temeritate permanserint, et obedire noluerint, a consortio fratrum ejiciantur; si vero poenituerint et humiles et quieti fuerint, 268 denuo recipiantur. Haec est etiam porta judicii in civitate Dei, hoc est sancta Ecclesia, ut contumaces et rebelles si corrigi nolunt, ferro 1260Aexcommunicationis tanquam putrida membra a corpore Ecclesiae praecidantur, de quibus scriptum est: Ex nobis quidem exierunt, sed non erant ex nobis (I Joan. II); porro poenitentes et suae malitiae finem imponentes, tanquam curata et sancta membra in corpus Ecclesiae reponantur. Igitur caetera quidem peccata toleranda sunt in domo Dei, contumaces autem et protervos filios severitas patrum sapientum obruit, ut auferat malum de medio sui, cum auctoritate legis Domini quam memoravimus; imo proprio exemplo Dei, qui inobedientes primos homines de paradiso expulit (Gen. III).

Verbum igitur traditionis quod de domino vineae pronuntiatur, non negligenter sed diligenter et cum timore cogitandum et pensandum est, quia utrobique 1260Bneglectum vel contemptum, sive a praelatis sive a subjectis, ad tradentis respicit judicium.

Vir affert pro fructu ejus mille argenteos. Diligens et studiosus inspector hujus capituli attendere debet quis vel qualis, aut quantus sit hujus vineae fructus, qui tanti pretii aestimatur, ut pro ejus assecutione, non decem, aut viginti, aut triginta, sed determinate mille sunt argentei deferendi, et qui hos deficiens, comparare hunc fructum possit non quilibet potens et dives, sive officialis vel privatus, sed absolute vir dici et esse debeat.

Quis igitur fructus est iste? nimirum quidem ille qui velut tribus pulchritudinis coloribus depingitur, videlicet potentia, sapientia, bonitate: potentia 1260Cquidem qua nihil efficacius, sapientia qua nihil rationabilius, bonitate qua nihil dulcius. Nam potentia nulla impossibilitatis vel infirmitatis lege constringitur, sapientia nihil admittit quod rationis virtute careat, bonitas tanta dulcedinis multitudine affluit, ut nihil supra. Praeterea hujusmodi fructus attactus et usus efficax et saluberrimum sanitatis toti homini praebet experimentum. Sed ubi hoc in creaturis et visibilibus invenitur? Nunquid in angelis? Scriptum est autem, quia et in angelis suis iniquitatem reperit (Job IV). Creatura enim corruptioni et mutabilitati subjacere potest, quod autem non potest, immutabile et incorruptibile esse necesse est.

Porro tres pulchritudines hujus fructus diximus 1260Dtales esse, ut nihil supra se suscipere possunt; potest tamen aliquid infra esse, quod ex earum affectione vel participatione dicatur aliquo modo potens, sapiens et bonum esse, 269 sed non substantialiter, potentia, sapientia, bonitas. Quod enim susceptibile et participabile est, non idem est quod suscipiens et participans, nam suscipiens et participans est, quando nec suscipit, nec participat, atque ideo mutabilitati subjacet et potest corrumpi: porro susceptibile et participabile in sui semper essentia immutabiliter consistens, nunquam potest corrumpi, nulla autem creatura susceptibilis et participabilis est, Deus igitur est. Cum ergo quaerimus quisnam fructus hujus vineae sit, et omnes ejus virtutis et pulchritudinis circumstantias attendimus. 1261Aprocul dubio Deum esse postremo concludimus. Susceptione autem et participatione hoc consequitur rationalis creatura, ut quandoque transeat in incorruptionem et immutabilitatem, non natura sed gratia, atque ita ex homine operante et Deo cooperante, quasi nascitur et crescit fructus iste, qui est praemium omnium ad Dei regnum pertinentium, et appellatur vera beatitudo. Vera autem beatitudo ipse est Deus quem habere et quo frui aeternaliter est vere beatum esse. Fructus igitur iste Deus est.

Porro de qualitate hujusmodi fructus quid dicemus, cum de ea scriptum sit, quod nec oculus vidit, nec auris audivit, nec in cor hominis ascendit? (I Cor. II.) Verumtamen superius eumdem fructum tribus distinximus coloribus, quod magis ad qualitatem 1261Bpertinet, non quod differentia colorum diversum faciat fructum, sed quod haec diversitas ita inseparabiliter uni substantiae cohaereat, ut nullam proprietatis virtutem et efficaciam aliquo modo adimat. Sicut enim, verbi gratia, in uno aliquo subjecto tres conveniunt colores, et unus nomen habet ut dicatur rubeus, alter albus, tertius viridis, una tamen substantia et eadem est, quae hos continet; sic in isto fructu, cum aliud non sit potentia, aliud sapientia, atque aliud bonitas, unus tamen et idem est fructus, et unam atque eamdem virtutem et efficaciam ubique habet, videlicet posse, sapere, vegetare, quae tamen efficiunt ut nihil boni sit, quod ejus plenitudini desit.

1261CDe quantitate vero hujus fructus quid dicendum est, cum tantae immensitatis sit ut nullo circumscribatur loco, nullo concludatur termino? Videtur tamen quaedam spatia habere, non secundum se, sed secundum participans: nullum autem hujus rei participans esse potest, nisi rationalis creatura. Porro rationalis 270 creatura, altera spiritualis est, ut angelus et anima, altera corporalis ut elementa, et quae ex his composita sunt. Sed quia non est hujus loci de corporalis rei dimensionibus disputare, quae linea, superficie, vel solido corpore constituuntur, fructus autem iste de cujus quantitate dicere coepimus, non corporalis sed spiritualis est; Deus enim spiritus est (Joan. IV), de cujus quantitate quia incomprehensibilis et incircumscriptus 1261Dest, nec cogitare, nec dicere aliquis potest, videamus tamen nunc quae sint spatia quae habere potest non secundum se, sed secundum participans. Quidquid enim bonitatis, honestatis, sanctitatis, disciplinae vel scientiae habere potest participans anima, de participabili Deo quasi profluentem in se gratiae sumit vigorem; atque per hoc videtur habere participans aliquid longius vel brevius, latius vel angustius, altius vel inferius, secundum quod illi placet distribuere, qui dat unicuique gratiam secundum mensuram fidei (Rom. XII). Unde Apostolus ad illos loquens quos ad hujusmodi dimensiones suscipiendos hortabatur: In charitate, inquit, radicati et fundati, ut possitis comprehendere cum omnibus sanctis quae sit longitudo, 1262Alatitudo, altitudo et profundum (Ephes. II).

Quia vero fructus iste, de quo loquimur, de radice charitatis nascitur et crescit, et ad maturitatem quasi ad perfectionem pervenit, non quantum ad capabilem Deum, qui semper perfectus, sed quantum ad capacem hominis mentem, qui augmento et detrimento subjacet, ut hoc modo proficiendo Deum quandoque comprehendat, cum quo suo modo perfectus et incommutabilis fiat, primo videamus de ipso nostro Domino Jesu Christo, quomodo juxta humanitatem de radice charitatis omnes has in se susceperit dimensiones, longitudinem videlicet, latitudinem, altitudinem et profundum: quis enim majorem eo charitatem habuit, qui animam suam pro ovibus suis posuit? (Joan. XV.)

1262BSi autem ponamus oculos mentis in genere et qualitate passionis ejus, videbimus omnes has dimensiones venerabiliter contineri, et hoc exemplo omnem Christianam animam viriliter promoveri. In figura quippe crucis, notandae sunt quatuor dimensiones istae, scilicet longitudo, altitudo, latitudo et profundum, quae ex radice charitatis Christi in totum protenduntur mundum, significantis et monentis omnem animam quae ejus passione redempta fuerit, si praedictum fructum, hoc est si aeternam beatitudinem consequi voluerit, ejusdem charitatis dimensionibus, juxta modum et naturam sibi concessam, ad eam pertingere debere.

271 Lata enim debet esse charitas, quia usque 1262Cad dilectionem inimicorum extendi debet, sicut Christus in cruce pendens pro inimicis oravit dicens: Pater, ignosce illis, quia nesciunt quid faciunt (Luc. XXIII). Longa debet esse, quia non horaria, sed usque ad finem vitae, sicut de Christo scriptum est: Cum dilexisset suos, in finem dilexit eos (Joan. XIII), tantam quippe perseverantiam debet habere charitas, ut pro nulla tribulatione vel angustia deficiat. Alta debet esse, propter causam finalem, ut scilicet attendat propter quid agat vel patiatur, hoc est propter aeternam beatitudinem, quae est fructus iste, de quo loquimur, propter quem semper sursum intendere, et in coelo conversationem habere monetur; profundum debet habere, quia nunquam absque timore debet esse, sed semper attendere 1262Dquod quidquid ex latitudine, longitudine, et altitudine consequitur, non ex suis meritis, sed ex Dei misericordia habet; et ideo quia ignorat occultum et profundum Dei judicium, quare unum eligat et alterum repellat, et semper finis incertus est dum multi vocantur, pauci cliguntur (Matth. XX), nunquam sine timore debet esse.

Itaque quoniam in Christo habitat omnis plenitudo divinitatis corporaliter (Coloss. II), et ei non ad mensuram dat Deus spiritum (Joan. III), omnes autem sancti de plenitudine ejus accipiunt, gratiam pro gratia (Joan. I), videntur ad harum dimensionum spatia, suo quique modo vel mensura pertingere, secundum quod eis dat qui plenarie habet et de sua plenitudine dare potest, quantum voluerit.

1263APorro quia charitas veluti centrum in meditullio posita omnes quasi per circumferentiam virtutes tangit, omnis enim virtus ex radice charitatis descendit; cumque omnis motus sex species habeat, sit namque ante et retro, sursum et deorsum, dextrorsum sinistrorsum; ad quamcunque partem mens hominis intentionem dirigit pro consequendo ejusmodi fructu, semper originem omnis boni motus a charitatis vigore accipit. Et quia ipse homo minor mundus dictus, ad instar majoris mundi quatuor constat elementis, quatuor quoque mensuratur partibus, quibus continetur totus, si ad Dei similitudinem conservandam fuerit institutus, videlicet prudentia, justitia, temperantia, fortitudine.

His quatuor partibus a centro mentis, hoc est 1263Bcharitate, aequa distantia porrectis, quidquid virtutis in anima potest esse, quasi circulum et circumferendo tangis et concludis.

Haec ergo aliquo modo esse potest mensura sive dimensio, quam potest habere fructus iste participans, non secundum se ut dictum est, sed secundum participans, ut quandoque a participante sicuti est 272 adeptus, omnem deinceps adimat dimensionis in crescendo passibilitatem sive mutabilitatem, et conferat perfecte aeternam impassibilitatem, immutabilitatem, immortalitatem Locus obscurus..

Igitur iste fructus vera est beatitudo, vera autem beatitudo est Deus cujus qualitas et immensitas incomprehensibilis est. Sed quia jam cognovimus qui sit fructus praescriptae vineae, videamus nunc de 1263Cofferente, qui sit, quia vir dicitur esse, nec aliter nisi vir sit, offerre possit. Vir quippe a virtute dicitur, et qui pro tanto fructu offerre debet, oportet ut virtutum pulchritudine et gratia resplendeat, quia non erit accepta oblatio, quam nulla virtutum commendat claritudo. In ratione enim dati et accepti ea debet esse forma ut talis sit in dante habitus compositio, et honestatis atque disciplinae gratia, ut in accipiente pariat beneplacitum et hilaritatem vultus, et munus reddat acceptius. Et si hoc disciplinae et honestatis bonum mortales inter se affectant, et approbant homines, quid putamus Deum omnipotentem et immortalem velle et quaerere a nobis, cujus natura bonitas, sanctitas, honestas 1263Dsingularis et disciplina est? Ergo qui tali Domino offert, indutus debet esse fortitudine et praecinctus virtute (Psal. XCII): fortitudine quidem mentis ad coercenda et repellenda vitia et peccata, virtute animi ad bona opera agenda et exercenda. Non enim recta est oblatio quam culpae repellit obfuscatio, quia et Cain Dominus dixit: Si recte offeras, recte autem non dividas, peccasti (Gen. IV). Recte quidem obtulit, qui fruges terrae Deo dedit, sed non recte divisit, qui cor in malo detinuit, et oblationem suam invidiae peste maculavit: secernere enim debuit bonum a malo, quia nulla participatio lucis ad tenebras, nec possunt in conspectu Dei simul esse 1264Averitas et falsitas, aequitas et malitia. Recte quidem obtulit, quia cui debuit Deo obtulit; sed non recte divisit, quia quod erat melius Deo recte negavit, quod vilius dedit: non enim satis Deo charus est, imo Deo indignus est, qui rem suam illi quidem offert, seipsum autem sibi retinet.

Talem ergo virum Propheta describit in primo psalmo, ubi hujusmodi habitum viri et propositum repraesentat, quem psalmum quia intelligentibus notus est, quicunque hunc virum assumere cupit, jugiter meditetur et opere exerceat: alio quoque loco hunc eumdem virum breviter commemorat dicens: Beatus vir qui timet Dominum, in mandatis ejus cupit nimis (Psal. CXI), et caetera, hoc est enim quod hunc virum efficit, et beatum, quia virtutis est 1264Btimere Deum, et mandata ejus considerare et servare; beatitudinis vero quod propter hoc, potens in terra erit semen ejus, et justitia ejus manet in saeculum saeculi (ibid).

273 Descripto offertore quem virum decet esse, videndum nunc quid pro tali fructu vir affert et afferre debet. Mille, inquit, argenteos. Millenarius numerus pro perfectione ponitur, argentum autem castorum eloquiorum purum et lucidum designat sensum, sicut scriptum est: Eloquia Domini, eloquia casta, argentum igne examinatum (Psal. XI). Sed quid possumus dicere argenteum de hoc argento formatum et inscriptum? Si diligenter inspiciamus, quid est quod format, vel inscribit in mente hominis imaginem Dei, imaginem sanctitatis et justitiae; 1264Cnisi praeceptum Domini lucidum illuminans oculos (Psal. XVIII), oculos videlicet hominis interioris? ubi autem praeceptum Domini audimus, et unde cognoscimus, nisi ex sancta Scriptura quae est eloquium Domini? Haec ergo Scriptura bene intellecta format, et quasi quamdam inscriptionem facit in mente hominis, ut cum ex lectione sanctae Scripturae charitatem perfecte assumpserit, de corde puro et conscientia bona, et fide non ficta (II Tim. II), argentei cujusdam monetam suscipiat, hoc modo inscriptam, ad imaginem et similitudinem Dei, hanc enim formam ipse rerum Conditor homini creando imprimendam instituit dum diceret: Faciamus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram (Gen. I), 1264Dquod est dicere: Faciamus hominem viventem, rationabilem, Deo similem: cuncta etenim animantia duplici honore praecellit hominis conditio, dum dicitur ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram; ad imaginem videlicet, ut sit rationalis, ad similitudinem nostram, ut rectus sit sectando justitiam Dei. Horum altero, scilicet rationalitate, carere non potest; alterum, hoc est divinae rectitudinis vel justitiae similitudinem, nisi per gratiam assequi non potest: sed ea qua carere non potest homo facultas rationalitatis instrumentum est, sive oculus quidam ad quaerendam similitudinem Dei. Est ergo inexcusabilis, cum ad Dei similitudinem non pervenerit, 1265Aquia videlicet bono instrumento ad hoc, propter quod sibi datum est, uti noluit.

Verum cum primum fecit Deus hominem, non solum rationalem, sed et similitudinis suae fecit honore pollentem, Deus enim, inquit Scriptura, fecit hominem rectum, ipse vero implicuit se multis quaestionibus (Eccle. VII). Nunc autem seductus perdidit quidem honorem similitudinis Dei, sed facultas rationis in eo permansit, per quam revocantem audire et ad restaurationem sui ducem ac praeceptorem valeat sequi. Argentum ergo hujusmodi divinus et summus ille trapezeta in anima hominis inscripsit, quando eam rationalem et suae sanctitatis participem fecit.

274 Quocirca debitor est homo Deo, ut, quia Deus 1265Beum hoc duplici honore insignivit, intelligat debitum suum, videlicet ut rationis capax, ipsa ratione duce, semper ad Dei similitudinem per sanctitatem proficiat, ne, si non intelligat, compararetur jumentis insipientibus, et similis fiat illis (Psal. XLVIII). Hoc denique debitum quia homo debeat Deo ostendit Dominus in Evangelio, quia cum tentaretur a Scribis et Pharisaeis dicentibus: Si licet censum dare Caesari an non, respondit: Ostendite mihi numisma census; qui cum ostendissent, dixit: Cujus est imago et superscriptio? Quibus respondentibus: Caesaris: Reddite, inquit, quae sunt Caesaris Caesari, et quae sunt Dei Deo (Matth. XXII).

Hac ergo sententia sua demonstrat Dominus et demonstrando docet, ut sicut justum est homini 1265Cmortali ea quae illius sunt; et quae ab illo donata sunt, tributaria subjectione reddi, ita justum, imo justissimum est, Deo omnipotenti et immortali ea quae illius sunt, et quae ab illo concessa sunt, homini summa devotione et humili subjectione deferri. Sunt autem homini a Deo concessi ratio et intellectus, quibus ita uti debet, ut ad Dei similitudinem bene vivendo proficiat, atque hanc superscriptionem argentei in anima et mente sua ex sanctitatis fulgore suscipiat, ad imaginem et similitudinem Dei.

Igitur hujuscemodi argenteum, unum vel duos sive tres aut plures, secundum mensuram donationis Dei, aliquis fidelis offert, ut comparet fructum 1265Dillum, hoc est vitam aeternam quae per dilectionem operatur, tendit et proficit ad Dei similitudinem. Sed mille affert argenteos, qui perfectae sanctitatis claritate Dei adeptus est imaginem et similitudinem.

Sive millena unitas unam significat fidem, unum baptisma, unum Deum qui operatur omnia in omnibus, et qui fructum illum, hoc est aeternam desiderat vitam, oportet ut veram et rectam fidem teneat et doceat, unum Deum et unum hominem habeat et colat, nomen Christianitatis quod in baptismo suscepit, fide et operibus exornet, veram, catholicam, et unam divinam Scripturam legat, doceat, amplectatur et sequatur. Igitur cum haec de semetipsa dilecta ad gratiam et gloriam 1266Adilecti dicit, continuo respondens ait: Vinea, etc.

VERS. 12.-- Vinea mea coram me est. Mille tui pacifici, et ducenti his qui custodiunt fructum ejus.

Vinea, inquit, mea coram me est, hoc est cognosco et approbo meam 275 vineam, ex hoc quod gratiam plantationis meae in ea invenio, quam si non invenirem, coram me esse non posset, nec mea vinea dici posset. Nam de vobis qui vinea mea dici et esse potestis, per prophetam locutus sum, quia aspiciam vos et crescere faciam, multiplicabimini, et firmabo pactum meum vobiscum (Levit. XXVI): qui enim coram me sic sunt, ut praesentia mea et visione digni sint, bonorum operum claritate fulgentes illos agnosco et custodio; quia oculi Domini super justos (Psal. XXXIII), sicut econtrario, 1266Bqui me postponunt contemnendo, illos quoque et ego postpono reprobando, atque ideo adjutorium gratiae meae non impendendo.

Mille tui pacifici, et ducenti his qui custodiunt fructus ejus; ex opposito illius vineae, quae in pravum conversa est, de qua dicitur, quia exspectavi ut faceret uvam, fecit autem labruscas (Isa. V), melius hujus capituli sensus patebit. Dicit enim Dominus per Osee de ea sub specie meretricis: Et fodi eam mihi quindecim argenteis, et coro hordei et dimidio coro hordei (Ose. III): sacramentum autem, in his numeris absconditum est pulcherrimum; hic in mille argenteis, illic in quindecim argenteis, et coro hordei et dimidio coro hordei; cujus videlicet haec summa est, quod ista et virgo sit et viro conjuncta, illa 1266Cautem neque virgo neque viro conjuncta, hujus namque virginitatem unitas millena; conjunctionem vero sive nuptias binarius centenus significat. Arithmetici vero sive abacistae melius norunt quod dicitur, et qua ratione unitas virgo pronuntietur, usu habent in suis tractatibus, quod videlicet in semetipsa multiplicata nihil creat, quia semel unus, unus est, quod nulli alii numero contingit: nam caeteri numeri in semetipsos ducti alios creant, ut bis duo quatuor, et tertia novem: porro nuptias hujus centenus designat binarius, et hoc felicissimum est, quia dilecta haec quae ex fide est, et semper viro conjuncta est, et semper virgo permanet, semper generat, semper tamen virgo permanet.

1266DE contra illius viduitatem simul et corruptionem illius designat, quod pretium ejus neque in unitate mansit, neque ad binarium pervenit, cum dicitur: Fodi eam mihi quindecim argenteis et coro hordei et dimidio coro hordei. Si argenteos attendas, neque decem sunt argentei, quae esset unitas decena, neque viginti qui esset binarius decenus, sed sunt quindecim, in quo videlicet numero plus unitate, minus est binario: similiter neque unus tantum corus hordei, neque duo sunt cori, sed corus et dimidius hordei, plus monade, minus binario. Itaque et illi hoc infelicissimum est, quia neque virgo est, neque virum habet. Igitur mille tui pacifici argentei, 276 hoc est omnes sermones in una fide consonantes; numerus enim iste, millena 1267Aunitas est, et pacem, hoc est remissionem peccatorum facientes vel acquirentes sunt tibi; quandoquidem unum Dominum, unam fidem, unum baptisma habere, est in catholica Ecclesia esse, ubi datur remissio peccatorum per pacem, id est Christum, qui est pax nostra, qui fecit utraque unum (Ephes. II). Sancta etenim Scriptura, quae haec tria resonat et docet, totam hujus pacis summam in se continet, quia quidquid legis, de Deo, de fide, de Christianitatis religione est, et omnia Ecclesiae sacramenta ex his sunt constituta, et qui ea habet, sicut habere debet, pacem illam consequitur, quae sentit bella vitiorum; cumque hac pace ad virtutum abundantiam profecerit, data sibi remissione peccatorum, ad illam perpetuam atque nunquam finiendam pacem pertinget, ubi nullus labor, nullus dolor, 1267Bnihil omnino erit, quod ei adversari possit.

Sunt igitur tria ista hujus pacis instrumenta, quia omni animae ad hanc tendenti semper considerandum cui credat, quid credat, quomodo credat. Si enim quaeras cui vel in quem credere debeas, Deus tibi proponitur; si vero quaeris quid credere, Ecclesiae tibi sacramenta ostenduntur; porro si quaeras quomodo credere debeas, Christianitatis tibi religio praescribitur. Fides enim sine operibus otiosa, imo mortua est (Jac. II), et: Sine fide impossibile est placere Deo (Hebr. XI). Proinde, ut diximus, propter istarum trium rerum unitatem, quae veram aeternamque constituunt et acquirunt pacem, recte quidem huic vineae mille dicatur esse pacifici.

1267CSed ducenti his qui custodiunt fructus ejus, cur esse dicuntur? Primo quidem videndum qui sunt hujus fructus custodes, deinde quid velit eis datus numerus iste binarius centenus de quo supra paululum praedicavimus. Custodes hujus fructus primo loco dicere possumus eos, qui in Ecclesia Dei praesunt verbo et opere, et ne per haereticos aliosque perversos homines fructus iste a fidelium mentibus rapiatur, lingua manuque, hoc est doctrina et operatione, student obsistere, nunquam steriles esse, sed in seipsis et in aliis semper virtutum sobolem procreare. Secundo vero loco generaliter omnes Christiani hujus fructus custodes esse debent, quia hoc ab eis exigit Christiana religio, ne male vivendo vitam aeternam perdant, sed semper cum Deo 1267Dunus Spiritus existentes, ex hac spirituali conjunctione bonorum operum fecunditate cumulentur, sicque tandem virginali conjugio in coelestibus nuptiis quas hic significat binarius centenus, cum Deo in sempiternum perfruantur. Cujus conjugii dos erit 277 duplex stola, videlicet beatitudo corporis et animae, quam etiam potest significare binarius centenus, quia et centenarius in dextera manu ejusdem beatitudinis exprimit coronam.

VERS. 13. Quae habitas in hortis, amici auscultant, fac me audire vocem tuam.

Post multa et diversa pulchre et laudabiliter prolata dilecti et dilectae colloquia, quasi summam et finalem epithalamii hujus deponens vocem idem 1268Adilectus, tanquam erudit jam, et ex consortio sermonis ejus ad plenum edoctae proclamat, atque ut specie sua et pulchritudine quam ex hac eruditione assumpsit, procedat in exemplum aliorum denuntiat. Quae habitas, inquit, in hortis. Qui sunt horti, nisi amoenitas Scripturarum vel delectatio virtutum? nihil enim jucundius floret, vel dulcius olet, quam circa rivos et fluenta sive germina sanctarum Scripturarum, et pulchram delectabilemque ac salubrem varietatem virtutum. Utrobique enim laudabilis et coelestis est disciplina, hic in dicendo, ibi in faciendo. Quid autem est in his hortis habitare, nisi sanctae legis frequenti meditatione et virtutum exercitatione requiescere? Cujus enim voluntas in lege Domini est, et in lege ejus meditatur die ac nocte, simpliciter cum Jacob domi habitat (Gen. XXV), hoc 1268Best in mentis suae tranquillitate secura stabilitate moratur, nihil varium, nihil mutabile in fidei, vel morum identitate recipiens. At contra in his hortis non habitat, qui cum Esau rerum saecularium venationi intendens (Gen. XXV), circa mundi strepitum per silvas cogitationum vagatur, neque unitatem fidei, neque morum integritatem conservans.

Igitur, o dilecta, quae in his hortis simpliciter ac salubriter habitas, fac me audire vocem tuam. Qualem vocem? vocem pii sermonis, vocem virtutis, vocem bene et recte docentis, vocem juste et pie viventis. Sicut enim vox magna est praedicatio vera et recta, sic et vox magna est conversatio pia et sancta. Vox magna est humilitas, vox magna est obedientia, vox 1268Cmagna est castitas, vox magna est patientia, vox magna et sonora est charitas, et quot virtutibus sancta anima radiat, quasi tot magnis vocibus ad Deum clamat.

Et quare volo audire vocem tuam? videlicet ut te verbo et opere clamantem audiam, sicut scriptum est: Filii qui nascentur et exsurgent, audiant et narrent ea filiis suis, ut ponant in Deo spem suam et non obliviscantur operum Dei, et mandata ejus exquirant (Psal. LXXVII). Et quid est meum audire? nimirum approbare, acceptare, et meo adjutorio 278 dignam judicare, cum enim audio approbo, cum exaudio adjuvo. Tu autem fac me audire vocem tuam. Quomodo facies? honeste et pie conversando, vera et pia docendo. Siquidem rationem et intellectum, 1268Dmemoriam et ingenium tibi concessi; ut sis inexcusabilis, neque dicas te nec scire, nec posse, omnem tibi impossibilitatis exemi necessitatem, quatenus ut debito habeas et facias: ego autem debitor tibi esse volo, ut cum feceris quod jure facere debes, vinear cum judicor (Psal. L); tuo, inquam, judicio vinci volo, quia valde delector si meo bene uteris dono, et idcirco tuum est facere ut velim vocem tuam audire: attamen tuum facere non est tuum, sed meum, quia ut velis et possis, munus est gratiae meae.

Fac me, inquit, audire vocem tuam. Quare? quia amici auscultant: cujus amici? Et mei et tui: mei per charitatem, quia me diligunt sermonem meum 1269Aservando; tui, quia te diligunt salutem tibi optando. Sunt enim amici quos corporalibus oculis non vides qui de profectu tuo et salute, sive de conversione tua gaudent, de quibus scriptum est, quia: Gaudium est angelis Dei super uno peccatore poenitentiam agente (Luc. XV). Hi nempe administratorii spiritus sunt in omnem terram propter eos qui haereditatem capiunt salutis (Hebr. I): hi enim solliciti sunt et agunt pro salute hominum, sicut a quodam istorum amicorum invisibilium cuidam amicorum visibilium dicitur, quia in tempore illo consurget Michael qui stat pro filiis populi tui (Dan. XII), ac subinde, et nemo est adjutor meus in omnibus his nisi Michael princeps vester (Dan. X).

Isti ergo amici auscultant, quia valde delectantur 1269Baudire vocem tuam, ad me clamantem sive orando, sive psallendo, sive praedicando, sive optando. Sunt et alii amici, quos prae oculis habes, qui etiam hujusmodi quadrifidam concentorum veluti pulchrum διατέσσαρον symphoniam audire delectantur, et idcirco aures adhibent et auscultant atque optant audire te canentem et dicentem: Ego autem sicut oliva fructificavi in domo Domini, speravi in misericordia Dei mei, et exspectabo nomen tuum ante conspectum sanctorum tuorum (Psal. LI). Hi, inquam, sancti et tales amici auscultant, optativo et desiderativo modo, ut fias quales ipsi sunt, ut unus eorum optabat anathema fieri pro fratribus suis (Rom. IX), quorum salutem desiderabat; et quia 1269Cipse in hortis virtutum sapientiae quoque et scientiae jam habitabat, sollicitus erat sic vocem suam in auribus meis temperare, ut et Deo et hominibus placeret, et quid saluti hominum competeret, vita et doctrina ostenderet. Unde haec vox ejus est ex hortis sapientiae et virtutis resonans, et mihi audibilis: Castigo corpus meum et servituti redigo, subjicio, ne forte dum aliis praedicavero, ipse reprobus efficiar (I Cor. IX). Hoc 279 modo dum caro ita spiritui subjicitur, ut nihil infra se cupiat, solum quod supra se est quaerat, haec est vox quae delectabiliter sonat in auribus meis, imo hoc est Canticum canticorum quo nihil dulcius in hac mortali vita cantare potest homo mortalis et passibilis, quali voce et quali cantico semper rapitur 1269Dad illam ineffabilem dulcedinem capiendam, quam nec oculus vidit, nec auris audivit (I Cor. II), cujus assecutio perficiet hominem immortalem et impassibilem. Hanc nempe vocem et hoc canticum, dum angeli et omnes sancti mei auscultant et audire desiderant, ad eamdem gloriam quam isti, hoc est angeli adepti sunt, et illi hoc est homines, sancti per fidem, spem et charitatem se adepturos, non dubitant, te quoque quae nondum adepta es, secum adipisci peroptant, atque pro hoc mihi incessabiliter supplicant. Quid tandem ad hanc vocem dilecta respondet? Fuge, dilecte mi, etc.

VERS. 14.-- Fuge, dilecte mi, et assimilare capreae hinnuloque cervorum super montes aromatum.

Si attente inspiciamus, magna haec vox humilis 1270Acorde, sive ad totam Ecclesiam referamus, sive ad quamlibet Deo devotam animam: cur enim sancta Ecclesia sive quaelibet sancta anima haec ad Deum non utatur voce in praesenti vita? Dicit nempe unus sanctorum: Ex parte cognoscimus et ex parte prophetamus; cum autem venerit quod perfectum est, evacuabitur quod ex parte est (I Cor. XIII). Quid iste persensit, qui cognoscendi et prophetandi imperfectionem in hac vita praesenti pronuntiavit? quod enim ex parte est, perfectum non est; sed hanc imperfectionem dicit evacuandam, quando in futura vita venerit quod perfectum est; cujusmodi autem imperfectionem si recte consideres, nimirum hujus dilecti fuga est.

Porro quidquid in sacramentis Ecclesiae agitur, 1270Bmagna et profunda mysteria continet, quae omnia hujus dilecti potentiam, virtutem et gratiam praedicant, sed quis est qui de his ad plenum disputare valeat? unde dilecta prae hujusmodi magnitudinis attonita, ex parte cognoscit et ex parte prophetat, sed quia ad plenum comprehendere non valet, deficit, et dilecto ut fugiat non pro neglectu, sed pro defectu proclamat: fuge enim subtilium rerum in discussione sacramentorum, dilecti hujus fuga est. Nam quando vim eorum et efficaciam ad plenum enarrare, vel discutere non possumus, fugit nos iste dilectus: item cum sacrae Scripturae faciem intendimus, sed eam plene pervidere et arcana thesaurorum ejus introire non possumus, profecto fugit 1270Cnos iste dilectus.

280 Sed fugientem non temere retineamus, verum quidquid in sacramento vel sanctarum Scripturarum subtilitate comprehendere non possumus, igni comburamus, hoc est sancto Spiritui reservemus, et ne in sensum haereticum nimis discutiendo incidamus, fugere dilectum sinamus. Nempe secundum exemplum beati Jacob qui cum angelo luctatus est, nos quidem cum verbo Dei luctari monemur, sed postquam, data benedictione, tactu nervi claudicamur, fugere Dei verbum permittamus. Quid namque est luctari cum verbo Dei, nisi infatigabiliter sensum sacrae Scripturae investigare? Quid denique victorem a victo benedictionem postulare et suscipere, nisi ipsius sensus intelligentiam quaerere et 1270Dinvenire? Sed victor a victo benedictione accepta femore emarcente claudicat, quia is qui sacram Scripturam, Deo inspirante, bene intellexerit, omni carnis voluptate restincta, in activa et contemplativa vita proficit, et grandi quidem spiritus commodo, sed magno carnis suae vincit detrimento. Denique is claudicat qui vicit, quia tetigit qui victus est, nervum femoris ejus et emarcuit; quomodo claudicat? videlicet uno pede terrae innitens, alterum a terra suspendens, id est activam vitam pro cura subditorum non omnino relinquens, et contemplativae prae ejus dulcedine totis viribus inhaerens.

Iste claudus salit vel ascendit sicut cervus, terramque vix tangere dignatur, nam conversatio ejus in coelis est (Philip. III): verumtamen ex parte, uno 1271Aenim tantum pede nunc interim illuc suspensus est, donec veniat quod perfectum est. Et idcirco quia nunc perfecte comprehendere non potest, recte dicit: Fuge, dilecte mi. Cum ergo verbi Dei sensum in monte cum Domino loquentes, mente percipimus, illud Apostoli attendamus: Noli altum sapere, sed time (Rom. XI), ne dum dilectum fugientem incaute prosequimur, in perversi dogmatis foveam dilabamur. Item hoc modo dilectum fugere dicimus, quia semper est incomprehensibilis; nam istud concedendum majestati ejus ut non possit comprehendi, semperque sit desideratus ac desiderabilis, nosque lateat, quandiu simus in hoc corpore, quam magna sit multitudo dulcedinis ejus, quam abscondit timentibus se (Psal. XXX).

1271BDicamus ergo ei: Fuge, fuge, cautus nobis ac providus, ne unquam dum vivimus, nos comprehendisse arbitremur, sequentes ut comprehendamus. Sive hoc modo dicat quaevis fidelis anima et sapiens Deo humili et devota mente: Domine, non sum digna ut intres sub tectum meum (Matth. VIII), non sum digna ut in me ostendas aliquod frequens praesentiae, vel visitationis tuae miraculum. Fuge, inquit, dilecte mi, non quaero in praesenti vita gloriam, sed desidero gratiam, non quaero claritatem miraculorum, sed opto remissionem peccatorum. Fuge, inquam, dilecte mi, et 281 saltus hujusmodi similes saltibus capreae aut hinnulo cervorum effice, non super me, sed super montes aromatum, super excelsa merita sanctorum atque perfectorum. Non est meum de 1271Cdivinitatis tuae arcano, de altissimis praeceptorum tuorum documentis, de profundis sacramentorum tuorum mysteriis tractare, vel disputare, sed illorum potius qui montes excelsi possunt dici propter eminentiam sapientiae et virtutum, qui tacti Spiritu tuo sancto fumigant tuum bonum odorem, ut possint dicere cum Apostolo: Christi bonus odor sumus 1272ADeo in omni loco (II Cor. II), atque ideo recte dicuntur montes aromatum.

Et quid mirum si te ego infirmitatis meae conscia, fugere dico, cum ipsi montes magni et docti, in ipsorum tuorum operum, sive praeceptorum, vel etiam sacramentorum consideratione obstupescant, et te nonnunquam fugere sinant? Nam unus istorum montium, qui usque ad tertium coelum porrectus fuerat, et quae non licet homini loqui audierat, (II Cor. XII), fugientem te dilectum persequi timens, O altitudo, inquit, divitiarum sapientiae et scientiae Dei, quam incomprehensibilia sunt judicia ejus et investigabiles viae ejus! Quis enim cognovit sensum Domini, aut quis consiliarius ejus fuit? aut quis prior dedit illi et retribuetur ei? quoniam ex ipso et 1272Bper ipsum et in ipso sunt omnia, ipsi honor et gloria in saecula saeculorum (Rom. XI).

Idcirco, dilecte mi, fuge, non ut me omnino derelinquas, sed quod hic, qui incomprehensibilis es, adipisci non valeo, in futura mihi vita, vera et aeterna beatitudine sine fine concedas. Similis esto capreae, hinnuloque cervorum super montes aromatum. Hoc est, etiam perfectorum sanctorum intellectum incomprehensibili divinitatis tuae cognitione transcende; sive in eorum cordibus tales fac saltus, ut de virtute in virtutem proficiant (Psal. LXXXIII), quia quoties electi de bonis ad meliora, de virtutibus ad virtutem proficiunt, quasi quosdam in eorum mentibus saltus Deus facit, quatenus his paulatim gradibus sive saltibus, ad illum summum et perfectum 1272Cperveniant statum, in quo videtur Deus Deorum in Sion (Psal. LXXXIII), ubi possint incessabiliter dicere et cantare in auribus Domini Sabaoth, non simpliciter canticum, sed Canticum canticorum, hoc est cognoscere et percipere illud summum et optimum bonum in saecula saeculorum. Amen.

BOOK FOUR.

  • 1243

1243D251 If the zeal of my littleness in this special kind of Canticle had so far profited with your love that, stirred up in your whole spirit, with the cares of temporal things put behind you, you could say with the Apostle: I will pray with the spirit, I will pray also with the power; I will sing with the spirit, I will sing also with the power (I Cor. XIV) [Vulg. 1Cor 14:15 mente, "with the understanding", both times], my heart would assuredly exult greatly in the Lord, because it would be no small rejoicing of mine to say with the Apostle: The joy and my crown are you in the Lord (Philip. V). For if 1244Dafter the manner of my singing you now already put forth leaves somewhat in the Lord, you rightly praise the canticle, because this assuredly is to praise the canticle: to experience the canticle and its measure. But what is the force of this canticle? According to its name, by which it is called Canticle of Canticles, to bear the mind more excellently and more sublimely to the love of its Maker, and perfectly to lay aside from it whatever from the things of the world can stand in the way of contemplation of this kind. If then you have 1245Aexperienced it somewhat, let the concord and harmony of flesh and spirit tell you, for which not to be opposed to one another is to sing beautifully and to make melody rightly. If the handmaid serves the free woman, that is, if the flesh consents to reason, there is no better nor sweeter harmony which may please the supreme Godhead; this indeed is to sing a new canticle and of this kind is the praise that is in the Church of the saints (Psal. CXLIX). For the praise of God is the pious life and conversation of the saints, because they have this such living of theirs from the grace and kindness of God: therefore God is to be praised, not man himself, because this is not the work of man, but the work of God who justifies man himself.

For what is a new canticle, but the venerable commandment of the New Testament? What is it to sing a new canticle 1245Bbut to put off the old man and put on the new? Put off, says the Apostle, the old man, and put on the new, who according to God is created in justice and holiness (Ephes. IV): therefore to be just and holy is assuredly to sing a new canticle, for all perfection of holiness is recognized from the instrument of the evangelical instruction. For whereas the law says: Thou shalt not kill, the Gospel teaches that one must not be angry without cause; and whereas the law 252 says that one must not commit adultery, the Gospel teaches that one must not sin even in concupiscence (Exod. XX; Matth. V). Such perfection of holiness is surely and assuredly the melody of the new canticle. This new canticle the Church of the saints sings, and by frequent singing of this kind attains to the singing of 1245Cthe Canticle of Canticles. For what indeed is it to sing the Canticle of Canticles, but to love the Lord with the whole mind, the whole soul, the whole strength? For as it is called the Canticle of Canticles because it surpasses all other canticles in its dignity, so charity can be called the virtue of virtues, because it surpasses all virtues by its excellence.

If then you, O beloved sisters, truly and sincerely love the Lord, assuredly you sing the Canticle of Canticles; and because praise is in the Church of the saints, in you certainly will be the praise of God, who, as we believe, are the Church of the saints. Bless therefore the Lord in his works and sing to him in the canticles of your lips, and with harps (Eccli. XXXIX). For whatever marks of religion and holiness are in you, they are 1245Dassuredly his works, in which, when you bless, when you ascribe all these things not to your own industry but to his grace.

Hence you ought to sing to him in the canticles of lips and harps, lest it be said of you: This people honoureth me with the lips, but their heart is far from me (Isa. XXIX). For what is it to sing in the canticles of lips and harps? Is it not when voice and life praise the Lord? for then lips and harp sound well together. Now in the harp are stretched strings made from the entrails of dead animals, which are fitted in the wood in so diverse a manner that they give a diverse sound according to the tension and the diversity of the measures. What then can be designated by the harp, but the mind of the just man? in which strings made from the entrails of dead animals are stretched, because in 1246Ait are presented the mortifications of vices, which it has learned from the sayings and writings, or the deeds, of the holy Fathers withdrawn from this life, by which it so chastises its senses inwardly and outwardly that in the ears of the Lord of Sabaoth it presses down with sweet melody the concord of flesh and Spirit. And a certain diversity of sounds is there in some manner denoted, as long as the mortification of pride is carried out in one way, that of lust in another, of wrath in another, and of avarice in another; rightly, with a certain most beautiful harmony, the mind is seen to sound forth delightfully to the Lord its God a new canticle, nay the Canticle of Canticles: you sing in the canticles then of lips and harps, when both by voice and by work you pay to the Lord your God the service of your holiness. If then at the voice of this canticle your mind has been for some time stirred up, as we believe, 1246Bto the love of the heavenly bridegroom, and if you have the ear of the heart ready for a harmony of this kind, your devotion will the more animate us to the things that remain. For no one willingly recounts to an unwilling hearer.

I shall begin, then, to touch the last part, as it were the final string of this Canticle, the Holy Spirit guiding the fingers of the mind, and in it, the Lord helping, I shall lay down the whole 253 harmony of the promised tetrachord.

VERSE 5.-- Who is she that goeth up from the desert, flowing with delights, leaning upon her beloved? Under the apple tree I raised thee up; there thy mother was corrupted corruvta, there she that bore thee was violated.

If I ascribe this voice to the Church wondering at the conversion 1246Cof Judaea, it will not be absurd; because it was assuredly to be wondered at that a people of hard neck and untamable heart, which after the passion of the Lord would not believe him, though many signs attested his Godhead, but rather, after many injuries inflicted upon him, fastened him to the cross, suddenly, when the apostles preached, seized the way of salvation and took up the doctrine of the new law.

And she wonders, and not without cause, because she greatly attends to this, that she goeth up from the desert, that flowing with delights, that leaning upon the beloved she goes up. For the Synagogue was a kind of desert, abandoned by God on account of unbelief, as he threatens concerning her through the prophet, And there shall be left, he says, 1246Dthe daughter of Sion as a covert in a vineyard, and as a lodge in a garden of cucumbers, as a city that is laid waste (Baruch VI). And the Lord in the Gospel: There shall be left, he says, to you your house deserted (Matth. XXIII). From this desert, then, Judaea, when she believed, went up through faith, because from that low-lying and weak understanding of carnal observance she passed over to the spiritual and sublime form of the evangelical instruction. But she could not go up except flowing with delights, because she could not attain to that sublimity of new understanding and grace except through the affluence of the virtues and the abundance of holy charity. But she could not flow with these delights of the virtues unless she leaned upon the beloved of holy Church, that is, Christ, because without his co-operating grace no 1247Aproclamations of holiness and faith could come to her.

Further, in another way, if thou look to each holy soul, attend carefully to what is above, where the beloved adjures the daughters of Jerusalem that they stir not up nor make the beloved to awake till she herself please. For what dost thou think the beloved attained in this her sleep, that the beloved should so earnestly forbid her now to be stirred up and awakened? What, I say, so beautiful, so delightful, and so pleasing to himself did almighty God attend to in this her sleep. Assuredly, if thou considerest rightly, this sweetest beloved regards with the placable countenance of his condescension something great and honourable and worthy of admiration. For he wonders at her ascending, at the place also of the ascent, 1247Bat the bearing of the one ascending and at the support of her ascending. What is this ascent as of one sleeping and resting, but a contemplative lifting up from earthly things to heavenly, from the world to the Lord? But because solitude of mind and body helps this ascent much, for the one is helped by the other, since that of the mind is defended by the solitude of the body, and solitude of the body profits little if the mind is busied about the din 254 of the world the almighty Father with a serene gaze of loving-kindness wonders at the soul going up from the desert, saying: Who she that goeth up from the desert? Who is she? he says, « who hath disposed ascents in her heart, in the vale of tears (Psal. LXXXIII), » going up from the desert, that is, from the solitude of a mind 1247Cdespising the din of this world and sleeping in the quiet of the Spirit and choosing only the observance of my commandments? For from this it follows that she conceives such a bearing that she seems to flow with delights, because this is what the observance of my commandments confers, that she flows with the delights of the virtues, nor is it anything else to flow with virtues than to keep my precepts. For whatever can be or be called virtue, this is all contained in the catalogue of my precepts. But whence has she this power, namely to go up, to flow with delights? Is it from herself? By no means, because every soul is infirm and weak without co-operating grace. But who is this beloved? My Son, I say, of whom I said to you: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased (Matth. 1247DIII). Because then she was leaning upon him, because she followed his footsteps, keeping and, as far as she could, imitating what he showed and taught through the flesh by doing and speaking, therefore she was able to go up in mind, and to flow with the delights of the virtues.

It will not be absurd to understand it in another way also, namely that we take the desert as the present life, and these delights with which the beloved flowing goes up as Holy Scripture. For why should Holy Scripture not be called delights, in which so great diversities of understanding for the profit of the soul are found, like diverse dishes of food at one table: for as among diverse dishes one food is more delicate than another, so in Holy Scripture among diverse understandings one sense is more subtle than another: for there, now 1248Athe bare history feeds those who read like a coarser food, now under the texture of the letter the moral allegory refreshes them to the marrow like a more subtle food, now contemplation, lifting them up to higher things, sweetly affects the mind like a singular and choice food. For whoever flows with delights, is loosened in a certain relaxation of himself, and is released from the pursuit of labour as if from weariness: because assuredly when the soul has begun to abound inwardly in delights, it by no means any longer consents to brood upon earthly desires, but, taken by the love of its Maker, and free in a sweet captivity, it sighs by fainting to contemplate his beauty, and as it were by growing weary grows strong, because while it can no longer carry sordid works, it hastens through quiet to him whom it loves inwardly. From the desert, then, of the present life of the world the soul flowing with 1248Bdelights goes up, because while it is fed with the mystical understandings of the Holy 255 Scriptures, it is lifted up daily to contemplate the things above.

Yet she is described as leaning upon the beloved, because unless she herself cleaves to Holy Scripture by studiously searching it, she by no means lifts the step of her ascent to grasp those sublime things of Spiritual understanding: for the mind intent on Holy Scripture leans upon her beloved, because while God is found and recognized in Scripture itself, the mind of the one recognizing and loving leans as it were upon him.

This voice, then, can be that of the Church exulting at the progress of each holy soul and saying: Who is she that goeth up from the desert, flowing with delights, leaning upon her beloved? As if she said in other words: 1248CWho is she that, intent on the meditation of the Holy Scriptures, cleaves with such zeal to my beloved, the Lord Jesus Christ, that by their mystical understandings, as it were flowing with certain delights, she is able to go up through contemplation to the love of eternal life.

Wherefore he at once adds: Under the apple tree I raised thee up: there thy mother was corrupted, there she that bore thee was violated.

After the beloved has approved his beloved, that is, the faithful soul, for the state of virtue and the bearing conferred by his own gift, he suddenly makes an apostrophe to her herself, bringing back to memory the victory of the good state, so that she may grow together into a greater 1248Dgrace of divine charity. Under the apple tree, he says, I raised thee up: as if he said: If thou considerest anidmavertis what thou wast in the first parent, whence together with the whole human race thou didst contract guilt as it were by descent, not in vain wilt thou cleave to me more zealously, when thou attendest to what manner of one I have now made thee, or how great a grace I have conferred. Under the apple tree indeed I raised thee up, because, that thou mightest persevere in my grace, I held out before thee the form of thy condition, and that thou mightest learn to be under my power, I bound thee with the law of obedience. For when I said to Adam: Of every tree of paradise eat, but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil do not eat (Gen. II); I raised him up as one still lukewarm and ignorant, and admonished him to the duty of using reason well, that he might learn to fit himself to disciplines di ciplinas and to the pursuit of obedience; but what? 1249Ahe transgressed the precept and despised the good of discipline and obedience.

There then thy mother was corrupted, there she that bore thee was violated. How? Eve was seduced and violated, she persuaded her husband, and both presumed upon the forbidden tree. Corrupted was then and violated under the apple tree thy mother or she that bore thee: corrupted in the incontinence of the outward senses, violated through the consent of spirit and soul, in the guilt of disobedience; for she saw and desired concapivit, she obeyed the persuasion of the serpent and, touching the forbidden fruit, ate, and offered it to her husband to eat (Gen. III). 256 This sin therefore, after it was consummated, begot death (Jac. I), and the penalty of this death, as if proceeding from this root of thy former parents, has been spread into the 1249Bposterity of the whole human race.

Therefore in thy first parents I raised thee up, and called thee forth to the pursuits of the virtues, but thou tui, in thy parents themselves, didst decline rather to vices, and didst not fear to become liable to death.

But when thou hadst been lost in such a way, who restored thee to salvation? who made thee such as thou art now seen to be? Did not I undertake death for thee and redeem thee from that death? Did I not again, thee under the apple tree, that is, under the wood of the cross, raise up, and lift thee to so great an honourableness and beauty of life?

But that thou mayest keep this honourableness and beauty of life inviolate, thou must needs persist with a strong mind in my charity.

1249CVERSE 6.-- Set me as a seal upon thy heart, as a seal upon thy arm: for love is strong as death, emulation hard as hell; its lamps are lamps of fire and of flames.

Two seals the beloved here proposes to his beloved, one namely to be set upon the heart, the other upon the arm. For what are these two seals, namely of the heart and of the arm, but the keeping of the heart and the keeping of work? For of the seal, that is, of the keeping of the heart, it is written: With all keeping keep thy heart, for from it life proceedeth (Prov. IV): but of the seal, that is, of the keeping of work, it is written: In all works remember thy last things, and thou shalt never sin (Eccle. VII).

1249DAnd well are these two necessary to man in all his life, and if the first keeping has been neglected, the other perishes; for as a good man out of the good treasure of his heart bringeth forth good, so an evil man, out of the evil treasure of his heart bringeth forth evil (Luc. VI). For whatever proceeds outward into work was first conceived in the heart, and therefore if the keeping of the heart is neglected, so that it is not ruled by reason, whatever is shown outwardly in work is judged irrational. If the heart is ordered by reason, what is brought forth from it into work is honourable, because according to the state or quality of the mind, every action of the agent is understood to be either good or evil.

What is it then that the bridegroom says to the bride: Set me as a seal upon thy heart, as a seal upon 1250Athy arm? What keeping can be safe and secure without God? Unless indeed the Lord keep the city, he watcheth in vain that keepeth it (Psal. CXXVI): and therefore the Psalmist prays: Keep me, O Lord, as the apple of the eye; under the shadow of thy wings protect me (Psal. XVI). But because, just as nothing of good work can be begun without him, 257 so neither can it be completed, the same Psalmist says: Unless the Lord build the house, they labour in vain that build it (Psal. CXXVI): Therefore also it is necessary that the seal of God upon the arm be set, lest the building of good work be destroyed.

Rightly then is it said to the bride: Set me as a seal upon thy heart, as a seal upon thy arm, because she cannot think or do right things 1250Bunless divine grace inspires and governs; nor bring these to the end by persevering, unless the same grace keeps her. For when the works of holiness are shut and as it were sealed, lest they be corrupted by any depravity, then truly the seal of God upon the heart and arm of each soul is not unfittingly understood to be set.

Or let us say that the seal of God is the impression of holiness which is to be set upon the heart and arm of each soul desiring to live holily and justly. For when the life and conversation or the teaching of the Lord Jesus Christ is set before the holy soul, to be imitated or to be observed, rightly his seal upon the heart and arm of her is fixed, so that as she has borne the image of the earthly she may bear also the image of the heavenly (I Cor. XV). 1250CDid not the Lord, when he said to his disciples: Learn of me, because I am meek and humble of heart (Matth. XI), seem as it were to say: Set me as a seal upon your heart? For there he wished to leave as it were a figure of meekness and humility impressed upon their hearts; but when he said: I have given you an example, that as I have done, so you also may do (Joan. III), did he not seem to say: Set me as a seal upon your arm? For there he wished to leave them a certain figure and image of good working and serviceable charity, which they themselves also afterwards might impress upon their hearers by teaching and working. Whence also the Apostle, writing to the Philippians, and wishing to impress the seal or signet of holiness from his own mind 1250Dupon their minds: Brethren, he says, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever modest, whatsoever just, whatsoever holy, whatsoever lovely, whatsoever of good fame, if any virtue, if any praise of discipline, think on these things, which you have both learned, and received, and heard, and seen in me, these things do, and the God of peace shall be with you (Philip. IV).

The bridegroom therefore, that is, Christ, says to his bride, that is, to the faithful soul: Set me as a seal upon thy heart, as a seal upon thy arm; as if he said to her in other words: Whatever thou readest in my teaching, whatever in my works, lay up in thy mind, and fulfil in acts, that from them thou mayest receive the form and image of holiness, through which 258 thou mayest lay aside every figure of the old man, which he assumed by sinning under the apple tree 1251A. And why? for love is strong as death.

Well and fittingly, when the beloved had first said: Set me as a seal upon thy heart, as a seal upon thy arm, he straightway adds, for strong as death is love, emulation hard as hell, because since God himself is charity, as John says (I Joan. IV), to set God upon the heart is to have his charity, but to set him upon the arm is to work good through the same charity, because, as it is written: Faith worketh through love (Gal. V). Now charity is the root of all the virtues, because as from one root many branches come forth, so from one charity many virtues are begotten. If then charity alone begets many virtues, and no one nourishes virtues 1251Bin himself but he who loves God, assuredly to have charity is to have God, and therefore, his seal being set upon heart and arm, the working through love is good and honourable.

But what is it that made God be incarnate and die, but charity? For God so loved the world, as to give his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him may not perish, but may have life everlasting (Joan. III): and so each faithful soul sets God as a seal upon its heart and arm, when, in imitation of him, as he laid down his life for it, so it does not hesitate to labour for him, and, if the cause demands, to undergo death also. Whence well is that very love strong as death so called, because it kindles the mind that truly loves God with so great a force 1251Cthat it does not hesitate to die for him whom it fears to offend by any love of a worldly thing. For whomever charity itself has perfectly possessed, it kills utterly to the love of worldly things. Strong then is love as death, because as death destroys temporal life, so the love of God in the mind of the just man slays the love of this world, and whomever charity has perfectly imbued within, it renders as it were insensible to all outward things to be carnally desired.

Hard also as hell is emulation, because the imitation of the works of Christ is as mighty to absolve and justify man from sins as hell is mighty to torment sinners: which emulation, however, proceeds from the ardour of charity, which brings so great a force of pain 1251Dfrom the desire of the supernal [felicity], as hell brings from the remembrance of their evils to the sinners whom it torments.

Whence it is added that its lamps are lamps of fire and of flames, that in the hearts of the elect charity itself may be understood to be not simply heat but fire and flame.

VERSE 7.-- Many waters could not quench charity, nor shall the floods overwhelm it; if a man shall give all the substance of his house for love, he shall despise it as nothing.

Because so great is its force in the mind of each saint that, as 259 waters cannot quench an immense fire, so the many tribulations of the world cannot take away the fervour of charity from the mind of the saint. 1252AWhence a certain one who was burning with this fire of charity says: Who shall separate us from the charity of Christ, tribulation or distress, persecution or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or the sword? But in all these things we overcome because of him that hath loved us. For I am sure that neither life, nor death, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor virtues, nor dominions, nor any creature shall be able to separate us from the charity which is in Christ Jesus our Lord (Rom. VII) [Vulg. Rom 8:35–39 sets persecutio after periculum, reads neque mors, neque vita, has no potestates or dominationes but instantia, futura, fortitudo, altitudo, profundum, and reads a caritate Dei, "from the love of God"].

Whence rightly it is added that if a man shall give all the substance of his house for love, he shall despise it as nothing.

For why should the holy soul not despise all its substance for the love of God, when it despises its very self 1252Bso far that for the same charity of God it does not fear death? For if it despises for the sake of his love all those things which are not God, what is there that it could set before that same love? And since there is nothing in heaven which it sets before charity, which is God, assuredly it is not a little but nothing if it despises all its substance for its sake. It follows therefore that charity is the highest good, if no good can be set before it.

VERSE 8.-- Our sister is a little one and hath no breasts; what shall we do to our sister in the day in which she is to be spoken to?

Above the beloved had commended the eminence of charity, and had shown of what kind or how great a good charity itself is; how it can be reached 1252Che now purposes to demonstrate: because, since it is of so great excellence, so great dignity, the way is not easy to lay hold of it, and to hold it in the peace of perpetual security. Necessary therefore for obtaining it are constancy or fortitude of mind, knowledge of the Scriptures, and perseverance in good work. Wherefore the beloved says of the beloved, that is, the Church, or any holy soul whatever, which he calls sister on account of faith and good working, that she is a little one and hath no breasts; and he gives at once counsel as to what is to be done for this imperfection.

Our sister, he says, is a little one: whence is she a little one? Because she is still tender in faith, in sense, in word and reason, in strength of mind and in the 1252Daction of a good life. And hath no breasts. How hath she no breasts? She does not yet have the understanding of Holy Scripture, which is contained in the two Testaments, because although she reads and hears what 260 the letter shows and sounds, she has not yet received the knowledge of spiritual understanding, in which all the force and method of speaking and disputing rightly consists, without which the power neither of teaching nor of preaching can be obtained. Wherefore she ought first to put away the things that are of a little one (I Cor. XIII), and to tend to perfection by believing and working, that after she has had breasts through the entire knowledge of the two Testaments, then at length she may fittingly take up the office of teaching and preaching.

What then shall we do, he says, to our sister, in the day 1253Awhen she is to be spoken to? Since our sister is still a little one, and therefore cannot speak to [others], yet let her grow daily and desire to attain to perfection; when the time of speaking to her shall have come, so that it may be said to her: Arise, make haste, my love, show me thy face, let thy voice sound in my ears (Cant. II), what counsel shall we find in the day of discretion now possessed, of understanding also and knowledge, and of an honourable life?

VERSE 9.-- If she is a wall, let us be built upon it bulwarks of silver: if she is a door, let us join it together with boards of cedar. [Vulg. Ct 8:9 aedificemus, "let us build"]

There are two qualities of prelates: one of those who, intent on the office of public preaching, against heretics and all reprobates themselves as a wall for the house 1253Bof Israel, that is, the Church, do oppose (Ezech. XIII). The other of those who, bearing only the office of teacher and cleaving to the contemplative life, kindle their subjects to the pursuit of good action by word and example, to whom they are as it were a door, when they show them the entrance of the heavenly kingdom by teaching rightly and working well.

What then shall we do to our sister, in the day such when she is to be spoken to, and admonished that she now begin to rise to preaching or teaching? She must have two things necessary for this office, namely a wall and a door, that she may be constant and learned, resisting heretics and instructing the people of God: for she will have the wall for defence, the door for leading in.

1253CIf then she is a wall, what shall we do? Let us build, he says, upon it bulwarks of silver: for bulwarks are necessary against the ambushes of enemies; but why of silver? because the words of the Lord are silver tried by the fire (Psal. XI). Bulwarks of silver therefore are the fortifications of the divine words, which are to be built in the mind of the preacher through the knowledge of the Holy Scriptures. If, he says, she is a wall, let us build upon this wall bulwarks of silver; if, he says, she has amid adversity and prosperity a spirit of fortitude 261 and of such constancy that she stands like a wall for the defence of justice, let us give her also the knowledge of the Holy Scriptures, from whose sentences, as from certain bulwarks, 1253Dshe may be able to fight against the depravities of heretics or of perverse men and to defend the reason of truth.

Further, if she is a door, and studiously keeps watch to this end, that she may instruct her hearers with the word of life, and lead them into a good manner of living, what shall we do? Let us join, he says, that door together with boards of cedar; for a painting is in place of reading to those who do not know letters. What then is the matter of this painting which is to be placed on this door, but the life and conversation of the saints? For when any prelate, for the sake of edification, sets before his subjects the examples of the saints, assuredly he paints as it were in their minds what they ought to love, what to fear, or how they ought to order their life in imitation of them.

1254AWhence also the painting itself is said dieitur to be composed with boards of cedar; for the cedar is of an incorruptible nature, and therefore boards of cedar are rightly understood as the saints, because they are corrupted by no rottenness of vices, nay they fill the Church with a good odour, because the good odour of Christ they are in every place (II Cor. II).

With boards of cedar then the door is joined together when any one of the preachers confirms his preaching by the virtues of the saints whom he brings in for example, so that he may open the gate of eternal life to those who imitate, or shut it to those who despise.

Therefore holy Church, or any holy soul whatever, which tends to the love of her bridegroom, while she is still a little one and tender in faith and knowledge, in morals and discipline, if she 1254Bdesires to attain that perfection which may bring forth in her the full charity of God, it will be necessary for her to have, with constancy of mind, the bulwarks of the divine words, and to stand with happy perseverance in doctrine also and a good life. For when she has had the breasts of preaching and teaching, so that she can also nourish others and lead them to perfection, she seems as it were bound by debt to share also with her neighbours this which she has from the grace of God, as the Apostle says: To the Greeks and to the barbarians, to the wise and to the unwise I am a debtor, so, as much as is in me, I am ready to preach the gospel to you also that are at Rome (Rom. I). Whence, at once after the grace of knowledge has been obtained, presenting herself of her own accord at the door of preaching she constantly answers her bridegroom: I am a wall and my breasts are as a tower.

1254C262 VERSE 10.-- I am a wall, and my breasts are as a tower since I became before him as one finding peace.

For she shows the cause of the grace conferred upon her, namely the finding of peace, through which she strives to tend constantly by preaching and working to her own profit and that of others; for since the life of man upon earth is a warfare (Job VII), when one is in the fight and suffers the force of adversaries, how should he stand for the defence of others, who is still labouring for his own? It is necessary therefore first to feel peace and quiet in oneself, to obtain inmost security for him, and then first to be a wall for the defence of others; first to know how to instruct, rule and teach oneself, then to extend the breasts of one's doctrine to the profit of others, 1254Dwhich also is a sign of a certain peace, because when the mind labours on account of ignorance, and struggles with itself to obtain knowledge, once knowledge has been obtained, after it long fought with itself, it is assuredly proved to have gained the fruit of great peace and quiet.

What peace then does she say she has found, and where? Assuredly that peace which surpasseth all understanding (Philip. IV), which the bridegroom himself left to his lovers, saying: Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you (Joan. XIV); for what peace can be preferred to this peace, which here indeed begins, but there abides eternally? For Christ himself is peace, of whom the Apostle says: For he is our peace, who 1255Ahath made both one (Ephes. II); whence also she says she found this before him. Since, she says, I became before him as one finding peace: for there she found peace, where she recognized as present him who is true peace. But how did she find him present and recognize him? and how, he being present, did she find peace? Assuredly in such a way as he himself taught, who says to his own: Have salt in you, and have peace among you (Marc. IX). For being about to teach concerning having peace, not without cause did he put first, have salt in you; for in no way can anyone attain this peace unless he has had a mind seasoned with the salt of wisdom; for as a certain one says. Wisdom is to have been free of folly, because as salt takes away rottenness from flesh, so wisdom takes away folly from the heart. And by the seasoning of wisdom, 1255Bfolly having been taken away from the heart, which begets the rottenness of vices, one is quickly drawn together to this peace, by which every fight between flesh and spirit is lulled to sleep, and the flesh desires nothing that is repugnant to the spirit; and so, this peace having been found in this land, one will at some time come to that which is to be taken away by no end. But how is this fight taken away, so that 263 peace may be granted, except before him, except in the presence of him who, consoling his own who are thus to fight, says: Have confidence, I have overcome the world (Joan. XVI); as if he said: Because I have overcome, through me you also shall overcome?

Rightly then the bride says: Since I became before him as one finding peace, I am a wall, and my breasts are as a tower; because since by his grace I have overcome carnal affections, and have been strengthened with spiritual peace, I can 1255Cstand for the salvation of others also, and constantly speak forth the words of exhortation. My breasts indeed are as a tower, because I have grown so much from the divine grace in the word of exhortation that I can, according to the prophet, ascend a high mountain and lift up my voice with strength that I may preach the gospel to Jerusalem (Isa. XL.) Indeed I am a wall, for defending and keeping the people of God, and my breasts are as a tower, that I may be able to look forth from on high, and to announce from afar things to come.

VERSE 11.-- The peaceable had a vineyard in that which hath peoples: he let it out to keepers, a man bringeth for the fruit thereof a thousand pieces of silver.

It is greatly to be considered who this peaceable one is, 1255Dor what is the vineyard of the peaceable one, and who the peoples, or who the keepers, or what the fruit of this vineyard.

This peaceable one is the Lord Jesus Christ: for the causes of the peace noted above he is called peaceable, whose place is made in peace (Psal. LXXV), and who called us in peace, dissolving the enmities in his flesh, making void the law of commandments in decrees, that he might make the two in himself, into one new man making peace, that he might reconcile both in one body to God, by the cross killing the enmities in himself, and coming he preached peace to them that were afar off and peace to them that were near (Ephes. II) [Vulg. Eph 2:17 pacem vobis, qui longe fuistis, "peace to you that were afar off"].

With the eye of the inner man illuminated it is to be carefully looked into how fittingly, how truly, and how uniquely this one is peaceable, who such and so great and so long-lasting 1256Aenmities dissolved in his flesh; the wonderful and adorable majesty of the reconciliation that was made is then the more recognized, when the quality and the quantity of the enmity is weighed; for how great an enmity did the first man contract toward God through the evil of disobedience, that he not only lost that felicity of paradise in which he had been placed, but also took upon himself death, the avenger of transgression? But the weight of this enmity grew through the succession of the human offspring by the increase of malice and wickedness, so that the Maker himself, as Scripture says, touched inwardly with sorrow of heart, said: It repenteth me to have made man (Gen. VI), and therefore, sentence of judgment having been given, save Noe, who alone was then saved with his wife and sons, the whole world was consumed by the avenging water.

1256BBut who would dissolve the weight of so great an enmity? Would 264 an angel? But an angel, equally with man a creature of God, needed the grace of God, and a creature could not free a creature from a necessity of this kind. There came therefore the Maker of the creature himself, needing nothing, almighty, and in every way sufficient to destroy the wall of this enmity, and to establish without any obstacle the eternal covenant of reconciliation and of true peace. And because he could not be seen through the Godhead, he came through the humanity that he might become visible; and at his birth the whole world met him with a sign of temporal peace, announcing and proclaiming the token of that highest and eternal peace which was to be established through him. Whence also at his nativity the angels cried: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men 1256Cof good will (Luc. II).

Who then is more and truly peaceable than this so great eternal maker of so great a peace? Solomon indeed, who was called from his name peaceable, for Solomon is interpreted peaceable, had temporal peace, a temporal king, by God's granting, so that he might build a house to God with no one hindering; but by his name, and his work, and his time he went before this true peaceable one, as night goes before day, the shadow before the truth; who, that he might found for himself a house, namely holy Church, laid as it were in the foundation the sign of this wonderful peace, which is to be kept, Peace, saying, I leave with you, my peace I give unto you (Joan. XIV).

To this peaceable one there was a vineyard, namely holy Church, which is therefore not unfittingly called a vineyard, because, 1256Dif the cultivation or the nature of the vine is attended to, she seems to draw to herself no small profit for her own progress from its likeness. For what indeed is the manner of cultivation that is applied to the vine? In the time of pruning, the useless shoots being cut back, it is as it were cleansed; then, dug about, it is raised up and tied to stakes: further, if thou attend to the quality of its nature, thou wilt see that first it fixes a living root, then, because it is pliant and apt to fall, with its tendrils, as with certain arms, it binds whatever it lays hold of, and by these it raises and lifts itself up. What then is the pruning in the Church or in any soul whatever, but the cutting away of vices from the hearts? and what the digging about, but the bringing back to the mind 1257Aof sins through compunction and confession? For as with a kind of hoe of compunction the mass of earthly works is brought back to memory, so that the mind, unburdened through confession and satisfaction, may be able to bear fruit better in good acts. And what does the minister of this office do who receives the penitent, and imposes on him as he confesses the measure of penance? He raises him with the hand of sure consolation and with the hope of the divine mercy, and sets before him, through the examples of the saints, what 265 purpose of life he should hold henceforth, by which he ought to support himself, as if tied to stakes, lest he fall.

Further, according to the nature of the vine the progress of the Church or of any soul whatever is considered, because after it has been planted and fixed in the root of faith, the layering of humility being pressed down, lest it could be bent back or drawn away by any storms or tempests 1257Bof the world, it embraces all its neighbours with the embraces of charity as with tendrils and coils, and rests in their compunction.

Such, then, was the vineyard to the true peaceable one, our Lord Jesus Christ; not that it is not so now, or ought not to be in the future, but we ought to take was as said in his foreknowledge and predestination, as it is written elsewhere of every creature: What was made in him was life (Joan. I), because in his foreknowledge all things already were and lived, just as in the mind of some craftsman there is the form or pattern of the thing to be made, whose likeness the hands of the worker imitate, so that he may bring the thing forth into the open.

The vineyard, moreover, was in that (understood: peace) which 1257Chath peoples, because the Church has been gathered not from the one nation of the Jews, but from the peoples of all nations, into the unity of faith, love and peace, as it is written: They had one heart and one soul (Act. IV). Further, it is to be noted that he does not say, in that peace which the peoples have, but which hath peoples, so that the grace of him who calls, justifies, glorifies may be the more attended to than the labour and zeal of him who wills, runs, strives to lay hold, because, as the Apostle says: It is not of him that willeth nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy (Rom. IX). For he is our peace who hath made both one (Ephes. II), and from it is the peace which surpasseth all understanding (Phil. IV). When therefore this peace hath peoples, no schism, or any dissension, can break into the unity of their faith, but they cleave so firmly 1257Din that peace that they become a most choice vineyard to the true peaceable one, our Lord Jesus Christ: for if they themselves had peace without the peace that has them, they would not be held by a firm root, because they would not be planted together in that peace in which in the selfsame they might sleep and rest (Psal. IV). Which sleep and rest is given after this life in the selfsame, because we shall see him as he is (I Joan. III), and there is no change there, nor shadow obrumbratio of alteration (Jac. I), but the peace which we shall once have received we shall keep for ever without any change.

But these peoples whom this peace hath, although in the first place we ought to take them as the universal Church gathered from Jews and Gentiles, yet in the second 1258Aplace we can, not unfittingly, take them as the particular Church established within the universal itself through the diverse kinds 266 of professions, which also can be called the vineyard of the Lord, and ought to be bound together by the same peace and unanimity.
