Further, if we descend to individuals, some faithful soul serving God can, not absurdly, be called the vineyard of the Lord, whose cultivator is the Holy Spirit through grace, since according to the form set down above, which we said befits the whole, it seems not unfittingly to suit the single one also, namely that this be its zeal: to cut away vices and sins like useless shoots with the hand of pious work through co-operating grace, to bring earthly works back to the mind through compunction and confession, as through a digging about, 1258Band so, by doing penance and doing good works, to offer fruit acceptable to God.

He let it out to keepers: the keepers of this vineyard, that is, of holy Church, were the holy apostles or their successors, apostolic men, whose zeal and diligence it was to instruct her in holiness and justice, and to defend her by word and example from the plague of evil works and of depraved doctrines; not that whatever progress they attained in this keeping was of their own work, but because they were ministers and officers of the divine operation and efficacy, as it is said by the Lord in Numbers to Aaron: Put ye my name upon the children of Israel, I the Lord will bless them (Num. VI) [Vulg. Nm 6:27 Invocabuntque nomen meum super filios Israel, et ego benedicam eis, "And they shall invoke my name upon the children of Israel, and I will bless them"] : as if he said in other words: Do you, through the ministry delivered to you, pour my grace 1258Cinto men by word and work; it will be mine to show the good of that grace in them and to bring it to effect.

Now the word of delivering which is uttered in this pronouncement is to be attended to, not without fear, by all the prelates of the Churches and by their subjects, because it forewarns both those to the virtue of prudence and these to the virtue of obedience, to be wary and careful. For the Apostle speaks to prelates: Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, wherein the Holy Spirit hath placed you bishops, to rule the Church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood (Act. XX); further, to subjects: Obey, he says, your prelates and be subject to them. For they watch as being to render an account for your souls, that they may do this with joy and not with grief, 1258Dfor this is not expedient for you (Hebr. XIII). Therefore it ought to make you, that is, the prelates, attentive with solicitude, providence, and these, that is, the subjects, with humility, patience, on account of the word of this delivering, in which it is said: He let it out to keepers.

If then God has delivered his Church to keepers, it is greatly to be feared lest, if the keepers neglect the keeping, and those to be kept despise the keepers, or resist and disparage the keeping, they gravely offend him who placed the keepers and established the keeping. These keepers indeed God calls watchmen, as he himself speaks by the prophet: I have made thee a watchman to the house of Israel; the things which thou seest, thou shalt announce to them from me 1259A(Ezech. III); 267 the things which thou seest, he says, thou shalt announce to them from me, that is, what thou understandest with the mental eye, or beholdest with the bodily eye, as needing to be corrected or amended, thou shalt announce to them, by exhortation, counsel and precept, from me, that is, according to the reason and manner which I shall have shown thee beforehand by inspiring. And in the delivering of this keeping God set before the keepers themselves, or watchmen, the danger, and the manner of escaping the danger, saying: If, when I say to the wicked: Thou shalt die the death, and thou declare it not to him, he indeed shall die in his iniquity, but his blood I will require at thy hand, behold the danger. But the manner of escaping this danger follows in what he says: But if thou declare it to the wicked, that he may be converted from his iniquity, and he hear thee not, he indeed shall die in 1259Bhis iniquity, but thou hast delivered thy soul (ibid). To the keepers therefore, that is, to the prelates in the Church, danger is set before them for negligence, security for vigilance, whence greater care and solicitude ought to hold them toward the office entrusted to them.

Further, the danger of private persons or subjects is not less, nay it is graver, for contempt and disobedience; because while prelates mostly sin from infirmity and negligence, these offend from pride and rashness, and the contempt and irreverence of those is the contempt or irreverence of God. So he himself says: He that heareth you heareth me, and he that despiseth you despiseth me (Luc. X); and to the prophet, whom he says he gave as a watchman to the house 1259Cof Israel: Therefore he says, they do not hear thee, because it is an exasperating house (Ezech. III). An evil and fearful appellation, that the house of the undisciplined and disobedient should be named an exasperating house, and in another place they are called of stiff neck and uncircumcised heart, because they resist the Holy Spirit (Act. VII). For they who resist the word of discipline and honourableness resist the word of God. The words, moreover, of God are spirit and life (Joan. VI), and therefore they resist the Holy Spirit. Whence the Prophet, because he saw that to resist the word of God is damnable, asked to be taught goodness and discipline by God, because he had believed his commandments and been obedient (Psal. CXVIII).

But the divine word commanded in the sacred law concerning the stubborn and wanton and disobedient son, that his parents, having seized him, 1259Dshould bring him to the elders of the city and to the gate of judgment (Deut. XXI), namely lest they hasten their own sentence, but that they bring in wise men as witness; for they ought to know that the first fault of our race, for which we all pay, is disobedience, and that the justice of God lays up no pardon for the stubborn and wanton, but, as it is written: God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace to the humble (I Petr. V).

For such are always to be examined at the gate of judgment, so that, if they remain in their stubbornness or rashness and will not obey, they be cast out from the fellowship of the brethren; but if they repent and become humble and quiet, 268 they be received again. This is also the gate of judgment in the city of God, that is, holy Church: that the stubborn and rebellious, if they will not be corrected, be cut off with the sword 1260Aof excommunication, like putrid members, from the body of the Church, of whom it is written: They went out from us, but they were not of us (I Joan. II); but that the penitent, and those putting an end to their malice, be restored like healed and holy members into the body of the Church. Therefore the other sins are indeed to be tolerated in the house of God, but the severity of wise fathers overwhelms stubborn and wanton sons, that it may take away the evil from its midst, with the authority of the law of the Lord which we have mentioned; nay, by the very example of God, who expelled the disobedient first men from paradise (Gen. III).

The word delivering, therefore, which is pronounced of the lord of the vineyard, is to be thought on and weighed not negligently but diligently and with fear, because on either side 1260Bneglect or contempt, whether by prelates or by subjects, looks to the judgment of him who delivers.

A man bringeth for the fruit thereof a thousand pieces of silver. The diligent and studious inspector of this chapter ought to attend who, or of what kind, or how great is the fruit of this vineyard, which is valued at so great a price that for the obtaining of it not ten, or twenty, or thirty, but determinately a thousand are the pieces of silver to be brought; and that he who, lacking these, could purchase this fruit, is not any powerful and rich man, whether official or private, but ought absolutely to be called, and to be, a man.

What, then, is this fruit? Surely that which is painted as it were with three colours of beauty, namely power, wisdom, goodness: power 1260Cindeed, than which nothing is more efficacious; wisdom, than which nothing is more reasonable; goodness, than which nothing is sweeter. For power is constrained by no law of impossibility or infirmity, wisdom admits nothing which lacks the virtue of reason, goodness abounds with so great a multitude of sweetness that there is nothing above it. Moreover, the touch and use of such a fruit affords an efficacious and most wholesome experience of health to the whole man. But where is this found among creatures and visible things? Is it in angels? But it is written that in his angels also he found iniquity (Job IV). For a creature can be subject to corruption and mutability; but that which cannot must be immutable and incorruptible.

Further, we have said that the three beauties of this fruit 1260Dare such that they can receive nothing above themselves; yet something can be below, which from affection for them or participation in them may be said in some manner to be powerful, wise and good, 269 but not substantially power, wisdom, goodness. For that which is receivable and participable is not the same as that which receives and participates; for the receiving and participating thing is such when it neither receives nor participates, and therefore it is subject to mutability and can be corrupted: but the receivable and participable, abiding ever immutably in its own essence, can never be corrupted; but no creature is receivable and participable; it is therefore God. When therefore we ask what the fruit of this vineyard is, and attend to all the circumstances of its virtue and beauty. 1261Abeyond doubt we conclude at the last that it is God. But by reception and participation the rational creature attains this, that at some time it may pass into incorruption and immutability, not by nature but by grace; and thus, from man working and God co-operating, this fruit is as it were born and grows, which is the reward of all who pertain to the kingdom of God, and is called true beatitude. But true beatitude is God himself, whom to have and whom to enjoy eternally is truly to be blessed. This fruit, therefore, is God.

Further, what shall we say of the quality of such a fruit, since it is written of it that eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither hath it entered into the heart of man? (I Cor. II.) Nevertheless above we distinguished the same fruit by three colours, which pertains rather to quality, 1261Bnot that the difference of the colours makes a different fruit, but that this diversity so inseparably coheres in one substance that it in no way takes away any virtue and efficacy of its property. For just as, for example, three colours come together in some one subject, and one has the name so that it is called red, another white, the third green, yet one and the same is the substance which contains them; so in this fruit, though power is not one thing, wisdom another, and goodness another, yet the fruit is one and the same, and has everywhere one and the same virtue and efficacy, namely to be able, to be wise, to quicken, which nevertheless bring it about that there is nothing good which is lacking to its fullness.

1261CBut what is to be said of the quantity of this fruit, since it is of such immensity that it is circumscribed by no place, enclosed by no boundary? Yet it seems to have certain extents, not according to itself, but according to the participant: but nothing can be a participant of this thing save the rational creature. Further, the rational 270 creature is in one kind spiritual, as the angel and the soul, in the other corporeal, as the elements and the things which are composed of them. But since this is not the place to dispute about the dimensions of a corporeal thing, which are constituted by line, surface, or solid body, while this fruit, of whose quantity we began to speak, is not corporeal but spiritual; for God is a spirit (Joan. IV), of whose quantity, because he is incomprehensible and uncircumscribed, 1261Dno one can either think or speak; let us nevertheless now see what are the extents which it can have, not according to itself, but according to the participant. For whatever of goodness, honourableness, holiness, discipline or knowledge the participating soul can have, it takes from the participable God, as it were the vigour of grace flowing forth into it; and through this the participant seems to have something longer or shorter, broader or narrower, higher or lower, according as it pleases him to distribute who gives grace to every one according to the measure of faith (Rom. XII). Whence the Apostle, speaking to those whom he was exhorting to receive such dimensions: In charity, he says, rooted and founded, that you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the length, 1262Abreadth, height and depth (Ephes. II) [Vulg. latitudo, et longitudo, et sublimitas, "breadth, and length, and height"].

But since this fruit of which we speak is born and grows from the root of charity, and comes to maturity as it were to perfection, not as regards God who is to be grasped, who is always perfect, but as regards the capable mind of man, which is subject to increase and loss, so that by advancing in this manner it may at some time comprehend God, with whom in its own manner it may become perfect and unchangeable, let us first see concerning our Lord Jesus Christ himself how, according to his humanity, he received in himself from the root of charity all these dimensions, namely length, breadth, height and depth: for who had greater charity than he, who laid down his life for his sheep? (Joan. XV.)

1262BBut if we set the eyes of the mind on the kind and quality of his passion, we shall see all these dimensions venerably contained, and every Christian soul manfully promoted by this example. For in the figure of the cross are to be noted these four dimensions, namely length, height, breadth and depth, which from the root of Christ's charity are stretched out into the whole world, signifying and admonishing every soul which has been redeemed by his passion that, if it wishes to attain the aforesaid fruit, that is, eternal beatitude, it must reach it by the dimensions of the same charity, according to the measure and nature granted to it.

271 For charity ought to be broad, because it ought to be extended even 1262Cto the love of enemies, as Christ hanging on the cross prayed for his enemies, saying: Father, forgive them, because they know not what they do (Luc. XXIII). It ought to be long, because not for an hour but to the end of life, as it is written of Christ: Having loved his own, he loved them unto the end (Joan. XIII); for charity ought to have such great perseverance that it fails for no tribulation or distress. It ought to be high, because of the final cause, namely that it attend for what it acts or suffers, that is, for eternal beatitude, which is this fruit of which we speak, for the sake of which it is admonished always to tend upward and to have its conversation in heaven; it ought to have depth, because it ought never to be without fear, but always to attend 1262Dthat whatever it attains from breadth, length and height, it has not from its own merits but from the mercy of God; and therefore, because it knows not the hidden and deep judgment of God, why he should choose one and reject another, and the end is always uncertain while many are called, few are chosen cliguntur (Matth. XX), it ought never to be without fear.

Since therefore in Christ dwelleth all the fullness of the Godhead corporeally (Coloss. II), and to him God doth not give the spirit by measure (Joan. III), while all the saints receive of his fullness, grace for grace (Joan. I), they seem to reach to the extents of these dimensions, each in his own manner or measure, according as he gives to them who has in full and can give of his fullness as much as he will.

1263AFurther, since charity, set like a centre in the middle, touches all the virtues as it were through the circumference, for every virtue descends from the root of charity; and since every motion has six species, for there is before and behind, up and down, to the right, to the left; to whatever part the mind of man directs its intention for attaining such a fruit, it always receives the origin of every good motion from the vigour of charity. And since man himself, called the lesser world, consists after the likeness of the greater world of four elements, he is also measured by four parts, by which he is wholly contained, if he has been established for preserving the likeness of God, namely prudence, justice, temperance, fortitude.

These four parts being stretched out from the centre of the mind, that is, 1263Bfrom charity, at an equal distance, whatever of virtue can be in the soul, thou, as with a circle, both touchest by carrying round and enclosest.

This, therefore, can in some manner be the measure or dimension which this fruit, participating, can have, not according to itself, as has been said, but according to the participant, so that when at some time it has been attained by the participant as it is, 272 it may take away from then on all passibility or mutability of dimension in growing, and confer perfectly eternal impassibility, immutability, immortality.

This fruit, therefore, is true beatitude, and true beatitude is God, whose quality and immensity is incomprehensible. But since we now know what is the fruit of the aforesaid vineyard, let us now see concerning the 1263Cone who offers, who he is, since he is said to be a man, and could not offer unless he were a man. For man is so called from virtue, and he who ought to offer for so great a fruit must shine with the beauty and grace of the virtues, because an oblation will not be accepted which no brightness of the virtues commends. For in the matter of what is given and received the form ought to be this: that there be in the giver such composure of bearing, and such grace of honourableness and discipline, that it bring forth in the receiver good pleasure and cheerfulness of countenance, and render the gift more acceptable. And if mortals affect this good of discipline and honourableness among themselves, and men approve it, what do we think the omnipotent and immortal God wills and seeks from us, whose nature is goodness, holiness, singular 1263Dhonourableness and discipline? Therefore he who offers to such a Lord ought to be clothed with strength and girded with virtue (Psal. XCII): with strength of mind, that is, for restraining and repelling vices and sins, with virtue of spirit for doing and exercising good works. For that oblation is not right which the darkening of guilt repels, since the Lord said even to Cain: If thou offer rightly, but divide not rightly, thou hast sinned (Gen. IV) [Vulg. nonne si bene egeris, recipies, "if thou do well, shalt thou not receive?"]. He offered rightly indeed, who gave the fruits of the earth to God, but he did not divide rightly, who kept his heart in evil and stained his oblation with the plague of envy: for he ought to have separated the good from the evil, because there is no participation of light with darkness, nor can there be together in the sight of God 1264Atruth and falsehood, equity and malice. He offered rightly indeed, because he offered to God, to whom he ought; but he did not divide rightly, because what was better he rightly denied to God, what was viler he gave: for he is not dear enough to God, nay, he is unworthy of God, who offers his goods to him indeed, but keeps himself for himself.

Such a man, therefore, the Prophet describes in the first psalm, where he represents the bearing and purpose of such a man; and since that psalm is known to those who understand, whoever desires to take on this man, let him meditate on it continually and exercise it in deed: in another place also he mentions this same man briefly, saying: Blessed is the man who feareth the Lord, he desireth exceedingly in his commandments (Psal. CXI) [Vulg. volet nimis, "he shall delight exceedingly"], and the rest; for this is what makes this man, and blessed, since it belongs to virtue 1264Bto fear God, and to consider and keep his commandments; but to beatitude, that for this, his seed shall be mighty upon earth, and his justice remaineth for ever and ever (ibid).

273 The offerer having been described, whom it befits to be a man, it is now to be seen what the man brings, and ought to bring, for such a fruit. A thousand, he says, pieces of silver. The number thousand is put for perfection, and silver designates the pure and bright sense of chaste words, as it is written: The words of the Lord are chaste words, silver tried by the fire (Psal. XI). But what can we call a piece of silver formed and inscribed from this silver? If we look diligently, what is it that forms or inscribes in the mind of man the image of God, the image of holiness and justice, 1264Csave the commandment of the Lord, lightsome, enlightening the eyes (Psal. XVIII), the eyes, namely, of the inner man? And where do we hear the commandment of the Lord, and whence do we know it, save from Holy Scripture, which is the speech of the Lord? This Scripture, therefore, well understood, forms, and makes as it were a kind of inscription in the mind of man, so that when from the reading of Holy Scripture he has perfectly taken on charity from a pure heart and a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith (II Tim. II), he receives the coin of a certain piece of silver, inscribed in this manner: to the image and likeness of God, for this form the Maker of things himself appointed to be impressed on man in creating him, when he said: Let us make man to our image and likeness (Gen. I), 1264Dwhich is to say: Let us make man living, rational, like to God: for the condition of man excels all living things by a twofold honour, when it is said to our image and likeness; to the image, namely, that he may be rational, to our likeness, that he may be upright by following the justice of God. The one of these, namely rationality, he cannot lack; the other, that is, the likeness of the divine uprightness or justice, he cannot attain save through grace: but the faculty of rationality, which man cannot lack, is the instrument, or as it were a kind of eye, for seeking the likeness of God. He is therefore inexcusable when he has not come to the likeness of God, 1265Abecause, namely, he would not use a good instrument for that for which it was given him.

But when God first made man, he made him not only rational, but also endowed with the honour of his likeness, For God, says Scripture, made man upright, but he entangled himself with many questions (Eccle. VII). But now, seduced, he has lost indeed the honour of the likeness of God, but the faculty of reason has remained in him, through which he may be able to hear him who calls him back and to follow him as leader and teacher to his restoration. Such silver, therefore, that divine and highest money-changer inscribed in the soul of man, when he made it rational and a partaker of his holiness.

274 Wherefore man is a debtor to God, so that, since God 1265Bmarked him with this twofold honour, he should understand his debt, namely that, being capable of reason, with reason itself as leader, he should always advance to the likeness of God through holiness, lest, if he understand not, he should be compared to senseless beasts, and become like to them (Psal. XLVIII). Finally, that man owes this debt to God the Lord shows in the Gospel, since, when he was tempted by the Scribes and Pharisees saying: Whether it be lawful to give tribute to Caesar or not, he answered: Show me the coin of the tribute; and when they had shown it, he said: Whose is the image and inscription? And when they answered: Caesar's: Render, he says, the things that are Caesar's to Caesar, and the things that are God's to God (Matth. XXII).

By this sentence of his, therefore, the Lord shows, and by showing teaches, that just as it is just that to a 1265Cmortal man the things which are his, and which have been given by him, be rendered in tributary subjection, so it is just, nay most just, that to the omnipotent and immortal God the things which are his, and which have been granted by him to man, be brought with the highest devotion and humble subjection. Now reason and understanding have been granted to man by God, which he ought so to use that by living well he may advance to the likeness of God, and receive in his soul and mind, from the brightness of holiness, this inscription of the piece of silver: to the image and likeness of God.

Such a piece of silver, therefore, one or two or three or more, according to the measure of God's gift, some faithful man offers, that he may purchase that fruit, 1265Dthat is, eternal life, which works through love, tends and advances to the likeness of God. But he brings a thousand pieces of silver, who by the brightness of perfect holiness has attained the image and likeness of God.

Or else the thousandfold unity signifies one faith, one baptism, one God who worketh all in all; and he who desires that fruit, that is, eternal life, must hold and teach the true and right faith, must have and worship one God and one man, must adorn with faith and works the name of Christianity which he received in baptism, must read, teach, embrace and follow the true, catholic, and one Holy Scripture. When, therefore, the beloved says these things of herself to the grace and glory 1266Aof the beloved, he at once answers and says: The vineyard, etc.

VERSE 12.-- My vineyard is before me. A thousand are thy peaceable ones, and two hundred for them that keep the fruit thereof. [Vulg. fructus, "the fruits"]

My vineyard, he says, is before me, that is, I know and approve my 275 vineyard, from this, that I find in it the grace of my planting; if I did not find it, it could not be before me, nor could it be called my vineyard. For of you who can be called and be my vineyard I spoke by the prophet, that I will look upon you and make you grow; you shall be multiplied, and I will establish my covenant with you (Levit. XXVI): for those who are so before me that they are worthy of my presence and sight, shining with the brightness of good works, I acknowledge and keep; because the eyes of the Lord are upon the just (Psal. XXXIII), just as on the contrary, 1266Bthose who set me behind them by despising, them too I set behind me by reprobating, and therefore by not bestowing the help of my grace.

A thousand are thy peaceable ones, and two hundred for them that keep the fruits thereof; from the opposite of that vineyard which was turned into perversity, of which it is said that I looked that it should bring forth the grape, but it brought forth wild grapes (Isa. V), the sense of this chapter will better appear. For the Lord says by Osee of her, under the figure of a harlot: And I bought her to me for fifteen pieces of silver, and for a core of barley, and for half a core of barley (Ose. III): now a most beautiful sacrament is hidden in these numbers; here in a thousand pieces of silver, there in fifteen pieces of silver, and a core of barley and half a core of barley; the sum of which is this, that this one is both a virgin and joined to a husband, that one 1266Cneither a virgin nor joined to a husband; for the thousandfold unity signifies the virginity of this one, but her conjunction or nuptials the hundredfold two. Arithmeticians or abacists know better what is said, and by what reason unity is pronounced a virgin they have in use in their treatises, namely that multiplied into itself it creates nothing, because once one is one, which befalls no other number: for the other numbers, led into themselves, create others, as twice two four, and the third [tertia; read ter tria, "thrice three"], nine: further, the hundredfold two designates her nuptials, and this is most happy, because this beloved who is of faith is both always joined to a husband and always remains a virgin, always brings forth, yet always remains a virgin.

1266DOn the contrary, it designates the widowhood and at the same time the corruption of that one, that her price neither remained in unity nor came to two, when it is said: I bought her to me for fifteen pieces of silver and a core of barley and half a core of barley. If thou attend to the pieces of silver, there are neither ten pieces of silver, which would be the tenfold unity, nor twenty, which would be the tenfold two, but there are fifteen, in which number, namely, it is more than unity, less than two: likewise there is neither one core of barley only, nor are there two cores, but a core and a half of barley, more than the monad, less than two. And so this too is most unhappy for her, that she is neither a virgin nor has a husband. Therefore a thousand are thy peaceable pieces of silver, 276 that is, all the discourses harmonizing in one faith; for this number is a thousandfold 1267Aunity, and they are thine, making or acquiring peace, that is, the remission of sins; since to have one Lord, one faith, one baptism is to be in the catholic Church, where the remission of sins is given through peace, that is, Christ, who is our peace, who hath made both one (Ephes. II). For Holy Scripture, which sounds forth and teaches these three things, contains in itself the whole sum of this peace, because whatever there is of law, of God, of faith, of the religion of Christianity, and all the sacraments of the Church are constituted from these, and he who has them as he ought to have them attains that peace which feels the wars of the vices; and when by this peace he has advanced to an abundance of virtues, the remission of sins having been given him, he will reach that perpetual and never-to-be-ended peace, where there will be no labour, no pain, 1267Bnothing at all which could oppose him.

These three, therefore, are the instruments of this peace, since every soul tending toward it must always consider in whom it believes, what it believes, how it believes. For if thou ask whom, or in whom, thou oughtest to believe, God is set before thee; but if thou askest what to believe, the sacraments of the Church are shown thee; further, if thou ask how thou oughtest to believe, the religion of Christianity is prescribed to thee. For faith without works is idle, nay, is dead (Jac. II), and: Without faith it is impossible to please God (Hebr. XI). Accordingly, as we have said, on account of the unity of these three things, which constitute and acquire the true and eternal peace, there may rightly indeed be said to be for this vineyard a thousand who are peaceable.

1267CBut two hundred for them that keep the fruits thereof, why are they said to be? First indeed it is to be seen who are these keepers of the fruit, then what this number, the hundredfold two, given to them, means, of which we spoke a little above. As keepers of this fruit we can name in the first place those who preside in the Church of God by word and work, and who, lest this fruit be snatched from the minds of the faithful by heretics and other perverse men, strive to withstand with tongue and hand, that is, with doctrine and working, never to be barren, but always to beget an offspring of virtues in themselves and in others. But in the second place all Christians generally ought to be keepers of this fruit, because the Christian religion requires this of them, that they lose not eternal life by living evilly, but, being always one Spirit with God, 1267Dbe heaped from this spiritual conjunction with the fruitfulness of good works, and so at length in a virginal wedlock, in the heavenly nuptials which the hundredfold two here signifies, may enjoy God for ever. The dowry of which wedlock will be 277 the double stole, namely the beatitude of body and soul, which the hundredfold two can also signify, because the hundred, too, on the right hand, expresses the crown of the same beatitude.

VERSE 13. Thou that dwellest in the gardens, the friends hearken: make me hear thy voice.

After many and diverse colloquies of the beloved and his beloved, beautifully and laudably uttered, the same 1268Abeloved, laying down as it were the sum and final voice of this epithalamium, as though he now instructs [erudit; read eruditae, "to one now instructed"], and proclaims to her fully taught out of the fellowship of his discourse, and announces that she should come forth as an example to others in her form and beauty which she has taken on from this instruction. Thou that dwellest, he says, in the gardens. What are the gardens, if not the pleasantness of the Scriptures or the delight of the virtues? for nothing flowers more delightfully or smells more sweetly than the region about the streams and flowing waters or shoots of the Holy Scriptures, and the beautiful, delightful and wholesome variety of the virtues. For on both sides the discipline is laudable and heavenly, here in speaking, there in doing. But what is it to dwell in these gardens, if not to rest in frequent meditation of the holy law and exercise of the virtues? For he whose will is in the law of the Lord, and who meditates on his law day and night, dwells simply at home with Jacob (Gen. XXV), that 1268Bis, abides in the tranquillity of his mind with secure stability, admitting nothing varied, nothing changeable into the sameness of faith or morals. But on the contrary he does not dwell in these gardens who, intent with Esau on the hunting of worldly things (Gen. XXV), wanders about the din of the world through the woods of thoughts, keeping neither the unity of faith nor the integrity of morals.

Therefore, O beloved, thou that dwellest in these gardens simply and wholesomely, make me hear thy voice. What voice? The voice of pious discourse, the voice of virtue, the voice of one teaching well and rightly, the voice of one living justly and piously. For as true and right preaching is a great voice, so also a pious and holy way of life is a great voice. Humility is a great voice, obedience is a great voice, chastity 1268Cis a great voice, patience is a great voice, charity is a great and resounding voice; and with as many virtues as the holy soul shines, with so many great voices, as it were, it cries to God.

And why do I wish to hear thy voice? Namely that I may hear thee crying out by word and work, as it is written: The children that shall be born and shall rise up, let them hear and tell it to their children, that they may put their hope in God and not forget the works of God, and may seek his commandments (Psal. LXXVII) [Vulg. et narrabunt filiis suis, "and shall declare to their children", without audiant]. And what is my hearing? Surely to approve, to accept, and to judge worthy of my help, 278 for when I hear I approve, when I hearken I help. But do thou make me hear thy voice. How wilt thou do it? By living honourably and piously, by teaching true and pious things. For reason and understanding, 1268Dmemory and wit I have granted thee; that thou mayest be inexcusable, and not say that thou neither knowest nor art able, I have taken away from thee every necessity of impossibility, so that thou mayest have and do as is due: but I wish to be a debtor to thee, so that when thou hast done what thou oughtest by right to do, I may be overcome when I am judged (Psal. L); by thy judgment, I say, I wish to be overcome, because I am greatly delighted if thou usest my gift well, and therefore it is thine to bring it about that I wish to hear thy voice: and yet thy doing is not thine, but mine, because that thou art willing and able is the gift of my grace.

Make me, he says, hear thy voice. Why? Because the friends hearken: whose friends? Both mine and thine: mine through charity, because they love me by keeping 1269Amy word; thine, because they love thee by wishing thee salvation. For there are friends whom thou seest not with bodily eyes, who rejoice over thy progress and salvation, or over thy conversion, of whom it is written that: There is joy to the angels of God upon one sinner doing penance (Luc. XV). These indeed are ministering spirits in all the earth for them who receive the inheritance of salvation (Hebr. I) [Vulg. in ministerium missi, "sent to minister", for in omnem terram]: for these are solicitous and act for the salvation of men, as it is said by one of these invisible friends to one of the visible friends, that at that time shall Michael rise up, who standeth for the children of thy people (Dan. XII), and presently, and none is my helper in all these things but Michael your prince (Dan. X).

Therefore these friends hearken, because they are greatly delighted 1269Bto hear thy voice crying to me, whether by praying, or by psalmody, or by preaching, or by wishing. There are also other friends, whom thou hast before thine eyes, who are likewise delighted to hear such a fourfold symphony of concords, like a beautiful διατέσσαρον, and therefore they give ear and hearken, and long to hear thee singing and saying: But I, like an olive tree, have borne fruit in the house of the Lord, I have hoped in the mercy of my God, and I will wait for thy name before the face of thy saints (Psal. LI) [Vulg. sicut oliva fructifera in domo Dei, "like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God"]. These, I say, holy and such friends, hearken, in the optative and desiderative mood, that thou mayest become such as they themselves are, as one of them wished to become anathema for his brethren (Rom. IX), whose salvation he desired; and because 1269Che himself was already dwelling in the gardens of the virtues, of wisdom also and of knowledge, he was solicitous so to temper his voice in my ears that he might please both God and men, and might show by life and doctrine what befitted the salvation of men. Whence this voice of his is sounding from the gardens of wisdom and virtue, and audible to me: I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, I subject it, lest perhaps, while I have preached to others, I myself become a castaway (I Cor. IX). In this 279 way, while the flesh is so subjected to the spirit that it desires nothing below itself, seeks only what is above itself, this is the voice which sounds delightfully in my ears; nay, this is the Canticle of canticles, than which mortal and passible man can sing nothing sweeter in this mortal life; by which voice and by which canticle he is ever caught up 1269Dto take hold of that ineffable sweetness which eye hath not seen, nor ear heard (I Cor. II), the attaining of which will make man immortal and impassible. While the angels and all my saints hearken to this voice and this canticle and desire to hear it, they, the ones (that is, the angels) having attained, and the others (that is, men) holy through faith, hope and charity not doubting that they will attain, the same glory, long greatly that thou also, who hast not yet attained, mayest attain it with them, and for this they unceasingly make supplication to me. What, at length, does the beloved answer to this voice? Flee away, O my beloved, etc.

VERSE 14.-- Flee away, O my beloved, and be like to the roe, and to the young hart upon the mountains of spices.

If we look attentively, great is this voice of one humble 1270Aof heart, whether we refer it to the whole Church, or to any soul devoted to God: for why should not holy Church, or any holy soul, use this voice toward God in the present life? For one of the saints says: We know in part and we prophesy in part; but when that which is perfect is come, that which is in part shall be done away (I Cor. XIII). What did he perceive, who pronounced the imperfection of knowing and prophesying in this present life? for that which is in part is not perfect; but he says this imperfection is to be done away when in the future life that which is perfect shall come; and such imperfection, if thou consider rightly, is surely the flight of this beloved.

Further, whatever is done in the sacraments of the Church 1270Bcontains great and profound mysteries, all of which proclaim the power, virtue and grace of this beloved; but who is there who is able to dispute of these to the full? whence the beloved, astonished before such greatness, knows in part and prophesies in part, but because she is not able to comprehend to the full, she fails, and cries out to the beloved to flee, not from neglect but from failing: for "flee", in the discussion of the subtle matters of the sacraments, is the flight of this beloved. For when we cannot fully set forth or discuss their force and efficacy, this beloved flees us: likewise when we direct our gaze on the face of sacred Scripture, but cannot see it fully through and enter the secrets of its treasures, assuredly 1270Cthis beloved flees us.

280 But let us not rashly hold him back as he flees; rather, whatever we cannot comprehend in a sacrament or in the subtlety of the holy Scriptures, let us burn with fire, that is, reserve to the Holy Spirit, and lest by discussing too much we fall into a heretical sense, let us suffer the beloved to flee. For according to the example of blessed Jacob, who wrestled with the angel, we indeed are admonished to wrestle with the word of God, but after, the blessing having been given, we are lamed by the touch of the sinew, let us permit the word of God to flee. For what is it to wrestle with the word of God, if not untiringly to search out the sense of sacred Scripture? What, then, is it for the victor to ask and receive a blessing from the vanquished, if not to seek and 1270Dfind the understanding of that sense? But the victor, the blessing received from the vanquished, limps with his thigh withering, because he who by God's inspiring has understood sacred Scripture well, every pleasure of the flesh being quenched, advances in the active and contemplative life, and conquers with great gain indeed to the spirit, but with great loss to his flesh. Lastly, he limps who conquered, because he who was conquered touched the sinew of his thigh, and it withered; how does he limp? Namely, resting one foot on the earth, holding the other up from the earth, that is, not wholly abandoning the active life, for the care of those subject to him, and cleaving with all his strength to the contemplative for its sweetness.

This lame man leaps or ascends like a hart, and scarcely deigns to touch the earth, for his conversation is in heaven (Philip. III): yet in part, for 1271Awith one foot only is he now meanwhile suspended there, until that which is perfect shall come. And therefore, because now he cannot comprehend perfectly, he rightly says: Flee away, O my beloved. When therefore, speaking with the Lord on the mountain, we perceive with the mind the sense of the word of God, let us attend to that saying of the Apostle: Be not highminded, but fear (Rom. XI), lest while we incautiously pursue the fleeing beloved we slip into the pit of perverse dogma. Again, we say in this manner that the beloved flees, because he is always incomprehensible; for this is to be granted to his majesty, that he cannot be comprehended, and that he is always desired and desirable, and that it is hidden from us, as long as we are in this body, how great is the multitude of his sweetness, which he hath hidden for them that fear him (Psal. XXX).

1271BLet us therefore say to him: Flee, flee, being cautious and provident for ourselves, lest ever while we live we think that we have comprehended, following that we may comprehend. Or let any faithful and wise soul say in this manner to God with a humble and devoted mind: Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldst enter under my roof (Matth. VIII), I am not worthy that thou shouldst show in me some frequent miracle of thy presence or visitation. Flee away, she says, O my beloved, I seek not glory in the present life, but I desire grace; I seek not the brightness of miracles, but I long for the remission of sins. Flee away, I say, O my beloved, and 281 make such leaps like the leaps of the roe or of the young hart, not upon me, but upon the mountains of spices, upon the lofty merits of the saints and of the perfect. It is not mine to treat or dispute of 1271Cthe secret of thy divinity, of the highest teachings of thy precepts, of the deep mysteries of thy sacraments, but rather of those who can be called lofty mountains for the eminence of their wisdom and virtues, who, touched by thy Holy Spirit, send forth as smoke thy good odour, so that they can say with the Apostle: We are the good odour of Christ 1272Aunto God in every place (II Cor. II) [Vulg. Deo in iis qui salvi fiunt, "unto God in them that are saved"], and therefore they are rightly called mountains of spices.

And what wonder if I, conscious of my infirmity, say to thee to flee, when the great and learned mountains themselves are astonished in the consideration of thy very works, or precepts, or even sacraments, and sometimes suffer thee to flee? For one of these mountains, who had been stretched up even to the third heaven, and had heard things which it is not granted to man to utter, (II Cor. XII), fearing to pursue thee, the beloved, as thou fleest, O the depth, he says, of the riches of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God! how incomprehensible are his judgments, and how unsearchable his ways! For who hath known the mind of the Lord, or who hath been his counsellor? or who hath first given to him, and recompense shall be made him? for of him and 1272Bby him and in him are all things; to him be honour and glory for ever and ever (Rom. XI).

Therefore, O my beloved, flee away, not that thou mayest forsake me wholly, but that what I cannot attain here, since thou art incomprehensible, thou mayest grant me in the life to come, in true and eternal beatitude without end. Be like to the roe, and to the young hart upon the mountains of spices. That is, transcend even the understanding of the perfect saints by the incomprehensible knowledge of thy divinity; or make such leaps in their hearts that they may advance from virtue to virtue (Psal. LXXXIII), because as often as the elect advance from good things to better, from virtues to virtue, God makes as it were certain leaps in their minds, so that by these steps or leaps little by little they may come to that highest and perfect 1272Cstate in which the God of gods is seen in Sion (Psal. LXXXIII), where they may unceasingly say and sing in the ears of the Lord of Sabaoth, not simply a canticle, but the Canticle of canticles, that is, to know and to perceive that highest and best good for ever and ever. Amen.

282 EPILOGI LOCO AUCTORIS PARAENESIS Ad sacras virgines quibus haec commentaria scripsit et inscripsit.

  • 1271

1271DEcce, dilectae sorores, ut potuimus vobis cantavimus, et quantum ille noster summus praeceptor donavit, sub cujus disciplina omnes sunt qui recte et bene canendi scientiam quaerunt. Sed quia bene et recte canendi scientia triplici constat instrumento, videlicet, corde, ore et opere, convincor peritus non esse cantor. Ore quidem cantare possum, sed si reliqua duo defuerint, omnis mei cantionis species coram Domino inanis erit: siquidem corde et opere cantare, potest Deo placere, etiam si non cantet ore; ore autem solummodo cantare, non 1272Dautem corde et opere, impossibile est Deo placere posse. Porro qui vult perfectam habere canendi scientiam, et summam ipsius nosse dignitatem, trium istorum oportet semper habere facultatem. Quam Apostolus se nosse et habere ostendens: Psallam, inquit, spiritu, psallam et mente (I Cor. XIV). Nam spiritu psallere est et verba spiritualia memoriter proferre, quod est ore cantare; et ad opera spiritu concepta procedere, quod est opere cantare; mente psallere est vitalem verborum sensum mente percipere, quod est corde cantare.

1273ADato autem instrumento ad recte et bene canendi scientiam consequendam opus est, ut etiam sciamus quid primum sit in canendo sciendum, et quale canticum, ut perveniamus ad canticum canticorum. Primo quippe discere et cantare nos oportet canticum illud novum, de quo cantando hortatur nos Spiritus sanctus in Psalmo: Cantate, inquit, Domino canticum novum, laus ejus in Ecclesia sanctorum (Psal. CXLIX). Si relativorum qualitatem consideres, ubi dicitur novum, consequitur ut et vetus sit. Sed primo videamus quid sit vetus canticum, ut ex ejus agnitione melius novum intelligamus.

Vetus illud canticum vetus homo Adam cantavit et docuit, sed novo cantico quod postea auditum est, valde oppositum et contrarium et ea distantia 1273Bdistans, quae est inter mortificans et vivificans. Et quod est illud canticum? nimirum illud, quo vetus ille homo Factori suo reclamavit, et contra justitiam et pietatem vociferatus est, videlicet superbia, inobedientia et peccati sui excusatio. Justum quippe fuit ut factori et rectori suo subditus esset, et obediret, miserum autem fuit, quod post culpam se non recognovit 283 neque de pietate Dei praesumpsit, sed contemptor culpae suae poenam in omnem suam posteritatem exsul paradisi transfudit. Hujus cantici flebilem tragoediam multi quanto plus cantant, illius praesumptionem et negligentiam imitando, tanto majorem impositae mortis exsolvunt vindictam.

Huic autem cantico oppositum est illud novum 1273Ccanticum, canticum pacis et laetitiae, canticum vitae et justitiae, canticum virtutis et salutis quod praecinuit ille novus homo, et non tantum simpliciter homo, sed Deus et homo; hujusmodi nempe praecentore qui dixit: Discite a me quia mitis sum et humilis corde et invenietis requiem animabus vestris (Matth. XI), monemur novum utilitatis cantare canticum. Porro exemplo ipsius Domini, de quo dicit Apostolus: Christus factus est obediens Deo Patri usque ad mortem (Philip. II), monemur suavis obedientiae cantare canticum; ad vocem quoque ejusdem novi praecentoris qui dicit: Poenitentiam agite, appropinquabit enim regnum coelorum (Matth. IV), monemur non declinare cor nostrum in verba malitiae, ad excusandas 1273Dexcusationes in peccatis (Psal. CXLVI); quia haec est gravissima, imo miserrima vox veteris hominis impoenitentis, vox, inquam, veteris et dolore pleni cantici, quin potius converso modo ejusmodi cantici et in novum mutato, laboriosam quidem quantum ad corpus sed salubrem quantum ad animam spiritus contribulati melodiam, quatuor modorum genere, hoc est compunctione, confessione, satisfactione, perseverantia Deo concinamus; et in quatuor ipsorum modorum finalis videlicet cogitationem, locutionem, actionem et consuetudinem quotidie deponamus.

Siquidem utriusque cantici, hoc est veteris et novi, isti sunt finales, cogitatio, locutio, actio, et consuetudo, et secundum praecedentis speciem modi 1274Adepositionem suscipiunt; sive et elegiacam quantum ad vetus, sive suavem et musicam quantum ad novum. Musica nempe depositio est, quae fit rationabile vocum sive tonorum, conjunctione, dispositione, tenore, et hanc magis, imo semper suscipit novum canticum, propter rationabilem motum mentis, bene et pulchre canentis, et ad bonum finem cogitando, loquendo, agendo, consuescendo semper tendentis. E contra elegiaca haec est tristis et misera depositio est, quae fit irrationabili et inaequali motu mentis; et quia confusa est hujusmodi cantionis species, in suavem et immitem depositionis generat qualitatem.

Est ergo inter hujusmodi duo cantica ea distantia, quae est inter vitam et mortem; quia vetus 1274Boccidit, novum autem vivificat, et hoc a simili, nam dicuntur quaedam marinae bestiae, quae syrenae nuncupantur, quae dum navigantes dulcedine cantus sui alliciunt et attrahunt, 284 subito incautos et negligentes submergunt: hoc autem modo dum carnales quique in hujus mundi pelago, quasi navigantes carnalis vitae dulcedine, peccati delectatione tenentur, repente salutem animae suae negligentes, et converti per poenitentiam nolentes ab immundis spiritibus ad aeternam mortem rapiuntur. Et hic est veteris cantici modus, quia a spiritu superbiae et inobedientiae inchoans, in aeternae damnationis barathrum, gravissimo et miserrimo cordis impoenitenti sono extremam deponit vocem.

Porro ex alia parte ea similitudo est, quae nobis 1274Costenditur ex divina et humana Scriptura. Ex divina quidem qua scribitur David cithara sua furorem Saulis mitigasse (I Reg. XVI): ex humana vero qua scribitur Orpheus cantu suo lenisse tigres et leones; et Amphion sono testitudinis saxa movisse, quod significat novi cantici hanc esse virtutem, ut contra salutem suam furentes mitiget bestiales hominum mentes et dura mortalium corda, rationali verborum et sensuum motu, ad bonum vivendi modum et rationabilem morum honestatem componat. Et iste est novi cantici modus, qui a spiritu humilitatis et obedientiae inchoans, in aeternae beatitudinis gaudium altissimo et laetissimo cordis innocentis sive poenitentis sono ultimam deponit vocem.

1274DSicut ergo contraria sibi sunt vita et mors, ita sibi contraria sunt vetus et novum canticum juxta qualitates personarum quarum auctoritate utrumque canticum initium accipit et finem. Veteris siquidem cantici auctor est diabolus, novi vero cantici auctor est Christus. Quocirca, contempto auctore mortis, auctorem vitae sequamur, cujus delectabilem et suavissimum sanctitatis concentum jugiter attendentes, ineptas sirenarum voces, hoc est stultas malignorum spirituum persuasiones, surda pertranseamus aure.

Officinae autem et mansiones, in quibus instrumenta hujus novi et salubris cantici parentur et servantur, et in quibus ipsum canticum audiamus et discamus, et cantandi consuetudine et exercitio 1275Aperveniamus ad illud Canticum canticorum, cujus suavitas et dulcedo nunquam deficiet, sunt dilecta Domini tabernacula, de quibus quondam divinus ille, qui dixit se auditorem sermonum Dei, et visionem Dei intuentem, qui cadit, et sic apertos habet oculos, percunctaturus est:

Quam dilecta, inquit, tabernacula tua, Jacob, et tentoria tua, Israel; ut valles nemorosae, ut horti juxta fluvios irrigui; ut tabernacula quae fixit Dominus, quasi cedri propter aquas multas (Num. XXIV). Veri autem Israel ac spiritualis Jacob peregrinantis vel militantis in praesenti saeculo, tabernacula sunt religiosi, et secundum 285 disciplinam Christi bene dispositi, ordines videlicet conjugatorum, continentium, viduarum atque virginum secundum 1275Butrumque sexum, haec plane tabernacula singula in suo proposito pulchra sunt.

Quam pulchra tabernacula, quam pulchra tentoria? ut valles nemorosae, ut horti juxta fluvios irrigui. Ista similitudo ex aliis Scripturae locis perspicua est: siquidem in Isaia Dominus derelictae quondam gentilitati spiritualium virtutum merita tanquam deserto arbusta promittens: Dabo, inquit, in solitudine cedrum et spinam, myrtum et lignum olivae: ponam in deserto abietem, ulmum et buxum simul, ut videant, et sciant et recogitent et intelligant pariter (Isa. XLI). Ergo pulchra tabernacula ut valles nemorosae. Valles propter humilitatem, nemorosae propter diversarum pulchritudinem virtutum.

1275CIn his enim tabernaculis Dei, hoc est professionibus sanctis, sunt cedri, hoc est sancti fide et opere incorrupti et imputribiles, atque odore virtutum redolentes: sunt spinae verbo et exemplo alios compungentes et ad bona opera provocantes: sunt myrtus proximorum tribulationes per compassionem verbo consolationis temperantes: sunt olivae misericordiae et pietatis actibus perfluentes; sunt abietes contemplationi virtute ad alta semper surgentes: sunt ulmi quamvis saeculares et minus fructificantes alios tamen bene viventes suis facultatibus sustentantes et adjuvantes: sunt buxus quamvis ad alta virtutum non surgentes, neque fructum facientes, parentum tamen fide semper viventes: 1275Dsunt ergo haec tabernacula Domini ut valles nemorosae, quia hoc ex humili corde, actu quoque et habitu infimo contrahunt, ut tantarum ubertate virtutum virescant atque florescant.

Sunt etiam ut horti juxta fluvios irrigui, sicut alibi dicitur: Et eris quasi hortus irriguus, et sicut fons aquarum cujus non deficient aquae (Isa. LVIII). Et in eisdem canticis: Hortus conclusus, fons signatus, fons hortorum, puteus aquarum viventium, quae fluunt impetu de Libano (Cant. IV). Ecce tabernacula pulchra ut horti juxta fluvios irrigui. Quia ex humore Spiritus sancti semper sunt virentes et florentes sermone et actione, et assidua divinorum praeceptorum meditatione.

Sunt quoque cedri propter aquas; quod Psalmista 1276Aostendit, qui cum dixisset: Rigans montes de superioribus suis, etc., continue subsecutus: Saturabuntur, inquit, campi et cedri Libani quas plantavit (Psal CIII). Ergo pulchra tabernacula ut cedri propter aquas, id est juxta aquas, videlicet in quibus passeres nidificant (Psal. CIII), quorum abundantia cum sunt divites homines, pauperum supplet inopiam.

Igitur, haec tabernacula sunt 286 ut tabernacula quae fixit Dominus, quia omnis ista eorum pulchritudo, ornatus et compositio, opus est Dei omnipotentis, sua gratia illa collocantis, promoventis, decorantis et sustentantis.

Fluet aqua de situla ejus, et semen ejus erit in aquas multas (Num. XXIV). Quae est situla ejus? Imo, quae est aqua ejus? Nimirum veri Jacob, hoc est supplantatoris, 1276Bsive veri Israel, hoc est mentis Dominum videntis. Quorum nonnulli in his tabernaculis, hoc est professionibus, habitant. Cujus situla est Christus de quo hauritur aqua, id est sancta Scriptura. Per eum quippe sancta Scriptura aperitur, imo ab illo sitis excitatur, ut haec aqua desideretur, ab illo sensus aperitur, ut Scripturae intelligantur. Fluet ergo aqua de situla ejus, id est vera manabit intelligentia Scripturarum de Christo ejus. Quid deinde? Et semen ejus erit in aquas multas. Quod est aqua de situla ejus, hoc est multitudo aquarum de semine illius. Nam semen illius, semen patris ejus Abrahae (Gen. XVII), illius videlicet, qui vere Pater excelsus, sive Pater multarum gentium Christus est.

Hoc semen illius erit in aquas multas, id est hoc 1276Csemen fundit aquas multas. Bibendo experti sumus quod vere in aquas multas sit semen illius. Qui in me credit, inquit, flumina de ventre ejus fluent aquae vivae (Joan. VII). Item: Qui biberit ex aqua quam ego dabo ei, non sitiet in aeternum, sed aqua quam ego dabo ei, fiet in eo fons aquae salientis in vitam aeternam (Joan. IV). Hoc, inquam, gratia ejus bibendo experti sumus. Ecce enim de hac situla, quae est Christus ipse, multa sancti Spiritus in una Ecclesia dona percepimus, multa et largissima Scripturarum mente possidemus.

Igitur in his tabernaculis Domini, novum illud semper resonat canticum quod cantant horum tabernaculorum habitatores septem vocum differentiis, 1276Dregente cantum Spiritu sancto sua septiformi gratia, videlicet sapientia et intellectu, consilio et fortitudine, scientia et pietate atque timore Domini. Porro ex his septem vocum differentiis diversae fiunt beatitudines quasi octo modorum species; videlicet humilitas, mansuetudo, luctus, sive tria secundum Dominum, pax, misericordia, munditia, justitiae appetitus, patientia.

Et iste cantus sive laus Dei non est nisi in Ecclesia sanctorum, quia quod sancti sunt et quod sciunt et possunt hoc unde sancti sunt, Dei solius gratiae munus est. Et tales quotidie exeuntes de Aegypto hujus mundi, contemptu propriae voluntatis tenentes citharas Dei, hoc est carnis mortificationem, non solum cantant canticum novum, sed et 1277Acanticum canticorum, quia hoc modo ad illam ineffabilem Dei charitatem proficiunt, quae est virtus virtutum, et ex qua procedit, et in qua continetur omnium virtutum plenitudo.

Vos itaque, dilectae sorores, quia tabernaculum Dei estis, sive in tabernaculis Dei habitatis, hoc novum semper concinite canticum humilitate, castitate, patientia, obedientia, carnis mortificatione, Dei et proximi dilectione. Cantabiles vobis sint justificationes 1278ADomini in loco peregrinationis vestrae, (Psal. CXVIII), ut quandoque de Aegypto hujus saeculi exeuntes et ad terram promissionis pervenientes atque bonis ipsius terrae, quae nec oculus vidit, nec auris audivit, nec in cor hominis ascendit (I Cor. II, Isa. LXIV), aeterna liter perfruentes, cum omni suavitate et dulcedine sine intermissione cantetis non solum canticum novum, sed et canticum canticorum, per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen.

282 IN PLACE OF AN EPILOGUE, THE AUTHOR'S PARAENESIS To the sacred virgins for whom he wrote and to whom he inscribed these commentaries.

  • 1271

1271DBehold, beloved sisters, as we were able we have sung to you, and as much as that highest master of ours has granted, under whose discipline are all who seek the knowledge of singing rightly and well. But since the knowledge of singing well and rightly consists of a threefold instrument, namely heart, mouth and work, I am convicted of not being a skilled singer. With the mouth indeed I can sing, but if the other two are lacking, every form of my singing will be empty before the Lord: for to sing with the heart and with work can please God, even if one sing not with the mouth; but to sing with the mouth only, and not 1272Dwith the heart and with work, it is impossible to be able to please God. Further, he who wishes to have the perfect knowledge of singing, and to know its highest dignity, must always have the faculty of these three. The Apostle, showing that he knew and had it: I will sing, he says, with the spirit, I will sing also with the mind (I Cor. XIV). For to sing with the spirit is both to utter spiritual words from memory, which is to sing with the mouth, and to proceed to the works conceived in the spirit, which is to sing with work; to sing with the mind is to perceive with the mind the living sense of the words, which is to sing with the heart.

1273AThe instrument, then, having been given for attaining the knowledge of singing rightly and well, there is need that we should also know what is first to be known in singing, and what canticle, that we may come to the canticle of canticles. For first we must learn and sing that new canticle to the singing of which the Holy Spirit exhorts us in the Psalm: Sing ye, he says, to the Lord a new canticle, his praise in the Church of the saints (Psal. CXLIX). If thou consider the quality of relatives, where new is said, it follows that there is also an old. But let us first see what the old canticle is, that from the knowledge of it we may better understand the new.

That old canticle the old man Adam sang and taught, but it is greatly opposed and contrary to the new canticle which was heard afterwards, and distant from it by that distance 1273Bwhich is between the mortifying and the vivifying. And what is that canticle? Surely that by which that old man cried out against his Maker, and clamoured against justice and piety, namely pride, disobedience and the excusing of his sin. For it was just that he should be subject to his maker and ruler, and obey; but it was wretched that after his fault he did not acknowledge himself, 283 nor presume upon the piety of God, but, a despiser of his fault, an exile from paradise, he transmitted its punishment to all his posterity. The more many sing the doleful tragedy of this canticle, by imitating his presumption and negligence, the greater the vengeance of the imposed death they pay.

But opposed to this canticle is that new 1273Ccanticle, the canticle of peace and gladness, the canticle of life and justice, the canticle of virtue and salvation, which that new man sang before us, and not simply man, but God and man; for by such a precentor, who said: Learn of me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you shall find rest to your souls (Matth. XI), we are admonished to sing the new canticle of usefulness [utilitatis; read humilitatis, "of humility"]. Further, by the example of the Lord himself, of whom the Apostle says: Christ became obedient to God the Father unto death (Philip. II), we are admonished to sing the canticle of sweet obedience; at the voice also of the same new precentor, who says: Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven will draw near (Matth. IV), we are admonished not to incline our heart to evil words, to make excuses 1273Din sins (Psal. CXLVI); because this is the most grievous, nay the most wretched voice of the old impenitent man, the voice, I say, of the old canticle full of sorrow; but rather, the manner of such a canticle being converted and changed into the new, let us sing together to God a melody of the contrite spirit, laborious indeed as regards the body but wholesome as regards the soul, in the genus of four modes, that is, compunction, confession, satisfaction, perseverance; and on the four finals of these modes, namely thought, speech, action and custom, let us daily make our cadence.

For of both canticles, that is, of the old and of the new, these are the finals, thought, speech, action, and custom, and according to the form of the preceding mode 1274Athey take their cadence; either the elegiac as regards the old, or the sweet and musical as regards the new. For the musical cadence is that which is made by a reasonable conjunction, disposition, and tenor of voices or tones, and this the new canticle takes more, nay always, on account of the reasonable motion of the mind singing well and beautifully, and always tending to a good end by thinking, speaking, acting, being accustomed. On the contrary, the elegiac, this is a sad and wretched cadence, is that which is made by an irrational and unequal motion of the mind; and because the form of such singing is confused, it generates an unpleasant in suavem and harsh quality of cadence.

There is therefore between such two canticles that distance which is between life and death; because the old 1274Bkills, but the new gives life, and this by a likeness; for certain sea beasts are spoken of, which are called sirens, which, while they allure and draw sailors by the sweetness of their song, 284 suddenly sink the incautious and negligent: and in this manner, while all carnal men in the sea of this world, sailing as it were, are held by the sweetness of the carnal life, by the delight of sin, suddenly, neglecting the salvation of their soul, and unwilling to be converted through penance, they are snatched by unclean spirits to eternal death. And this is the mode of the old canticle, since, beginning from the spirit of pride and disobedience, it makes its last cadence in the abyss of eternal damnation with the most grievous and most wretched sound of an impenitent heart.

Further, on the other side, there is that likeness which is 1274Cshown us from divine and human Scripture. From the divine, where it is written that David with his harp calmed the fury of Saul (I Reg. XVI): from the human, where it is written that Orpheus by his song soothed tigers and lions; and that Amphion by the sound of the lyre testitudinis moved stones; which signifies that this is the power of the new canticle, that it calms the bestial minds of men raging against their own salvation, and composes the hard hearts of mortals, by a reasonable motion of words and senses, to a good manner of living and a reasonable honourableness of morals. And this is the mode of the new canticle, which, beginning from the spirit of humility and obedience, makes its last cadence in the joy of eternal beatitude with the highest and most joyful sound of an innocent or penitent heart.

1274DAs therefore life and death are contrary to each other, so the old and the new canticle are contrary to each other, according to the qualities of the persons by whose authority each canticle takes its beginning and end. For the author of the old canticle is the devil, but the author of the new canticle is Christ. Wherefore, despising the author of death, let us follow the author of life, and, continually attending to his delightful and most sweet harmony of holiness, let us pass by with deaf ear the foolish voices of the sirens, that is, the foolish persuasions of malignant spirits.

But the workshops and dwellings in which the instruments of this new and wholesome canticle are prepared and kept, and in which we may hear and learn the canticle itself, and by the custom and exercise of singing 1275Amay come to that Canticle of canticles whose sweetness and delightfulness will never fail, are the beloved tabernacles of the Lord, of which once that diviner, who said that he was a hearer of the words of God, and one beholding the vision of God, who falleth, and so hath his eyes open, was about to inquire:

How beloved, he says, are thy tabernacles, O Jacob, and thy tents, O Israel; as woody valleys, as watered gardens beside the rivers; as tabernacles which the Lord hath pitched, as cedars by many waters (Num. XXIV). Now the tabernacles of the true Israel and spiritual Jacob, sojourning or serving as a soldier in the present age, are the religious, and those well ordered according to the 285 discipline of Christ, namely the orders of the married, the continent, widows and virgins, according to 1275Beither sex; these tabernacles plainly are each beautiful in its own purpose.

How beautiful the tabernacles, how beautiful the tents? as woody valleys, as watered gardens beside the rivers. This likeness is clear from other places of Scripture: for in Isaias the Lord, promising to the gentiles, once forsaken, the merits of spiritual virtues like trees to a desert: I will give, he says, in the wilderness the cedar and the thorn, the myrtle and the olive tree: I will set in the desert the fir tree, the elm and the box tree together, that they may see, and know, and consider, and understand together (Isa. XLI). Therefore the tabernacles are beautiful as woody valleys. Valleys on account of humility, woody on account of the beauty of diverse virtues.

1275CFor in these tabernacles of God, that is, in holy professions, there are cedars, that is, saints incorrupt and incorruptible in faith and work, and fragrant with the odour of the virtues: there are thorns, pricking others by word and example and provoking them to good works: there is the myrtle, tempering the tribulations of neighbours through compassion by the word of consolation: there are olives, overflowing with acts of mercy and piety; there are firs, rising ever on high by virtue for contemplation: there are elms, who, though secular and less fruitful, yet sustain and help others who live well with their means: there is the box, who, though not rising to the heights of the virtues, nor bearing fruit, yet live always by the faith of their parents: 1275Dthese tabernacles of the Lord are therefore as woody valleys, because they draw this from a humble heart, and from lowly action also and bearing, that they grow green and flower with the fullness of such great virtues.

They are also as watered gardens beside the rivers, as it is said elsewhere: And thou shalt be like a watered garden, and like a fountain of waters whose waters shall not fail (Isa. LVIII). And in the same canticles: A garden enclosed, a fountain sealed, the fountain of gardens, the well of living waters, which run with a strong stream from Libanus (Cant. IV). Behold the tabernacles beautiful as watered gardens beside the rivers. Because from the moisture of the Holy Spirit they are always green and flowering in speech and action, and in the assiduous meditation of the divine precepts.

They are also cedars by the waters; which the Psalmist 1276Ashows, who, when he had said: Watering the hills from his upper rooms, etc., continued at once: The plains, he says, shall be filled, and the cedars of Libanus which he hath planted (Psal CIII) [Vulg. Saturabuntur ligna campi, "the trees of the field shall be filled"]. Therefore the tabernacles are beautiful as cedars by the waters, that is, beside the waters, namely, in which the sparrows make their nests (Psal. CIII), by whose abundance, when they are rich men, the need of the poor is supplied.

Therefore these tabernacles are 286 as tabernacles which the Lord hath pitched, because all this their beauty, adornment and ordering is the work of the omnipotent God, who by his grace places, advances, adorns and sustains them.

Water shall flow out of his bucket, and his seed shall be in many waters (Num. XXIV). What is his bucket? Nay, what is his water? Surely of the true Jacob, that is, the supplanter, 1276Bor of the true Israel, that is, the mind seeing the Lord. Some of whom dwell in these tabernacles, that is, professions. Whose bucket is Christ, from whom water is drawn, that is, Holy Scripture. For through him Holy Scripture is opened, nay by him thirst is aroused, that this water may be desired; by him the sense is opened, that the Scriptures may be understood. Water therefore shall flow out of his bucket, that is, the true understanding of the Scriptures shall stream from his Christ. What next? And his seed shall be in many waters. What is water out of his bucket, this is the multitude of waters from his seed. For his seed, the seed of his father Abraham (Gen. XVII), namely of him who truly is the lofty Father, or the Father of many nations, Christ.

This seed of his shall be in many waters, that is, this 1276Cseed pours forth many waters. By drinking we have experienced that his seed truly is in many waters. He that believeth in me, he says, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water (Joan. VII). Again: He that shall drink of the water that I will give him shall not thirst for ever, but the water that I will give him shall become in him a fountain of water springing up into life everlasting (Joan. IV). This, I say, we have experienced by drinking of his grace. For behold, from this bucket, which is Christ himself, we have received many gifts of the Holy Spirit in the one Church, we possess in mind many and most abundant things of the Scriptures.

In these tabernacles of the Lord, therefore, that new canticle ever resounds which the dwellers of these tabernacles sing with the seven differences of voices, 1276Dthe Holy Spirit ruling the song with his sevenfold grace, namely wisdom and understanding, counsel and fortitude, knowledge and piety and the fear of the Lord. Further, from these seven differences of voices diverse beatitudes come about, as it were eight species of modes; namely humility, meekness, mourning, or three [tria; read tristitia, "sorrow"] according to the Lord, peace, mercy, cleanness, the desire of justice, patience.

And this song, or praise of God, is not save in the Church of the saints, because that they are saints, and that they know and are able to do that whereby they are saints, is the gift of the grace of God alone. And such, going out daily from the Egypt of this world, by contempt of their own will holding the harps of God, that is, the mortification of the flesh, sing not only a new canticle, but also 1277Athe canticle of canticles, because in this manner they advance to that ineffable charity of God, which is the virtue of virtues, and from which proceeds, and in which is contained, the fullness of all the virtues.

You therefore, beloved sisters, since you are the tabernacle of God, or dwell in the tabernacles of God, sing together always this new canticle with humility, chastity, patience, obedience, mortification of the flesh, love of God and of neighbour. Let the justifications 1278Aof the Lord be songs to you in the place of your pilgrimage, (Psal. CXVIII), that at some time, going out from the Egypt of this age and coming to the land of promise, and eternally aeterna liter enjoying the good things of that land, which eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither hath it entered into the heart of man (I Cor. II, Isa. LXIV), you may sing with all sweetness and delightfulness, without intermission, not only the new canticle, but also the canticle of canticles, for ever and ever. Amen.

On this text

Cruces for this work — where the plate is defective or the reading uncertain →

A twelfth-century abbot of Cologne expounds the Song of Songs, verse by verse, for a community of nuns on an island in the Rhine. Wolbero's frame is the canticle itself: married people sing the canticle of praise, widows the canticle of gladness, and virgins the new canticle that only those who follow the Lamb can sing, and his whole commentary is offered to the sisters as that song. The Bride is read now as the Church and now as the single soul, the Bridegroom as Christ, and the book moves by patient, numbered distinctions: seven gifts, four fears, threefold senses, a square of virtues and vices that Migne prints as a diagram.

The edition is Migne's reprint of Henricus Gravius's Cologne printing of 1630, with the editor's dedication, preface and the approving censure of the abbot of Gerodhen in front of the text. The bold numbers in the text are that edition's page numbers, kept as printed. Every page of the work was read at the plate while it was translated. Migne's four foot notes, which the digital transcription omits, were recovered and stand in the Latin column, among them his own verdicts Deest aliquid (something is missing, col. 1213A) and Locus obscurus (an obscure passage, col. 1263B). The volume's scan fills in some letters with ink, so every place where this translation says the printed type is at fault was checked again on a second copy of the same printing. The judgements behind the markers are set out in the apparatus.
